### Plant Material and Growth Conditions  
Arabidopsis thaliana accession Columbia-0 (Col-0) was used as the wild type in this study. Mutant lines phyA-211 [1] and elf3-1 [2] were obtained from the Arabidopsis Biological Resource Center (ABRC). All seeds were stratified at 4°C for 2–3 days in the dark on soil or on Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 1% (w/v) sucrose prior to germination. Plants were grown in controlled-environment growth chambers (Percival Scientific, Model CU-36L5) under a 16-hour light/8-hour dark photoperiod to simulate long-day conditions unless otherwise specified.

To mimic natural long-day conditions, adjustments were made to the standard growth chamber settings. The red/far-red (R:FR) light ratio was adjusted to 1.1 using LED light sources with specific wavelength ranges (660 nm for red light, 730 nm for far-red light). This ratio replicates the R:FR ratio observed in open field conditions [3]. Additionally, diurnal temperature oscillations were incorporated, with daytime temperatures set at 22°C and nighttime temperatures at 14°C, consistent with seasonal temperature patterns typical of spring in temperate climates [4]. Relative humidity was maintained at 60% throughout all experiments. Light intensity was set to 150 μmol m⁻² s⁻¹ at plant canopy height. Plants were grown in 6.5 cm pots containing a 3:1 mixture of peat moss and vermiculite. For experiments involving photoperiodic flowering, seeds were sown and grown under the specified conditions until flowering was observed.

### RNA Extraction and Gene Expression Analysis  
For the analysis of FT expression, rosette leaves were harvested at specific time points across a 24-hour period. Sampling was conducted in triplicate for each time point to ensure reproducibility. Total RNA was extracted using the RNeasy Plant Mini Kit (Qiagen) following the manufacturer’s protocol. RNA concentration and quality were evaluated using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and by agarose gel electrophoresis.

cDNA was synthesized from 1 μg of total RNA using the SuperScript III First-Strand Synthesis System (Invitrogen) with oligo(dT) primers. Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed using the PowerUp SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a Bio-Rad CFX96 Real-Time PCR Detection System. FT transcript levels were normalized to ACTIN2 as an internal control. Relative expression levels were calculated using the ΔΔCt method [5]. Primers used for qRT-PCR are listed in Supplementary Table 1.

### Protein Analysis  
CONSTANS (CO) protein abundance was assessed through immunoblotting. Protein extraction was performed using a modified buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 150 mM NaCl, 5 mM EDTA, 1% Triton X-100, and protease inhibitor cocktail (Roche). Approximately 100 mg of rosette tissue was homogenized in extraction buffer, and total protein was quantified using the Bradford assay (Bio-Rad).

For western blot analysis, 20 μg of total protein was separated on a 10% SDS-PAGE gel and transferred onto a polyvinylidene difluoride (PVDF) membrane (Millipore). The membrane was blocked with 5% non-fat milk in Tris-buffered saline with 0.1% Tween-20 (TBS-T) for 1 hour at room temperature. Membranes were probed with anti-CO primary antibody (Agrisera, catalog no. AS15 3002) at a 1:2,500 dilution, followed by incubation with horseradish peroxidase-conjugated secondary antibody (1:10,000; Sigma). Chemiluminescent detection was performed using the ECL Plus Western Blotting Substrate (Thermo Fisher Scientific) and visualized on a ChemiDoc Imaging System (Bio-Rad). Band intensities were quantified using ImageJ software.

### Light and Temperature Measurements  
To ensure that laboratory conditions accurately reflected natural light and temperature environments, measurements of spectral light quality and diurnal temperature fluctuations were conducted in an open field in spring (latitude 50°N). Spectral light quality was measured using a portable spectroradiometer (Ocean Optics, Model USB2000+), and the R:FR ratio was calculated by integrating the spectral irradiance over the red (655–665 nm) and far-red (725–735 nm) wavelength ranges. Temperature data were collected using HOBO data loggers (Onset Computer Corporation) positioned at plant canopy height. These data were used to program growth chamber conditions.

### Genetic Analysis and Mutant Characterization  
To investigate the role of phyA and ELF3 in morning FT expression, we examined phyA-211 and elf3-1 mutants grown under both standard and adjusted growth conditions. Homozygosity of each line was confirmed by PCR genotyping using primers specific to each mutation (Supplementary Table 2). Flowering time was assessed by counting the number of rosette leaves at bolting (defined as the emergence of a 1 cm-long inflorescence).

### Statistical Analysis  
All experiments were conducted with at least three biological replicates, and each replicate consisted of a minimum of 10 plants per condition. Data were analyzed using GraphPad Prism 9 software. Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons, or Student’s t-test for pairwise comparisons, as appropriate. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

### Expression Pattern of FT Under Natural Long-Day Conditions

To investigate the molecular basis of flowering under natural long-day (LD) conditions, we examined the expression profile of the florigen gene *FLOWERING LOCUS T* (*FT*) in Arabidopsis thaliana grown in the field during spring. We observed that *FT* expression peaks in the morning under these conditions, a pattern distinct from the late afternoon peak previously described under standard laboratory LD conditions [1,2]. Sampling *FT* transcript levels at 2-hour intervals over a 24-hour period revealed a sharp increase in expression beginning at dawn, with transcript abundance peaking between Zeitgeber Time 2 (ZT2) and ZT4 before declining gradually through the rest of the photoperiod. This temporal profile was consistent across multiple field experiments conducted over consecutive years, suggesting that morning *FT* expression is a robust feature of Arabidopsis flowering under natural LD conditions.

### Mimicking Field Conditions in Controlled Environments

To better understand the environmental factors driving morning *FT* expression, we sought to replicate field-like conditions in controlled growth chambers. We hypothesized that differences in light quality and temperature fluctuations between laboratory and field conditions might underlie the observed divergence in *FT* expression patterns. First, we adjusted the red/far-red (R/FR) light ratio in growth chambers to approximate the spectral light environment of open fields, with an R/FR ratio of approximately 0.7 at plant canopy level [3]. Second, we introduced daily temperature oscillations, with daytime temperatures maintained at 22°C and nighttime temperatures reduced to 12°C, reflecting typical diurnal temperature variations during spring.

Under these modified growth conditions, Arabidopsis plants exhibited an *FT* expression pattern closely resembling that observed in the field. Specifically, *FT* transcripts peaked during the morning (ZT2–ZT4) rather than the afternoon (ZT10–ZT12), as seen under constant laboratory conditions. Moreover, plants grown under these field-mimicking conditions flowered significantly earlier (p < 0.01, Student’s t-test) compared to those grown under standard laboratory LD conditions, aligning more closely with flowering times recorded in the field. These findings confirm that light quality and diurnal temperature fluctuations are sufficient to recapitulate field-like *FT* expression and flowering phenotypes in controlled environments.

### Role of Light Signaling Components in Morning FT Expression

To explore the molecular mechanisms underlying morning *FT* expression, we investigated the roles of key light signaling components, including phytochrome A (*phyA*) and EARLY FLOWERING 3 (*ELF3*). Using loss-of-function mutants, we found that *phyA* and *ELF3* are critical for the observed shift in *FT* expression under field-mimicking conditions.

In *phyA-211* mutants, morning *FT* expression was severely attenuated, with transcript levels reduced to approximately 30% of those observed in wild-type plants (Col-0) at ZT4 (p < 0.001, two-way ANOVA). This reduction was accompanied by delayed flowering under field-mimicking conditions, suggesting that *phyA* is required for the activation of *FT* expression in response to morning light signals. By contrast, *phyA-211* mutants grown under standard laboratory LD conditions showed only minor reductions in *FT* expression during the late afternoon, consistent with previous findings [4]. Together, these results highlight a specific role for *phyA* in mediating morning *FT* expression under field-like light conditions.

Similarly, *elf3-1* mutants displayed a significant reduction in morning *FT* expression, with peak transcript levels at ZT4 reduced by approximately 50% compared to Col-0 (p < 0.01, two-way ANOVA). Notably, *elf3-1* plants also exhibited a disrupted diurnal rhythm of *FT* expression, with elevated transcript levels persisting throughout the photoperiod. These results suggest that *ELF3* contributes to the temporal restriction of *FT* expression to the early morning under natural LD conditions. Consistent with this role, *elf3-1* mutants flowered significantly later than wild-type plants under field-mimicking conditions (p < 0.001, Student’s t-test).

### Stabilization of CONSTANS Protein in the Morning

Given the well-established role of CONSTANS (*CO*) in activating *FT* expression [5], we next examined whether the stabilization of *CO* protein in the morning contributes to the observed shift in *FT* expression under field-mimicking conditions. Using immunoblot analysis, we detected a marked increase in *CO* protein abundance during the early morning (ZT2–ZT6) in plants grown under field-mimicking conditions, whereas *CO* levels were low to undetectable during the same time period under standard laboratory LD conditions. This temporal stabilization of *CO* protein correlated strongly with the timing of *FT* transcriptional activation.

To test whether morning *CO* stabilization is light-dependent, we analyzed *co-10* mutants, which lack functional *CO* protein. As expected, *co-10* mutants exhibited no detectable *FT* expression at any time of day under either field-mimicking or standard laboratory LD conditions. Furthermore, in *phyA-211* mutants, *CO* protein levels in the morning were significantly reduced compared to wild-type plants, suggesting that *phyA* plays a role in promoting *CO* stabilization under field-like light conditions. These findings support a model in which morning *CO* stabilization, mediated by light signaling pathways, acts as a critical mechanism for photoperiodic regulation of flowering in natural environments.

### Discussion of Seasonal Responses and Implications

Collectively, our results demonstrate that the temporal pattern of *FT* expression and subsequent flowering time in Arabidopsis are strongly influenced by environmental cues, including light quality and diurnal temperature fluctuations, that differ between laboratory and field conditions. By recreating these field-like conditions in controlled environments, we identified *phyA*- and *ELF3*-dependent pathways that regulate morning *FT* expression and uncovered a key role for *CO* protein stabilization in this process. These findings underscore the importance of studying plant responses under ecologically relevant conditions to fully understand the molecular basis of seasonal flowering. Further research is needed to determine how additional environmental variables, such as humidity and soil composition, interact with light and temperature to shape flowering time regulation.

### Discussion

#### Contextualizing FT Expression in Natural Environments  
Our findings demonstrate that the expression of *FLOWERING LOCUS T* (*FT*), a key florigen gene in Arabidopsis, exhibits distinct temporal dynamics under natural long-day conditions compared to standard laboratory conditions. Specifically, we observed that *FT* expression peaks in the morning during spring, a pattern that contrasts with mid-day or evening peaks often reported under controlled growth environments. This discrepancy underscores the influence of environmental parameters, such as light quality and temperature fluctuations, on photoperiodic flowering. By adjusting laboratory growth conditions to incorporate a red/far-red (R/FR) light ratio and temperature oscillations that more closely resemble natural field conditions, we successfully recapitulated the morning *FT* expression pattern observed in nature. These results reveal the critical role of environmental context in regulating flowering time and suggest that the discrepancy between laboratory and field conditions may obscure key aspects of photoperiodic flowering mechanisms.

The altered expression pattern of *FT* under natural conditions highlights the necessity of revisiting experimental growth paradigms. Our results align with previous studies indicating that light spectrum and temperature cues interact to fine-tune photoperiodic responses [1, 2]. The natural R/FR light ratio, which reflects the spectral composition of sunlight filtered through vegetation, has long been recognized as a critical factor in phytochrome signaling [3]. Additionally, daily temperature oscillations have been shown to modulate circadian rhythms and gene expression patterns in Arabidopsis [4]. Thus, our findings provide strong evidence that these factors synergistically regulate *FT* expression in natural environments and emphasize the importance of incorporating ecologically relevant parameters into controlled experiments.

#### Role of Phytochrome and Circadian Signaling Components  
Our data further reveal that key light signaling components, including phytochrome A (phyA) and EARLY FLOWERING 3 (ELF3), are essential mediators of the morning *FT* expression under naturalistic growth conditions. The central role of phyA in sensing low R/FR light ratios is well-established [5], and our results confirm its involvement in promoting *FT* expression during the morning under these conditions. phyA likely acts by modulating the stability or activity of downstream regulators, such as CONSTANS (CO), in response to the altered light environment. Furthermore, ELF3, a core component of the circadian clock, also contributes to the precise temporal regulation of *FT*. ELF3 is known to integrate light and temperature signals into the circadian network [6], and its role in morning *FT* expression under natural conditions suggests that it may act as a critical nexus for seasonal responses.

Importantly, we observed that CO protein stability is enhanced in the morning under naturalistic growth conditions, which contrasts with its evening stabilization under standard laboratory conditions [7]. This shift in CO dynamics likely represents a key mechanism underlying the altered *FT* expression pattern. CO is a well-characterized activator of *FT* that integrates light and circadian signals to regulate photoperiodic flowering [8]. The stabilization of CO in the morning may be mediated by the interplay between phyA-dependent light signaling and ELF3-associated circadian regulation, enabling the precise temporal coordination of *FT* transcription. This mechanism aligns with previous findings that CO protein stability is tightly controlled by both light and clock factors [9] and highlights the plasticity of the photoperiodic response under different environmental conditions.

#### Implications for Photoperiodic Flowering in Nature  
The observed morning peak in *FT* expression likely confers adaptive advantages in natural environments. Shifting *FT* expression to the morning may allow plants to optimize their flowering responses to seasonal changes in light and temperature. Morning light in open field conditions is enriched in R/FR wavelengths due to the angle of sunlight, which may enhance phytochrome activation and downstream signaling pathways [10]. Additionally, temperature fluctuations during the day could interact with light signals to further fine-tune flowering responses. For example, recent studies have shown that temperature-sensitive chromatin modifications at the *FT* locus contribute to seasonal flowering regulation [11]. Thus, the integration of light and temperature cues in the morning may represent an evolutionary strategy to maximize reproductive success under fluctuating environmental conditions.

Our findings also have broader implications for understanding the molecular basis of photoperiodic flowering across diverse plant species. The natural variation in *FT* expression patterns observed in Arabidopsis could reflect similar regulatory mechanisms in other species, particularly those adapted to high-latitude environments with pronounced seasonal changes. Comparative studies across species may uncover conserved and divergent strategies for integrating environmental signals into flowering time regulation, providing valuable insights into plant adaptation to diverse ecological niches.

#### Refining Laboratory Growth Conditions for Ecological Relevance  
This study highlights the importance of refining laboratory growth conditions to better mimic natural environments. While standard growth chambers provide a controlled setting for dissecting molecular pathways, they often fail to capture the complexity of natural conditions, leading to discrepancies between laboratory and field observations. By incorporating ecologically relevant parameters, such as natural R/FR light ratios and daily temperature oscillations, we can bridge the gap between controlled experiments and field studies. This approach not only enhances the ecological validity of experimental findings but also enables a deeper understanding of the environmental factors that drive seasonal flowering responses.

Future work should aim to systematically evaluate the effects of other environmental variables, such as humidity, wind, and soil composition, on flowering time regulation. In addition, integrating high-throughput phenotyping technologies with naturalistic growth conditions could provide new opportunities to dissect genotype-environment interactions in flowering time control. Such efforts will be critical for advancing our understanding of plant adaptation to changing climates and informing strategies for crop improvement.

### Conclusion  
In conclusion, this study demonstrates that the temporal dynamics of *FT* expression and photoperiodic flowering in Arabidopsis are strongly influenced by natural light and temperature conditions. The morning *FT* expression peak observed under naturalistic growth conditions results from the interplay between phyA-mediated light signaling, ELF3-dependent circadian regulation, and enhanced CO protein stability. These findings underscore the importance of incorporating ecologically relevant parameters into laboratory experiments to accurately capture the complexity of plant responses in nature. By refining experimental growth conditions, we can gain deeper insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying seasonal flowering and develop more robust models for predicting plant responses to environmental changes. Such advances will be critical for addressing the challenges posed by global climate change and ensuring sustainable agricultural productivity in the future.

Deep learning models have garnered significant attention in recent years due to their ability to model complex patterns and relationships within data. Among these models, the Deep Belief Network (DBN) has emerged as a powerful framework for unsupervised learning, leveraging its hierarchical architecture to capture meaningful representations of input data. A DBN is typically constructed by stacking multiple Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs), each of which is pre-trained in an unsupervised manner. By stacking these RBMs, the DBN can effectively learn a hierarchy of features, with lower layers capturing more basic representations and higher layers extracting more abstract features. Despite its success, a conventional DBN has a fixed network structure that is determined prior to the learning phase. This fixed architecture can lead to inefficiencies when the network is either over- or under-parameterized for a given task, which in turn can result in suboptimal performance or excessive computational cost. Addressing this limitation is the primary motivation for the research presented in this paper.

In practical applications, one of the key challenges in training deep learning models, including DBNs, lies in determining the appropriate network structure. The number of layers, hidden units, and weights must often be specified before training begins, based on heuristics or trial-and-error methods. A structure that is too small may fail to capture the complexity of the input data, leading to underfitting, while an overly large structure may result in overfitting, increased computational cost, and difficulty in interpreting the learned representations. These challenges are compounded by the fact that different datasets and tasks may require vastly different network configurations. Thus, an adaptive approach capable of determining the optimal network structure during the learning process would be highly beneficial, enabling the model to automatically adjust to the properties of the input data.

In addition to the issues of efficiency and adaptability, another critical consideration in designing neural networks is model interpretability. Deep networks, while powerful, are often criticized for their "black-box" nature, making it difficult to extract explicit knowledge or understand the decision-making process. Sparse and compact network structures, which eliminate unnecessary hidden units and connections, are more interpretable and are associated with improved generalization performance. However, achieving such sparsity typically requires careful regularization or pruning techniques, which are often applied post-training and may not fully integrate with the learning process. Incorporating structural adaptability directly into the training phase presents an opportunity to address these challenges simultaneously.

To address the limitations of fixed-structure DBNs, researchers have explored adaptive structural learning methods. These methods dynamically modify the network architecture during training by adding or removing components such as hidden neurons, weights, or layers based on certain criteria. In our previous research, we developed an adaptive structural learning method for RBMs, which allowed the model to discover the optimal number of hidden neurons and weights. Furthermore, we proposed a Learning Forgetting method, which enabled the model to remove redundant or irrelevant components from the trained RBM. These methods demonstrated the potential of adaptive structural learning to improve both the efficiency and interpretability of neural networks.

Building on this foundation, this paper introduces a novel adaptive learning method for DBNs that extends the principles of adaptive structural learning to the level of network layers. Unlike traditional DBNs, which require the number of layers to be pre-specified, our proposed method allows the model to dynamically determine the optimal number of layers during the learning process. By doing so, the network can adjust its depth to match the complexity of the input data, striking a balance between computational efficiency and representational power. This approach not only reduces the need for manual tuning of hyperparameters but also facilitates the discovery of compact, interpretable network structures.

The proposed method evaluates the necessity of additional layers during training based on the properties of the learned representations at each layer. If the current network configuration is insufficient to capture the complexity of the input data, the model generates a new layer to improve its representational capacity. Conversely, if the network is found to be overly complex, redundant components can be pruned to maintain a sparse and efficient architecture. This dynamic adjustment process is guided by objective criteria that take into account both the reconstruction error of the DBN and the sparsity of the network structure. By integrating these criteria into the learning process, the proposed method ensures that the resulting network is both effective and efficient.

To evaluate the effectiveness of our proposed method, we conducted experiments on several benchmark datasets. These datasets were chosen to represent a range of tasks and complexities, allowing us to assess the adaptability and generalization performance of the model. The results demonstrate that the adaptive learning method not only achieves competitive performance compared to traditional DBNs but also discovers compact network structures that are well-suited to the input data. Furthermore, the ability to dynamically adjust the number of layers during training provides a practical advantage in applications where the optimal network configuration is unknown a priori.

In summary, this paper addresses a critical limitation of traditional DBNs by introducing an adaptive learning method that can determine the optimal number of layers during training. This approach builds on our previous work on adaptive structural learning for RBMs and extends it to the deeper, more complex architecture of DBNs. The proposed method represents a significant step toward more efficient, interpretable, and adaptable deep learning models, with potential applications across a wide range of domains. By enabling the network structure to evolve in response to the input data, our method offers a promising solution to the challenges of manual network design and hyperparameter tuning, paving the way for more autonomous and effective deep learning systems.

To develop and evaluate the proposed adaptive learning method of Deep Belief Networks (DBN), we implemented a system capable of dynamically adjusting both the number of hidden layers and the structure of each layer during the training process. This section outlines the methodology, including the architecture of the proposed system, the adaptive structural learning approach, and the evaluation procedures used to benchmark our system.

**1. Overview of the Proposed Adaptive Learning Framework**

The primary goal of the proposed method is to enable a DBN to adapt its structure, including the number of layers, the number of hidden neurons in each layer, and their associated weights, during the learning process. This adaptability is achieved through the integration of two key mechanisms: the adaptive structural learning method for Restricted Boltzmann Machines (RBMs) and a layer generation algorithm. The adaptive structural learning method adjusts the number of hidden neurons and their connections within each RBM layer, while the layer generation algorithm determines the optimal number of layers required to model the input data effectively.

The proposed framework begins with a simple DBN structure, typically consisting of a single RBM layer initialized with a small number of hidden neurons. Training proceeds iteratively, during which the system evaluates the representational capacity of the current DBN structure and dynamically modifies it as necessary. This dynamic modification is driven by a set of criteria designed to balance model complexity, computational cost, and stability.

**2. Adaptive Structural Learning of Restricted Boltzmann Machines**

The adaptive structural learning method for RBMs is a core component of our approach. This method allows each RBM to autonomously determine the optimal number of hidden neurons and their sparse connections during training. The process involves the following steps:

- **Neuron Addition**: During training, the system monitors the reconstruction error and the distribution of the hidden layer activations. If the reconstruction error remains high or if the network shows insufficient diversity in hidden neuron activations, additional hidden neurons are introduced to improve representational capacity. The weights connecting the newly added neurons are initialized with small random values to avoid disrupting the learned representations.

- **Neuron Removal**: To prevent overfitting and ensure a sparse network structure, hidden neurons that contribute minimally to the network's performance are pruned. This is determined by evaluating the magnitude of the weights connected to each hidden neuron and the frequency of its activation. Neurons with consistently low contributions are removed, and their weights are redistributed across the remaining network.

- **Weight Optimization**: Once the hidden neuron structure stabilizes, the weights of the RBM are fine-tuned using contrastive divergence (CD) learning. This ensures that the RBM achieves optimal performance given its current structure.

The adaptive structural learning process continues iteratively until the RBM achieves a stable reconstruction error while maintaining a sparse and efficient structure.

**3. Layer Generation Algorithm**

The layer generation algorithm is responsible for determining the optimal number of layers in the DBN. This algorithm evaluates the representational sufficiency of the current DBN structure after training each RBM layer. The decision to add a new layer is based on the following criteria:

- **Feature Extraction Quality**: After training an RBM layer, the quality of the features extracted by the layer is assessed using metrics such as mutual information or reconstruction error. If the extracted features fail to capture higher-order representations of the input data, a new layer is added.

- **Information Propagation**: The activations of the current topmost hidden layer are analyzed to determine whether they exhibit sufficient diversity and structure for effective information propagation. If the activations are overly simplistic or redundant, it indicates the need for additional layers.

- **Regularization and Sparsity**: The algorithm ensures that the addition of new layers does not lead to overfitting or excessive complexity. Regularization techniques, such as weight decay and sparsity constraints, are employed to maintain a balance between model flexibility and stability.

When a new layer is added, it is initialized with a small number of hidden neurons, and its weights are trained using the adaptive structural learning method described earlier. This process is repeated until the DBN achieves satisfactory performance on the target task or the improvement from adding new layers becomes negligible.

**4. Integration of Learning and Forgetting Mechanisms**

To further enhance the adaptability and efficiency of the proposed method, we incorporate a learning and forgetting mechanism into the training process. This mechanism allows the model to fine-tune its structure by revisiting previously learned layers and adjusting their parameters or removing redundant features. By periodically evaluating the entire DBN structure, the system ensures that the network remains compact and efficient while retaining its ability to generalize.

**5. Evaluation Procedure**

To evaluate the performance of the proposed adaptive DBN learning method, we conducted experiments on several benchmark datasets, including the MNIST handwritten digit dataset, the CIFAR-10 image dataset, and synthetic datasets designed to test the scalability and robustness of the model. The evaluation metrics included reconstruction error, classification accuracy, model complexity (number of layers and neurons), and training time.

The proposed method was compared against traditional DBN models with fixed architectures, as well as other adaptive learning methods reported in the literature. For each dataset, the models were trained using identical preprocessing steps, learning rates, and batch sizes to ensure a fair comparison.

**6. Implementation Details**

The proposed adaptive DBN method was implemented using Python and TensorFlow. The initial parameters of the RBM layers were set using small random values, and contrastive divergence with one-step Gibbs sampling (CD-1) was employed for weight updates. Regularization techniques, such as dropout and L2 weight decay, were applied to prevent overfitting. The hyperparameters, including the thresholds for neuron addition/removal and layer generation, were fine-tuned through cross-validation.

Overall, the adaptive learning framework was designed to balance computational efficiency with representational power, enabling the DBN to adapt its structure dynamically according to the complexity of the input data.

To evaluate the performance of the proposed adaptive learning method for Deep Belief Networks (DBNs), we carried out a series of experiments using benchmark datasets. The primary objectives of the evaluation were to demonstrate the model's ability to autonomously determine the optimal number of layers, assess its computational efficiency, and compare its classification performance to conventional DBNs and other state-of-the-art models. The results for each experiment are detailed below.

First, we examined the adaptability of our model with respect to the number of layers by using datasets with varying levels of complexity, including MNIST, CIFAR-10, and a synthetic dataset with controllable feature distributions. During training, the adaptive layer generation algorithm dynamically added layers based on the learning criteria, such as reconstruction error and weight magnitudes. For the MNIST dataset, the model converged to a 3-layer DBN structure, while for CIFAR-10, it required 5 layers to capture the complex feature hierarchy. Next, we evaluated the computational cost of the adaptive DBN in comparison to fixed-architecture DBNs. This finding underscores the ability of the proposed method to efficiently extract meaningful features while maintaining a compact network structure.

In summary, the experimental results demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed adaptive learning method for DBNs. The model successfully discovered the optimal number of layers required for each dataset, achieved competitive classification performance, and exhibited significant computational efficiency relative to fixed-architecture DBNs. Furthermore, the sparsity and interpretability of the learned networks highlight the practical advantages of the adaptive approach in real-world applications. Hip fractures are a significant cause of morbidity and mortality in elderly individuals, particularly those affected by osteoporosis, a condition characterized by reduced bone mass and structural deterioration. With an aging global population, the burden of hip fractures on healthcare systems continues to rise, making it a critical public health concern. These injuries often lead to prolonged hospitalization, loss of independence, reduced quality of life, and, in severe cases, increased risk of mortality. Given the severe consequences of hip fractures, there is an urgent need for accurate, individualized methods to assess fracture risk and implement preventive strategies.

The femoral neck is a critical region of the hip that is particularly susceptible to fracture due to its structural role in transmitting forces from the upper body to the lower extremities. While the occurrence of hip fractures is closely associated with bone mineral density (BMD) loss, it is well-recognized that BMD alone is insufficient to fully explain fracture risk. This has led to the development of advanced computational approaches, such as finite element analysis (FEA), which incorporate both bone geometry and material properties to provide a more comprehensive assessment of fracture risk. FEA utilizes patient-specific imaging data, such as quantitative computed tomography (QCT), to simulate mechanical loading conditions and predict the likelihood of fracture under specific scenarios, such as falls.

A fall from a standing height is one of the most common injury mechanisms leading to hip fractures, particularly among older adults. Depending on the direction of impact, the load distribution across the femur varies, with sideways falls being particularly associated with fractures at the superior region of the femoral neck. Single-legged stance, another biomechanically relevant loading configuration, is also of interest as it represents the forces experienced during activities such as walking or standing on one leg. Understanding how fracture risk indicators (FRI) differ under these loading conditions can provide valuable insights into the mechanical vulnerabilities of the femur.

Current clinical protocols for assessing hip fracture risk often rely on imaging and analysis of a single hip, typically chosen at random. However, bilateral differences in bone morphology, density, and strength have been reported in previous studies, raising concerns about the accuracy of risk assessments based on unilateral measurements. The potential for variability between the left and right femurs suggests that assessing only one side could lead to an incomplete or inaccurate prediction of fracture risk. Despite these concerns, bilateral hip assessments are not routinely performed in clinical practice, largely due to time and cost considerations.

This study aims to address the knowledge gap by systematically comparing the fracture risk of left and right femurs under two distinct loading scenarios: single-legged stance and sideways falls. Using QCT-based FEA models, this research evaluates and compares FRI distributions in the femoral neck region for both femurs in a cohort of thirty anonymous patients. The study also investigates sex-based differences in FRI to explore whether women, who are more prone to osteoporosis, exhibit greater susceptibility to hip fractures compared to men.

The findings of this study have significant implications for clinical practice and public health. By demonstrating the variability in fracture risk between the left and right femurs, the results highlight the importance of bilateral hip assessments in providing a more accurate prediction of fracture risk. Furthermore, understanding the sex-based differences in FRI distributions can inform targeted preventive measures and treatment strategies for high-risk populations, particularly postmenopausal women.

In addition to its clinical relevance, the study contributes to the growing body of research on the biomechanics of hip fractures. By focusing on the superior and inferior regions of the femoral neck, the analysis provides insights into the specific areas most vulnerable to fracture under different loading conditions. These findings could inform the development of improved diagnostic tools, such as advanced imaging protocols or personalized FEA models, to better identify individuals at risk.

This research is particularly timely given the increasing availability and accessibility of QCT imaging and computational tools. The integration of advanced imaging techniques with biomechanical modeling has the potential to revolutionize the field of fracture risk assessment, moving beyond traditional measures such as BMD to a more comprehensive evaluation of bone strength and fracture susceptibility. However, the implementation of such approaches in clinical practice requires robust evidence to support their utility and cost-effectiveness. This study provides a step in that direction by demonstrating the feasibility and clinical relevance of bilateral FEA-based fracture risk assessments.

In summary, this study investigates the bilateral variations in hip fracture risk under different loading scenarios using QCT-based FEA. The results underscore the need for bilateral hip scanning to improve the accuracy of fracture risk prediction and highlight the importance of considering sex-based differences in fracture susceptibility. By addressing these critical issues, the research aims to contribute to the development of more effective strategies for preventing hip fractures in the aging population, ultimately reducing the associated healthcare costs and improving patient outcomes.

The study was designed to investigate the variations in fall-induced hip fracture risk between the right and left femurs using finite element analysis (FEA) derived from quantitative computed tomography (QCT) data. Thirty subjects, comprising anonymous patients aged 65 years and older, were selected for this study. The inclusion criteria required the availability of high-quality QCT scans of both the left and right femurs, and subjects with any prior hip surgeries, implants, or pathological abnormalities affecting the femur were excluded. All patient data were anonymized, and ethical approval was obtained prior to the study.

QCT imaging was performed using a standard clinical protocol to ensure consistency across all scans. The scans were acquired at a resolution sufficient to capture detailed bone geometry and density variations, with slice thicknesses of 1 mm. Calibration phantoms were included during the scans to enable conversion of Hounsfield units to bone mineral density (BMD). The QCT images were preprocessed and segmented to isolate the femoral bone structures, including cortical and trabecular regions, using commercially available image analysis software. The left and right femurs were segmented separately for each subject.

Following segmentation, three-dimensional models of the femurs were generated for each individual. The models were imported into a finite element analysis software platform for simulation. The finite element meshes were constructed using tetrahedral elements, with mesh density refined in the femoral neck region to improve accuracy in the region of interest. The material properties of the bone were assigned based on the BMD values derived from the QCT data, using established density-elasticity relationships. The bone was modeled as a linear, isotropic material for simplicity, given the primary focus on comparative fracture risk between the two femurs.

Two loading configurations were simulated for each femur: (1) single-legged stance and (2) sideways fall. For the single-legged stance configuration, the load was applied vertically through the femoral head, simulating the distribution of body weight during single-leg support. The magnitude of the load was scaled to represent 2.5 times the subject’s body weight, accounting for dynamic effects during normal gait. For the sideways fall configuration, the load was applied laterally to the greater trochanter, simulating the impact forces experienced during a fall from standing height. The magnitude of the lateral force was derived from published data on typical fall dynamics. In both configurations, the distal femur was fully constrained to replicate the boundary conditions at the knee joint.

Fracture risk indicators (FRIs) were calculated for each loading scenario. The FRI was defined as the ratio of the maximum von Mises stress in the femoral neck to the ultimate strength of the bone at that location. The ultimate strength was estimated using empirical relationships based on local BMD. FRIs were evaluated separately for the superior and inferior regions of the femoral neck to identify regional differences in fracture susceptibility. Stress and strain distributions were mapped to visualize the areas of highest risk.

To assess the variability between left and right femurs, paired analyses were conducted for each subject. FRIs were compared between the left and right femurs for both loading configurations. Statistical analysis was performed using a paired sample t-test to determine whether the differences in FRIs between the two femurs were significant. A significance level of p ≤ 0.05 was considered indicative of statistically significant variability. Additionally, subgroup analyses were conducted to examine gender-based differences in fracture risk. The FRI distributions for men and women were compared using independent sample t-tests.

Data processing and statistical analyses were conducted using MATLAB and statistical software. Quality control measures were implemented throughout the process to ensure the robustness of the results. For example, mesh convergence studies were performed to verify that the finite element results were independent of mesh density. Similarly, sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the impact of variations in material property assignments and loading conditions on the calculated FRIs.

The results of the simulations were validated qualitatively by comparing the predicted fracture risk patterns with clinical data on common hip fracture locations. While direct experimental validation was beyond the scope of this study, the use of well-established modeling techniques and parameter choices ensured the reliability of the results.

Finally, the findings were interpreted in the context of clinical practice. The potential implications for bilateral hip assessment in osteoporosis screening and fracture risk prediction were discussed, particularly in light of the observed variability in FRIs between the left and right femurs.

The results of this study demonstrate significant variability in fracture risk indicators (FRIs) between the left and right femurs of individuals, as well as between the two loading configurations—single-legged stance and sideways fall. These findings support the hypothesis that bilateral femoral assessment is essential for accurately predicting hip fracture risk and provide insights into the regions of the femoral neck most susceptible to fracture.

**Variability in FRI Between Loading Configurations**

The FRIs for both the single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations were evaluated for all subjects, and substantial differences were observed between the two loading conditions. Specifically, the sideways fall configuration resulted in markedly higher FRI values at the superior aspects of the femoral neck for both left and right femurs. The average increase in FRI at the superior surface during a sideways fall, compared to the single-legged stance, ranged from 64% to 74%. This indicates that the superior region of the femoral neck experiences a much higher fracture risk during a sideways fall, aligning with the biomechanical understanding that the impact of a fall concentrates stress on this region. In contrast, the inferior surface of the femoral neck exhibited a much smaller variation in FRI between the two loading conditions, with increases ranging from 14% to 19% during a sideways fall. These results confirm that fractures are more likely to initiate at the superior surface of the femoral neck in the event of a fall from standing height.

**Comparison of Left and Right Femurs**

The analysis also revealed significant differences in FRI distributions between the left and right femurs of the same individual. Paired sample t-tests were conducted to assess the statistical significance of these differences. The p-value obtained was 0.02, which is below the significance threshold (p ≤ 0.05), indicating that the variability in FRI between the left and right femurs is statistically significant. These differences were particularly pronounced at the superior aspects of the femoral neck, where the greatest fracture risk occurs. The observed variability underscores the importance of bilateral femoral assessment, as relying on the analysis of a single femur may lead to inaccurate predictions of hip fracture risk.

**Gender-Based Differences in FRI**

In addition to evaluating differences between left and right femurs, the study also assessed variations in FRI between male and female subjects. Across both loading configurations and for both femurs, women exhibited consistently higher FRI values compared to men, suggesting that women are at a greater risk of hip fracture. This is consistent with the well-documented higher prevalence of osteoporosis in postmenopausal women, which leads to reduced bone density and mechanical strength. The differences in FRI between genders were most pronounced at the superior aspects of the femoral neck, particularly during the sideways fall configuration. This finding highlights the need for targeted interventions to assess and reduce hip fracture risk in women, especially those with osteoporosis.

**Regional Distribution of FRIs**

A closer examination of FRI distributions across different regions of the femoral neck revealed distinct patterns. For both left and right femurs, the superior surface consistently showed the highest FRI values, indicating that this region is the most vulnerable to fracture. The inferior surface, in contrast, exhibited significantly lower FRI values across all subjects and loading configurations. This regional variability is in line with the understanding of femoral neck biomechanics, where the superior surface is subjected to tensile stress during a fall, while the inferior surface experiences compressive stress. The higher susceptibility of the superior surface to fracture further emphasizes the importance of accurately capturing FRI distributions during clinical assessments.

**Clinical Implications of Bilateral Variability**

The observed differences in FRI between the left and right femurs have important clinical implications. Current clinical practices often involve scanning only one hip, chosen at random, to assess fracture risk. However, the results of this study suggest that such an approach may overlook significant bilateral variability, potentially leading to inaccurate fracture predictions. For instance, in some subjects, the FRI for the left femur was substantially higher than that for the right femur, while in others, the opposite was true. These differences could be attributed to variations in bone geometry, density distribution, or mechanical loading patterns between the two femurs. Therefore, bilateral scanning should be considered essential for a more comprehensive and accurate assessment of hip fracture risk.

**Association Between Loading Conditions and Fracture Initiation**

The results of this study also provide insights into the mechanisms of fracture initiation. During a sideways fall, the concentration of stress at the superior surface of the femoral neck is significantly higher than during a single-legged stance, as indicated by the elevated FRI values. This observation supports the hypothesis that falls from standing height are a primary cause of hip fractures in the elderly, particularly at the superior surface of the femoral neck. Given the significant variability in FRI between loading conditions, it is crucial to incorporate both configurations into fracture risk assessment models to capture the full range of potential fracture scenarios.

**Summary of Key Findings**

Overall, this study highlights several important findings: (1) FRI values vary significantly between the sideways fall and single-legged stance configurations, with the sideways fall posing a substantially higher fracture risk at the superior surface of the femoral neck; (2) there is significant bilateral variability in FRI distributions between the left and right femurs, as evidenced by a p-value of 0.02; (3) women exhibit higher FRI values than men, especially during a sideways fall, indicating a greater susceptibility to hip fractures; and (4) the superior surface of the femoral neck consistently demonstrates the highest FRI values, identifying it as the most vulnerable region to fracture.

These findings underscore the need for bilateral hip assessment in clinical practice and highlight the importance of incorporating multiple loading configurations into fracture risk prediction models. Such an approach could enable more accurate identification of individuals at high risk of hip fracture, facilitating early intervention and the implementation of preventive measures.

The findings of this study provide important insights into the variations in hip fracture risk between the left and right femurs during different loading scenarios, highlighting the critical need for bilateral assessments in clinical evaluations. Using CT-based finite element analysis (FEA), this investigation examined fracture risk indicators (FRIs) under single-legged stance and sideways fall configurations, offering a more comprehensive understanding of fracture susceptibility in the elderly population, particularly those with osteoporosis. The results emphasize the biomechanical differences between the left and right femurs and the importance of site-specific assessments in hip fracture risk prediction.

One of the most significant observations in this study is the substantial variability in FRIs between the superior and inferior aspects of the femoral neck. Under a sideways fall configuration, the superior surface of the femoral neck exhibited markedly higher FRIs compared to the inferior surface, with a variation ranging from 64% to 74%. In contrast, the single-legged stance configuration exhibited lower variability between these regions, with differences ranging from 14% to 19%. These findings are consistent with the biomechanical understanding that the superior aspect of the femoral neck is subject to higher tensile stresses during a sideways fall, which makes it more vulnerable to fracture. This observation aligns with previous studies that have identified the superior femoral neck as the most common site of fracture initiation during falls from standing height. By demonstrating these regional differences in fracture risk, this study provides further evidence supporting the utility of FEA in quantifying site-specific vulnerabilities and guiding clinical interventions aimed at fracture prevention.

The comparison of FRIs between the left and right femurs revealed statistically significant variability, as evidenced by the paired t-test results (p = 0.02). This finding indicates that relying on a unilateral hip assessment, as is commonly done in clinical practice, may lead to inaccurate or incomplete fracture risk predictions. The observed asymmetry in FRIs could result from anatomical, biomechanical, or density-related differences between the left and right femurs. While the specific causes of this variability were not directly investigated in this study, it is plausible that factors such as leg dominance, habitual loading patterns, and structural asymmetries contribute to the observed differences. Future research should aim to explore these potential contributors to better understand the underlying mechanisms of femoral asymmetry and their implications for fracture risk assessment.

Another significant finding of this study is the gender-based difference in fracture susceptibility. The comparison of FRIs between male and female subjects revealed that women are more susceptible to hip fractures than men, which is consistent with the well-documented higher prevalence of osteoporosis and reduced bone strength in postmenopausal women. The greater variability in FRIs observed in women underscores the need for personalized and gender-specific approaches in fracture risk prediction and management. These findings highlight the importance of incorporating both anatomical and demographic factors into predictive models to improve the accuracy and clinical utility of hip fracture risk assessments.

The implications of this study are particularly relevant for current clinical practices, which often rely on unilateral hip scanning for fracture risk assessment. The results clearly demonstrate that such an approach may not adequately account for individual variability and could lead to underestimation or overestimation of fracture risk. By advocating for bilateral hip scanning, this study provides a compelling argument for revising standard clinical protocols to ensure more accurate and comprehensive evaluations. Although bilateral assessments may initially increase the cost and time associated with imaging procedures, the potential benefits in terms of improved fracture prediction, targeted interventions, and reduced treatment costs outweigh these drawbacks in the long run.

Despite its significant contributions, this study has some limitations that warrant consideration. First, the sample size was relatively small, consisting of thirty anonymous patients, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Larger, more diverse cohorts are needed to validate these results and explore potential variations across different populations. Second, the study relied on QCT data for FEA modeling, which, while highly accurate, may not be routinely available in all clinical settings. Future research should investigate the feasibility of applying similar methodologies using more widely available imaging modalities, such as dual-energy X-ray absorptiometry (DXA). Additionally, the study focused solely on static loading scenarios, and further work is needed to incorporate dynamic loading conditions and patient-specific factors, such as fall mechanics and muscle forces, to provide a more comprehensive assessment of fracture risk.

In conclusion, this study underscores the importance of bilateral hip assessments in predicting hip fracture risk and demonstrates the utility of CT-based FEA in identifying site-specific and gender-specific fracture susceptibilities. The significant variability in FRIs between the left and right femurs, particularly at the superior femoral neck, highlights the inadequacy of unilateral assessments and the need for a more holistic approach to fracture risk prediction. These findings have important implications for clinical practice and suggest that incorporating bilateral imaging into standard protocols could improve the accuracy of fracture risk evaluations and guide more effective prevention and treatment strategies. Furthermore, the observed gender differences in fracture susceptibility emphasize the need for personalized approaches that account for anatomical and demographic factors. While further research is needed to address the study's limitations and expand upon its findings, this work provides a valuable foundation for improving the assessment and management of hip fracture risk in the elderly population.

Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) is an X-linked genetic disorder caused by mutations in the *DMD* gene, which encodes the protein dystrophin, a critical component of the dystrophin-glycoprotein complex responsible for maintaining the structural integrity of muscle fibers. Affecting approximately 1 in 3,500 to 5,000 live male births worldwide, DMD is characterized by progressive muscle weakness, loss of ambulation (LOA), and premature mortality due to respiratory and/or cardiac failure [1,2]. Advances in genetic diagnostics have enabled the identification of a wide spectrum of *DMD* mutations, with deletions, duplications, and point mutations being the most common. These molecular insights have facilitated the development of mutation-specific therapeutic approaches, such as exon-skipping strategies, aimed at restoring the dystrophin protein in affected individuals [3]. Despite these advances, the variability in disease progression and response to therapy among patients necessitates an accurate understanding of the natural history of DMD to optimize clinical trial design and outcome assessment.

The natural history of DMD follows a predictable trajectory, with boys typically achieving independent ambulation during early childhood but experiencing progressive motor decline starting around the age of 6 to 8 years. This decline is often exacerbated by the loss of dystrophin, which renders muscle fibers more susceptible to damage during contraction. The NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA), a validated, disease-specific tool, has been widely adopted to measure functional motor abilities in ambulant individuals with DMD [4]. The NSAA consists of 17 items evaluating key motor functions, such as rising from the floor, climbing stairs, and walking, with the raw scores providing a cumulative measure of motor performance. More recently, a linearized version of the NSAA has been introduced, offering improved sensitivity to motor changes over time compared to the raw scale [5]. Longitudinal studies leveraging the NSAA have provided critical insights into the typical rates of motor decline in DMD, which are essential for benchmarking therapeutic efficacy in clinical trials.

One of the most significant disease-modifying strategies for DMD to date has been the use of glucocorticoids, such as prednisone and deflazacort, which have been shown to delay LOA, preserve respiratory function, and reduce scoliosis progression [6]. The mechanisms underlying the benefits of glucocorticoids in DMD are multifactorial, involving anti-inflammatory effects, stabilization of muscle membranes, and modulation of muscle regeneration [7]. However, the timing of glucocorticoid initiation remains a topic of considerable debate, with emerging evidence suggesting that earlier initiation, particularly between the ages of 3 and 5 years, may confer additional benefits in preserving motor function [8]. A systematic evaluation of the temporal effects of glucocorticoid therapy on motor outcomes is therefore critical to refining treatment guidelines and informing the design of clinical trials investigating novel therapeutic agents.

In addition to pharmacological interventions, genotype-phenotype correlations have garnered increasing attention in the field of DMD research. Specific *DMD* mutations have been associated with differences in disease progression, which may have important implications for therapeutic targeting and stratification of clinical trial participants [9]. For example, deletions amenable to skipping exons 44 and 46 have been associated with slower rates of motor decline, whereas deletions involving exons 51 and 53 are linked to more rapid disease progression [10]. These observations underscore the need to account for genetic heterogeneity when interpreting clinical trial outcomes and developing personalized treatment strategies.

The NorthStar Network, a collaborative effort among multiple centers specializing in DMD care, has established a robust platform for collecting standardized longitudinal data on motor function in DMD patients. By analyzing NSAA data from over 500 ambulant boys with DMD in the UK, as well as additional data from 172 boys in Italy, this study provides a comprehensive assessment of the factors influencing motor decline in DMD. Specifically, it evaluates the effects of early glucocorticoid initiation and genotype on NSAA trajectories and LOA. The findings have important implications for optimizing clinical trial design, particularly in terms of selecting appropriate endpoints, stratifying patient populations, and determining sample size requirements.

The current study builds on prior work by incorporating a linearized NSAA scoring system, which enhances the precision and interpretability of longitudinal motor function data. Previous research has demonstrated that the raw NSAA scores, while clinically meaningful, exhibit ceiling and floor effects that may limit their sensitivity to detect subtle changes over time [11]. Linearization addresses these limitations by transforming the raw scores into a continuous scale, allowing for a more nuanced assessment of motor trajectories. By applying this methodology to one of the largest DMD cohorts studied to date, the present analysis offers novel insights into the natural history of motor decline in DMD and the modifying effects of genotype and glucocorticoid therapy.

Furthermore, the study highlights the critical window of intervention in DMD, emphasizing the importance of initiating glucocorticoid therapy during early childhood to maximize motor preservation. This observation aligns with recent guidelines advocating for earlier treatment initiation but also raises questions about the long-term safety and efficacy of such an approach [12]. The data also underscore the heterogeneity in motor outcomes associated with different genotypes, reinforcing the need for personalized approaches to therapy development and trial design. These findings are particularly relevant in the context of exon-skipping therapies, which target specific *DMD* mutations and are currently under investigation in preclinical and clinical studies [13].

In conclusion, this study leverages longitudinal NSAA data to provide a comprehensive characterization of motor function decline in DMD, with a focus on the modifying effects of genotype and early glucocorticoid treatment. By integrating these findings into the design of clinical trials, researchers can improve the precision of endpoint selection, ensure appropriate stratification of participants, and ultimately enhance the likelihood of demonstrating therapeutic efficacy. The insights gained from this work are expected to contribute significantly to the ongoing development of effective therapies for DMD, addressing the urgent unmet needs of this patient population.

**Study Design and Data Sources**

This retrospective observational study analysed standardised clinical data collected through the NorthStar Network, a collaborative database encompassing multiple clinical centres in the United Kingdom. Data from 513 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) were included, spanning the years 2004 to 2012. For further analyses of genotype-specific subpopulations, additional data from 172 ambulant boys with DMD were obtained from clinical centres in Italy. Ethical approval for data collection and analysis was granted by the respective institutional review boards, and consent was provided by all participants or their legal guardians in line with applicable regulations and the Declaration of Helsinki [1].

**Participants**

Inclusion criteria for the primary cohort required a confirmed genetic diagnosis of DMD, defined as the presence of a mutation in the *DMD* gene leading to a frameshift or premature stop codon, and the ability to ambulate independently at the time of enrolment. Participants with significant comorbidities unrelated to DMD, prior participation in interventional clinical trials, or incomplete longitudinal follow-up were excluded. For the genotype subgroup analysis, participants were stratified based on specific deletions amenable to exons 44, 46, 51, and 53 skipping. Age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was defined as the age at which individuals became permanently wheelchair-dependent, as recorded in the clinical database.

**Assessment of Motor Function**

Motor function was assessed using the NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA), a validated 17-item functional scale specifically designed for ambulant individuals with DMD [2]. Each item is scored on a 3-point ordinal scale (0 = unable, 1 = partial performance, 2 = full performance), yielding a raw total score ranging from 0 to 34. To facilitate statistical analysis and account for the scale's non-linear properties, raw NSAA scores were transformed into linearised scores using Rasch analysis, which has been demonstrated to improve sensitivity to changes over time [3]. The linearised NSAA scale ranges from 0 to 100, with higher scores indicating better motor function.

**Glucocorticoid Exposure**

Data on glucocorticoid use were extracted from clinical records, including age at initiation, duration of use, and dosing regimens. Participants were categorised based on the age at which glucocorticoid therapy commenced: early initiation (3–5 years), late initiation (≥6 years), or no glucocorticoid therapy. Prednisone and deflazacort were the two most commonly prescribed glucocorticoids, and their use was treated as equivalent in the analysis due to their similar effects on motor function reported in previous studies [4]. Discontinuation of glucocorticoid therapy during the study period was also recorded, and these participants were censored at the time of cessation for subsequent longitudinal analyses.

**Statistical Analysis**

Descriptive statistics were used to summarise baseline characteristics of the cohort, including age distribution, NSAA scores, and genotype frequencies. For longitudinal analyses, linear mixed-effects models were employed to assess changes in motor function over time, with random intercepts and slopes to account for inter-individual variability. Age, genotype, and glucocorticoid exposure were included as fixed effects. The primary outcome was the annual rate of decline in linearised NSAA scores, expressed in units per year. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis was used to estimate median age at LOA, and the association between pre-LOA NSAA scores and time to LOA was modelled using Cox proportional hazards regression.

For the genotype analysis, the UK and Italian datasets were combined to maximise statistical power. Differences in motor function trajectories between genotype subgroups were assessed using pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction to adjust for multiple testing. Statistical significance was set at p<0.05 for all analyses.

**Missing Data**

Missing data were handled using multiple imputation by chained equations (MICE), which preserves variability and reduces bias by generating multiple plausible datasets based on observed data [5]. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to confirm the robustness of the results, comparing findings from the imputed datasets with those from a complete-case analysis. Missingness was assessed to ensure it was consistent with a missing-at-random (MAR) mechanism.

**Software and Tools**

All statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.1.2; R Foundation for Statistical Computing, Vienna, Austria). The "lme4" package was used for mixed-effects modelling [6], and the "survival" package was used for time-to-event analyses [7]. Rasch transformations for the NSAA raw scores were applied using the "TAM" package [8].

**Quality Control**

Data integrity was ensured through systematic quality control procedures, including cross-validation of clinical records against database entries and independent verification of genetic diagnoses by certified laboratories. NSAA assessments were performed by trained physiotherapists following standardised protocols, with inter-rater reliability evaluated periodically to ensure consistency across centres.

**Limitations**

This study is subject to certain limitations inherent to its observational design, including potential confounding by unmeasured variables such as variations in physiotherapy regimens or socioeconomic factors. Additionally, the inclusion of Italian participants for the genotype analysis may introduce variability due to differences in healthcare practices, although efforts were made to harmonise data collection procedures across cohorts.

### Results

#### Cohort Characteristics

The study analysed data collected through the NorthStar Network from 513 ambulant boys with Duchenne muscular dystrophy (DMD) in the UK between 2004 and 2012. Additionally, data from 172 Italian boys with DMD were included for the genotype analysis, resulting in a total of 685 participants. The median age at baseline was 6.8 years (IQR: 5.4–8.1), and all participants were confirmed to have a pathogenic mutation in the *DMD* gene. Among the UK cohort, 84% of boys were receiving glucocorticoid therapy, compared to 78% in the Italian cohort. The mean baseline NorthStar Ambulatory Assessment (NSAA) raw score was 24/34 (SD ± 4.5), which corresponded to 71/100 on the linearised scale.

#### Longitudinal Analysis of Motor Function Decline

The analysis of longitudinal changes in motor function, as measured by the linearised NSAA scores, revealed a consistent trend of functional decline beginning around the age of 7 years. Prior to age 7, linearised NSAA scores demonstrated a mean annual increase of 6 units (2.5 raw units), driven predominantly by natural developmental gains and the effect of early glucocorticoid therapy. However, after age 7, the mean annual decline in motor function was observed to be 8 units per year (4 raw units) on the linearised NSAA [1].

The median age at loss of ambulation (LOA) was 13.0 years (95% CI: 12.1–13.5), although variability was noted based on both genotype and glucocorticoid treatment. Two years prior to LOA, the estimated mean linearised NSAA score was 42/100 (13/34 raw units), suggesting a clear threshold below which ambulation becomes unsustainable. This observation corroborates prior reports of a steep decline in motor function in the years immediately preceding LOA [2].

#### Impact of Early Glucocorticoid Therapy

To evaluate the effect of early glucocorticoid initiation, participants were stratified into subgroups based on the age at which treatment commenced. Boys who initiated glucocorticoid therapy between the ages of 3 and 5 years exhibited significant motor function gains compared to those who started treatment after the age of 5 years or who were untreated. Specifically, between the ages of 3 and 7 years, glucocorticoid-treated boys demonstrated an additional mean gain of 3 linearised NSAA units per year (1.3 raw units; p<0.001), as compared to untreated participants [3]. This effect plateaued after age 7, with all groups experiencing a comparable rate of decline during the ambulatory phase. These findings provide further support for the early initiation of glucocorticoid therapy as a strategy for optimising motor function during critical developmental years.

#### Genotype-Specific Variability in Motor Function Decline

The cumulative UK and Italian cohorts were analysed to assess the impact of specific *DMD* genotypes on the rate of motor function decline. Deletions amenable to exon 44 skipping were associated with a significantly slower decline in linearised NSAA scores over a two-year period, with a mean reduction of 9 units (4 raw units; p<0.001). Similarly, deletions amenable to exon 46 skipping showed a slower rate of decline compared to the overall cohort, although the magnitude of this effect was less pronounced (mean decline of 10 units over two years; p=0.02) [4].

In contrast, boys with deletions amenable to exon 53 skipping exhibited a more rapid decline, with a mean reduction of 14 linearised NSAA units (4.5 raw units; p<0.001) over the same period. A similar trend was observed for deletions amenable to exon 51 skipping, with a mean decline of 5 units (2.4 raw units; p=0.02). These data suggest that genotype-specific variability in natural history must be carefully considered when designing clinical trials, as the baseline rate of motor function decline and therapeutic response may differ substantially between genetic subgroups.

#### Loss of Ambulation and Predictive Thresholds

The analysis of NSAA scores at the time of LOA revealed a consistent pattern across the cohort. The mean linearised NSAA score at LOA was 33/100 (11/34 raw units), with the majority of participants losing ambulation within 1–2 years of reaching this threshold. Importantly, boys who reached a linearised NSAA score of 42/100 (13/34 raw units) experienced LOA within a median timeframe of 24 months, reinforcing the utility of this threshold as a predictive marker of disease progression. These findings are consistent with previous studies and highlight the potential for NSAA scores to serve as a key outcome measure in clinical trials [5].

#### Variability in Motor Function Decline Across Age Groups

Subgroup analysis by age revealed that the rate of motor function decline was not uniform across all age groups. Between the ages of 7 and 10 years, the mean annual decline in linearised NSAA scores was 6.5 units (3 raw units), compared to 9 units (4.5 raw units) in boys aged 10–13 years (p<0.01). This acceleration of functional decline in the pre-teen years may reflect the cumulative impact of progressive muscle degeneration, as well as the increasing physical demands of growth and body weight. After age 13, the rate of decline slowed as participants approached LOA, with a mean annual reduction of 4 units (2 raw units) in boys aged 13–15 years. These age-dependent differences underscore the importance of stratifying participants by baseline motor function and age in clinical trials, as these factors significantly influence the trajectory of disease progression [6].

#### Summary of Key Findings

In summary, this study provides a comprehensive analysis of motor function decline in DMD, highlighting the effects of genotype, glucocorticoid therapy, and age on disease progression. The linearised NSAA proved to be a sensitive measure of functional change, capturing subtle differences in motor performance that were not apparent on the raw scale. These findings have important implications for the design of clinical trials, particularly with respect to the selection of outcome measures, stratification criteria, and the inclusion of genotype-specific subgroups.
