The cortical microtubule (CMT) array is a highly dynamic and self-organizing network that plays a pivotal role in the growth and development of plant cells. Localized at the inner surface of the plasma membrane, CMTs are key regulators of cell wall deposition and the overall mechanical properties of plant cells. By guiding the deposition of cellulose microfibrils, CMTs influence cell shape, tissue architecture, and organ morphogenesis. Unlike animal cells, which rely on centrosomes to organize their microtubule arrays, plant cells utilize an acentrosomal system, where microtubules nucleate, grow, and interact in a decentralized manner. This unique organizational mode has made the plant CMT array a valuable model for studying the principles of microtubule dynamics and interactions.

A defining feature of CMTs is their dynamic instability, characterized by stochastic transitions between growth and shrinkage at their plus ends. This dynamic behavior is modulated by a variety of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs) and is critical for the establishment and maintenance of CMT arrays. In addition to intrinsic dynamic instability, CMTs interact with one another through a range of mechanisms, including bundling, severing, and polymerization-induced encounters. These interactions not only contribute to the spatial organization of the array but also influence the functional output of the CMT network, such as the control of cellulose microfibril orientation. Despite substantial progress in understanding the molecular players that regulate CMT dynamics and interactions, how the overall organization of a CMT array feeds back to influence individual microtubule behaviors remains an open question.

One specific interaction of interest is encounter-based catastrophe, a phenomenon in which the growing end of a microtubule contacts another microtubule and subsequently undergoes a transition to depolymerization. This mechanism has been observed in both in vitro and in vivo systems and is thought to play a central role in shaping microtubule arrays. In plant cells, where CMTs are closely associated with the plasma membrane and are subject to frequent interactions with surrounding microtubules, encounter-based catastrophe is likely to be a major determinant of CMT organization. However, the extent to which the spatial arrangement of CMTs—ranging from highly ordered, parallel arrays to more disordered, net-like configurations—influences encounter-based catastrophe rates and microtubule dynamics as a whole is not well understood.

The mechanical basis of encounter-based catastrophe adds an additional layer of complexity to the regulation of CMTs. When a growing microtubule encounters another microtubule, the outcome of the interaction depends on several factors, including the angle of contact, the structural rigidity of the microtubules, and the anchoring of the microtubules to the plasma membrane. It has been hypothesized that disordered CMT arrays, characterized by a wide range of microtubule orientations, may increase the likelihood of microtubule interactions and consequently elevate encounter-based catastrophe rates. Conversely, ordered arrays, in which microtubules are aligned in parallel, may reduce such interactions and promote sustained growth. These potential feedback mechanisms between CMT organization and individual microtubule behavior have yet to be systematically explored in plant cells.

In this study, we sought to investigate the relationship between CMT array organization and encounter-based catastrophe in Arabidopsis epidermal cells. We hypothesized that disordered CMT arrays, with their mixed orientations, would lead to higher rates of encounter-based catastrophe compared to ordered arrays. Using live-cell imaging and quantitative analysis, we examined the dynamics of CMTs in cotyledon and leaf pavement cells, which exhibit varying degrees of CMT organization. We further assessed how plasma membrane anchoring and CMT pause behavior influence the likelihood of encounter-based catastrophe. Our findings reveal that encounter-based catastrophe is the predominant mechanism of CMT depolymerization in Arabidopsis epidermal cells and that its frequency is strongly influenced by the spatial arrangement of the CMT array.

In addition to demonstrating the prevalence of encounter-based catastrophe, we show that disordered CMT arrays exhibit higher proportions of encounter-based catastrophe relative to free catastrophe, as well as an overall increase in catastrophe events. Microtubules in disordered arrays were more likely to pause upon encountering another microtubule, a behavior that often preceded depolymerization. Moreover, the anchoring strength of CMTs to the plasma membrane emerged as a key factor influencing encounter outcomes, with tightly anchored CMTs being more prone to undergo encounter-based catastrophe. These results suggest that the organization of the CMT array not only reflects the dynamic properties of individual microtubules but also exerts a feedback effect on their behavior through mechanical constraints and interaction opportunities.

Our study provides new insights into how CMT organization influences microtubule dynamics in plant cells. By linking CMT array patterning to encounter-based catastrophe rates, we highlight a bidirectional relationship in which the collective behavior of the array shapes, and is shaped by, the dynamics of its individual components. These findings underscore the importance of considering both intrinsic microtubule dynamics and higher-order organizational features when studying the plant cytoskeleton. Furthermore, our results have implications for understanding the mechanical principles underlying acentrosomal microtubule organization, not only in plant cells but also in other systems that rely on similar mechanisms for cytoskeletal regulation.

Plant Material and Growth Conditions  
Arabidopsis thaliana plants (Columbia-0 ecotype) were used for all experiments. Seeds were surface sterilized with 70% ethanol and 0.05% Tween-20 for 5 minutes, followed by three washes with sterile water. Sterilized seeds were plated on 1/2 Murashige and Skoog (MS) medium supplemented with 1% sucrose and 0.8% agar. Plates were stratified at 4°C in the dark for 3 days and then transferred to a growth chamber at 22°C under long-day conditions (16 h light/8 h dark). For imaging, 4- to 7-day-old seedlings were used. When specified, clasp-1 mutants were used to study the effects of microtubule anchoring on encounter-based catastrophe.

Live-Cell Imaging  
Live-cell imaging of cortical microtubules (CMTs) was performed using epidermal cells from cotyledons and leaves. Seedlings were mounted in water between a glass slide and a coverslip with a thin layer of 1% agar to stabilize the sample. Imaging was conducted on a spinning disk confocal microscope (Andor or Yokogawa system) equipped with a 60× oil immersion objective lens (NA 1.4). GFP-tagged TUA5 (GFP-TUA5) was used to visualize microtubules. For time-lapse imaging, images were acquired at 2-second intervals for a total duration of 3–5 minutes to capture the dynamic behavior of CMTs. Imaging conditions were maintained to minimize photobleaching and photodamage.

Quantification of Microtubule Catastrophes  
CMT catastrophe events were defined as the transition from a polymerizing or paused state to a depolymerizing state. Catastrophes were further categorized into two types: encounter-based catastrophes, which occurred when a growing CMT collided with another CMT, and free catastrophes, which occurred independently of any observable interaction. To distinguish between these, the position and timing of catastrophe events were analyzed in relation to nearby CMTs. Encounters were identified as instances where the growing tip of a CMT came into close proximity (within 0.5 μm) of another CMT and subsequently underwent catastrophe. Free catastrophes were assigned when no such encounter was observed.

Measurement of CMT Ordering  
To assess the overall organization of CMT arrays, the angular distribution of CMTs was quantified using ImageJ with the FibrilTool plugin. The degree of ordering was calculated as the nematic order parameter (S), which ranges from 0 (completely disordered) to 1 (perfectly aligned). Ordered arrays were defined as regions with S > 0.5, while disordered arrays had S ≤ 0.5. Analysis was performed on maximum intensity projections of confocal z-stacks.

Analysis of CMT Anchoring  
The strength of CMT anchoring to the plasma membrane was assessed qualitatively by observing the mobility of CMTs during growth and interactions. CMTs were categorized as tightly anchored if they exhibited minimal lateral movement during polymerization or depolymerization, and as weakly anchored if they displayed noticeable sliding or detachment from the membrane. To further validate these observations, clasp-1 mutant plants were used as a model for reduced microtubule anchoring. Comparisons of catastrophe rates between wild-type and clasp-1 mutants were used to assess the impact of anchoring strength on encounter-based catastrophe.

Data Analysis and Statistical Methods  
Quantitative data on catastrophe events, encounter frequencies, and angular distributions were extracted from time-lapse images using custom MATLAB scripts and ImageJ. The proportion of encounter-based catastrophes relative to total catastrophes was calculated for each region of interest. Rates of catastrophe (Fcat) were determined as the total number of catastrophes per unit time divided by the total CMT polymerization time. To compare ordered and disordered arrays, regions of interest were manually selected based on nematic order parameter values. Statistical analyses were performed using R software. Differences between groups were evaluated using Student’s t-tests or one-way ANOVA, followed by post hoc Tukey tests, with a significance threshold of p < 0.05. Data are presented as mean ± standard error of the mean.

Validation of Encounter-Based Catastrophe Mechanism  
To test the hypothesis that encounter-based catastrophe is influenced by CMT organization, the frequency and spatial distribution of encounters were compared between ordered and disordered arrays. Encounters were further classified by the angle of interaction between CMTs. Acute-angle encounters (<45°) and wide-angle encounters (≥45°) were analyzed separately to determine their contribution to catastrophe rates. Additionally, the duration of pause events preceding depolymerization was recorded for each encounter-based catastrophe to assess the mechanistic basis of this phenomenon.

Control Experiments  
To ensure that observed differences in catastrophe rates were not due to variations in imaging conditions or artifacts, control experiments were performed under identical imaging settings across all samples. Photobleaching was minimized by using low laser power and short exposure times. To confirm that GFP-TUA5 labeling did not alter microtubule dynamics, catastrophe rates in GFP-TUA5 lines were compared to those reported in unlabeled wild-type cells from the literature.

Reproducibility and Replication  
All experiments were performed using at least three independent biological replicates, with a minimum of five cells analyzed per replicate. Each cell was imaged in multiple regions to capture both ordered and disordered arrays. Data from replicates were pooled for statistical analysis, and trends were validated across independent experiments to ensure reproducibility.

To investigate the relationship between cortical microtubule (CMT) patterning and encounter-based catastrophe, we employed live-cell imaging in Arabidopsis cotyledon and leaf epidermal cells expressing GFP-tubulin. This approach allowed us to analyze both the spatial organization of CMT arrays and the frequency and type of catastrophe events. The results revealed a strong dependence of encounter-based catastrophe rates on CMT array organization and highlighted the role of mechanical interactions in influencing CMT dynamics.

We first quantified the relative contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophe events in Arabidopsis epidermal cells. Across all observed arrays, approximately 87% of catastrophe events were encounter-based, wherein a growing CMT polymer collided with another CMT and subsequently depolymerized. The remaining catastrophes (13%) occurred in the absence of direct CMT encounters and were classified as free catastrophes. These data indicate that encounter-based catastrophe is the dominant mechanism driving CMT depolymerization in vivo.

To determine whether the organization of CMT arrays influences catastrophe dynamics, we compared ordered (parallel) and disordered (mixed orientation) CMT arrays. Ordered arrays were characterized by largely parallel CMTs with a high degree of alignment, whereas disordered arrays displayed mixed orientations and intersecting CMTs. Disordered arrays exhibited significantly higher proportions of encounter-based catastrophes relative to free catastrophes compared to ordered arrays. Specifically, disordered arrays showed a 1.7-fold increase in encounter-based catastrophes. This suggests that the increased frequency of CMT intersections in disordered arrays provides more opportunities for MT-MT interactions that lead to catastrophe.

In addition to differences in the relative contributions of encounter-based and free catastrophes, disordered arrays also had a higher overall frequency of catastrophe events. We calculated the catastrophe frequency (Fcat) as the number of catastrophes per unit time normalized to the total length of CMTs in the array. Disordered arrays exhibited a significantly higher Fcat than ordered arrays, consistent with the hypothesis that increased CMT interactions drive higher rates of catastrophe. This result highlights the feedback between CMT organization and individual microtubule dynamics, wherein disordered arrays promote more frequent catastrophe events, potentially contributing to further disorganization.

Next, we examined the dynamics of encounter-based catastrophe events to better understand their underlying mechanisms. Encounters that led to catastrophe were often associated with a pause phase, during which the growing CMT temporarily stalled before undergoing depolymerization. We observed that pause durations preceding encounter-based catastrophes were significantly longer than those preceding free catastrophes, suggesting that mechanical interactions at CMT intersections may stabilize the growing CMT tip momentarily before triggering depolymerization. These pauses were particularly frequent and sustained in disordered arrays, where intersecting CMTs are more common.

To address whether physical properties of CMTs influence their susceptibility to encounter-based catastrophe, we analyzed the role of CMT anchoring to the plasma membrane. CMTs with tight anchoring, as indicated by reduced lateral movement and strong association with the membrane, were more prone to encounter-based catastrophe than loosely anchored CMTs. This suggests a mechanical basis for encounter-based catastrophe, wherein tightly anchored CMTs form physical barriers that growing CMTs are unable to cross. In contrast, loosely anchored CMTs may flex or shift upon collision, reducing the likelihood of catastrophe.

Finally, we investigated the effect of CMT array organization on the commonly used metric for microtubule catastrophe, Fcat. Consistent with our observations of higher catastrophe frequencies in disordered arrays, Fcat was significantly influenced by both CMT alignment and plasma membrane anchoring. These results suggest that Fcat should be interpreted cautiously in the context of plant CMT dynamics, as it reflects not only intrinsic microtubule properties but also the organizational state of the array and the mechanical properties of individual CMTs.

Taken together, our results demonstrate that CMT array organization strongly influences the frequency and distribution of encounter-based catastrophes in Arabidopsis epidermal cells. Disordered arrays, characterized by mixed CMT orientations and frequent intersections, promote encounter-based catastrophes through increased opportunities for MT-MT interactions. The mechanical properties of CMTs, including their anchoring to the plasma membrane, further modulate their susceptibility to encounter-based catastrophe. These findings add new complexity to our understanding of CMT dynamics, highlighting how array-level organization feeds back to shape the behavior of individual microtubules.

The results of this study provide significant insights into the interplay between cortical microtubule (CMT) array organization and the behavior of individual microtubules (MTs), particularly in the context of encounter-based catastrophe. Our findings reveal that the spatial arrangement of CMTs in Arabidopsis epidermal cells has a profound impact on both the frequency and mechanism of MT catastrophe, highlighting a feedback loop between CMT dynamics and array organization. This feedback mechanism adds a new layer of complexity to our understanding of plant MT organization and its regulation.

One of the key findings of our study is the predominance of encounter-based catastrophes in CMT arrays, with approximately 87% of catastrophes resulting from MT-MT interactions. This observation underscores the importance of physical interactions between MTs in shaping their dynamic behavior. The remaining 13% of catastrophes, which occur without encounters, likely represent intrinsic stochastic events associated with MT dynamic instability. However, the high proportion of encounter-based catastrophes emphasizes the mechanical constraints imposed by the dense and dynamic CMT network in plant cells.

Our study further demonstrates that the degree of CMT array disorder significantly influences the frequency of encounter-based catastrophes. Disordered arrays, characterized by mixed orientations of CMTs, exhibit higher rates of encounter-based catastrophe compared to ordered arrays with parallel CMTs. This observation aligns with our hypothesis that disordered arrays create more opportunities for MT-MT interactions due to the increased likelihood of intersecting trajectories. In contrast, the alignment of MTs in ordered arrays reduces the chances of encounters, leading to lower rates of encounter-based catastrophes. These findings suggest that CMT array organization is not merely a passive outcome of MT dynamics but actively shapes the behavior of individual MTs through the modulation of encounter frequencies.

The mechanical basis of encounter-based catastrophe is further supported by our observations of sustained pauses prior to depolymerization and the influence of plasma membrane anchoring. MTs that were tightly anchored to the plasma membrane were more prone to undergo encounter-based catastrophe than those with weaker attachments. This suggests that mechanical resistance at the encounter site, potentially mediated by anchoring proteins, plays a critical role in determining whether an MT undergoes catastrophe. Tight anchoring likely increases the rigidity of the MT at the point of interaction, making it less able to deform or bypass a physical barrier formed by another MT, ultimately leading to catastrophe.

Interestingly, we also observed that the commonly used measure of catastrophe frequencies (Fcat) is influenced by CMT array organization and MT anchoring. This finding has important implications for the interpretation of MT dynamic parameters in studies of plant cytoskeletons. Researchers should take into account the structural context of CMT arrays when comparing Fcat values across different experimental conditions or genetic backgrounds. For instance, mutants or treatments that alter CMT array organization may indirectly affect catastrophe frequencies by changing the likelihood of encounters, rather than directly influencing the intrinsic dynamics of MT polymerization and depolymerization.

Our findings have broader implications for understanding the functional roles of CMT arrays in plant cells. CMTs play a critical role in directing the deposition of cellulose microfibrils in the cell wall, which in turn influences cell shape and tissue mechanics. The feedback loop between CMT organization and MT dynamics described in this study suggests that plants may use this mechanism to modulate the structural and mechanical properties of CMT arrays in response to developmental or environmental cues. For example, increased encounter-based catastrophes in disordered arrays may serve as a mechanism to break down and reorganize CMT arrays under conditions where rapid remodeling is required, such as during changes in cell growth direction or response to mechanical stress.

From a broader perspective, this study contributes to our understanding of acentrosomal MT organization in plant cells. Unlike animal cells, which rely on centrosomes as primary MT organizing centers, plant cells organize their MTs through a combination of nucleation, severing, and dynamic instability, all of which are influenced by MT-MT interactions. The predominance of encounter-based catastrophes in plant CMT arrays reflects the importance of these interactions in shaping MT organization in an acentrosomal context. This study also raises intriguing questions about the molecular mechanisms underlying encounter-based catastrophe. While our results suggest a mechanical basis, further studies are needed to identify the proteins and molecular pathways that mediate this process. For example, the role of microtubule-associated proteins (MAPs), such as CLASP, in modulating encounter-based catastrophe remains an open question. The clasp-1 mutant, which exhibits defects in MT dynamics and organization, provides a valuable tool for investigating these mechanisms in future studies.

In conclusion, our findings demonstrate that CMT array organization has a strong influence on the behavior of individual MTs, particularly in the context of encounter-based catastrophe. Disordered arrays create more opportunities for MT-MT interactions, leading to higher rates of encounter-based catastrophe. These interactions are governed by mechanical constraints, including plasma membrane anchoring, which modulate the probability of catastrophe at encounter sites. This feedback between CMT organization and MT dynamics provides a mechanism for plants to regulate CMT array structure and function in response to developmental and environmental signals. By shedding light on the interplay between MT organization and dynamics, this study advances our understanding of the plant cytoskeleton and its role in shaping cell architecture and function. Future research should explore the molecular basis of encounter-based catastrophe and its regulation by MAPs and other cellular factors, as well as the functional consequences of this process for cell wall patterning and mechanical properties in plant tissues.

Accommodation is the process by which the eye changes its optical power to maintain focus on objects at varying distances. This dynamic adjustment is primarily facilitated by the ciliary muscle, which alters the shape of the crystalline lens to achieve focal changes. In phakic eyes, accommodation is a well-documented phenomenon, extensively studied due to its critical role in visual function. However, the accommodative mechanism is altered in pseudophakic eyes, where the natural crystalline lens is replaced by an intraocular lens (IOL). While the IOL lacks the deformable properties of the natural lens, pilocarpine-induced accommodation has been shown to influence the position of the IOL and the geometry of the eye. Understanding these changes is important for optimizing visual outcomes in pseudophakic patients, particularly in the context of presbyopia-correcting IOLs and other advanced lens designs.

Pilocarpine, a muscarinic cholinergic agonist, is commonly used to pharmacologically induce accommodation by stimulating the ciliary muscle. This agent has been extensively employed in research to investigate the accommodative response in both phakic and pseudophakic eyes. In pseudophakic eyes, where the mechanical properties of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures differ from those of the natural lens, pilocarpine-driven accommodation provides unique insights into the dynamics of ocular biometry. Previous studies have demonstrated anterior movement of the IOL and changes in anterior chamber depth (ACD) during accommodation, underscoring the interaction between the ciliary muscle, the zonules, and the IOL. These findings raise intriguing questions about the extent to which other ocular parameters, such as vitreous length (VL) and axial length (AL), may change during accommodation in pseudophakic eyes.

The axial length of the eye is a parameter of significant clinical relevance, particularly in refractive surgery, myopia progression studies, and the design of IOLs for cataract surgery. Changes in AL during accommodation have been reported in phakic eyes, with elongation attributed to forward movement of the lens and posterior displacement of the retina. However, the mechanisms underlying AL changes in pseudophakic eyes remain poorly understood. It has been hypothesized that ciliary muscle contraction during pilocarpine-induced accommodation might exert forces that influence the position of the IOL and the surrounding ocular structures, potentially leading to measurable changes in axial biometry. Despite these theoretical considerations, few studies have systematically examined AL changes in pseudophakic eyes during accommodation, and those that have are often limited by measurement techniques with insufficient precision or scan depth.

Advances in optical imaging technology, particularly the development of ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT), offer new opportunities to investigate these phenomena with unprecedented accuracy and comprehensiveness. Unlike traditional imaging modalities, UL-OCT enables high-resolution, full-length imaging of the eye, from the cornea to the retina, in a single scan. This capability allows for precise measurement of individual biometric components, including central corneal thickness (CCT), ACD, IOL thickness (IOLT), and VL, which collectively contribute to the overall AL. By leveraging this technology, it is possible to gain deeper insights into the structural changes that occur during accommodation, as well as to disentangle the contributions of different ocular components to changes in AL.

In this study, we aimed to investigate the effects of pilocarpine-induced accommodation on axial biometry in pseudophakic eyes using a custom-built UL-OCT system. Specifically, we sought to quantify changes in key ocular parameters, including CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL, to better understand the accommodative response in eyes with implanted IOLs. Our study builds on previous research by employing a highly precise imaging modality, enabling us to characterize subtle changes that may have been overlooked in earlier investigations. Furthermore, by focusing on pseudophakic eyes, our findings contribute to the growing body of knowledge on the functional behavior of IOLs in response to pharmacologically induced accommodation.

We hypothesized that pilocarpine-induced contraction of the ciliary muscle would result in measurable changes in ACD, VL, and AL, consistent with the mechanical effects of accommodation. Additionally, we expected that CCT and IOLT would remain stable, as these parameters are not directly influenced by accommodative forces. By testing these hypotheses, our goal was to elucidate the biomechanical interactions between the IOL and surrounding ocular structures during accommodation, thereby providing insights that may inform the design of future IOLs with enhanced accommodative properties.

The results of this study have important implications for both clinical practice and research. From a clinical perspective, understanding the accommodative behavior of pseudophakic eyes is essential for optimizing refractive outcomes and managing patient expectations following cataract surgery. For example, subtle changes in AL during accommodation could influence the effective lens position (ELP) and, consequently, the refractive performance of the IOL. From a research perspective, our findings contribute to the broader understanding of how pharmacological agents like pilocarpine interact with the biomechanical properties of the eye, offering potential avenues for the development of novel therapeutic strategies to enhance accommodation in both phakic and pseudophakic patients.

In summary, this study leverages the capabilities of UL-OCT to provide a detailed characterization of axial biometry during pilocarpine-induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes. By examining changes in CCT, ACD, IOLT, VL, and AL, we aim to shed light on the structural adaptations that occur in response to ciliary muscle contraction, thereby contributing to a deeper understanding of the accommodative process in eyes with implanted IOLs.

This study employed a custom-built ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system to investigate changes in axial biometry of pseudophakic eyes during pilocarpine-induced accommodation. The study adhered to the tenets of the Declaration of Helsinki and was approved by the institutional ethics committee. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to their enrollment.

**Participants**  
The study included 25 healthy subjects (age range: 49 to 84 years) with pseudophakic right eyes implanted with monofocal intraocular lenses (IOLs). Inclusion criteria required clear ocular media, no ocular pathologies or previous surgeries other than cataract surgery, and the ability to provide informed consent. Subjects with any history of retinal surgery, glaucoma, macular disease, or systemic conditions affecting accommodation were excluded. All participants underwent a comprehensive ophthalmic examination, including visual acuity testing, slit-lamp biomicroscopy, and fundus examination, to ensure eligibility.

**Instrumentation**  
The imaging was conducted using a custom-built UL-OCT system capable of capturing high-resolution, wide-depth scans of the entire eye. The system employed a swept-source OCT design with a central wavelength of 1060 nm, providing an axial scan depth of up to 14 mm in tissue. This configuration allowed for simultaneous imaging of the anterior segment, the IOL, and the posterior segment of the eye. The system's axial resolution was approximately 6 µm in tissue, ensuring accurate and reliable biometric measurements.

**Experimental Protocol**  
Each subject was imaged under two conditions: non-accommodative (baseline) and accommodative states. For the baseline measurements, the subjects were asked to fixate on a distant target to ensure a relaxed accommodative state. Following baseline imaging, accommodation was pharmacologically induced using two drops of 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride administered in the right eye, with a 5-minute interval between drops. Thirty minutes after the administration of the first drop, imaging was repeated under the accommodative state. The sequence of pilocarpine administration and imaging was standardized to minimize variability across subjects. The left eye was left untreated to serve as a control, although it was not analyzed in this study.

**Imaging Procedure**  
During each imaging session, participants were seated comfortably in front of the UL-OCT system and instructed to maintain steady fixation on the internal target light. The head was stabilized using a chin and forehead rest. A single trained operator performed all imaging to ensure consistency. Multiple volumetric scans were acquired for each subject to capture the entire axial length of the right eye. Care was taken to ensure proper alignment of the optical axis during image acquisition. The best-quality scan from each session, as determined by signal strength and absence of motion artifacts, was selected for analysis.

**Biometric Measurements**  
Custom-developed automated image analysis software was used to process the UL-OCT data and extract biometric parameters. The following measurements were obtained:  
1. **Central Corneal Thickness (CCT):** Measured as the distance between the anterior and posterior corneal surfaces.  
2. **Anterior Chamber Depth (ACD):** Measured as the distance from the posterior surface of the cornea to the anterior surface of the IOL.  
3. **IOL Thickness (IOLT):** Measured as the axial dimension of the IOL.  
4. **Vitreous Length (VL):** Measured as the distance from the posterior surface of the IOL to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE).  

The axial length (AL) was calculated as the sum of the above parameters: AL = CCT + ACD + IOLT + VL. Measurements were performed twice for each parameter to ensure reproducibility, and the average values were used for analysis.

**Statistical Analysis**  
All biometric data were analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Paired t-tests were used to compare measurements between the non-accommodative and accommodative states. A significance level of P < 0.05 was considered statistically significant. The mean and standard deviation (SD) were reported for each parameter.

**Validation and Reproducibility**  
To assess the reliability of the UL-OCT system and the automated measurement software, repeatability testing was performed on a subset of 10 subjects. Each subject underwent three consecutive imaging sessions under the same conditions, and the coefficients of variation (CoV) and intraclass correlation coefficients (ICC) were calculated for all biometric parameters. The results demonstrated high reproducibility and minimal variation (<2% CoV) for all measurements.

**Safety Considerations**  
The use of pilocarpine hydrochloride was considered safe for this study population. All subjects were monitored for potential side effects, including ocular discomfort, headache, or systemic symptoms, during and after the imaging sessions. No adverse events were reported during the study.

This methodological approach ensured high accuracy and reliability in the assessment of changes in axial biometry during pharmacologically induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes.

A total of 25 pseudophakic eyes from 25 healthy subjects (mean age: 65.4 ± 11.2 years; range: 49–84 years) were analyzed in this study. All participants underwent imaging in both the non-accommodative and accommodative states using the ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system. The key biometric measurements included central corneal thickness (CCT), anterior chamber depth (ACD), intraocular lens thickness (IOLT), vitreous length (VL), and axial length (AL). Accommodation was pharmacologically induced with 0.5% pilocarpine hydrochloride, and biometric changes were assessed 30 minutes after the first drop of pilocarpine.

In the non-accommodative state, the mean CCT was measured at 0.54 ± 0.03 mm, and this value did not exhibit a statistically significant change during accommodation (P > 0.05). Similarly, the IOLT remained stable between the non-accommodative and accommodative states, with a mean value of 0.93 ± 0.07 mm in both conditions (P > 0.05). These findings suggest that the corneal and intraocular lens thicknesses were unaffected by pilocarpine-induced accommodation.

The ACD, defined as the distance from the posterior surface of the cornea to the anterior surface of the IOL, showed a statistically significant increase during accommodation. In the non-accommodative state, the mean ACD was 3.99 ± 0.37 mm, which increased to 4.07 ± 0.38 mm in the accommodative state. This represented a mean change of +0.08 ± 0.09 mm (P < 0.05). The increase in ACD indicates a posterior displacement of the IOL during accommodation, likely attributable to contraction of the ciliary muscle and changes in zonular tension.

The VL, defined as the distance from the posterior surface of the IOL to the retinal pigment epithelium (RPE), decreased significantly during accommodation. In the non-accommodative state, the mean VL was 18.01 ± 0.90 mm, which decreased to 17.97 ± 0.90 mm after pilocarpine administration. This represented a mean change of −0.04 ± 0.09 mm (P < 0.05). The decrease in VL is consistent with a posterior shift of the IOL, leading to a slight reduction in the vitreous cavity length.

The AL, calculated as the sum of the CCT, ACD, IOLT, and VL, demonstrated a small but statistically significant increase during accommodation. In the non-accommodative state, the mean AL was 23.47 ± 0.93 mm, which increased to 23.51 ± 0.93 mm in the accommodative state. The mean change in AL was +0.04 ± 0.04 mm (P < 0.01). This elongation of the axial length can be attributed to the combined effects of the increased ACD and the posterior displacement of the IOL. Notably, the magnitude of axial elongation was small and consistent across the study population, indicating a relatively uniform accommodative response in pseudophakic eyes.

To explore the relationship between ACD and VL changes, a correlation analysis was performed. A significant negative correlation was observed between the change in ACD and the change in VL (r = −0.58, P < 0.01). This finding supports the hypothesis that the posterior displacement of the IOL, reflected as an increase in ACD, is associated with a corresponding decrease in VL. The stability of CCT and IOLT during accommodation further reinforces the conclusion that the observed changes in AL are primarily due to dynamic shifts in the anterior chamber and vitreous cavity dimensions.

The variability in accommodative responses was also evaluated. While the majority of subjects exhibited an increase in ACD and a decrease in VL during accommodation, a small subset of participants showed minimal or no changes in these parameters. This variability may reflect individual differences in ciliary muscle function, zonular mechanics, or IOL positioning. However, the overall trends were consistent across the cohort, with statistically significant changes in ACD, VL, and AL observed at the group level.

No adverse effects of pilocarpine administration were reported by study participants. Ocular discomfort was minimal, and all subjects tolerated the imaging procedures well. The high repeatability and resolution of the UL-OCT system allowed for precise measurements of ocular biometry, facilitating the detection of subtle changes during accommodation.

In summary, pilocarpine-induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes resulted in a posterior displacement of the IOL, as evidenced by an increase in ACD and a decrease in VL. These changes collectively contributed to a small but statistically significant elongation of the AL. CCT and IOLT remained stable throughout the accommodative process, highlighting the localized nature of the structural changes. These findings provide insights into the dynamics of accommodation in eyes implanted with IOLs and underscore the utility of UL-OCT for investigating ocular biometry in vivo.

The findings of this study provide novel insights into the axial biometry changes that occur in pseudophakic eyes during pilocarpine-induced accommodation, as measured by an ultra-long scan depth optical coherence tomography (UL-OCT) system. Our results demonstrate that pilocarpine, a cholinergic agonist, induces a measurable increase in axial length (AL) in eyes implanted with intraocular lenses (IOLs). This elongation is accompanied by posterior movement of the IOL, as evidenced by the increase in anterior chamber depth (ACD) and decrease in vitreous length (VL). These observations provide valuable information about the biomechanical behavior of pseudophakic eyes in response to pharmacologically stimulated accommodation.

The observed increase in AL during accommodation (+0.04 ± 0.04 mm) is consistent with prior studies that have reported changes in ocular biometry in response to accommodation in phakic eyes. In the natural crystalline lens, accommodation is achieved through a combination of ciliary muscle contraction and changes in lens shape and position. However, in pseudophakic eyes, the IOL is fixed in position within the capsular bag, precluding shape changes. Instead, the increase in AL observed in this study suggests that pilocarpine-induced contraction of the ciliary muscle exerts forces on the zonules and surrounding ocular structures, ultimately leading to posterior displacement of the IOL. The backward movement of the IOL is reflected by the increase in ACD (+0.08 ± 0.09 mm) and the corresponding decrease in VL (−0.04 ± 0.09 mm). These findings align with previous reports of IOL movement during accommodation, but our study provides direct and objective measurements using advanced OCT technology.

Interestingly, the central corneal thickness (CCT) and IOL thickness (IOLT) remained unchanged during accommodation, indicating that the observed changes in AL were primarily driven by alterations in the position of the IOL rather than changes in its geometry or optical properties. This finding further supports the hypothesis that ciliary muscle contraction causes mechanical changes in the zonular apparatus and posterior segment of the eye, which are transmitted to the IOL. The stability of CCT during pilocarpine-induced accommodation also suggests that corneal biomechanics are not significantly affected by the pharmacological stimulation of the ciliary muscle.

The magnitude of the changes in AL, ACD, and VL observed in this study is relatively small, raising the question of the functional significance of these alterations in pseudophakic eyes. It is well-established that pilocarpine-induced accommodation in phakic eyes can result in significant refractive changes, primarily due to the ability of the crystalline lens to alter its curvature and power. In pseudophakic eyes, however, the refractive impact of IOL movement is likely to be limited, as the IOL is designed to maintain a fixed optical power. Nevertheless, even small shifts in IOL position could influence postoperative refractive outcomes, particularly in premium IOLs designed for multifocal or extended depth-of-focus correction. Future studies are needed to investigate whether the observed changes in AL and IOL position translate to clinically significant refractive effects.

The use of UL-OCT in this study represents a significant advancement in the ability to quantify changes in ocular biometry during accommodation. The extended scan depth of this custom-built system allowed for precise imaging of the entire eye, enabling the accurate measurement of AL and its individual components. This level of precision is particularly important in pseudophakic eyes, where small changes in IOL position may have subtle but relevant effects. Additionally, the automated software used for biometry analysis minimized operator bias and ensured reproducibility of the measurements. The combination of these technological advancements underscores the utility of UL-OCT as a powerful tool for studying dynamic changes in ocular biometry.

The findings of this study have several clinical implications. First, the backward movement of the IOL during pilocarpine-induced accommodation may have implications for the design and selection of IOLs, particularly in the context of accommodating or pseudo-accommodating IOLs. Understanding the biomechanical interactions between the IOL, capsular bag, and ciliary muscle could inform the development of IOLs that better mimic the accommodative response of the natural crystalline lens. Second, the ability to induce and measure changes in AL pharmacologically may provide a non-invasive method for assessing ciliary muscle function in pseudophakic eyes. This could be particularly useful in evaluating the effectiveness of pharmacological or surgical interventions aimed at restoring accommodation.

Despite its strengths, this study is not without limitations. The use of pilocarpine to induce accommodation may not fully replicate the natural accommodative process, as pharmacological stimulation of the ciliary muscle can differ from voluntary accommodation in terms of both magnitude and dynamics. Additionally, the study population included only healthy pseudophakic eyes; therefore, the findings may not be generalizable to eyes with pathological conditions or different types of IOLs. Future studies should explore the effects of pilocarpine-induced accommodation in a broader range of IOL designs and patient populations, as well as investigate the long-term implications of IOL movement on visual function and ocular health.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that pilocarpine-induced accommodation in pseudophakic eyes is associated with a small but significant increase in AL, driven by posterior movement of the IOL. These findings highlight the dynamic nature of ocular biometry in pseudophakic eyes and provide new insights into the biomechanical interactions between the ciliary muscle, zonules, and IOL. The use of UL-OCT enabled precise and reproducible measurements of these changes, underscoring its potential as a valuable tool for studying accommodation and IOL behavior. Further research is warranted to explore the clinical implications of these findings and to evaluate the impact of IOL movement on postoperative refractive outcomes.

Endotracheal intubation is a critical component of airway management during general anesthesia, but it is often associated with significant hemodynamic responses, including elevations in heart rate (HR) and blood pressure (BP). These responses, primarily mediated by sympathetic stimulation due to laryngoscopy and tracheal manipulation, can lead to adverse outcomes, particularly in patients with cardiovascular comorbidities. The transient yet pronounced hemodynamic alterations, such as hypertension, tachycardia, and sometimes arrhythmias, may increase the risk of myocardial ischemia, stroke, or other complications in susceptible individuals. Thus, effective attenuation of these responses is a crucial aspect of perioperative anesthetic management.

Various pharmacological approaches have been explored to mitigate the hemodynamic fluctuations associated with laryngoscopy and intubation. Agents such as opioids, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, and alpha-2 adrenergic agonists have been widely studied, with varying degrees of success. Among these, remifentanil and dexmedetomidine have emerged as promising candidates due to their unique pharmacological properties. Remifentanil, a potent, ultra-short-acting opioid, is widely used for its rapid onset and titratable effects, making it particularly suitable for managing acute hemodynamic changes. However, its use may be associated with dose-dependent adverse effects, such as bradycardia and hypotension. On the other hand, dexmedetomidine, an alpha-2 adrenergic agonist, has gained attention for its sedative, analgesic, and sympatholytic properties, which contribute to its ability to attenuate the stress response during intubation. Additionally, dexmedetomidine has been shown to provide hemodynamic stability without significant respiratory depression, making it an attractive alternative or adjunct to opioids.

Despite the individual benefits of remifentanil and dexmedetomidine, there is limited evidence comparing their efficacy in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. Furthermore, the potential synergistic effects of combining these two agents remain underexplored. It is plausible that a combination of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil at lower individual doses may provide superior hemodynamic control while minimizing the adverse effects associated with higher doses of either drug alone. This hypothesis is supported by the complementary mechanisms of action of the two drugs: remifentanil primarily modulates the nociceptive response via opioid receptor activation, while dexmedetomidine exerts its effects through central alpha-2 adrenergic receptor agonism, resulting in reduced sympathetic outflow.

The present study was designed to address these gaps in the literature by evaluating the efficacy of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation. Conducted as a double-blind, randomized clinical trial, the study sought to provide a comprehensive comparison of these pharmacological strategies in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. A placebo group receiving normal saline was included to establish a baseline for the hemodynamic changes typically observed during intubation without pharmacological intervention.

The primary objectives of the study were to compare the effects of dexmedetomidine, remifentanil, and their combination on mean blood pressure (MBP) and heart rate (HR) immediately following intubation and during the subsequent peri-intubation period. Secondary objectives included assessing the temporal trends in MBP and HR over time and evaluating the safety profiles of the interventions. By addressing these objectives, the study aimed to provide evidence-based guidance for anesthesiologists in selecting the optimal pharmacological approach to manage hemodynamic responses during intubation, particularly in high-risk patient populations.

The findings of this study have significant clinical implications. The ability to effectively control BP and HR during laryngoscopy and intubation can enhance patient safety, reduce perioperative complications, and improve surgical outcomes. Moreover, understanding the potential benefits of combining dexmedetomidine and remifentanil may pave the way for more personalized and nuanced approaches to anesthetic management, particularly in patients with complex medical conditions.

In this randomized clinical trial, 124 patients were enrolled and assigned to one of four groups: dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), a combination of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil (DEX-REM), and normal saline (NS). The interventions were administered one minute prior to intubation, and hemodynamic parameters, including BP, HR, and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), were meticulously recorded at various time points. The baseline characteristics of the participants were comparable across the groups, ensuring the validity of the comparisons. The results demonstrated that all three intervention groups (DEX, REM, and DEX-REM) effectively attenuated the hemodynamic response to intubation compared to the NS group, with the combination group showing the most pronounced reductions in BP and HR.

This study is among the first to systematically evaluate the comparative efficacy of dexmedetomidine and remifentanil, both individually and in combination, in controlling hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation. The findings contribute to the growing body of literature on perioperative hemodynamic management and underscore the potential benefits of a multimodal pharmacological approach. By shedding light on the relative advantages and limitations of these agents, the study provides valuable insights for optimizing anesthetic care and improving patient outcomes during surgery.

This randomized, double-blind clinical trial was conducted at Amirkabir Hospital, Arak, Iran, to evaluate the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (DEX) versus remifentanil (REM) in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation in patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia. The study was approved by the local ethics committee and registered in the Iranian Registry of Clinical Trials (registration number: IRCT2016092722254N1). Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to enrollment.

A total of 124 adult patients, aged 18–65 years, with American Society of Anesthesiologists (ASA) physical status I or II, scheduled for elective surgery requiring general anesthesia with orotracheal intubation, were recruited for the study. Exclusion criteria included a history of cardiovascular disease, uncontrolled hypertension, arrhythmias, neurological disorders, hepatic or renal dysfunction, pregnancy, known allergies to the study drugs, use of beta-blockers or calcium channel blockers, and a body mass index (BMI) greater than 30 kg/m².

Participants were randomly assigned into one of four groups, each consisting of 31 patients: the DEX group, the REM group, the DEX + REM group, and the normal saline (NS) group as the control. Randomization was performed using a computer-generated random number table, and group allocation was concealed in sealed opaque envelopes. The study drugs were prepared by an independent anesthesiologist who was not involved in patient management or data collection to ensure blinding of both participants and investigators.

On arrival to the operating room, standard monitoring was applied, including non-invasive blood pressure (BP), heart rate (HR), and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2). Baseline measurements of these hemodynamic parameters were recorded. Patients were pre-oxygenated with 100% oxygen via a face mask for 3 minutes.

Study drugs were administered intravenously 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation. The DEX group received dexmedetomidine at a dose of 1 µg/kg diluted in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The REM group received remifentanil at a dose of 1 µg/kg diluted in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The DEX + REM group received a combination of dexmedetomidine (0.5 µg/kg) and remifentanil (0.5 µg/kg), diluted together in 10 mL normal saline and infused over 1 minute. The NS group (control) received 10 mL of normal saline infused over 1 minute. All infusions were administered using identical syringes to maintain blinding.

Anesthesia was induced 1 minute after the completion of drug infusion with intravenous propofol (2 mg/kg) and cisatracurium (0.15 mg/kg) to facilitate tracheal intubation. Following adequate muscle relaxation, direct laryngoscopy was performed using a Macintosh laryngoscope blade, and the trachea was intubated with an appropriately sized cuffed endotracheal tube. Laryngoscopy and intubation were performed by an experienced anesthesiologist to minimize variability. Anesthesia was maintained with isoflurane (1.2%) in a 50:50 mixture of oxygen and air. Additional doses of cisatracurium were administered as needed, and mechanical ventilation was adjusted to maintain end-tidal carbon dioxide (EtCO2) between 35 and 40 mmHg.

Hemodynamic parameters, including mean blood pressure (MBP), HR, and SaO2, were recorded at the following time points: on arrival to the operating room (baseline), 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation (post-drug infusion), immediately after intubation, and at 5-minute intervals for 15 minutes after intubation. All measurements were performed by a blinded observer who was unaware of the group allocation.

Any adverse events, such as bradycardia (HR < 50 beats per minute) or hypotension (systolic BP < 90 mmHg), were recorded and managed appropriately. Bradycardia was treated with intravenous atropine (0.5 mg), and hypotension was treated with intravenous ephedrine (5–10 mg) or fluid boluses as required. Patients who developed complications or required rescue interventions were excluded from the final analysis.

Sample size calculation was performed based on a pilot study, with a power of 80% and a significance level of 0.05, to detect a 20% difference in MBP and HR among the groups. A total of 31 patients per group were required to account for potential dropouts.

Statistical analysis was conducted using SPSS version 18.0. Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation (SD), and categorical variables were expressed as frequencies or percentages. Comparisons of demographic data and baseline hemodynamic variables among the groups were performed using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) for continuous variables and the chi-square test for categorical variables. Repeated measures ANOVA was used to assess changes in MBP, HR, and SaO2 over time within and between groups. Post-hoc analysis with the Tukey test was conducted to compare pairwise differences among the groups. A P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

In this randomized clinical trial, 124 patients undergoing elective surgery under general anesthesia were assigned to four groups to evaluate the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), their combination (DEX + REM), and normal saline (NS) in blunting the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation. The demographic characteristics of the patients, including age and sex, were comparable between the groups, and there were no significant differences in baseline hemodynamic parameters, including mean blood pressure (MBP), heart rate (HR), and arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2), among the four groups (P > 0.05).

Hemodynamic variables were recorded at multiple time points: on arrival to the operating room, 1 minute before laryngoscopy and intubation, immediately after intubation, and subsequently at 5-minute intervals up to 15 minutes. The results demonstrated significant differences in the hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation among the four groups.

Immediately following laryngoscopy and intubation, the NS group exhibited a marked increase in MBP and HR compared to the other three groups (P < 0.05). In contrast, the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups demonstrated significantly attenuated hemodynamic responses. The Tukey post-hoc test revealed no statistically significant differences in MBP and HR between the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups at any time point (P > 0.05). However, all three intervention groups showed significantly lower MBP and HR compared to the NS group at all measured time points after laryngoscopy and intubation.

A decreasing trend in MBP and HR was observed in the intervention groups over time, with the DEX + REM group exhibiting the most pronounced reduction in MBP. This group consistently maintained the lowest blood pressure values compared to the DEX and REM groups, although the differences were not statistically significant (P > 0.05). Similarly, all three intervention groups had lower HR values compared to the NS group at all time points, with no significant differences among the DEX, REM, and DEX + REM groups.

The repeated measures analysis further confirmed a significant interaction effect of time and group on both MBP and HR (P < 0.05). This finding indicates that while all three intervention groups effectively mitigated the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation, the NS group failed to control the increase in MBP and HR. Additionally, the DEX + REM combination not only prevented a rise in hemodynamic parameters but also induced a gradual decline in MBP and HR over time, suggesting a synergistic effect of the two drugs.

Arterial oxygen saturation (SaO2) remained stable across all groups throughout the study period, with no significant changes or differences observed between groups (P > 0.05). This indicates that the administration of DEX, REM, or their combination did not compromise oxygenation during the peri-intubation period.

In summary, the findings of this study demonstrate that both dexmedetomidine and remifentanil, either alone or in combination, are effective in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation. The combination of DEX and REM appeared to have the most favorable effect, resulting in the lowest MBP and a consistent decline in HR and MBP over time. These observations highlight the potential advantages of combining DEX and REM to achieve optimal hemodynamic stability during laryngoscopy and intubation. Conversely, the NS group exhibited significantly higher MBP and HR at all time points, underscoring the importance of pharmacological intervention to blunt the hemodynamic response during these procedures.

The present randomized clinical trial investigated the efficacy of dexmedetomidine (DEX), remifentanil (REM), and their combination (DEX-REM) in mitigating the hemodynamic responses associated with laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation, comparing these interventions to normal saline (NS) as a control. The results demonstrated that all three intervention groups (DEX, REM, and DEX-REM) were effective in significantly blunting the hemodynamic responses to laryngoscopy and intubation when compared to the NS group. Among the three interventions, the combination of DEX and REM resulted in the lowest blood pressure (BP) values, indicating a synergistic effect in controlling the hemodynamic response.

Laryngoscopy and orotracheal intubation are known to provoke a sympathetic response, characterized by transient increases in heart rate (HR) and BP, which can have deleterious effects, particularly in patients with cardiovascular comorbidities. The attenuation of these hemodynamic changes is critical in minimizing perioperative complications, especially during the induction of anesthesia. In this study, the use of DEX, REM, and their combination demonstrated superior attenuation of these responses compared to the control group, underscoring their value in clinical practice.

Dexmedetomidine, an α2-adrenergic receptor agonist, has been widely studied for its sedative, anxiolytic, and analgesic properties, as well as its ability to modulate sympathetic activity. In this study, the DEX group exhibited a significant reduction in HR and BP following laryngoscopy and intubation compared to the NS group. These findings are consistent with previous reports highlighting the efficacy of DEX in blunting the hemodynamic surge during airway manipulation. The ability of DEX to provide hemodynamic stability is largely attributed to its central sympatholytic effects and its capacity to reduce the release of norepinephrine, thereby mitigating the cardiovascular stress response.

Remifentanil, an ultra-short-acting opioid, has also been extensively used to attenuate the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation due to its potent analgesic and sympatholytic effects. In this study, the REM group exhibited comparable efficacy to the DEX group in controlling HR and BP, with no significant differences observed between the two groups. This finding aligns with existing literature suggesting that REM is highly effective in suppressing the cardiovascular response to airway instrumentation. The rapid onset and short duration of action of REM make it particularly suitable for procedures requiring precise hemodynamic control.

Interestingly, the combination of DEX and REM demonstrated the greatest efficacy in attenuating the hemodynamic response, as evidenced by the lowest BP values observed in the DEX-REM group. This suggests a potential synergistic interaction between DEX and REM, whereby the central sympatholytic effects of DEX and the peripheral opioid-mediated effects of REM complement each other to achieve superior hemodynamic stability. The use of a lower dose of each drug in the combination group (0.5 µg/kg each) may also reduce the risk of adverse effects associated with higher doses of either agent alone, such as bradycardia with DEX or respiratory depression with REM.

The results of this study have important clinical implications. First, the use of either DEX or REM alone can effectively blunt the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation, providing anesthesiologists with multiple options for achieving hemodynamic stability during induction. Second, the combination of DEX and REM may offer an even greater benefit in patients at high risk for cardiovascular complications, as it provides more pronounced attenuation of BP and HR changes without the need for higher doses of a single agent. Finally, the ability to reduce the hemodynamic response with these agents may improve perioperative outcomes by minimizing the risk of myocardial ischemia, arrhythmias, and other complications associated with sympathetic activation.

However, some limitations of this study should be acknowledged. First, the sample size, while sufficient to detect significant differences between groups, may limit the generalizability of the findings. Future studies with larger cohorts are warranted to confirm these results. Second, the study did not evaluate the potential side effects of the interventions, such as bradycardia, hypotension, or respiratory depression, which could influence the choice of agent in clinical practice. Third, the study was conducted in a single center, which may limit the external validity of the findings. Multicenter trials are needed to assess the reproducibility of these results across diverse patient populations and healthcare settings.

In conclusion, this study demonstrated that both DEX and REM are effective in attenuating the hemodynamic response to laryngoscopy and intubation, with the combination of DEX and REM providing the greatest efficacy. These findings suggest that the combination of these agents, even at reduced doses, may offer a superior strategy for achieving hemodynamic stability during airway management. Further research is needed to explore the long-term outcomes and safety profile of these interventions, as well as their applicability in specific patient populations, such as those with significant cardiovascular comorbidities. By optimizing the management of hemodynamic responses during laryngoscopy and intubation, anesthesiologists can improve the safety and quality of care for patients undergoing general anesthesia.

Natural transformation is a fundamental mechanism of horizontal gene transfer (HGT) in prokaryotes, facilitating the uptake and incorporation of exogenous DNA into the genome of competent cells. This process is central to bacterial evolution, allowing the acquisition of novel traits such as antibiotic resistance, metabolic versatility, and virulence [1, 2]. Beyond its evolutionary role, natural transformation has been proposed to provide immediate physiological benefits to individual cells, including the use of extracellular DNA as a nutrient source or as a template for DNA repair [3–5]. Despite its importance, the factors driving the evolution and maintenance of natural competence remain poorly understood. While the long-term adaptive value of transformation is evident in shaping genomic plasticity, elucidating its short-term costs and benefits to individual cells is essential for understanding its ecological and evolutionary dynamics.

### Mechanism and Evolution of Natural Transformation

Natural transformation is a highly conserved and regulated process, requiring the coordinated expression of multiple competence genes [6]. In model organisms such as *Acinetobacter baylyi*, the process involves the binding and uptake of double-stranded DNA (dsDNA) from the environment, its processing into single-stranded DNA (ssDNA), and the subsequent integration of this ssDNA into the bacterial chromosome via homologous recombination [7]. While this machinery is well characterized, its evolutionary origin remains a topic of debate. Hypotheses for the evolution of natural competence include DNA acquisition for genetic diversification, the utilization of extracellular DNA as a nutrient source, and its role in repairing damaged DNA [8, 9]. Each hypothesis suggests distinct selective pressures favoring the maintenance of this complex trait.

The DNA repair hypothesis posits that the uptake of environmental DNA provides templates for homologous recombination, thereby facilitating the repair of DNA damage, particularly double-strand breaks (DSBs) [10]. This idea is supported by the observation that competence genes are often induced under stress conditions, such as exposure to UV radiation or oxidative stress, which cause DNA damage [11]. However, the benefits of DNA uptake for repair are likely conditional, depending on both the nature of the stress and the availability of homologous DNA in the environment [12]. Moreover, the recombinational integration of DNA may itself introduce strand breaks or replication fork collapse, potentially imposing a fitness cost under certain conditions [13].

### Short-Term Benefits of DNA Uptake

Beyond its role in genetic exchange and repair, the immediate utility of DNA uptake has garnered considerable attention. Extracellular DNA can serve as a source of carbon, nitrogen, and phosphorus in nutrient-limited environments, providing a direct physiological benefit to competent cells [3, 14]. In this context, natural transformation may represent a metabolic strategy, enabling cells to scavenge resources from their surroundings. This hypothesis is supported by the observation that DNA uptake occurs even in the absence of homologous recombination in some bacteria, suggesting that the metabolic benefits of extracellular DNA can be decoupled from its genetic contributions [15].

Recent studies have also highlighted the context-dependent nature of DNA uptake benefits. For example, in heterologous environments where homologous DNA is scarce, the primary advantage of natural competence may lie in nutrient acquisition rather than genetic repair or recombination [16]. Conversely, in genotoxic environments, such as those with elevated UV radiation, the repair hypothesis predicts that competence should enhance survival. However, the relationship between DNA uptake, recombination, and fitness under such conditions remains complex and poorly understood.

### Costs of Recombination During Transformation

Despite its potential benefits, natural transformation is not without costs. The integration of exogenous DNA into the genome requires strand invasion and processing of ssDNA, which can interfere with other cellular processes, including replication and transcription [17]. Additionally, recombination with non-homologous or partially homologous DNA can lead to genomic instability, insertional mutagenesis, and the generation of deleterious alleles [18]. These risks are particularly pronounced in stressful environments, where DNA damage and replication stress are already elevated.

A less well-recognized cost of natural transformation is the potential for strand breaks introduced during the recombination process itself. Homologous recombination requires the generation of DSBs at sites of strand invasion, a process mediated by recombination repair pathways such as RecBCD and RecFOR [19]. While these pathways are essential for the successful integration of exogenous DNA, they may also exacerbate DNA damage under certain conditions, particularly when environmental stressors such as UV radiation induce additional genomic lesions. This interplay between DNA uptake, recombination, and repair pathways suggests that the costs and benefits of natural transformation are tightly linked to environmental context and genetic background.

### Study Objectives and Rationale

In this study, we investigate the immediate costs and benefits of natural transformation in *Acinetobacter baylyi*, a model organism for studying bacterial competence. Specifically, we aim to disentangle the physiological benefits of DNA uptake from the genetic consequences of recombination. By comparing the fitness of DNA uptake-proficient and -deficient strains under both benign and genotoxic conditions, we seek to determine the relative contributions of nutrient acquisition and DNA repair to the maintenance of competence. Furthermore, we explore the role of recombination in mediating the fitness effects of transformation, focusing on its impact on survival and genomic stability under UV-induced stress.

Our findings provide new insights into the selective pressures shaping the evolution of natural transformation and highlight the dual nature of recombination as both a benefit and a cost. By demonstrating that DNA uptake confers a physiological advantage independent of recombination, we challenge the traditional view that natural competence evolved primarily for genetic exchange or repair. At the same time, we reveal a previously unrecognized cost of recombination during transformation, with important implications for understanding the trade-offs associated with this process. Together, these results contribute to a more nuanced understanding of the ecological and evolutionary dynamics of natural competence in bacteria.

### Bacterial Strains and Growth Conditions  
The bacterial strains used in this study were derived from *Acinetobacter baylyi* ADP1. The wild-type strain (referred to as wt in this study) is naturally competent for DNA uptake and transformation. Mutant strains deficient in DNA uptake (ΔcomA) and recombination repair pathways (ΔrecBCD, ΔrecFOR) were constructed and verified by PCR and Sanger sequencing. For experiments requiring heterologous DNA, genomic DNA was extracted from *Escherichia coli* K-12 MG1655. Bacteria were cultured at 30°C in LB medium or minimal medium supplemented with 20 mM succinate as the sole carbon source, following standard protocols [1]. Where indicated, kanamycin (50 μg/mL) was added for selection.

### Construction of Mutant Strains  
Gene deletions were generated using homologous recombination with linear PCR products containing upstream and downstream flanking regions of the target genes fused to a kanamycin resistance cassette. PCR products were transformed into competent cells, and mutants were selected on LB agar containing kanamycin. The absence of the target gene was confirmed by colony PCR, and the functionality of the mutation was verified phenotypically. For example, ΔcomA mutants were tested for their inability to uptake plasmid DNA, and ΔrecBCD and ΔrecFOR mutants were tested for impaired recombination repair during transformation assays under UV-induced stress.

### DNA Preparation  
Genomic DNA from *A. baylyi* ADP1 and *E. coli* K-12 MG1655 was extracted using the Qiagen DNeasy Blood and Tissue Kit following the manufacturer's protocol. DNA concentrations were determined using a NanoDrop ND-1000 spectrophotometer, and DNA integrity was confirmed by agarose gel electrophoresis. DNA was sterilized by UV irradiation (254 nm, 100 J/m²) prior to transformation experiments to eliminate viable cells.

### Transformation Assays  
Natural transformation was assessed by incubating competent *A. baylyi* cells with genomic DNA derived from either homologous (ADP1) or heterologous (*E. coli*) sources. Cells were grown to mid-log phase (OD600 = 0.4–0.5) in LB medium and then washed twice with sterile 0.9% NaCl solution. Approximately 10⁸ cells were resuspended in 1 mL of transformation buffer (20 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.5, 1 mM CaCl₂, 0.1 mM MgCl₂) containing 1 μg of DNA. Transformations were carried out at 30°C for 30 min with gentle shaking. Following incubation, cells were plated on selective or non-selective LB agar to quantify transformants and total viable cells, respectively. Transformation frequency was calculated as the ratio of transformants to total viable cells.

### Competition Experiments  
Competition experiments were performed to assess the fitness effects of DNA uptake under benign and stressful conditions. Wild-type (wt) and ΔcomA strains were mixed at a 1:1 ratio and inoculated into LB medium at an initial density of 10⁶ CFU/mL. Cultures were incubated at 30°C with shaking (200 rpm) for 24 hours. To impose genotoxic stress, UV irradiation was applied at varying doses (50–200 J/m²) to cultures prior to incubation. Colony-forming units (CFUs) were determined by plating dilutions on LB agar and LB agar containing kanamycin to differentiate strains. Relative fitness (W) was calculated as the ratio of Malthusian growth parameters between wt and ΔcomA strains [2].

### UV Survival Assays  
The impact of UV-induced DNA damage on survival and transformation efficiency was evaluated by exposing mid-log-phase cultures to UV irradiation at doses ranging from 50 to 200 J/m². Following irradiation, cells were resuspended in transformation buffer containing homologous or heterologous DNA and incubated as described above. Survival was assessed by plating on LB agar, and transformation efficiency was calculated as described in the transformation assay. For recombination-deficient mutants (ΔrecBCD, ΔrecFOR), survival and transformation were evaluated under identical conditions to assess the role of recombination pathways in DNA repair.

### Microscopy and Cell Viability Assays  
To examine cell viability and morphological changes during transformation, cells exposed to UV stress were stained with the LIVE/DEAD BacLight Bacterial Viability Kit (Thermo Fisher Scientific) following the manufacturer's protocol. Samples were imaged using a Leica DMi8 epifluorescence microscope equipped with a 100× oil immersion objective. Green fluorescence indicated viable cells, while red fluorescence indicated membrane-compromised cells. Quantification was performed by analyzing at least 10 randomly chosen fields per sample.

### Statistical Analysis  
All experiments were performed with at least three independent biological replicates. Data are presented as means ± standard deviation (SD). Statistical significance was determined using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons or unpaired two-tailed Student's t-tests where appropriate. A p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant. All analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism 9.0 software.

### Ethical Statement  
This study did not involve human participants, animals, or genetically modified organisms requiring special regulatory approval. All experimental protocols followed institutional biosafety guidelines.
