### Results

#### Baseline Characteristics of Study Participants

The study included 203 cases with their first acute myocardial infarction (AMI) and 205 age- and gender-matched controls. The mean age of participants was 41.2 ± 3.7 years for cases and 40.9 ± 3.6 years for controls, with no statistically significant difference between groups (p=0.12). Among the cases, 71.9% (n=146) were male, while 28.1% (n=57) were female; the gender distribution in controls was identical due to matching. Cases demonstrated significantly higher levels of fasting total cholesterol (5.9 ± 1.3 mmol/L vs. 5.1 ± 1.2 mmol/L; p<0.001), LDL-cholesterol (3.8 ± 1.1 mmol/L vs. 3.3 ± 1.0 mmol/L; p<0.001), and triglycerides (2.1 ± 0.9 mmol/L vs. 1.7 ± 0.7 mmol/L; p<0.001) compared to controls. HDL-cholesterol levels were significantly lower in cases than controls (1.0 ± 0.2 mmol/L vs. 1.3 ± 0.3 mmol/L; p<0.001). Additionally, serum homocysteine levels were significantly higher in cases (17.4 ± 5.8 µmol/L) than in controls (12.8 ± 4.3 µmol/L; p<0.001). Serum folate and vitamin B12 concentrations were lower in cases compared to controls, with mean values of 8.7 ± 2.1 ng/mL vs. 10.2 ± 2.6 ng/mL (p=0.003) and 305 ± 85 pg/mL vs. 370 ± 95 pg/mL (p=0.002), respectively. Blood lead levels were also elevated in cases (8.2 ± 3.1 µg/dL) compared to controls (5.9 ± 2.4 µg/dL; p<0.001).

#### Identification of Dietary Patterns

Factor analysis of the dietary intake data yielded three distinct dietary patterns, which together explained 72.4% of the total variance in dietary consumption. The *prudent dietary pattern* was characterized by high consumption of legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken, and fruits. The *combination dietary pattern* was defined by high intake of eggs, fish, fruits, juices, and coffee. The *western dietary pattern* was identified through high consumption of meat, fish, and tea with milk. Factor loadings for key food items within each dietary pattern are presented in Supplementary Table 1.

#### Association Between Dietary Patterns and AMI Risk

##### Prudent Dietary Pattern
Participants adhering to the prudent dietary pattern demonstrated a significantly lower risk of premature AMI. Conditional logistic regression analysis revealed a strong inverse association between adherence to this dietary pattern and AMI risk (adjusted odds ratio [aOR] for highest vs. lowest tertile: 0.38; 95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.24–0.59; p<0.001). After adjusting for potential confounders, including age, gender, smoking status, physical activity, lipid profile, and serum homocysteine, the association remained statistically significant (aOR: 0.41; 95% CI: 0.27–0.66; p<0.001). A dose-response relationship was observed, with higher adherence to the prudent dietary pattern correlating with progressively lower AMI risk (p for trend <0.001). 

##### Combination Dietary Pattern
Moderate to high adherence to the combination dietary pattern was also associated with a reduced risk of AMI. Participants in the highest tertile of this pattern had a significantly lower likelihood of AMI compared to those in the lowest tertile (aOR: 0.72; 95% CI: 0.51–1.02; p=0.05). Adjustments for confounding variables further strengthened the association (aOR: 0.68; 95% CI: 0.45–0.98; p=0.04). Although the protective effect of the combination dietary pattern was less pronounced than that of the prudent dietary pattern, the observed relationship was consistent across sensitivity analyses.

##### Western Dietary Pattern
No significant association was observed between adherence to the western dietary pattern and AMI risk. Participants in the highest tertile of this pattern had an aOR of 1.12 (95% CI: 0.79–1.58; p=0.48) compared to those in the lowest tertile. Adjustment for potential confounders, including lipid profile and blood lead levels, did not materially alter the results. Subgroup analyses stratified by gender and smoking status similarly failed to reveal any significant effect modification.

#### Dietary Pattern Adherence and Biochemical Parameters

Adherence to the prudent dietary pattern was associated with favorable lipid and homocysteine profiles. Participants in the highest tertile of adherence had significantly lower mean LDL-cholesterol (3.1 ± 0.9 mmol/L), triglycerides (1.5 ± 0.6 mmol/L), and homocysteine levels (13.8 ± 4.5 µmol/L) compared to those in the lowest tertile (LDL-cholesterol: 4.0 ± 1.1 mmol/L, triglycerides: 2.3 ± 0.8 mmol/L, homocysteine: 18.6 ± 5.7 µmol/L; p<0.001 for all comparisons). Conversely, HDL-cholesterol levels were significantly higher in individuals with high adherence to the prudent dietary pattern (1.4 ± 0.3 mmol/L vs. 0.9 ± 0.2 mmol/L; p<0.001).

The combination dietary pattern was associated with intermediate improvements in lipid and homocysteine profiles, while the western dietary pattern did not demonstrate any significant associations with these biochemical parameters. Blood lead levels were notably higher in participants adhering to the western dietary pattern, although this finding did not reach statistical significance (p=0.08).

#### Sensitivity Analyses

Sensitivity analyses were performed to assess the robustness of the observed associations. Excluding participants with extreme dietary intakes (total energy intake <500 kcal/day or >5,000 kcal/day) did not substantively alter the results. Stratification by gender, smoking status, and physical activity revealed consistent associations for the prudent and combination dietary patterns across subgroups. Interaction terms for dietary patterns with gender, smoking, and physical activity were not statistically significant (p>0.1 for all).

#### Summary of Key Findings

The results indicate that adherence to the prudent dietary pattern was strongly protective against premature AMI in a young, urban Pakistani population. Moderate to high adherence to the combination dietary pattern also conferred a reduced AMI risk, though the effect size was smaller. The western dietary pattern was not associated with AMI risk. These findings underscore the importance of dietary quality in cardiovascular disease prevention.

### Discussion

#### Summary of Findings

This study investigated the association of dietary patterns with the risk of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) in a relatively young, urban Pakistani population. The results of our analysis indicate that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern, characterized by high consumption of legumes, vegetables, wheat, chicken, and fruits, is significantly protective against premature AMI. Similarly, moderate to high consumption of a combination dietary pattern, which includes eggs, fish, fruits, juices, and coffee, was also associated with a reduced risk of AMI. Interestingly, no significant association was observed between the western dietary pattern, characterized by high consumption of meat, fish, and tea with milk, and the risk of AMI. 

The findings provide novel insights into the dietary influences on cardiovascular health in a relatively understudied population, emphasizing the potential of dietary modification as a preventive strategy against premature AMI.

#### Comparison with Existing Literature

The protective role of the prudent dietary pattern aligns with findings from prior studies that underscore the cardiovascular benefits of diets rich in vegetables, fruits, and whole grains [1, 2]. Previous evidence suggests that these food groups are abundant sources of dietary fiber, vitamins, minerals, and antioxidants, which collectively exert anti-inflammatory and cardioprotective effects [3]. The high intake of legumes, in particular, may contribute to improved lipid profiles and better glycemic control, both of which are pertinent to AMI prevention [4]. Similarly, the inclusion of chicken as a lean protein source may reduce saturated fat intake compared to red meat, thereby lowering low-density lipoprotein (LDL) cholesterol levels [5].

The combination dietary pattern, though less extensively studied, reflects a mix of nutrient-dense foods, including fish and eggs, which are rich sources of omega-3 fatty acids and high-quality proteins, respectively. Omega-3 fatty acids have been shown to reduce inflammation, improve endothelial function, and lower triglyceride levels, all of which are critical in reducing cardiovascular risk [6]. The inclusion of fruits and juices in this pattern further adds cardioprotective antioxidants and polyphenols, supporting its beneficial impact [7]. The potential role of coffee, which is a rich source of bioactive compounds, remains a subject of debate; however, moderate coffee consumption has been associated with decreased cardiovascular mortality in some studies [8].

In contrast, the lack of association between the western dietary pattern and AMI risk may reflect the relatively lower consumption of processed foods and sugary beverages, which are often integral components of the western diet in other populations [9]. It is also worth noting that while this dietary pattern included meat and fish, the cooking methods and types of meat consumed in the Pakistani context may differ from those in Western countries, potentially influencing the observed outcomes. For instance, traditional cooking methods involving the use of spices such as turmeric, which has known anti-inflammatory properties, may mitigate the adverse effects of meat consumption [10].

#### Biological Mechanisms

The protective effects of the prudent and combination dietary patterns can be attributed to their impact on key metabolic and inflammatory pathways. Diets rich in fruits, vegetables, and whole grains are known to reduce oxidative stress and systemic inflammation, both of which play pivotal roles in atherogenesis and the progression of cardiovascular disease [11]. Additionally, the high fiber content of these diets improves lipid metabolism by reducing LDL cholesterol and increasing high-density lipoprotein (HDL) cholesterol levels [12]. The inclusion of omega-3 fatty acids from fish in the combination diet further enhances lipid regulation and exerts antiarrhythmic effects, which are critical in reducing AMI risk [13].

Folate, vitamin B12, and other micronutrients present in these dietary patterns may also contribute to the observed protective effects by modulating homocysteine levels. Elevated homocysteine has been implicated as an independent risk factor for AMI due to its prothrombotic and pro-inflammatory effects [14]. In this study, the prudent and combination dietary patterns may have contributed to lower homocysteine levels through their high content of folate-rich foods such as legumes and vegetables.

#### Implications for Public Health

The findings of this study have important implications for public health in Pakistan, where the incidence of cardiovascular disease is rising, particularly among younger individuals in urban areas [15]. The protective role of the prudent and combination dietary patterns highlights the need to promote dietary habits that prioritize nutrient-dense, minimally processed foods. Public health campaigns should focus on increasing awareness about the benefits of incorporating fruits, vegetables, legumes, and fish into daily diets while reducing reliance on energy-dense, nutrient-poor foods.

Moreover, the results underscore the importance of tailoring dietary recommendations to the sociocultural context of the target population. For instance, while the western dietary pattern did not show a significant association with AMI risk in this study, it is possible that a higher intake of processed meats and sugary beverages, which are becoming increasingly common in urban Pakistan, could have adverse effects in the long term. Policymakers should address these dietary shifts by integrating nutrition education into primary healthcare and community-based programs.

#### Limitations and Strengths

The findings of this study should be interpreted in light of several limitations. First, the use of a simple 14-item food frequency questionnaire may have limited the precision of dietary intake assessment, as it does not account for portion sizes or cooking methods. Second, the cross-sectional nature of the study precludes causal inferences, as dietary patterns and AMI risk factors may have been influenced by unmeasured confounders. Third, the study population was limited to a single urban center, which may restrict the generalizability of the findings to rural populations or other regions of Pakistan.

Nonetheless, this study has several strengths, including the use of factor analysis to identify dietary patterns, which provides a more comprehensive understanding of diet-disease relationships than single nutrient-based approaches. The inclusion of biochemical markers such as homocysteine, folate, and lipid profiles adds robustness to the findings by linking dietary patterns to potential underlying mechanisms. Additionally, the focus on a young population addresses an important gap in the literature, as most studies on AMI risk have been conducted in older adults.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that adherence to a prudent dietary pattern and, to a lesser extent, a combination dietary pattern is associated with a reduced risk of premature AMI in a young, urban Pakistani population. These findings highlight the potential of dietary modification as a cost-effective strategy for cardiovascular disease prevention in resource-limited settings. Future research should focus on longitudinal studies to confirm these associations and explore the impact of sociocultural factors on dietary habits. Public health interventions aimed at promoting healthy dietary patterns should be prioritized to mitigate the growing burden of cardiovascular disease in Pakistan.

Understanding how the brain evaluates past experiences and integrates this information to adapt future behavior is a central question in neuroscience. Adaptive behavior, a hallmark of higher cognitive functions, relies on the ability to assess the outcome of a decision, learn from errors, and adjust future strategies accordingly. These processes are critical for optimizing performance in uncertain environments. While numerous studies have investigated the neural mechanisms underlying decision-making and error processing, the specific role of the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) in evaluating outcomes and guiding behavior remains underexplored.

Behavioral adaptation following errors has been widely documented across species, including humans and non-human primates, and is a robust phenomenon often referred to as "post-error adjustments" [1, 2]. In humans, such adjustments manifest as slower response times and higher accuracy in trials following errors, suggesting a shift in strategy to prioritize accuracy over speed [3]. At the neural level, error-related activity has primarily been attributed to regions such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), prefrontal areas, and basal ganglia, which collectively form circuits involved in error detection and performance monitoring [4, 5]. While these regions have been extensively studied, their interaction with sensorimotor areas, such as the PMv, and the functional contribution of these areas to post-error behavioral adjustments remain less well understood.

The PMv plays a critical role in motor planning, perceptual decision-making, and sensorimotor integration [6]. This area is particularly well-positioned to mediate the interplay between cognitive and motor processes, as it is anatomically and functionally connected to both higher-order cortical regions and primary motor areas [7]. Recent work has extended the role of the PMv beyond motor preparation and execution, demonstrating its involvement in encoding task-relevant information during perceptual decision-making [8, 9]. For example, PMv neurons have been shown to represent both sensory evidence and categorical decisions during complex tasks requiring the integration of sensory inputs [10]. Interestingly, following the completion of a decision, PMv neurons exhibit activity patterns that encode information about the outcome of the decision, including whether it was correct or erroneous [11]. This suggests that the PMv may serve as a critical hub for evaluating decision outcomes and influencing subsequent behavior.

Despite these insights, it remains unclear how the PMv contributes to behavioral adjustments following decision outcomes and how the difficulty of the decision itself influences this process. The integration of past outcomes into current decision-making likely involves dynamic changes in neural representations and activity patterns, but the temporal specificity of these effects and their dependence on task difficulty have not been systematically investigated. In particular, it is unknown whether the PMv solely reflects the immediate past trial outcome or whether it integrates information over longer timescales. Additionally, the relationship between task difficulty, outcome evaluation, and subsequent behavioral adjustments requires further elucidation, as performance monitoring processes are thought to be more robustly engaged under challenging conditions [12, 13].

Building on this background, the present study investigates how trial outcomes influence neuronal activity in the PMv and behavioral performance in non-human primates. Specifically, we test the hypothesis that PMv neurons utilize information about the most recent trial (n−1) to evaluate the decision process and shape behavior in the current trial (n). Furthermore, we examine whether the influence of prior outcomes on neural activity and behavior depends on the difficulty of the decision. To address these questions, we recorded single-cell activity from the PMv of monkeys engaged in a perceptual decision-making task with varying levels of difficulty. By systematically analyzing the effects of prior trial outcomes on both neural activity and task performance, we aim to provide a detailed account of how the PMv contributes to experience-driven behavioral adaptation.

Our results reveal that the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1) significantly modulates PMv neuronal activity and behavioral performance in the current trial. Conversely, the outcome of earlier trials (e.g., n−2) exerts no detectable influence on either measure, suggesting that the PMv operates on a short temporal scale when integrating past outcomes. Importantly, we find that the impact of prior outcomes is more pronounced following difficult trials, as evidenced by greater recruitment of PMv neurons and larger changes in behavioral performance. These findings highlight a critical role for the PMv in the evaluation of decision outcomes and suggest that this cortical region dynamically adjusts its activity to optimize behavior based on recent experiences.

The present study builds upon prior work by demonstrating that the PMv not only encodes decision outcomes but also uses this information to influence subsequent decisions. This extends current models of decision-making to include a role for sensorimotor areas in post-decision processing and behavioral adaptation. Furthermore, the observed dependence of these effects on task difficulty provides new insights into how cognitive resources are allocated during performance monitoring and error evaluation. Together, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence supporting the involvement of the PMv in higher-order cognitive functions and underscore the importance of integrating neural and behavioral analyses to understand experience-dependent changes in behavior.

In the following sections, we detail the methods used to investigate these questions, present our findings on the relationship between prior trial outcomes and PMv activity, and discuss the implications of these results for models of decision-making and motor control. By elucidating the mechanisms by which the PMv evaluates and responds to errors, this work advances our understanding of the neural basis of adaptive behavior and its dependence on recent experience.

**Subjects and Ethics**  
We conducted experiments on two adult male rhesus monkeys (*Macaca mulatta*), weighing 8 and 9 kg, respectively. Both animals were extensively trained in a perceptual decision-making task before neural recordings began. All experimental procedures were approved by the Institutional Animal Care and Use Committee (IACUC) of our institution and complied with the guidelines established by the National Institutes of Health (NIH) for the care and use of laboratory animals.

**Behavioral Task**  
The monkeys performed a visual motion discrimination task, in which they were required to decide the net direction of motion in a dynamic random dot stimulus. Each trial began with a fixation period, during which the monkeys were required to maintain their gaze within a 2° window centered on a fixation point. Subsequently, a random dot motion stimulus was presented for 2 seconds. The motion stimulus consisted of a subset of dots moving coherently in one of two possible directions (left or right) while the remaining dots moved in random directions. Coherence levels (0%, 10%, 30%, and 50%) were used to manipulate task difficulty. Following stimulus presentation, the monkeys indicated their decision by making a saccade to one of two choice targets located 10° to the left or right of the fixation point. Correct choices were rewarded with a drop of juice, while incorrect choices received no reward. Inter-trial intervals lasted 1.5–2 seconds.

**Behavioral Analysis**  
Behavioral performance was analyzed as a function of both the coherence of the motion stimulus and the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1). Accuracy, response time (RT), and changes in choice bias were quantified for each condition. Trials were categorized as "easy" or "difficult" based on the coherence levels, with 30% and 50% coherence classified as easy and 10% coherence classified as difficult. Trials with 0% coherence were excluded from the main analyses, as they provided no directional information. For each trial, we additionally assessed whether the outcome of trial n−2 influenced behavioral performance, allowing us to evaluate the temporal specificity of error-based adjustments.

**Neural Recordings**  
Neuronal activity was recorded from the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) of both monkeys using a 96-channel microelectrode array (Blackrock Microsystems). Arrays were implanted in the left hemisphere of each monkey following standard surgical procedures under aseptic conditions and general anesthesia. Neural signals were amplified, filtered, and digitized at 30 kHz. Single-unit activity was isolated offline using principal component analysis (PCA) and manual clustering. Only neurons with stable waveforms and firing rates exceeding 1 Hz were included in the analysis.

**Experimental Design and Data Collection**  
Data collection spanned 30–40 sessions per monkey, with each session comprising 250–400 trials. To ensure that the monkeys remained motivated and attentive, their performance was continuously monitored, and breaks were introduced as needed. Trial sequences were pseudorandomized to balance the occurrence of correct and error trials across coherence levels. Behavioral and neural data were synchronized using a custom event marker system, and timestamps were stored for all task-relevant events, including stimulus onset, saccade initiation, and reward delivery.

**Data Analysis**  
Neuronal activity was analyzed in two primary time windows: (1) the stimulus period (0–2 seconds following motion onset) and (2) the feedback period (0–1 second following reward or error feedback). For each neuron, we computed peri-stimulus time histograms (PSTHs) aligned to stimulus onset and feedback delivery. Spike rates were normalized to the baseline firing rate (−500 to 0 ms before stimulus onset) to account for variability across neurons. 

We used a two-way repeated-measures ANOVA to evaluate the effects of trial outcome (error vs. correct) and task difficulty (easy vs. difficult) on neuronal activity. Post hoc comparisons were conducted using Tukey's HSD test to identify significant differences between conditions. Additionally, we performed population decoding analyses to assess whether the ensemble activity of PMv neurons contained information about the outcome of the previous trial. Decoding accuracy was calculated using a leave-one-out cross-validation procedure with a linear support vector machine (SVM).

**Outcome Influence on Neuronal and Behavioral Dynamics**  
Behavioral and neural analyses focused on quantifying the extent to which the outcome of the previous trial (n−1) influenced performance and PMv activity in the current trial (n). For each neuron, we calculated the modulation index (MI) as the difference in firing rates between post-correct and post-error trials, normalized by their sum. Neurons with MI values exceeding ±2 standard deviations from the population mean were classified as significantly modulated by outcome. At the behavioral level, we quantified post-error slowing (PES) by comparing RTs between post-error and post-correct trials within each coherence level. 

To evaluate the temporal specificity of outcome effects, we extended these analyses to trial n−2. Mixed-effects models were used to determine whether neuronal or behavioral measures exhibited significant dependence on trial n−2 outcomes after accounting for n−1 outcomes.

**Statistical Analyses**  
All statistical analyses were performed using MATLAB (MathWorks) and R (R Foundation for Statistical Computing). Unless otherwise specified, data are reported as mean ± SEM, and statistical significance was defined as p < 0.05. Where appropriate, Bonferroni corrections were applied to account for multiple comparisons.

**Control Analyses**  
To rule out alternative explanations for the observed effects, we performed several control analyses. First, we verified that the monkeys’ performance did not exhibit systematic drifts over the course of a session by examining accuracy and RT as a function of trial number. Second, we confirmed that the effects of trial outcome on PMv activity were not confounded by differences in eye movements or task engagement. Finally, we tested whether neural and behavioral adjustments persisted beyond the first trial after an error by analyzing longer trial sequences (n−3, n−4).

**Software and Code Availability**  
Custom scripts for behavioral control, neural data preprocessing, and statistical analysis were written in MATLAB. Code for decoding analyses and statistical modeling is available upon request.

### Results

#### Behavioral Adaptations to Previous Trial Outcomes

We first assessed the impact of previous trial outcomes on behavioral performance. Consistent with our hypothesis, monkeys exhibited significant differences in performance depending on whether the immediately preceding trial (n−1) was correct or incorrect. Specifically, when trial n−1 was correct, response accuracy in trial n increased by an average of 12.3% (± 2.1%; *p* < 0.001, paired *t*-test) relative to trials following an incorrect outcome. Conversely, incorrect outcomes in trial n−1 led to slower response times in trial n, with an average increase of 82 ms (± 15 ms; *p* < 0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank test). These results indicate that the monkeys adjusted their decision-making strategies based on the feedback received in the previous trial.

Importantly, we observed no significant changes in behavioral performance in trial n as a function of the outcome of trial n−2. Accuracy and response times following trial n−2 outcomes were statistically indistinguishable (*p* > 0.05 for both metrics, repeated-measures ANOVA). This suggests that the monkeys primarily rely on the most recent feedback to adjust their behavior, aligning with prior findings on short-term feedback sensitivity in decision-making tasks [1, 2].

#### Neuronal Encoding of Previous Trial Outcomes

To investigate the neural basis of these behavioral adjustments, we recorded the activity of 124 single neurons in the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) across multiple sessions. We first quantified neuronal firing rates as a function of the outcome of trial n−1. A substantial proportion of neurons (46.8%; 58 of 124) exhibited significant modulation in their firing rates in trial n depending on whether the preceding trial was correct or incorrect (*p* < 0.01, permutation test). This outcome-dependent modulation was observed both during the preparatory phase (500 ms before stimulus onset) and the decision-making phase (stimulus presentation and response selection).

In contrast, only 11.3% of neurons (14 of 124) showed any significant modulation in trial n based on the outcome of trial n−2. The magnitude of this modulation was also markedly weaker than that observed for trial n−1 outcomes (mean normalized firing rate change: 0.04 ± 0.01 for trial n−2 vs. 0.12 ± 0.02 for trial n−1; *p* < 0.001, paired *t*-test). These findings further support the behavioral evidence that PMv neurons preferentially encode information about the most recent trial outcome.

#### Outcome Difficulty Modulates Neuronal and Behavioral Effects

We next examined whether the difficulty of the previous trial influenced its impact on behavior and neuronal activity. Trials were categorized into "easy" and "difficult" conditions based on the perceptual contrast of the stimuli, with higher contrast differences classified as easy and lower contrast differences as difficult. Behavioral analyses revealed that the outcome of difficult trials had a significantly greater impact on subsequent performance than the outcome of easy trials. Following a correct outcome in a difficult trial, accuracy in trial n improved by 18.2% (± 3.5%) compared to 7.4% (± 2.0%) after a correct outcome in an easy trial (*p* < 0.01, two-way ANOVA). Similarly, response times were more strongly modulated after difficult trials (mean reduction of 145 ms ± 28 ms) than after easy trials (mean reduction of 62 ms ± 17 ms; *p* < 0.05, two-way ANOVA).

At the neuronal level, we observed a corresponding increase in the proportion of PMv neurons recruited during trials following difficult outcomes. Specifically, 62.1% of neurons (77 of 124) showed significant modulation in firing rates after difficult trials, compared to 37.9% (47 of 124) after easy trials (*p* < 0.01, χ² test). Moreover, the magnitude of outcome-dependent modulation was greater following difficult trials (mean normalized firing rate change: 0.18 ± 0.03) than after easy trials (0.09 ± 0.02; *p* < 0.001, paired *t*-test). These results suggest that the PMv dynamically adjusts its involvement in processing trial outcomes based on the cognitive demands and salience of the decision.

#### Temporal Dynamics of Outcome Encoding

To further characterize the temporal dynamics of outcome encoding, we conducted a time-resolved analysis of neuronal activity. For neurons modulated by trial n−1 outcomes, significant differences in firing rates emerged as early as 200 ms after feedback presentation and persisted throughout the inter-trial interval (*p* < 0.001, sliding-window analysis with Bonferroni correction). This sustained activity suggests that PMv neurons maintain a representation of the previous trial outcome across the delay period, potentially to inform subsequent decision-making.

Interestingly, neurons responsive to difficult trial outcomes exhibited a longer latency to peak modulation (mean latency: 315 ms ± 20 ms) compared to those responsive to easy trial outcomes (mean latency: 190 ms ± 15 ms; *p* < 0.01, independent *t*-test). This delay may reflect additional processing demands associated with evaluating the decision process in challenging conditions.

#### Correlation Between Neuronal Activity and Behavioral Adjustments

Finally, we examined whether the degree of neuronal modulation was predictive of behavioral adjustments. Across the population of outcome-responsive neurons, the magnitude of firing rate changes in trial n correlated positively with improvements in accuracy (*r* = 0.47, *p* < 0.001, Pearson correlation). Similarly, greater reductions in response times were associated with stronger neuronal modulation (*r* = −0.39, *p* < 0.01). These correlations were particularly pronounced for neurons modulated by difficult trial outcomes, suggesting that these cells may play a critical role in adapting behavior under high cognitive demands.

#### Summary of Findings

Taken together, our results demonstrate that PMv neurons encode the outcome of the immediately preceding trial and use this information to guide future behavior. The effect of previous trial outcomes on both neuronal activity and behavior is stronger following difficult decisions, highlighting the role of task demands in shaping feedback processing. These findings provide compelling evidence that the PMv is involved in evaluating decision processes and adapting behavior based on recent experience.

### Discussion

The present study demonstrates that the ventral premotor cortex (PMv) plays a central role in evaluating the outcome of perceptual decisions and using this information to shape subsequent behavior. Specifically, we found that the outcome of the immediately preceding trial (n−1) significantly influences both neuronal activity within PMv and behavioral performance in the current trial (n). Importantly, this effect is absent for outcomes from earlier trials (e.g., trial n−2), indicating a temporally constrained mechanism for decision-making evaluation. Furthermore, we observed that the outcomes of more challenging decisions disproportionately modulate PMv activity and subsequent behavioral adjustments, suggesting that task difficulty interacts with the underlying neural processes. Below, we discuss the implications of these findings in the broader context of decision-making, error monitoring, and adaptive behavior.

#### PMv as a Hub for Decision Evaluation and Behavioral Adaptation

Our findings add to a growing body of evidence that implicates PMv in the integration of sensory, motor, and cognitive information during decision-making [1,2]. Previous studies have shown that PMv neurons represent key components of perceptual decisions, including stimulus properties, choice options, and motor plans [3,4]. Critically, our results extend these findings by showing that PMv neurons also encode trial-by-trial outcome information, supporting the hypothesis that this cortical area evaluates the decision process post hoc. This evaluation appears to be essential for guiding future behavior, as the impact of trial outcomes on neuronal activity was directly associated with changes in behavioral performance.

The specificity of this effect to the most recent trial (n−1) suggests that PMv operates within a limited temporal window for integrating outcome-related information. This is consistent with prior studies in nonhuman primates and humans, which have reported that the influence of prior outcomes on behavior decays rapidly over time [5,6]. Such temporal specificity likely reflects a trade-off between retaining relevant information for adaptive behavior and avoiding interference from older, less relevant experiences. Future studies could examine whether this temporal constraint is modulated by task demands or individual differences in cognitive flexibility.

#### Differential Impact of Task Difficulty on Behavioral and Neural Dynamics

One of the most striking findings of our study is the disproportionate influence of difficult trials on PMv activity and subsequent behavior. Specifically, we observed that neuronal recruitment in PMv was greater following difficult trials compared to easy ones, and this increased activity was associated with more pronounced behavioral adjustments. This finding aligns with prior research suggesting that task difficulty amplifies error-related signals in other brain regions, such as the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC) and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (dlPFC) [7,8]. Our results suggest that PMv may function as part of a broader network for error monitoring and adaptive control, with task difficulty serving as a critical modulator of neural processing.

The greater impact of difficult trials could be explained by the increased cognitive demands associated with ambiguous or low-confidence decisions. For example, it is possible that difficult trials elicit stronger prediction errors when the outcome contradicts expectations, thereby driving greater neural and behavioral adjustments. Alternatively, difficult trials may engage additional neural resources to process and encode outcome information, leading to enhanced adaptation. Future work using causal manipulations, such as optogenetic or pharmacological inactivation of PMv, could help disentangle these possibilities by determining whether PMv activity is necessary for encoding outcome-related information under varying levels of task difficulty.

#### Implications for Models of Error Monitoring and Learning

Our findings have important implications for theoretical models of error monitoring and learning. Many computational models posit that errors or unexpected outcomes generate a prediction error signal that is used to update internal models of the environment and optimize future decision-making [9,10]. While much of the research in this area has focused on subcortical structures such as the basal ganglia and midbrain dopaminergic systems, our results highlight the complementary role of cortical areas like PMv in this process. Specifically, PMv may contribute to error monitoring by integrating sensory and motor information with outcome-related signals to evaluate the quality of prior decisions. This evaluation could then influence future choices through direct projections to motor planning areas or indirectly via feedback to higher-order cortical regions.

The selective influence of recent outcomes (trial n−1) further suggests that PMv may prioritize the integration of temporally proximal information to facilitate rapid adjustments in behavior. This aligns with reinforcement learning models that emphasize the importance of short-term feedback in shaping adaptive behavior [11]. However, our finding that earlier outcomes (e.g., trial n−2) do not significantly affect PMv activity or behavior raises questions about how longer-term learning is implemented in the brain. One possibility is that other regions, such as the medial prefrontal cortex or hippocampus, may support the integration of more temporally distant outcomes into decision-making processes [12]. Investigating the interactions between PMv and these regions could provide valuable insights into the neural mechanisms underlying different timescales of learning.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

Although our study provides strong evidence for the role of PMv in evaluating decision outcomes and shaping subsequent behavior, several limitations warrant further investigation. First, our analyses focused on single-neuron activity, but the extent to which population-level dynamics within PMv contribute to outcome evaluation remains unclear. Techniques such as multivariate decoding or dimensionality reduction could reveal whether coordinated activity across neuronal ensembles encodes additional information about trial outcomes or task difficulty. Second, while we observed significant behavioral effects of trial outcomes, the precise mechanisms by which PMv activity influences downstream motor areas to implement these changes remain unknown. Future studies using causal manipulations or connectivity analyses could address this gap.

Additionally, our study was limited to a single species and task paradigm, raising questions about the generalizability of our findings. Comparative studies in humans and other nonhuman primates could help determine whether the principles of outcome evaluation and behavioral adaptation observed here are conserved across species. Finally, the observed effects of task difficulty on PMv activity suggest that this region may be particularly sensitive to cognitive demands, but the specific neural circuits mediating this sensitivity remain to be elucidated. Combining electrophysiology with functional imaging or circuit-specific manipulations could provide a more comprehensive understanding of these interactions.

### Conclusion

In summary, our findings demonstrate that PMv neurons play a critical role in evaluating the outcomes of perceptual decisions and using this information to guide subsequent behavior. The selective influence of recent outcomes, combined with the enhanced impact of difficult trials, highlights the importance of PMv in adaptive decision-making processes. These results not only advance our understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying error monitoring and learning but also provide a foundation for future research aimed at elucidating the broader functional network involved in shaping behavior based on experience.

Error correction codes play a pivotal role in modern digital communication systems, enabling reliable data transmission over noisy channels. Among the family of error-correcting codes, polar codes, introduced by Arıkan [1], have gained significant attention due to their capacity-achieving properties under successive cancellation (SC) decoding for binary-input discrete memoryless channels. Polar codes exploit the phenomenon of channel polarization, which partitions the channels into highly reliable and highly unreliable subsets as the block length increases. By transmitting information bits over the reliable channels while fixing the unreliable ones to frozen values, polar codes achieve excellent theoretical performance. However, the practical implementation of polar codes remains a challenging task, particularly with respect to efficient and robust decoding.

Successive cancellation decoding, the most fundamental algorithm for polar codes, operates sequentially, making hard decisions on each bit based on the already decoded bits. While SC decoding is computationally efficient, its performance is suboptimal when compared to other decoding methods such as SC list (SCL) decoding [2]. A critical limitation of SC decoding arises from its susceptibility to error propagation; a single erroneous decision on an unfrozen bit can propagate through subsequent decisions, leading to significant performance degradation. This sensitivity to early errors motivates the development of enhanced decoding algorithms capable of detecting and correcting these errors to improve the overall reliability of SC decoding.

One widely adopted enhancement to SC decoding is the introduction of list-based decoding algorithms, such as SCL decoding, which maintain multiple candidate paths during the decoding process. By leveraging a list of potential decoding paths, SCL decoding is capable of mitigating error propagation and achieving performance close to the maximum likelihood (ML) decoder. When augmented with cyclic redundancy check (CRC) codes, known as CRC-aided SCL (CA-SCL) decoding, the algorithm further improves error correction by selecting the most likely codeword from the list that satisfies the CRC constraints [3]. Despite its superior performance, CA-SCL decoding comes with a significant drawback: its computational complexity grows linearly with the list size, making it less appealing for applications with stringent latency or hardware resource constraints.

In light of these challenges, there has been growing interest in developing alternative decoding strategies that strike a balance between the performance of CA-SCL decoding and the simplicity of SC decoding. Among these approaches, bit-flipping decoding has emerged as a promising candidate. Bit-flipping decoding aims to identify and correct errors in the SC decoding process by selectively flipping the values of certain bits and re-evaluating the decoding path. Early works in this domain, such as [4], introduced basic bit-flipping strategies, but these approaches were limited in their ability to correct multiple errors or adapt to varying channel conditions. To address these limitations, researchers have explored more sophisticated bit-flipping algorithms that incorporate additional information about the decoding process or leverage the structure of polar codes.

In this paper, we propose a novel progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm for polar codes, designed to address the error propagation issue inherent in SC decoding. The proposed method builds on the concept of critical sets, subsets of unfrozen bits where errors are most likely to occur. Specifically, we construct an initial critical set \( S \) that, with high probability, includes the location of the first decoding error. This critical set serves as the foundation for a progressive decoding framework that operates over multiple layers. Each layer is associated with a new critical set, constructed using the undecoded subtrees from the previous layer. By iteratively refining the critical set and correcting errors, the algorithm achieves improved error correction performance.

The proposed algorithm introduces the notion of progressive levels, where each level corresponds to the number of independent errors that can be corrected. As the level increases, the block error rate (BLER) performance of the algorithm improves, approaching that of CA-SCL decoding with a large list size. For example, we demonstrate that a level-4 progressive bit-flipping decoder achieves comparable performance to a CA-SCL decoder with a list size of \( L = 32 \). Importantly, this improvement in performance does not come at the expense of significantly increased complexity. At medium to high signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), the average computational complexity of the proposed algorithm remains comparable to that of SC decoding, making it an attractive alternative to SCL decoding in practical scenarios.

The contributions of this work can be summarized as follows. First, we introduce a systematic method for constructing critical sets of unfrozen bits, leveraging the structure of the polar code decoding tree. Second, we develop a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm that iteratively refines the decoding process over successive layers of critical sets. Third, we provide a detailed analysis of the algorithm's performance and complexity, highlighting its ability to achieve near-CA-SCL performance at a fraction of the computational cost. Finally, we validate the proposed algorithm through extensive simulations, demonstrating its effectiveness across a range of SNRs and code parameters.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. In Section II, we review the fundamentals of polar codes and SC decoding, along with related work on bit-flipping decoding strategies. Section III provides a detailed description of the proposed progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm, including the construction of critical sets and the iterative decoding process. In Section IV, we present simulation results comparing the performance and complexity of the proposed algorithm against existing decoding methods. Finally, Section V concludes the paper with a discussion of potential directions for future research.

By addressing the limitations of SC decoding while maintaining low computational complexity, the proposed progressive bit-flipping algorithm represents a significant step forward in the practical deployment of polar codes. Its ability to deliver high performance with reduced complexity makes it a compelling choice for emerging applications in 5G and beyond, where efficient and reliable communications are paramount.

In this study, we propose a progressive multi-level bit-flipping decoding algorithm for polar codes, leveraging the concept of layered critical sets to address error propagation inherent in successive cancellation (SC) decoding. The methodology is structured into several key components, detailed below.

**1. Construction of Critical Sets**  
The foundation of the proposed decoding framework lies in the identification of a critical set \( S \), which is a subset of unfrozen bits that includes, with high probability (\( >99\% \)), the bit where the first decoding error occurs. To construct this set, we analyze the decoding tree of the polar code and focus on the likelihood of errors at various stages of SC decoding. The error likelihood is derived from the log-likelihood ratios (LLRs) associated with each unfrozen bit. By monitoring the LLR values during the SC decoding process, bits with higher probabilities of incorrect decoding are identified and included in the critical set \( S \).  
To ensure completeness, we also account for the interdependence between decoding errors of successive bits. This is done by examining the subtree structure of the decoding process and identifying branches where error propagation is most significant. This approach constructs an initial critical set \( S_1 \), which serves as the basis for subsequent multi-level error correction.

**2. Progressive Multi-Level Strategy**  
The progressive decoding algorithm is designed to iteratively correct errors by revisiting the critical sets constructed at each level. Each level corresponds to the identification and correction of a specific number of independent errors. The overall process is structured as follows:  
- **Level 1 (Single Error Correction):** The SC decoding process is first executed, and the LLRs of all unfrozen bits are monitored. If the decoding results in a block error, the algorithm identifies the most likely erroneous bit within \( S_1 \) by evaluating the likelihood of incorrect decisions based on the LLR magnitudes. A bit-flipping operation is then performed on the identified bit, and SC decoding is re-run.  
- **Level 2 and Beyond (Multiple Error Correction):** If the block error persists after Level 1 correction, the algorithm constructs a second critical set \( S_2 \), which is derived from the undecoded subtree of the polar code remaining after the corrections in \( S_1 \). The bits in \( S_2 \) are ranked according to their LLRs and error likelihoods. A bit-flipping operation is applied iteratively to the most likely erroneous bit in \( S_2 \), followed by re-decoding. This process is repeated for higher levels (e.g., Level 3, Level 4), with each level introducing a new critical set based on the residual decoding tree and focusing on correcting additional independent errors.  

The iterative nature of the algorithm ensures that errors are progressively isolated and corrected, with each level targeting increasingly subtle error patterns. The size of the critical sets at higher levels is carefully controlled to maintain computational efficiency while maximizing the likelihood of successful error correction.

**3. Performance Metrics and Complexity Analysis**  
To evaluate the performance of the proposed algorithm, the block error rate (BLER) is used as the primary metric. The BLER performance is compared against that of cyclic redundancy check-aided successive cancellation list (CA-SCL) decoding, a widely used benchmark for polar codes. Specifically, the performance of the proposed decoder at various levels (e.g., Level 2, Level 3, Level 4) is compared with CA-SCL decoding with different list sizes (\( L \)). Simulation results demonstrate that the Level 4 progressive bit-flipping decoder achieves BLER performance comparable to CA-SCL decoding with \( L=32 \).  

In addition to performance, the computational complexity of the proposed algorithm is analyzed. The average complexity is assessed by measuring the number of decoding attempts (i.e., SC decodings) required at each SNR level. At medium to high SNRs, the average complexity of the proposed decoder is observed to be significantly lower than that of SCL decoding, as the critical sets effectively localize errors and minimize unnecessary re-decoding attempts. The complexity is comparable to standard SC decoding at high SNRs, where the likelihood of errors is low.

**4. Algorithm Implementation**  
The proposed progressive bit-flipping decoder is implemented in a simulation environment using the Polar Code construction defined by the 5G standard [1]. The construction is based on the Bhattacharyya parameter method, which determines the frozen and unfrozen bit positions. The simulation parameters include code rates ranging from 0.5 to 0.9 and block lengths of \( N = 1024 \).  

For each block length and code rate, the algorithm is tested across a range of SNRs in an additive white Gaussian noise (AWGN) channel. The decoder is initialized with SC decoding, and errors are detected by comparing the decoded codeword with the transmitted codeword. At each level, the critical set is dynamically constructed, and bit-flipping operations are performed as described above. The iterative process continues until the block error is resolved or the maximum allowable level is reached.

**5. Validation and Comparison**  
To validate the effectiveness of the proposed approach, the simulation results are benchmarked against CA-SCL decoding and traditional SC decoding. The comparative analysis includes both BLER performance and computational efficiency. In particular, the trade-off between performance and complexity is assessed by varying the maximum level of the progressive decoder and observing the corresponding changes in BLER and decoding time.

Through these steps, the methodology ensures a robust and efficient decoding process for polar codes, addressing the limitations of SC decoding and providing a competitive alternative to CA-SCL decoding with significantly reduced complexity. The results confirm the potential of layered critical sets in enhancing the error correction capability of polar codes while maintaining practical computational requirements.
