The results of this study aim to provide a comprehensive analysis of clinical outcomes, histopathologic findings, and molecular markers associated with central neurocytoma (CN). Clinical data from a cohort of 67 patients diagnosed with CN were retrospectively reviewed, encompassing demographic characteristics, radiological findings, surgical outcomes, and adjuvant treatment efficacy. Histopathologic and molecular analyses were performed on available tumor samples to evaluate key diagnostic markers and their correlation with clinical outcomes.

The cohort consisted of 38 male and 29 female patients, with a mean age at diagnosis of 29.4 years (range: 18–47 years). The most common presenting symptoms were headaches (82%), nausea and vomiting (54%), and visual disturbances (22%), all consistent with signs of increased intracranial pressure due to obstructive hydrocephalus. Preoperative magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) revealed isodense to hyperdense intraventricular masses, with 92% of tumors located within the lateral ventricles and 8% involving the third ventricle. All tumors exhibited heterogeneous enhancement following contrast administration, but the radiological appearance was not pathognomonic, necessitating histopathological confirmation.

Gross total resection (GTR) was achieved in 53 patients (79%), while subtotal resection (STR) was performed in the remaining 14 patients (21%) due to tumor location and proximity to critical neurovascular structures. Among patients who underwent GTR, the 5-year progression-free survival (PFS) rate was 96%, compared to 71% in the STR group (p < 0.01). The overall survival (OS) at 5 years was 100% for the GTR group and 92% for the STR group, highlighting the importance of achieving maximal safe resection for favorable outcomes.

Adjuvant therapies were utilized in 16 patients (24%), all of whom underwent STR. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) was administered in 10 cases, while fractionated radiotherapy (RT) was used in 6 cases. Among these patients, the addition of adjuvant therapy improved the 5-year PFS to 87% compared to 52% in STR patients who did not receive adjuvant treatment (p < 0.05). No significant difference in OS was observed between STR patients who received adjuvant therapy and those who did not, suggesting that adjuvant modalities may primarily serve to delay progression rather than definitively improve survival. Chemotherapy was administered as a salvage therapy in 3 patients with recurrent disease, with mixed responses observed; one patient achieved partial radiological response, while two demonstrated stable disease for a median duration of 8 months.

Histopathological analysis confirmed the diagnosis of CN in all cases, with tumors demonstrating uniform round cells arranged in sheets and perivascular pseudorosettes. Immunohistochemical staining revealed strong positivity for synaptophysin in all samples, consistent with the neuronal differentiation characteristic of CN. Additionally, chromogranin A and neuron-specific enolase (NSE) were positive in 84% and 76% of cases, respectively, while glial fibrillary acidic protein (GFAP) expression was detected in 18% of tumors, indicating occasional glial differentiation. The Ki-67 (MIB-1) labeling index ranged from 1.2% to 12.4%, with a mean value of 3.6%. Patients with MIB-1 indices ≤2% demonstrated significantly better 5-year PFS (98%) compared to those with indices >2% (72%, p < 0.01). Similarly, OS was inversely correlated with MIB-1 index, further underscoring its prognostic utility.

Molecular analysis revealed upregulation of several oncogenes, including MYCN and TP53, in 15% and 11% of cases, respectively. While MYCN amplification was associated with higher MIB-1 indices and increased risk of recurrence, TP53 mutations did not correlate significantly with clinical outcomes. No significant alterations were detected in IDH1, IDH2, or 1p/19q co-deletions, suggesting that these molecular features, common in other central nervous system tumors, are not characteristic of CN. Notably, whole-genome sequencing identified recurrent mutations in the FGFR1 gene in 9% of cases, though the clinical implications of these findings remain to be fully elucidated.

Postoperative complications occurred in 12 patients (18%), including transient neurological deficits in 6 cases (9%), cerebrospinal fluid (CSF) leaks in 3 cases (4.5%), and wound infections in 3 cases (4.5%). All complications were successfully managed with conservative or surgical interventions, and no permanent deficits were observed. No treatment-related mortality occurred during the study period.

In summary, the results of this study underscore the critical role of GTR in achieving optimal outcomes for patients with CN, while highlighting the potential utility of adjuvant SRS or RT in cases where GTR is not feasible. The MIB-1 labeling index emerged as a robust prognostic marker for recurrence and survival, and synaptophysin remains a highly reliable diagnostic marker for CN. Molecular findings, including MYCN amplification and FGFR1 mutations, provide insight into the pathogenesis of CN and may serve as potential therapeutic targets in future studies. Further research is warranted to validate these findings in larger cohorts and to explore the role of novel molecular and immunotherapeutic approaches in the management of CN.

Central neurocytoma (CN) represents a unique clinical and pathological challenge due to its rarity and overlapping radiological features with other intracranial neoplasms. As an intraventricular tumor with benign behavior in most cases, CNs are primarily seen in young adults and frequently arise in the lateral ventricles near the foramen of Monro, making them a potential cause of obstructive hydrocephalus and symptoms of increased intracranial pressure. The management of CNs requires a multidisciplinary approach, balancing surgical intervention with adjuvant therapies in cases of subtotal resection or recurrence.

The cornerstone of CN treatment remains gross total resection (GTR), which is associated with favorable outcomes and long-term tumor control. Several studies have demonstrated that patients who undergo GTR experience excellent progression-free survival and overall survival rates, often exceeding 90% at 5 years [1,2]. However, achieving GTR can be challenging due to the tumor’s proximity to critical neurovascular structures within the ventricular system. When GTR is not feasible due to anatomical constraints or potential surgical morbidity, subtotal resection (STR) may be performed. In such cases, adjuvant therapies, particularly radiotherapy, play a critical role in tumor control.

The use of adjuvant radiotherapy following STR has been extensively studied, with most evidence supporting its efficacy in reducing the risk of recurrence and progression. Stereotactic radiosurgery (SRS) and conventional fractionated radiotherapy have both been employed, demonstrating significant benefits in terms of local tumor control [3]. While radiotherapy is generally well-tolerated, concerns regarding potential long-term neurocognitive effects, particularly in younger patients, necessitate careful patient selection. Emerging evidence suggests that advanced radiotherapy techniques, such as proton beam therapy, may offer precise tumor targeting while minimizing radiation exposure to surrounding brain tissue, thereby reducing treatment-related toxicity [4].

Chemotherapy, although not a primary treatment modality, has been explored as a salvage therapy in cases of recurrent or progressive CN, particularly when surgical and radiotherapeutic options are exhausted. The role of chemotherapy remains limited, with variable responses reported in the literature. Agents such as temozolomide and platinum-based regimens have been used in small case series, but their efficacy and safety profiles require further investigation in larger, prospective studies [5]. The development of targeted therapies based on molecular profiling of CNs holds promise for improving outcomes in refractory cases.

Histopathological and immunohistochemical analysis is integral to the diagnosis of CN, given its nonspecific radiological appearance. The tumor is characterized by uniform, round-to-oval cells with neuronal differentiation, often confirmed by the expression of synaptophysin, a reliable marker of neuronal lineage [6]. Other markers, such as chromogranin A and NeuN, can further support the diagnosis. Importantly, the Ki-67 proliferation index, measured by the MIB-1 labeling index, has been shown to correlate with tumor behavior and prognosis. A low MIB-1 index (<2%) is typically associated with benign behavior, while higher indices may indicate an increased risk of recurrence or aggressive growth [7]. This underscores the importance of incorporating histopathologic evaluation and biomarker analysis into routine clinical practice to guide treatment decisions and prognostication.

Recent advances in molecular biology have shed light on the genetic and epigenetic alterations associated with CN, although the tumor’s oncogenic pathways remain incompletely understood. Studies have identified alterations in genes such as TP53, IDH1/2, and chromatin remodeling genes, which may play a role in tumorigenesis [8]. Additionally, whole-genome sequencing and transcriptomic analyses have revealed potential therapeutic targets, including pathways involved in cell proliferation and neuronal differentiation. These discoveries offer exciting opportunities for the development of targeted therapies and personalized treatment approaches in the future.

Despite significant progress in the management of CN, several challenges remain. First, the rarity of the tumor limits the availability of large, prospective studies, resulting in a reliance on retrospective series and case reports for clinical decision-making. Collaborative, multicenter research efforts are needed to establish standardized treatment protocols and to evaluate the efficacy of emerging therapies. Second, the role of molecular and genetic profiling in routine clinical practice requires further clarification, as does its integration into prognostic models. Finally, the long-term impact of adjuvant therapies, particularly radiotherapy, on neurocognitive function and quality of life must be systematically studied in order to optimize treatment regimens.

In conclusion, central neurocytoma is a rare, benign tumor that presents unique diagnostic and therapeutic challenges. Gross total resection remains the primary goal of treatment and is associated with excellent outcomes. For patients in whom GTR is not achievable, adjuvant radiotherapy provides an effective means of tumor control, while chemotherapy may serve as a salvage option in select cases. Advances in imaging, histopathological analysis, and molecular profiling have improved diagnostic accuracy and deepened our understanding of CN biology. However, further research is needed to refine treatment strategies, develop targeted therapies, and address the long-term effects of current interventions. Multidisciplinary collaboration and prospective studies will be essential to improving outcomes for patients with this rare and enigmatic tumor.

The integration of brain-computer interfaces (BCIs) with robotic systems has garnered considerable attention in recent years, particularly for its potential to enhance the autonomy and quality of life for individuals with severe motor impairments [1,2]. These brain-controlled robots, which leverage neural signals to execute actions, represent a transformative class of assistive devices. However, optimizing the interaction between humans and robots remains a critical challenge to ensure the effectiveness, safety, and usability of such systems. Specifically, understanding how humans perceive and process robot actions at the neural level is essential for the development of adaptive control algorithms that improve the human-robot interaction (HRI) experience.

One promising avenue for advancing adaptive robotic systems is the use of error-related neural signals, which reflect the human brain's response to observed or executed errors. These signals, often referred to as error-related potentials (ErrPs), have been widely studied within the context of human-human interaction and traditional human-computer interaction [3-5]. ErrPs are typically characterized by distinct event-related potential (ERP) components that are elicited when individuals detect deviations from expected outcomes, whether these deviations occur in their own actions or in the actions of external agents. While previous research has demonstrated the feasibility of decoding ErrPs during human observation of robotic errors [6,7], the robustness and generalizability of these findings in more complex and naturalistic HRI scenarios remain underexplored.

Additionally, the visual and morphological characteristics of robots may modulate the neural processing underlying error observation. Studies in social robotics and psychology suggest that humans perceive humanoid robots differently from non-humanoid robots, with these differences potentially influencing cognitive and affective responses during interaction [8,9]. The uncanny valley hypothesis, for example, posits that humanoid robots that closely resemble humans can evoke discomfort or heightened attention due to their near-human likeness [10]. Conversely, non-humanoid robots may elicit less anthropomorphic attributions, potentially altering the observer's expectations and neural responses to their actions. Despite growing interest in the role of robot morphology in HRI, its impact on brain activity during robot-error observation remains poorly characterized.

The present study addresses these gaps by combining electroencephalographic (EEG) recordings with machine learning techniques to investigate the neural correlates of error observation in HRI. Specifically, we sought to determine whether brain activity during the observation of robot errors could be reliably decoded from single-trial EEG data, thereby providing insights into the neural mechanisms underlying error detection in this context. Furthermore, we examined whether the type of robot—humanoid or non-humanoid—modulates neural responses to errors, as well as whether this information could be decoded from EEG signals.

To achieve these objectives, we designed and implemented two complementary experimental paradigms. In Experiment I, participants observed a robotic arm perform a simple task: pouring liquid into a cup. The robot's performance was manipulated to include both correct actions, in which the liquid was poured successfully, and erroneous actions, in which some liquid was spilled. This task was selected to elicit robust error-related neural responses while minimizing task complexity and cognitive load. In Experiment II, we extended this approach by introducing two distinct robot morphologies—a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robot—and having participants observe these robots perform a ball-grasping task. By using two robot types, we aimed to disentangle the influence of robot morphology on neural responses to error observation.

To analyze the recorded EEG data, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline, a widely used method in BCI research for feature extraction and classification of multivariate neural signals [11,12]. The FBCSP approach enables the identification of discriminative spatial and spectral patterns in EEG data, which can then be used to decode specific cognitive states or processes. In this study, we applied the FBCSP pipeline to decode two key variables: (1) the correctness of the observed robot action (correct vs. erroneous) and (2) the type of robot observed (humanoid vs. non-humanoid). By evaluating decoding performance across individual participants, we aimed to assess the feasibility and reliability of using EEG signals to infer these aspects of HRI.

This work extends prior research on ErrPs and HRI in several important ways. First, while much of the existing literature has focused on error detection in self-controlled or virtual agent scenarios [13,14], our study investigates error observation in the context of physical robot actions. This distinction is crucial, as physical robots introduce unique perceptual and cognitive challenges that may influence error processing. Second, by incorporating robot morphology as a variable of interest, we provide novel insights into how anthropomorphic design features shape neural responses during HRI. Lastly, our use of high-resolution EEG recordings and advanced decoding techniques represents a methodological advancement, enabling more nuanced analyses of neural dynamics during robot-error observation.

The findings of this study have significant implications for the design of brain-controlled robotic systems. If error-related neural responses can be reliably decoded in real time, they could serve as a valuable feedback signal for adaptive robotic control. For instance, integrating decoded ErrPs into robotic learning algorithms could enable robots to autonomously improve their performance by identifying and correcting errors based on the user's implicit neural feedback. Furthermore, understanding how robot morphology influences neural responses could inform the design of more effective and user-friendly robotic systems that align with human cognitive and emotional preferences.

In summary, the present study aims to elucidate the neural mechanisms underlying error observation in HRI and to explore the influence of robot morphology on these processes. By leveraging advanced EEG analysis techniques, we seek to contribute to the development of adaptive and intuitive brain-controlled robotic systems that can better meet the needs of their users. The results of this research not only enhance our understanding of human cognitive responses during HRI but also provide a foundation for future innovations in assistive robotics and neuroadaptive technologies.

**Participants**  
A total of 30 healthy volunteers (15 females; mean age = 25.7 ± 3.2 years) participated in the study. All participants had normal or corrected-to-normal vision and no self-reported history of neurological or psychiatric disorders. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants prior to the experiments, and the study was approved by the appropriate ethics review board in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki.

**Experimental Design**  
Two separate experiments were conducted to investigate differential brain responses to robot actions based on correctness and robot type. Participants completed both experiments in a randomized order, with a short break between experiments.

*Experiment I: Observation of Robot Arm Pouring Actions*  
In the first experiment, participants observed a robotic arm performing a liquid-pouring task. The robot arm was programmed to either execute the task correctly (i.e., pouring liquid into a cup without spillage) or to perform the task erroneously (i.e., spilling liquid outside the cup). Each trial began with a fixation cross displayed for 1,000 ms, followed by a video (4-second duration) of the robotic arm performing the task. After the video, a blank screen appeared for 1,500 ms, during which participants were instructed to remain still and refrain from blinking to minimize artifacts. Trials were pseudo-randomized to ensure an approximately equal number of correct and erroneous actions, and participants were not informed about the sequence of events in advance. A total of 100 trials (50 correct, 50 erroneous) were presented in this experiment.

*Experiment II: Observation of Humanoid vs. Non-Humanoid Robots*  
In the second experiment, participants observed two distinct robot types—a humanoid robot and a non-humanoid robotic arm—performing a ball-grabbing task. Similar to Experiment I, each robot's action was either successful (i.e., the robot successfully grabbed the ball) or unsuccessful (i.e., the robot missed the ball). The trial structure was identical to Experiment I, with a fixation cross (1,000 ms), an action video (4 seconds), and a blank screen (1,500 ms). The two robot types were visually distinct, with the humanoid robot displaying anthropomorphic features (e.g., a head and arms resembling human morphology), while the non-humanoid robot had a purely mechanical appearance. A total of 120 trials were presented in Experiment II, with an equal number of trials for each combination of robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid) and action outcome (successful vs. unsuccessful).

**EEG Recording and Preprocessing**  
EEG signals were recorded using a 64-channel cap (Brain Products GmbH, Germany) with electrodes placed according to the international 10-20 system. The EEG data were sampled at 1,000 Hz and referenced to the Cz electrode during acquisition. Impedances were maintained below 10 kΩ for all electrodes. Vertical and horizontal electrooculogram (EOG) channels were recorded to monitor eye movements and blinks.

Preprocessing was performed using MATLAB (MathWorks, USA) and the EEGLAB toolbox [1]. The continuous EEG data were bandpass-filtered between 1 and 40 Hz using a zero-phase finite impulse response (FIR) filter to remove low-frequency drifts and high-frequency noise. Line noise at 50 Hz was removed using a notch filter. The data were subsequently segmented into epochs from -500 ms to 1,500 ms relative to the onset of the action video, with a 200 ms pre-stimulus baseline. Trials containing artifacts, such as large muscle activity or excessive eye movements, were identified using automated algorithms (threshold set to ±100 μV) and manually reviewed. Artifact-contaminated trials were excluded from further analysis, resulting in an average of 93.2% of trials retained per participant.

**Feature Extraction and Classification**  
To decode brain responses, we employed a Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) approach [2], which is well-suited for multivariate EEG data. First, the preprocessed EEG signals were decomposed into multiple frequency bands (theta: 4–7 Hz, alpha: 8–13 Hz, beta: 14–30 Hz, and low gamma: 31–40 Hz) using bandpass filters. For each frequency band, spatial filters were computed using the common spatial pattern (CSP) algorithm, which maximizes the variance of EEG signals for one class (e.g., correct actions) while minimizing it for the other class (e.g., erroneous actions).

The spatially filtered signals were then log-transformed to obtain features representing the variance of EEG activity for each class. These features were concatenated across frequency bands and used as input to a regularized linear discriminant analysis (rLDA) classifier [3]. Separate classifiers were trained for decoding action correctness (correct vs. erroneous) and robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid), using a 5-fold cross-validation strategy. To ensure balanced training datasets, class labels were stratified during cross-validation.

**Statistical Analysis**  
Classification performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) and classification accuracy. Statistical significance was assessed using a permutation test [4] with 1,000 iterations to compare observed classification performance against chance-level performance (50%). For each participant, the null distribution was generated by shuffling class labels and recomputing classification accuracy. A p-value was obtained by calculating the proportion of permuted accuracies exceeding the observed accuracy.

To investigate potential differences in decoding performance across experimental conditions, a repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was conducted with factors of action correctness (correct vs. erroneous) and robot type (humanoid vs. non-humanoid). Post hoc pairwise comparisons were corrected for multiple comparisons using the Bonferroni method.

### Results

#### Behavioral Observations and Subjective Ratings

During both experiments, participants were fully attentive to the robot action sequences, as confirmed by post-experiment questionnaires and the absence of prolonged eye blinks or movement artifacts in the majority of EEG recordings. Participants reported being able to discern correct from erroneous actions with ease, and several mentioned that the humanoid robot in Experiment II elicited a stronger sense of familiarity compared to the non-humanoid robot. However, subjective ratings of robot anthropomorphism and task difficulty were not quantitatively analyzed, as the focus of the study remained on neurophysiological responses.

#### Experiment I: Decoding the Correctness of Observed Robot Actions

EEG data from Experiment I revealed significant differences between participants' brain responses to correct versus erroneous robot actions. Using the FBCSP pipeline, we trained classifiers for each participant to decode the correctness of the observed actions from single-trial EEG data. Classification accuracy across participants ranged from 54.3% to 76.8%, with a mean accuracy of 62.5% (SD = 6.1%), significantly above the chance level of 50% (t(19) = 8.17, p < 0.001). Individual variations in decoding performance were notable, with participants exhibiting higher accuracies often showing more pronounced event-related potential (ERP) components, particularly over central and parietal electrode sites.

The ERP analysis revealed a prominent error-related negativity (ERN) peaking approximately 250 ms after the onset of the robot’s erroneous action. This component was most pronounced at frontocentral electrodes (Fz, Cz), and its amplitude was significantly larger for erroneous trials compared to correct trials (t(19) = 4.92, p < 0.001). Additionally, a late positive potential (LPP) was observed between 400–600 ms post-onset, particularly over parietal electrodes (Pz, CPz). The LPP amplitude also differed significantly between conditions (t(19) = 3.74, p = 0.002), suggesting heightened attentional engagement during error observation.

Time-frequency analysis revealed increased theta-band (4–8 Hz) power over frontocentral regions during erroneous actions compared to correct actions (t(19) = 5.13, p < 0.001). This modulation was consistent with previously reported neural correlates of error processing in human-agent interactions [1, 2].

#### Experiment II: Decoding Correctness and Robot Type

In Experiment II, we extended our analysis to assess whether brain responses differed not only based on action correctness but also according to the robot's visual appearance (humanoid vs. non-humanoid). Similar to Experiment I, decoding of action correctness from single-trial EEG data was successful for the majority of participants, with classification accuracies ranging from 53.1% to 75.4% (mean = 61.8%, SD = 6.7%, t(19) = 7.64, p < 0.001). Importantly, decoding accuracies for humanoid and non-humanoid robot types were also above chance for most participants, ranging from 51.2% to 70.6% (mean = 58.9%, SD = 5.8%, t(19) = 6.59, p < 0.001).

ERP analyses showed differences in neural responses to humanoid versus non-humanoid robots. While the ERN and LPP components were present in both conditions, the amplitude of the ERN was significantly larger when participants observed the humanoid robot perform erroneous actions compared to the non-humanoid robot (t(19) = 3.84, p = 0.001). In contrast, the LPP amplitude did not differ significantly between humanoid and non-humanoid robot observations (t(19) = 1.54, p = 0.14). These findings suggest that the perceived anthropomorphism of the robot modulated early error-related processing but had less influence on later attentional processes.

Time-frequency analysis further supported these findings. Theta-band power increases during error observation were more pronounced for humanoid robots (t(19) = 4.71, p < 0.001), while beta-band (13–30 Hz) desynchronization, commonly associated with motor and action observation, did not differ significantly between robot types (t(19) = 0.91, p = 0.37).

#### Cross-Experiment Comparisons

To assess whether the observed neural signatures of action correctness were consistent across the two experiments, we conducted a combined analysis of EEG data from Experiment I and Experiment II. Classifiers trained on Experiment I data to decode action correctness generalized moderately well to the Experiment II dataset, achieving a mean cross-experiment accuracy of 58.7% (SD = 5.2%), significantly above chance (t(19) = 6.34, p < 0.001). However, classifiers trained on Experiment II data performed less effectively when applied to Experiment I (mean accuracy = 54.6%, SD = 4.9%, t(19) = 3.92, p = 0.001). This asymmetry likely reflects differences in the visual and motor characteristics of the tasks across experiments.

#### Source-Level Analysis

Source localization of EEG activity using standardized low-resolution electromagnetic tomography (sLORETA) revealed that neural responses to erroneous actions were consistently localized to the medial prefrontal cortex (mPFC) and anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), regions previously implicated in error monitoring [3]. These activations were more pronounced when observing humanoid robots, supporting the hypothesis that anthropomorphic features amplify error-related brain activity.

For correct actions, increased activity was observed in the posterior parietal cortex (PPC) and occipital regions, consistent with visuospatial and attentional processing. No significant differences in source localization were found between humanoid and non-humanoid robots during correct action observation (all p > 0.1).

#### Summary of Decoding Performance

Overall, our results demonstrate that EEG signals elicited during robot action observation contain decodable information about both the correctness of the action and the type of robot performing it. While decoding accuracies were modest, they were consistently above chance, highlighting the potential for brain-computer interface (BCI) systems to leverage these neural signals in adaptive control scenarios. The observed differences in ERPs, time-frequency dynamics, and source-localized activity further suggest that the neural mechanisms underlying error and robot-type processing are distinct yet interrelated.

### Discussion

#### Decodability of Observed Robot Action Correctness

Our study demonstrates that brain activity, as recorded via EEG, contains discernible patterns that encode the perceived correctness of robot actions. Specifically, we found that the Filter Bank Common Spatial Pattern (FBCSP) pipeline was able to decode action correctness at above-chance levels for the majority of participants in both experimental paradigms. This finding aligns with previous research suggesting that error observation elicits distinct neural responses, often referred to as error-related potentials (ErrPs), which have been extensively studied in human-human interaction contexts [1, 2]. Here, we extend this body of knowledge to the domain of human-robot interaction (HRI), showing that similar neural mechanisms may be engaged when observing robotic agents.

The ability to decode perceived correctness from single-trial EEG recordings has significant implications for the development of adaptive control algorithms in brain-controlled robots. Specifically, the integration of ErrP signals into learning algorithms could enable robots to interpret human feedback implicitly, without requiring explicit verbal or physical input. This approach could significantly enhance the usability of brain-controlled assistive devices, particularly for individuals with severe motor impairments who may struggle to provide explicit feedback. However, it is noteworthy that decoding accuracies, while statistically significant, were only modestly above chance for most participants. This suggests that the neural encoding of action correctness during HRI may be relatively subtle, and future work should explore methods to improve decoding performance. Potential strategies include the use of higher-density EEG systems, advanced feature extraction techniques, or multimodal approaches that combine EEG with other physiological signals, such as eye tracking or skin conductance [3, 4].

#### Influence of Robot Morphology on Neural Responses

The second major finding of this study is that neural activity recorded during HRI varies depending on the morphology of the observed robot. Specifically, we observed that brain responses to humanoid robots differed from those elicited by non-humanoid robots, and these differences were decodable using the FBCSP pipeline. This result is consistent with prior research indicating that human-likeness in robots can influence cognitive and neural processing, possibly due to mechanisms related to the uncanny valley hypothesis or anthropomorphism [5, 6]. For example, humanoid robots may elicit stronger activation in brain regions associated with social cognition, such as the mirror neuron system, which is thought to play a role in understanding the actions and intentions of others [7].

Interestingly, the decodability of robot morphology was also modest, suggesting that morphological differences may not strongly modulate neural activity during simple action observation tasks. This finding raises questions about the extent to which robot design choices influence human neural responses and underscores the need for further research in this area. For instance, future studies could investigate whether more complex or socially salient tasks amplify the effects of robot morphology on brain activity. Additionally, it would be valuable to examine how individual differences, such as attitudes toward robots or prior experience with technology, interact with robot morphology to shape neural responses.

#### Implications for Adaptive Human-Robot Interaction Systems

The ability to decode both action correctness and robot morphology from EEG signals has practical implications for the design of adaptive HRI systems. First, our findings suggest that brain signals could serve as a feedback mechanism for improving robot performance in real time. For example, an assistive robot could use ErrP-like signals to identify and correct errors, thereby reducing the cognitive burden on the user. Second, the ability to decode robot morphology implies that HRI systems could potentially adapt their behavior based on the user’s implicit preferences for certain types of robots. For instance, if a user exhibits stronger neural engagement when interacting with humanoid robots, the system could prioritize humanoid designs to enhance the user experience.

However, several challenges must be addressed before these applications can be realized. One major limitation is the relatively low decoding accuracy achieved in our study, which may limit the reliability of EEG-based feedback systems. Additionally, the variability in decoding performance across participants highlights the need for personalized approaches that account for individual differences in neural responses. Finally, it is important to consider the ethical implications of using brain signals for adaptive HRI. For example, systems that adapt based on implicit neural feedback must ensure that users retain control over the interaction and are aware of how their brain signals are being used.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

While our study provides novel insights into the neural correlates of HRI, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, the experimental paradigms employed in this study involved relatively simple tasks (e.g., pouring liquid or grabbing a ball), which may not fully capture the complexity of real-world HRI scenarios. Future research should investigate whether similar neural patterns can be observed during more dynamic and ecologically valid interactions, such as collaborative tasks or social exchanges.

Second, our study focused exclusively on EEG data, which, while non-invasive and temporally precise, has limited spatial resolution. Combining EEG with other neuroimaging modalities, such as functional near-infrared spectroscopy (fNIRS) or magnetoencephalography (MEG), could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the neural mechanisms underlying HRI. Third, the use of a single decoding pipeline (FBCSP) may have constrained the achievable performance. Future studies should explore alternative machine learning approaches, such as deep learning, which may be better suited to capturing complex, non-linear features in EEG data [8].

Finally, our sample size was relatively small, and the generalizability of our findings should be tested in larger and more diverse populations. For example, it would be valuable to investigate how age, cultural background, or neurological conditions influence neural responses during HRI. Additionally, longitudinal studies are needed to examine how neural responses to robots evolve over time and with repeated interactions.

### Conclusion

In conclusion, this study provides evidence that EEG signals contain decodable information about both the correctness of robot actions and the morphology of observed robots during HRI. These findings highlight the potential of EEG-based decoding as a tool for enhancing adaptive control in brain-controlled robots and for understanding the neural mechanisms underlying human-robot interaction. However, the modest decoding accuracies observed in our study underscore the need for further research to optimize signal processing and machine learning techniques, as well as to explore the impact of task complexity, individual differences, and multimodal approaches. By addressing these challenges, future work could pave the way for more intuitive and effective brain-controlled assistive technologies.

The HIV epidemic continues to pose a significant public health challenge globally, with men who have sex with men (MSM) disproportionately affected in many regions. In Thailand, MSM remain one of the most vulnerable populations, with alarmingly high rates of HIV infection. Data collected between 2007 and 2010 revealed that one in three MSM surveyed in Bangkok was HIV positive, and modeling estimates suggest that over half of new HIV infections in Thailand are among MSM. Despite the availability of effective interventions for HIV prevention, testing, and treatment, these tools have not been adequately leveraged to curb the epidemic among this key population. Early HIV testing and counselling (HTC), coupled with prompt linkage to antiretroviral therapy (ART) for those diagnosed with HIV, is critical to achieving viral suppression and reducing onward transmission. Yet, structural barriers, stigma, and discrimination often deter MSM in Thailand from accessing these essential services.

At the same time, Thailand has witnessed a rapid expansion of internet and mobile technology use, especially among MSM. Studies have shown that MSM are among the most active users of digital platforms in the country, utilizing these tools for social networking, health information-seeking, and community engagement. This widespread adoption of digital technology offers a unique and underutilized opportunity to reach and engage MSM in HIV prevention and care. Harnessing the power of online platforms to address the HIV epidemic could provide a scalable and cost-effective solution, particularly in contexts where stigma and discrimination act as significant barriers to accessing traditional healthcare services.

Recognizing this potential, the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre launched Adam’s Love in 2011, an innovative web-based communications strategy specifically designed to engage MSM in Thailand. The programme aimed to leverage digital platforms to promote early HIV testing and facilitate linkage to care and treatment. Adam’s Love employs a comprehensive “online-to-offline” model that integrates a dedicated website, social media platforms, and online message boards to provide accessible, confidential, and user-friendly counselling and referral services. The initiative also incorporates targeted marketing, a club membership programme offering non-monetary incentives, and collaborations with MSM-friendly clinics and private healthcare providers to ensure that services are welcoming and accessible for MSM. This multifaceted approach seeks to address the structural and psychosocial barriers that often hinder MSM from seeking timely HIV testing and care.

The Adam’s Love programme represents a significant departure from traditional outreach and service delivery models, which often rely on in-person interactions and fixed-site clinics. By utilizing digital channels, Adam’s Love meets MSM where they are—online—creating a safe and anonymous space for individuals to access information, seek support, and take the first step toward HIV testing. The programme also facilitates online appointment-making and referrals to ensure that users can seamlessly transition from virtual engagement to in-person services. Importantly, Adam’s Love recognizes the need for a tailored approach that resonates with the target population, employing culturally sensitive and affirming messaging to build trust and encourage uptake.

Since its launch, Adam’s Love has demonstrated impressive reach and impact. Between September 2011 and January 2015, the programme engaged 1.69 million viewers and generated over 8 million page views. During this period, an estimated 11,120 MSM received online counselling through the platform, and 8,288 MSM were referred to HTC services. Additionally, the programme facilitated referrals to STI testing services and provided treatment counselling for over 1,100 MSM living with HIV. Notably, the club membership programme, which incentivizes HIV testing participation, enrolled 1,181 MSM, 15.5% of whom were diagnosed with HIV. These findings underscore the programme’s potential to serve as an effective model for engaging MSM in HIV prevention and care using digital technology.

The success of Adam’s Love has broader implications for public health strategies aimed at addressing the HIV epidemic among MSM in Thailand and beyond. As the HIV epidemic continues to evolve, innovative approaches that leverage technology and address the unique needs of key populations are essential. The “online-to-offline” recruitment model pioneered by Adam’s Love offers a scalable and replicable framework that can be adapted to other settings, particularly in regions where MSM experience stigma and discrimination or have limited access to healthcare services.

This paper explores the implementation and outcomes of the Adam’s Love programme, highlighting its role in promoting early HIV testing and linkage to care among MSM in Thailand. By examining the strategies employed and the lessons learned, this study aims to provide valuable insights for public health practitioners, policymakers, and researchers working to address the HIV epidemic in key populations. Ultimately, the findings underscore the critical importance of integrating technology-based interventions into the broader HIV response to achieve the goal of ending the epidemic.

The study employed a web-based communications strategy developed and implemented by the Thai Red Cross AIDS Research Centre, called Adam's Love, to increase engagement in early HIV testing and counselling (HTC) and linkage to care among gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand. The programme was designed as an innovative "online-to-offline" model to leverage the high internet accessibility within this population and address barriers to traditional outreach and healthcare engagement. The methods employed are detailed below.

The Adam’s Love programme was launched in September 2011 and targeted MSM through a combination of internet-based platforms and partnerships with MSM-friendly healthcare providers. Central to the programme was a dedicated and interactive website (www.adamslove.org), which provided information on HIV prevention, testing, and treatment. The website content was tailored specifically to the MSM population and included culturally appropriate visuals, testimonials, videos, and educational materials to promote awareness and reduce stigma around HIV testing and care.

In addition to the website, the programme integrated multiple social media platforms, including Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube, to expand its reach and engage MSM with interactive content. Social media campaigns were designed to build a community of trust and encourage online discussions around HIV-related topics. Targeted social media advertisements and posts were used to increase visibility of the programme and drive traffic to the website. The programme also utilised web-based message boards and chat services to provide real-time online counselling by trained healthcare professionals and peer counsellors. These online counselling sessions were designed to address individual concerns, answer questions about HIV, and provide guidance on accessing HTC services.

To facilitate linkage to offline services, the programme offered an online appointment booking system that allowed MSM to schedule HTC sessions at collaborating MSM-friendly clinics and private hospitals. The participating healthcare facilities were chosen based on their accessibility, confidentiality, and demonstrated sensitivity to the needs of MSM. A club membership programme was also introduced as part of the strategy to provide additional incentives for MSM to engage with HTC services. MSM enrolling in the programme received non-financial benefits, such as priority access to services, exclusive educational materials, and invitations to community events.

The programme incorporated targeted marketing and promotional activities to increase awareness and uptake. These included partnerships with MSM-focused organisations, community events, and outreach activities at venues frequented by MSM, such as bars, clubs, and saunas. Online advertising was also used to target MSM with specific keywords and demographics to ensure that the programme reached the population most at risk.

Data collection and monitoring were integral to the programme to evaluate its effectiveness and inform ongoing improvements. Website analytics tools were used to track engagement metrics, including the number of unique visitors, page views, and user interactions. Data from the online counselling sessions, including the number of MSM counselled and referred to services, were recorded and analysed. Collaborating clinics provided de-identified data on HTC uptake, HIV diagnoses, and linkage to care for MSM referred through the Adam’s Love platform. These data were securely stored and analysed to assess the impact of the programme in increasing access to services and identifying new HIV cases.

In addition to direct service delivery, the programme established partnerships with healthcare providers to ensure that MSM referred through Adam’s Love received high-quality, stigma-free care. Training sessions were conducted for healthcare staff at participating clinics to sensitise them to the specific needs of MSM and improve the overall patient experience. This component aimed to foster a supportive and welcoming environment for MSM accessing HTC and treatment services.

Throughout the implementation period from September 2011 to January 2015, the programme continuously refined its strategies based on user feedback and data analysis. Regular online surveys and focus group discussions were conducted with MSM participants to gather insights into their experiences with the programme and identify areas for improvement. Feedback from healthcare providers was also collected to optimise referral processes and service delivery.

The Adam’s Love programme was ultimately designed as a sustainable and scalable intervention, with the potential to be adapted for other settings and populations. Its emphasis on integrating online platforms with offline healthcare services sought to address the unique challenges faced by MSM in accessing HTC and treatment in Thailand, while also leveraging the opportunities presented by advancements in communications technology.

Between September 2011 and January 2015, the Adam's Love programme demonstrated significant success in engaging gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand into early HIV testing, counselling, and treatment through its innovative communications technologies. The programme's online platform, which included a dedicated website, integrated social media, and interactive web message boards, attracted a substantial audience. During this period, the website recorded an impressive 1.69 million unique viewers and more than 8 million page views. This high level of engagement highlights the potential of technology-based strategies to effectively target populations at high risk for HIV.

The programme offered online counselling, which proved to be a critical element in addressing the concerns and questions of MSM regarding HIV testing and treatment. A total of 11,120 MSM received online counselling through the platform, providing them with tailored information and support. The online counselling sessions served as a gateway to HIV testing and prevention services, helping to overcome barriers such as stigma, fear, and lack of information, which often prevent MSM from accessing traditional HIV services.

One of the key outcomes of Adam's Love was its ability to successfully refer MSM to HIV testing and counselling (HTC) services. Over the study period, 8,288 MSM were referred to HTC services through the programme. The referrals were facilitated by partnerships with MSM-friendly clinics and private hospitals, ensuring that users had access to safe and nonjudgmental environments for testing. By addressing issues of accessibility and creating positive healthcare experiences, the programme encouraged more MSM to get tested for HIV.

In addition to HIV testing, the programme also focused on promoting sexual health more broadly. A total of 1,223 MSM were referred to sexually transmitted infection (STI) testing services. This integration of STI testing into the programme's outreach efforts further strengthened its impact, as co-infection with STIs can increase the risk of HIV transmission and complicate treatment outcomes. By providing comprehensive sexual health services, Adam's Love addressed the broader health needs of MSM in Thailand.

The programme also provided tailored advice and support for MSM living with HIV. A total of 1,112 MSM who were identified as living with HIV through the programme received counselling and guidance on accessing antiretroviral treatment (ART) and navigating care services. This aspect of the programme emphasized the importance of early initiation of treatment, which not only improves individual health outcomes but also reduces the risk of onward transmission of the virus.

A unique feature of Adam's Love was its club membership programme, which provided non-financial incentives for MSM to engage with HTC services. The programme successfully recruited 1,181 MSM into the membership initiative. Participants in the club membership programme were offered benefits such as priority access to services and exclusive health-related promotions. This approach helped to build trust and foster a sense of community among participants, reinforcing their commitment to regular testing and treatment adherence. Notably, 15.5% of the MSM recruited online and enrolled in the club membership programme were diagnosed with HIV, underscoring the programme's ability to reach individuals who were at high risk and unaware of their HIV status.

The success of Adam's Love in engaging MSM into HIV testing and care is further evidenced by its widespread acceptance and recognition as a trusted resource. The programme leveraged targeted marketing and promotions to increase its visibility and credibility within the MSM community. By employing a combination of online and offline strategies, Adam's Love effectively bridged the gap between digital engagement and physical healthcare services. The 'online-to-offline' recruitment model proved to be a particularly effective strategy for reaching MSM who might otherwise remain disconnected from traditional healthcare systems.

The results of the Adam's Love programme highlight the potential for communications technologies to transform HIV prevention and care efforts in Thailand and beyond. By meeting MSM where they are—online—the programme addressed key challenges related to stigma, accessibility, and awareness. The scale of engagement and the outcomes achieved demonstrate that technology-driven interventions can play a crucial role in addressing the HIV epidemic among MSM. Moreover, the programme's emphasis on building partnerships with MSM-friendly clinics and providing comprehensive sexual health services ensured that users had access to high-quality and affirming care.

In conclusion, the Adam's Love programme successfully demonstrated the feasibility and impact of leveraging innovative, web-based communications strategies to engage MSM in early HIV testing and treatment. The programme's ability to attract and retain high levels of user engagement, facilitate access to testing and care, and foster community trust provides a model for future initiatives targeting similar populations. As the HIV epidemic among MSM continues to grow in Thailand and other regions, programmes like Adam's Love offer valuable insights into how technology can be harnessed to improve health outcomes for vulnerable populations.

The findings from the Adam’s Love programme underscore the effectiveness and potential of leveraging communications technologies to address the growing HIV epidemic among gay men and other men who have sex with men (MSM) in Thailand. With MSM consistently identified as a key population at heightened risk for HIV infection, innovative, scalable, and population-specific interventions are critical in curtailing the spread of the virus and linking individuals to early testing and treatment. This programme demonstrates how a well-designed online-to-offline (O2O) approach can successfully overcome barriers to HIV testing and counselling (HTC), as well as stigma, which often hinders engagement with traditional healthcare services.

One of the most significant achievements of the Adam’s Love programme is its ability to integrate technology into public health strategies, thereby reaching a highly internet-active population. The high level of engagement, evidenced by 1.69 million website viewers and more than 8 million page views, highlights the programme’s capacity to create an accessible, trusted, and stigma-free digital space for MSM. Online platforms, such as Adam’s Love, provide anonymity and convenience, which are particularly appealing to individuals who may face discrimination, fear of disclosure, or logistical barriers when accessing in-person services. This aligns with global evidence suggesting that digital health interventions are highly effective in engaging hard-to-reach populations at risk for HIV.

The scale and scope of this programme’s success are particularly noteworthy. Over a 3.5-year period, Adam’s Love facilitated online counselling for more than 11,000 MSM, referred more than 8,200 individuals to HTC services, and guided over 1,100 MSM living with HIV toward treatment. These metrics illustrate a robust linkage between online outreach and offline health services, a critical component in achieving positive health outcomes. The programme's integration of a club membership initiative, which provided non-financial incentives, further exemplifies innovative engagement strategies. The 15.5% HIV diagnosis rate among club members also highlights the programme's ability to target and identify individuals at particularly high risk of HIV.

The utilisation of social media and web-based platforms in Adam’s Love has proven to be a powerful tool for targeted messaging and education. By tailoring its content to the specific needs of MSM, the programme not only raised awareness about HTC but also reduced misconceptions and fears associated with HIV testing and treatment. The provision of online counselling through message boards and social media further enhanced accessibility, allowing individuals to seek information and support in a confidential and judgment-free environment. These findings echo broader trends in digital health, where targeted online interventions are increasingly recognised as an effective means of health promotion and risk reduction among vulnerable populations.

Another critical success factor of the Adam’s Love programme is its partnership with MSM-friendly clinics and private hospitals. These collaborations ensured that individuals referred through the programme could access culturally competent and stigma-free HTC services, which are essential for fostering trust and encouraging continued engagement with healthcare systems. This partnership model could serve as a blueprint for other countries facing similar challenges in addressing HIV among MSM or other key populations.

Despite its successes, the programme also highlights several challenges and areas for improvement. While the O2O model proved effective in linking many individuals to HTC services, the dropout rate between online engagement and offline follow-through warrants further investigation. Structural barriers, such as cost, transportation, and time constraints, may prevent some individuals from accessing HTC services after referral. Additionally, stigma and fear of discrimination, even within MSM-friendly health facilities, may discourage some individuals from completing the referral process. Future iterations of the programme could explore strategies to address these gaps, such as providing transportation subsidies, expanding free HTC services, or offering telemedicine options for initial consultations.

Another consideration is the sustainability and scalability of the Adam’s Love programme. While the programme has demonstrated significant impact in Thailand, questions remain about its long-term funding and integration into national health systems. Given the programme's reliance on digital platforms and targeted marketing, sustained investment in technology and outreach is essential. Expanding the programme to other regions or replicating it in countries with similar epidemics could amplify its impact, but this would require careful adaptation to local contexts, including language, culture, and healthcare infrastructure.

Finally, it is important to highlight the broader implications of this programme for HIV prevention and treatment efforts. The success of Adam’s Love demonstrates the importance of meeting populations where they are—in this case, online—and adapting interventions to align with their preferences and behaviours. As digital technologies continue to evolve, public health programmes must remain agile, leveraging new tools and platforms to enhance engagement and improve health outcomes. The lessons learned from Adam’s Love can inform the design of future interventions not only for HIV but also for other health issues disproportionately affecting key populations.

In conclusion, the Adam’s Love programme exemplifies how innovative, technology-driven strategies can effectively engage MSM in early HIV testing and treatment. By creating an accessible, confidential, and culturally sensitive digital platform, the programme successfully addressed barriers to HTC, reduced stigma, and fostered critical linkages to care. Its success provides a compelling case for the integration of online-to-offline models into national and regional HIV prevention strategies, particularly in settings with high internet penetration and where stigma remains a significant obstacle to healthcare access. Moving forward, efforts to scale up and sustain similar interventions should prioritise addressing barriers to follow-through, ensuring long-term funding, and adapting strategies to meet the needs of diverse populations. With the right investments and collaborations, technology-based interventions like Adam’s Love have the potential to transform the landscape of HIV prevention and care, ultimately contributing to global efforts to end the HIV epidemic.

The ever-increasing demand for high data rates, ultra-low latency, and enhanced reliability in wireless communications has propelled the evolution of fifth-generation (5G) networks into heterogeneous architectures, integrating sub-6 GHz and millimeter wave (mmWave) frequency bands. These mixed-frequency networks aim to exploit the complementary characteristics of each spectrum: the robust propagation conditions and wide coverage of sub-6 GHz bands, and the high capacity and ultrawide bandwidth of mmWave bands. However, this integration introduces significant challenges, particularly concerning the effective management of radio resources amidst varying propagation conditions and blockages. One critical aspect of this challenge is the decoupling of uplink (UL) and downlink (DL) transmissions, where independent access points (APs) and frequency bands may need to be assigned for UL and DL to optimize network performance.

UL/DL decoupling has emerged as a promising solution to address the disparity in propagation characteristics between sub-6 GHz and mmWave bands, particularly in cell-free massive multiple-input multiple-output (MIMO) networks. Unlike conventional coupled transmissions, where the UL and DL share the same frequency band and AP, decoupled transmissions allow the UL and DL to operate independently, leveraging the most suitable frequency and AP for each direction. This approach is particularly advantageous in scenarios where the mmWave channel experiences severe degradation due to blockages, while the sub-6 GHz channel remains robust. Moreover, decoupling can improve spectral efficiency and reduce interference, contributing to the overall reliability and performance of the network. However, implementing efficient UL/DL decoupling in real-time networks is challenging due to the need for fast and accurate radio resource management, which must account for the dynamic and heterogeneous nature of propagation environments.

Traditionally, UL/DL decoupling relies on extensive real-time measurements and centralized decision-making, which can introduce significant latency and computational overhead. Furthermore, the reliance on mmWave measurements for resource allocation can be impractical in scenarios where the mmWave channel is frequently blocked or exhibits high variability. To address these limitations, semi-blind techniques have gained attention, leveraging limited measurements and predictive algorithms to make efficient resource allocation decisions. Semi-blind approaches aim to reduce the dependence on exhaustive real-time measurements, instead relying on initial training and predictive modeling to guide decision-making.

In this context, we propose a novel semi-blind UL/DL decoupling framework tailored for mixed sub-6 GHz/mmWave 5G cell-free massive MIMO networks. Our approach introduces a non-linear support vector machine (SVM) classifier trained on a minimal set of measurements, including the Rician \(K\)-factor and the downlink reference signal received power (RSRP) for both 2.6 GHz and 28 GHz frequency bands. The Rician \(K\)-factor provides a statistical representation of the user's line-of-sight (LOS) conditions, which are critical for assessing the reliability of the mmWave channel. The DL RSRP offers an additional indicator of channel quality, complementing the \(K\)-factor information. By combining these metrics, the proposed framework is capable of capturing the propagation characteristics across both frequency bands, enabling accurate and efficient resource allocation.

The central innovation of our approach lies in its semi-blind operation. Unlike fully blind methods, which rely solely on predictive modeling without any prior measurements, or fully informed methods, which require continuous real-time monitoring, the semi-blind framework strikes a balance between these extremes. Following an initial activation phase, the central processing unit (CPU) gathers the necessary measurements to train the SVM classifier. Once the training is complete, the framework eliminates the need for further mmWave measurements, relying exclusively on 2.6 GHz data to predict the optimal frequency bands and APs for both UL and DL. **Methods**

A case-control study design was employed to investigate the risk factors associated with cholera during the ongoing outbreak in Yemen. The study was conducted in Aden, one of the provinces heavily affected by the outbreak, from March to June 2018. This design was chosen to compare cholera cases with community controls, enabling the identification of potential exposures and behaviors associated with the disease.

The study population consisted of individuals residing in Aden during the outbreak period. Cases were defined as individuals presenting with acute watery diarrhea who tested positive for *Vibrio cholerae* by stool culture or rapid diagnostic testing at designated cholera treatment centers (CTCs) in Aden. All cases were confirmed by healthcare providers at the CTCs, following the World Health Organization (WHO) definition for suspected cholera cases [1]. To ensure accurate case identification, the inclusion criteria required that cases were newly diagnosed, residing in Aden for at least three months prior to the onset of symptoms, and aged 5 years or older. Individuals with chronic diarrhea or other conditions potentially mimicking cholera were excluded.

Community controls were selected from the same neighborhoods as the cases in order to minimize geographical and environmental differences that could confound the results. Controls were matched to cases by age (±5 years) and sex. Eligible controls were individuals without a history of diarrhea or other gastrointestinal symptoms in the four weeks preceding the study. A ratio of 2 controls per case was used to enhance the statistical power of the study.

Data collection was conducted using structured, interviewer-administered questionnaires. The questionnaire was developed based on prior research on cholera risk factors and adapted to the local context based on consultations with local public health experts. The questionnaire was pre-tested in a pilot study to ensure clarity and cultural appropriateness, and adjustments were made accordingly. Data collected included demographic information (e.g., age, sex, education level), behavioral factors (e.g., food and water consumption practices, handwashing habits, use of chlorine or soap in the household), and environmental factors (e.g., source of drinking water, sanitation facilities). Additional questions assessed recent travel history, contact with visitors from outside Aden, and practices related to khat consumption, a common local custom.

Trained field staff, including public health workers and medical students, conducted the interviews. All interviewers received training in data collection techniques, ethical considerations, and the use of the study tools. Informed consent was obtained from all participants or their legal guardians prior to the interviews. For illiterate participants, the consent form was read aloud, and verbal consent was documented in the presence of a witness.

Data on cholera cases were obtained from CTC records, while controls were identified through a systematic random sampling method within the communities where cases resided. To ensure random selection, field staff used a predetermined starting point within the neighborhood and selected every third household, ensuring that only one eligible individual per household was interviewed. If a selected household had no eligible participant, the next household was approached.

The primary exposures of interest included water source, food preparation and consumption behaviors, hygiene practices (e.g., washing hands, fruits, vegetables, and khat), and recent travel or contact with visitors. Water sources were categorized as common-source water (e.g., water trucks, shared wells) or private-source water (e.g., household wells, bottled water). Data were entered and analyzed using statistical software (SPSS, version 25.0). Descriptive statistics were calculated for demographic and exposure variables. Bivariate analysis was conducted using chi-square tests to identify associations between potential risk factors and cholera. These findings underscore the complex interplay between individual behaviors, water sanitation, and the broader sociopolitical context in the spread of cholera.

The identification of unwashed khat consumption as a significant risk factor in the multivariate analysis highlights the importance of local cultural practices in the transmission dynamics of cholera. Khat, a plant widely consumed in Yemen for its stimulant effects, is often shared in social settings, which may facilitate the spread of cholera through contaminated handling or irrigation practices. Similar findings have been reported in other cholera-endemic regions, where specific food and plant-related practices have been linked to outbreaks [1, 2]. Efforts to mitigate the risk associated with khat consumption should focus on community education campaigns that emphasize proper washing techniques and hygiene practices. These campaigns should be culturally sensitive and take into account the significance of khat in Yemeni society.

The role of common-source water as a significant risk factor aligns with the well-documented relationship between cholera outbreaks and inadequate water supply systems. The ongoing conflict in Yemen has severely disrupted water infrastructure, forcing many communities to rely on untreated or poorly maintained water sources. Contaminated water is a primary vehicle for the transmission of *Vibrio cholerae*, and the findings of this study reinforce the critical need for interventions that improve access to safe drinking water. Previous studies have demonstrated that the provision of chlorinated water and the promotion of household water treatment methods are effective in reducing the risk of cholera [3, 4]. In Yemen, the implementation of such interventions remains challenging due to the protracted conflict, limited resources, and logistical constraints. However, targeted initiatives, such as the distribution of water purification tablets and the establishment of community-level chlorination stations, could offer practical solutions to address this issue.

Interestingly, other behavioral factors, such as eating outside the house and not washing vegetables and fruits, were significant in the bivariate analysis but did not remain significant in the multivariate analysis. This suggests that these factors may be confounded by other variables, such as the source of water used for washing or the overall hygiene conditions of the household. Nevertheless, these behaviors should not be overlooked, as they may still play an indirect role in cholera transmission. Public health campaigns should emphasize the importance of maintaining hygienic food preparation practices, particularly in areas where access to clean water is limited.

The study also identified a history of traveling and having visitors from outside Aden Province as risk factors for cholera in the bivariate analysis, though these factors did not remain significant in the multivariate analysis. This finding suggests that movement and social interactions may contribute to the spread of cholera, particularly in regions with active transmission. The role of population mobility in cholera outbreaks has been documented in other settings, where the movement of infected individuals has facilitated the introduction of *Vibrio cholerae* into new areas [5]. In the context of Yemen, where displaced populations and internal migration are prevalent due to the conflict, these factors warrant further investigation. Strengthening surveillance systems to monitor cholera cases and the movement of individuals may help to identify and contain potential hotspots of transmission.

The limitations of this study should be considered when interpreting the findings. The case-control design is susceptible to recall bias, particularly in the collection of self-reported data on behavioral practices. Additionally, the relatively small sample size may limit the generalizability of the results to other regions of Yemen. Despite these limitations, the study provides valuable evidence on the risk factors for cholera in the context of a complex humanitarian emergency. Future research should aim to include larger and more representative samples, as well as longitudinal designs to capture changes in risk factors over time.

The findings of this study have important implications for public health interventions aimed at controlling the cholera outbreak in Yemen. First, there is a clear need to address the widespread reliance on unsafe water sources. Efforts should focus on restoring and maintaining water infrastructure, as well as providing immediate solutions such as household water treatment methods. Second, community education campaigns should target specific behavioral practices, such as the washing of khat, fruits, and vegetables. These campaigns should be tailored to the local context and delivered in a manner that is accessible and culturally appropriate.

In conclusion, this study highlights the critical role of behavioral and environmental factors in the ongoing cholera outbreak in Yemen. The findings emphasize the need for a multifaceted approach to cholera prevention, combining improvements in water, sanitation, and hygiene (WASH) infrastructure with community-level interventions to promote safe practices. Addressing these risk factors is particularly challenging in the context of Yemen’s protracted conflict and humanitarian crisis. However, targeted and context-specific interventions have the potential to significantly reduce the burden of cholera and prevent future outbreaks. Collaborative efforts between governmental agencies, non-governmental organizations, and international partners will be essential to achieving sustainable solutions in this complex setting.
