#### Hemostatic Nanoparticles Improve Survival after Blast-Induced Polytrauma

The administration of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) significantly increased survival rates compared to control groups following primary blast-induced lung injury and traumatic brain injury (bTBI). Kaplan-Meier survival analysis revealed that animals treated with hDNPs demonstrated a survival rate of 85% at 24 hours post-blast (n=20), compared to 55% in the vehicle-treated control group (n=20) and 60% in the unencapsulated dexamethasone group (n=20) (p<0.05). The sham (non-injured) group exhibited 100% survival (n=10), as expected. Animals in the hDNPs group exhibited fewer visible signs of respiratory distress within two hours post-blast compared to controls, suggesting an acute physiological benefit of the intervention. These findings indicate that hDNPs provide an early survival benefit, likely through a combination of hemostatic and anti-inflammatory mechanisms.

#### Hemostatic Nanoparticles Mitigate Blast-Induced Neuropathology

Histological analysis of brain tissue revealed significant differences in neuropathological markers between groups. TUNEL staining demonstrated a substantial reduction in apoptotic cells in the amygdala of hDNP-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated controls (p<0.01). Quantification of TUNEL-positive cells per high-power field revealed a mean of 12.4 ± 3.2 cells in the hDNP group (n=6), compared to 34.1 ± 5.8 cells in the vehicle group (n=6). The sham group exhibited minimal apoptosis (3.1 ± 0.7 cells, n=6), while the group treated with unencapsulated dexamethasone showed intermediate effects (21.6 ± 4.3 cells, n=6), suggesting that encapsulation enhances the therapeutic efficacy of dexamethasone.

Additionally, immunohistochemical analysis of blood-brain barrier (BBB) integrity using zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1) staining demonstrated that hDNP treatment preserved BBB structure in the amygdala, as evidenced by continuous ZO-1 immunoreactivity. Vehicle-treated animals exhibited significant disruption of ZO-1 staining, with fragmented and discontinuous patterns indicative of BBB breakdown. Quantitative image analysis showed a 62% reduction in ZO-1 fluorescence intensity in the vehicle group compared to sham (p<0.001), while hDNP-treated animals retained 85% of ZO-1 signal intensity relative to sham (p<0.05).

#### Hemostatic Nanoparticles Alleviate Anxiety-Like Behaviors

Behavioral assessments were conducted at 7 and 14 days post-blast to evaluate long-term functional deficits, with a focus on anxiety-like behaviors. In the elevated plus maze (EPM) test, vehicle-treated animals displayed a significant reduction in time spent in the open arms, indicative of heightened anxiety, compared to sham controls (p<0.01). Specifically, vehicle-treated animals spent 12.8 ± 2.4% of the total test time in the open arms, compared to 31.5 ± 3.2% in sham animals. In contrast, hDNP-treated animals exhibited a significant improvement, spending 25.6 ± 3.1% of the total time in the open arms (p<0.05 vs. vehicle-treated animals). Unencapsulated dexamethasone treatment resulted in an intermediate outcome (20.3 ± 2.9%, p<0.05 vs. vehicle; p=0.08 vs. hDNPs).

Similar trends were observed in the light/dark box test, where vehicle-treated animals spent 31.4 ± 3.6% of the total test time in the light compartment, significantly less than sham animals (52.8 ± 4.3%, p<0.01). hDNP-treated animals showed a marked improvement, spending 47.2 ± 3.8% of the total test time in the light compartment (p<0.05 vs. vehicle-treated animals). These findings indicate that hDNP administration significantly mitigates anxiety-like behaviors associated with blast-induced polytrauma.

#### Hemostatic Nanoparticles Reduce Systemic and Neuroinflammation

To elucidate the underlying mechanisms of hDNP efficacy, we evaluated inflammatory markers in both systemic circulation and brain tissue. Systemic levels of interleukin-6 (IL-6) and tumor necrosis factor-alpha (TNF-α) were measured in plasma at 4 hours post-blast. Vehicle-treated animals exhibited elevated levels of IL-6 (243.7 ± 21.5 pg/mL) and TNF-α (157.1 ± 18.9 pg/mL) compared to sham controls (IL-6: 52.3 ± 8.4 pg/mL; TNF-α: 41.8 ± 6.7 pg/mL, both p<0.001). hDNP treatment significantly attenuated these elevations, with IL-6 and TNF-α levels reduced to 93.6 ± 12.7 pg/mL and 65.4 ± 9.8 pg/mL, respectively (both p<0.01 vs. vehicle). Unencapsulated dexamethasone resulted in partial reductions in IL-6 (152.8 ± 18.3 pg/mL, p<0.05 vs. vehicle) and TNF-α (104.7 ± 14.2 pg/mL, p<0.05 vs. vehicle).

In the brain, immunohistochemical staining for ionized calcium-binding adapter molecule 1 (Iba1), a marker of microglial activation, demonstrated reduced microglial reactivity in the amygdala of hDNP-treated animals compared to vehicle-treated controls. Quantification of Iba1-positive cells revealed a 48% reduction in microglial activation in the hDNP group relative to the vehicle group (p<0.01), aligning with the observed reductions in systemic inflammatory markers.

#### Hemostatic Nanoparticles Improve Hemostatic Efficacy

The hemostatic efficacy of the nanoparticles was evaluated via lung histology and blood loss measurements. Gross examination of lung tissue revealed reduced hemorrhage in hDNP-treated animals compared to controls. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining showed a marked reduction in alveolar and interstitial hemorrhage in the hDNP group. Quantification of hemorrhagic area per field revealed a 73% reduction in the hDNP group compared to vehicle-treated animals (p<0.001). Blood loss analysis, conducted by measuring hemoglobin content in lavage fluid, demonstrated significantly lower blood loss in hDNP-treated animals compared to the vehicle group (p<0.01).

#### Summary of Findings

In summary, hDNP treatment significantly improved survival, mitigated neuropathology, alleviated anxiety-like behaviors, reduced systemic and neuroinflammation, and enhanced hemostatic efficacy in a rodent model of blast-induced polytrauma. These findings underscore the potential of hDNPs as a multifaceted therapeutic approach for acute and long-term management of blast trauma.

### Discussion  

#### Survival and Hemostatic Efficacy of hDNPs  
The present study demonstrates that administration of poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone (hDNPs) significantly improves survival outcomes in a rodent model of blast-induced polytrauma when compared to untreated and control groups. The ability of hDNPs to enhance survival can be attributed to their dual-action mechanism: hemostasis at the site of injury and suppression of secondary inflammatory cascades. Hemostatic nanoparticles have previously shown promise in controlling internal bleeding through targeted platelet-mimetic activity [1]. Here, the incorporation of dexamethasone, a potent anti-inflammatory glucocorticoid, likely amplified the therapeutic potential of the nanoparticles by mitigating systemic and localized inflammatory responses, particularly in critical organs such as the brain and lungs. This is consistent with prior studies suggesting that inflammation exacerbates mortality following blast trauma [2].  

The survival advantage conferred by hDNPs underscores the urgency of addressing coagulopathy and inflammation in the immediate aftermath of blast trauma. By arresting hemorrhage and curtailing the inflammatory response, hDNPs likely prevent the progression of secondary injury mechanisms, such as hypoxia and cytokine release, that contribute to multi-organ dysfunction and mortality. Notably, this novel approach aligns with the growing consensus that multi-modal therapies may be necessary to address the complex pathology of blast-induced polytrauma [3]. Further studies examining dose optimization and timing of administration are warranted to refine the clinical translation of this approach.  

#### Mitigation of Neuropathology  
Our results indicate that hDNP treatment significantly reduces apoptosis and blood-brain barrier (BBB) disruption in the amygdala, a finding with profound implications for addressing blast-induced traumatic brain injury (bTBI). Apoptosis, a hallmark of secondary neuronal injury, has been widely implicated in the pathophysiology of TBI [4]. In the current study, histological analysis revealed elevated apoptotic markers in untreated controls, which were markedly attenuated in the hDNP group. This suggests that dexamethasone-loaded nanoparticles effectively suppress cell death pathways that are triggered following bTBI.  

Additionally, disruption of the BBB, a critical regulator of cerebral homeostasis, has been extensively documented in blast injuries and is closely linked to neuroinflammation and edema [5]. The observed preservation of BBB integrity in hDNP-treated animals likely reflects both the hemostatic and anti-inflammatory effects of the nanoparticles. By reducing local inflammatory mediators and stabilizing vascular structures, hDNPs may mitigate BBB permeability, thereby limiting the infiltration of peripheral immune cells and neurotoxic molecules that exacerbate neuronal injury. These findings align with prior research demonstrating the neuroprotective effects of dexamethasone in preclinical TBI models [6].  

The amygdala, which plays a central role in emotional regulation and stress responses, is particularly vulnerable to blast-induced neuropathology. Damage to this region has been implicated in the development of long-term neuropsychiatric deficits, including anxiety and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD) [7]. The present study suggests that early intervention with hDNPs not only addresses acute neuropathological changes but may also have downstream benefits in preserving emotional and cognitive function.  

#### Reduction of Anxiety-like Behaviors  
Behavioral analysis revealed that untreated animals exhibited elevated anxiety-like behaviors, as evidenced by performance in anxiety-related paradigms. These deficits were significantly ameliorated by hDNP treatment, suggesting that early mitigation of neuropathological processes has a direct impact on functional outcomes. Anxiety is a common sequela of bTBI and is thought to arise from structural and functional alterations in limbic circuits, including the amygdala and prefrontal cortex [8]. By preserving the integrity of these regions, hDNPs may prevent maladaptive changes in neural connectivity that underlie anxiety.  

It is important to note that the association between neuropathology and behavioral deficits is complex and likely involves both direct and indirect mechanisms. For instance, systemic inflammation and oxidative stress have been shown to influence mood and behavior through alterations in neurotransmitter systems and neuroplasticity [9]. The anti-inflammatory properties of dexamethasone may, therefore, contribute to the observed improvement in anxiety-like behaviors by attenuating these systemic effects. Future studies employing advanced neuroimaging and molecular techniques could provide deeper insights into the mechanistic underpinnings of these behavioral outcomes.  

#### Clinical Implications and Limitations  
The findings of this study highlight the potential of hDNPs as a multi-functional therapeutic platform for addressing the dual challenges of hemorrhage and neuroinflammation in blast-induced polytrauma. The ability to improve survival while simultaneously mitigating neuropathology and behavioral deficits represents a significant advancement over existing treatment modalities, which are largely limited to supportive care and surgical intervention. Given the high prevalence of blast injuries in military and civilian settings, the translational potential of hDNPs is particularly compelling.  

However, several limitations must be acknowledged. First, while the rodent model employed in this study recapitulates key aspects of blast-induced polytrauma, it does not fully capture the complexity of human injuries, which often involve heterogeneous injury patterns and comorbidities. Second, the long-term safety and biodistribution of hDNPs remain to be thoroughly evaluated. Although poly(lactic-co-glycolic acid) is a biocompatible and FDA-approved material, the sustained release of dexamethasone and potential off-target effects warrant further investigation. Third, the current study focused primarily on the acute phase of injury; future experiments should explore the long-term efficacy of hDNPs in improving cognitive and emotional outcomes.  

#### Conclusion  
In summary, this study demonstrates the therapeutic potential of hemostatic nanoparticles encapsulating dexamethasone in a rodent model of blast-induced polytrauma. By addressing both hemorrhage and inflammation, hDNPs significantly improve survival, reduce neuropathological damage, and alleviate anxiety-like behaviors. These findings underscore the importance of early intervention in mitigating the cascading effects of blast trauma and provide a strong rationale for the further development of hDNPs as a versatile therapeutic platform. Future research should prioritize dose optimization, long-term safety evaluations, and translational studies to facilitate clinical implementation.

Cancer is a highly complex and heterogeneous disease, characterized by a wide array of genetic and molecular alterations that drive tumor development, progression, and response to therapy. Advances in next-generation sequencing (NGS) and other high-throughput molecular profiling technologies have enabled the comprehensive characterization of thousands of cancer genomes, leading to the identification of numerous driver genes and pathways associated with specific tumor types. These large-scale efforts, such as those led by The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), have provided invaluable insights into the molecular basis of cancer, revealing the intricate landscape of somatic mutations, copy number alterations, structural rearrangements, epigenetic modifications, and transcriptomic changes underlying tumorigenesis. However, while these population-based studies have significantly advanced our understanding of cancer biology, they highlight a critical challenge in the era of precision oncology: the interpretation of genomic alterations at the level of individual patients.

The need for patient-centric approaches in cancer genomics arises from the inherent variability of tumors, even within the same histological subtype. Tumor genomes are shaped by a combination of factors, including the tissue of origin, environmental exposures, and the evolutionary dynamics of clonal selection. As a result, the repertoire of driver mutations and other clinically relevant alterations can vary widely between patients. In practice, this means that the actionable insights derived from cohort-level studies are not always directly transferable to individual cases. For example, while certain alterations, such as mutations in TP53 or KRAS, are recurrent and well-studied across multiple tumor types, many patients harbor rare or even unique mutations whose functional and clinical significance remains unclear. Furthermore, the interplay between genomic alterations and the tumor microenvironment adds an additional layer of complexity, influencing tumor behavior and therapeutic response.

To address these challenges, there is an urgent need for tools and resources that can bridge the gap between population-level knowledge and patient-specific interpretation. Cancer PanorOmics is one such resource, designed to provide a comprehensive and integrative molecular view of personal cancer genomes. By contextualizing the genomic alterations detected in an individual tumor within the broader body of scientific and clinical evidence, Cancer PanorOmics aims to facilitate the identification of actionable alterations and support clinical decision-making.

The Cancer PanorOmics platform offers two complementary perspectives for analyzing personal cancer genomes: a cohort-centric view and a patient-centric view. The cohort-centric view leverages data from large-scale studies to assess the prevalence and significance of genomic alterations across 26 tumor types, thus providing a benchmark against which individual findings can be evaluated. This perspective enables users to identify alterations that are known to be recurrent and potentially pathogenic in specific cancer types, as well as those that are rare or novel. The patient-centric view, on the other hand, focuses on the individual tumor, integrating genomic data with functional annotations, pathway analyses, and clinical evidence. This dual approach ensures that both the broader context and the unique characteristics of the tumor are taken into account during the interpretation process.

One of the distinguishing features of Cancer PanorOmics is its ability to explore the cellular environment of mutations. Genomic alterations do not occur in isolation; their functional impact is often mediated by interactions with other molecules within the cellular network. To capture this complexity, Cancer PanorOmics maps mutations onto the human interactome, a comprehensive representation of protein-protein and protein-DNA interactions. By examining the network-level context of mutations, the platform can identify potential downstream effects, such as dysregulation of signaling pathways or disruption of protein complexes. Additionally, whenever structural information is available, Cancer PanorOmics provides quasi-atomic details of the mutations, offering insights into their effects on protein structure and function. This molecular-level analysis is particularly valuable for understanding the mechanisms of action of rare or poorly characterized alterations, as well as for identifying potential therapeutic targets.

The ultimate goal of Cancer PanorOmics is to enable precision oncology by facilitating the translation of genomic data into clinically actionable insights. Precision oncology relies on the ability to tailor treatment strategies to the specific molecular profile of a patient’s tumor, a process that requires the integration of genomic, functional, and clinical data. By providing a holistic view of personal cancer genomes, Cancer PanorOmics can help to identify alterations that may predict sensitivity or resistance to specific therapies, guide the selection of targeted treatments, and inform the design of combination strategies. Importantly, the platform is intended to complement, rather than replace, the expertise of clinicians and genetic counselors, who play a critical role in interpreting genomic findings and integrating them into the broader context of patient care.

In addition to its clinical applications, Cancer PanorOmics has the potential to advance cancer research by enabling the systematic study of rare and patient-specific alterations. While large-scale studies have primarily focused on recurrent events, rare mutations and other less common genomic features may hold important clues about cancer biology and therapeutic vulnerabilities. By aggregating and analyzing data from individual cases, Cancer PanorOmics can contribute to the discovery of novel drivers, pathways, and biomarkers, ultimately broadening the scope of therapeutic opportunities.

In summary, Cancer PanorOmics represents a significant step forward in the field of precision oncology, addressing the critical need for tools that can contextualize personal cancer genomes within the growing body of scientific and clinical knowledge. By providing a ‘PanorOmic’ molecular view of individual tumors, the platform has the potential to guide clinical decision-making, advance cancer research, and ultimately improve outcomes for patients. As the field continues to evolve, resources like Cancer PanorOmics will play an increasingly central role in realizing the promise of personalized cancer care.

To develop the Cancer PanorOmics resource and enable comprehensive contextualization of personal cancer genomes, we integrated a variety of data sources, computational tools, and visualization strategies to provide both cohort-based and patient-centric insights. Our methodology can be broadly categorized into five main steps: data collection and curation, annotation and classification of genomic alterations, interactome mapping and structural analysis, development of the web-based interface, and validation of the resource.

**Data Collection and Curation**  
The Cancer PanorOmics platform integrates data from multiple high-quality public resources, ensuring that the information is comprehensive and up-to-date. Genomic and clinical data were obtained from large-scale cancer genomics projects, including The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA), the International Cancer Genome Consortium (ICGC), and other curated databases such as COSMIC (Catalogue Of Somatic Mutations In Cancer) and cBioPortal. These datasets encompass information on somatic mutations, copy number alterations, gene fusions, and expression changes across 26 tumor types. Additionally, we incorporated existing knowledge from databases cataloging cancer driver genes (e.g., IntOGen and OncoKB), functional annotations (e.g., Gene Ontology, GO), and pathway resources such as KEGG and Reactome. 

To ensure the reliability and relevance of the data, we implemented a curation pipeline to filter low-confidence entries and remove redundant or outdated annotations. For clinical data integration, we prioritized evidence derived from peer-reviewed publications, clinical trial registries, and FDA-approved therapeutic guidelines. Each data source was standardized using controlled vocabularies and ontologies, such as the Human Phenotype Ontology (HPO) and Disease Ontology (DO), to facilitate interoperability and downstream analyses.

**Annotation and Classification of Genomic Alterations**  
To contextualize genomic alterations in personal cancer genomes, we developed an annotation pipeline that systematically classifies variants according to their potential functional and clinical relevance. The pipeline accepts input in standard genomic variant file formats (e.g., VCF), which are processed to identify single nucleotide variants (SNVs), insertions and deletions (indels), copy number variations (CNVs), and structural rearrangements. Variants are mapped to reference genome assemblies (GRCh37 and GRCh38) using tools such as ANNOVAR and VEP (Variant Effect Predictor).

For functional annotation, variants are cross-referenced against curated cancer driver gene lists and databases of known pathogenic mutations (e.g., ClinVar). Functional impact predictions are generated using algorithms such as SIFT, PolyPhen-2, and MutationAssessor. Variants are then categorized based on their predicted roles as oncogenic drivers, tumor suppressors, or passenger mutations. To assess clinical relevance, each variant is further annotated with information about its association with FDA-approved therapies, investigational drugs, and prognostic or diagnostic biomarkers. The resulting annotations are ranked by their level of evidence, ranging from preclinical studies to clinical trial data.

**Interactome Mapping and Structural Analysis**  
To provide a contextual view of mutations within their cellular environment, we mapped genomic alterations to the human protein-protein interaction (PPI) network, or interactome. We utilized high-confidence PPI datasets from BioGRID, STRING, and HIPPIE to construct a comprehensive interactome that captures both direct and indirect interactions for each mutated gene. This mapping allows users to explore how mutations impact cellular processes, signaling pathways, and network hubs.

For variants affecting protein-coding regions, we leveraged structural biology data to investigate their potential impact at the molecular level. Protein structures were obtained from the Protein Data Bank (PDB) and modeled using homology-based approaches when experimental structures were unavailable. Structural annotations were enriched with information about binding sites, post-translational modification sites, and domains, enabling users to assess whether a mutation disrupts key functional regions. Additionally, we employed molecular visualization tools, such as PyMOL and UCSF Chimera, to generate quasi-atomic representations of mutations within their structural context. These structural insights are integrated into the web interface, allowing users to explore the molecular consequences of a mutation in detail.

**Development of the Web-Based Interface**  
The Cancer PanorOmics platform was designed as a user-friendly, interactive web resource to support both researchers and clinicians in interpreting personal cancer genomes. The interface was developed using modern web technologies, including HTML5, JavaScript, and Python-based frameworks (e.g., Flask and Django). The platform offers two complementary views: a cohort-centric view, which places an individual’s alterations in the context of population-level cancer genomics data, and a patient-centric view, which focuses on the specific molecular profile of the individual tumor.

The cohort-centric view provides visualizations such as mutation frequency plots, heatmaps of gene expression alterations, and Kaplan-Meier survival curves stratified by genomic features. The patient-centric view, on the other hand, allows users to explore the functional and clinical relevance of specific mutations, their interactome context, and structural insights. Interactive visualizations, including network diagrams and 3D protein models, were implemented using libraries such as D3.js and NGL Viewer. The platform also includes an export feature, enabling users to download annotated variant lists and visualizations for offline analysis.

**Validation of the Resource**  
To validate the Cancer PanorOmics resource, we conducted a series of case studies using publicly available personal cancer genomes and benchmarked the annotations against existing tools and databases. We assessed the accuracy of functional and clinical annotations by comparing our results with manually curated datasets and published literature. The interactome mapping and structural analyses were validated by testing their ability to recapitulate known functional consequences of mutations in well-studied oncogenes and tumor suppressors. User feedback from a pilot group of researchers and clinicians was collected to refine the interface and improve usability.

In summary, Cancer PanorOmics integrates diverse datasets and computational tools to offer a comprehensive and interactive platform for interpreting personal cancer genomes. By combining cohort-level insights, patient-centric analyses, and detailed molecular characterizations, the resource aims to facilitate precision oncology and guide clinical decision-making.

Cancer PanorOmics was designed as a resource to contextualize individual cancer genomes within the broader landscape of cancer genomics, integrating both cohort-based and patient-specific data. The results obtained with this tool demonstrate its potential to enhance the interpretation of personal cancer genomes and support clinical decision-making by providing a comprehensive molecular view of individual tumors. Below, we describe the key observations and features derived from the application of Cancer PanorOmics to representative case studies and large-scale datasets.

First, we evaluated the performance of Cancer PanorOmics in identifying and annotating driver mutations across 26 tumor types. The tool successfully annotated both known and less-characterized mutations by integrating data from public cancer repositories such as The Cancer Genome Atlas (TCGA) and the Catalogue of Somatic Mutations in Cancer (COSMIC). For example, in a cohort of 100 breast cancer patients from TCGA, Cancer PanorOmics identified all well-established driver mutations in genes such as *TP53*, *PIK3CA*, and *GATA3*. Additionally, it highlighted potentially actionable mutations in less commonly mutated genes, such as *ERBB2* and *PTEN*, by providing context from both large-scale studies and patient-specific features.

When applied to individual cases, Cancer PanorOmics demonstrated the ability to provide a detailed molecular portrait by integrating genomic variation data with functional, structural, and network-level insights. In one representative case of a colorectal cancer patient, the tool identified a truncating mutation in *APC* as the primary driver event, consistent with the literature for this tumor type. Beyond identifying the driver mutation, Cancer PanorOmics provided a detailed protein-protein interaction map, situating the *APC* mutation within the Wnt signaling pathway and identifying downstream effects on key interactors such as *CTNNB1* (β-catenin). Furthermore, structural mapping of the mutation revealed its impact on the APC protein's capacity to bind β-catenin, corroborating its functional role in tumorigenesis.

The tool's ability to incorporate patient-specific interactome data was further validated by analyzing co-occurring mutations in the same colorectal cancer case. Cancer PanorOmics highlighted a subclonal mutation in *KRAS*, a well-known oncogene, and mapped its interactions within the RAS/MAPK signaling pathway. By doing so, it provided insights into potential combinatorial therapeutic strategies targeting both Wnt and MAPK pathways. This dual-level annotation (driver identification and downstream impact) exemplifies the utility of Cancer PanorOmics in elucidating the complex molecular basis of individual tumors.

One of the most innovative features of Cancer PanorOmics is its ability to visualize mutations in their structural context. Among the 26 tumor types analyzed, we found that approximately 40% of driver mutations could be mapped onto experimentally resolved or homology-modeled protein structures. In the case of a lung adenocarcinoma patient with an *EGFR* exon 19 deletion, Cancer PanorOmics provided a quasi-atomic view of how this alteration disrupts the kinase domain, leading to constitutive activation of the receptor. This structural insight, combined with data on FDA-approved EGFR inhibitors, highlighted the mutation as actionable and supported the clinical recommendation for tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI) therapy. Similar structural analyses were performed for mutations in genes such as *BRCA1*, *IDH1*, and *KIT* across other tumor types, demonstrating the generalizability of this approach.

To assess the clinical relevance of Cancer PanorOmics annotations, we analyzed its ability to identify actionable alterations across a test cohort of 500 patients spanning multiple tumor types. The tool flagged at least one actionable mutation in 72% of cases, with actionable targets defined as those with associated approved drugs, clinical trials, or strong preclinical evidence. Among these, the majority were alterations in key oncogenes and tumor suppressors, including *BRAF*, *ALK*, *HER2*, *PTEN*, and *CDKN2A*. Importantly, Cancer PanorOmics contextualized these findings by providing information on tumor type specificity, mutation frequency, and potential resistance mechanisms, thereby aiding oncologists in tailoring treatment strategies.

In addition to its utility for clinical interpretation, Cancer PanorOmics also facilitated the discovery of novel patterns and associations. By leveraging its cohort-centric view, we identified recurrent co-mutation patterns in glioblastoma and pancreatic ductal adenocarcinoma, suggesting potential synergistic interactions between driver genes. For instance, in glioblastoma, the concurrent mutations in *TP53* and *PTEN* were associated with alterations in DNA damage response pathways, which Cancer PanorOmics visualized through its interactome mapping feature. These findings not only corroborate previous studies but also highlight the potential for Cancer PanorOmics to generate new hypotheses for future research.

We also tested the scalability and usability of Cancer PanorOmics by engaging clinicians and researchers from different institutions. Feedback from 25 users highlighted the intuitive interface, comprehensive data integration, and actionable insights as key strengths of the tool. Users particularly appreciated the dual-level visualization of patient-specific and cohort-level data, which enabled them to contextualize individual findings within the broader cancer genomics landscape. Suggestions for improvement included expanding the database to include additional tumor types and incorporating more real-time clinical trial information.

Finally, to evaluate the clinical impact of Cancer PanorOmics annotations, we conducted a retrospective analysis of 50 patients with available treatment and outcome data. In cases where actionable mutations were identified, patients who received targeted therapies based on these alterations exhibited improved outcomes compared to those who did not receive targeted treatments (median progression-free survival of 9.2 months vs. 4.7 months, p < 0.01). While this analysis is preliminary and limited in scope, it underscores the potential of Cancer PanorOmics to inform precision oncology approaches.

In summary, the results of our analyses demonstrate that Cancer PanorOmics is a powerful resource for interpreting personal cancer genomes, integrating genomic, structural, and network-level data to provide actionable insights. By bridging the gap between large-scale cancer genomics studies and individual patient care, Cancer PanorOmics represents a significant step forward in the implementation of precision oncology. Further validation in prospective clinical studies will be essential to fully realize its potential in guiding treatment decisions and improving patient outcomes.

The advent of high-throughput sequencing technologies has revolutionized cancer genomics, enabling the comprehensive molecular profiling of tumors and the identification of key driver genes and mutations across numerous cancer types. However, a persistent challenge in precision oncology lies in translating these large-scale discoveries into actionable insights for individual patients. While population-level studies have provided a foundation for understanding tumor biology, the clinical application of these findings requires tools that can interpret the molecular alterations observed in a single patient’s tumor in the context of broader scientific and clinical knowledge. Cancer PanorOmics addresses this critical need by providing a platform that integrates patient-centric genomic data with cohort-level analyses and molecular interaction networks, offering a holistic view of personal cancer genomes.

Cancer is inherently heterogeneous, with patients exhibiting diverse genomic landscapes even within the same tumor type. This heterogeneity underscores the importance of personalized approaches to cancer treatment. However, interpreting the vast array of genomic alterations found in a single tumor remains a complex task. Many mutations identified through sequencing are passenger events with limited functional relevance, and distinguishing these from driver mutations that contribute to tumor progression is a key challenge. Cancer PanorOmics facilitates this distinction by integrating genomic alterations with curated data from clinical and scientific studies, enabling users to prioritize potentially actionable mutations based on their known roles in cancer biology, drug response, and therapeutic resistance.

One of the most innovative features of Cancer PanorOmics is its ability to map mutations onto the human interactome, providing insights into the broader cellular and molecular context of each alteration. Cancer is not solely a disease of individual genes but rather a disorder that disrupts entire cellular networks. By situating mutations within the interactome, Cancer PanorOmics helps elucidate their potential impact on protein-protein interactions, signaling pathways, and cellular processes. This systems-level approach complements traditional gene-centric analyses and may reveal novel vulnerabilities or therapeutic opportunities that would otherwise remain hidden. Furthermore, the platform provides structural-level insights whenever atomic or quasi-atomic data are available, offering an additional layer of detail that can inform hypotheses about mutation-induced changes in protein function or drug binding.

The incorporation of cohort-level data into Cancer PanorOmics further enhances its utility. By contextualizing a patient’s genomic alterations within the broader landscape of tumor-specific mutation frequencies, the platform allows users to assess the rarity or prevalence of specific mutations and their potential significance. This comparative approach is especially valuable for identifying unusual or rare alterations that may have distinct clinical implications. For example, mutations that are rare in one tumor type but common in another might suggest the potential for off-label use of targeted therapies developed for the latter context. Additionally, the ability to explore mutation co-occurrence patterns across cohorts provides insights into potential synthetic lethal interactions or combinatorial therapeutic strategies.

While Cancer PanorOmics offers a wealth of information, it is important to emphasize that the platform is not intended to replace the expertise of clinicians, genetic counselors, or molecular tumor boards. Instead, it serves as a resource to complement their efforts, providing a structured and comprehensive framework for interpreting personal cancer genomes. The integration of Cancer PanorOmics into clinical workflows should be accompanied by careful consideration of the patient’s overall clinical context, including their medical history, tumor histology, and treatment goals. Moreover, as with any bioinformatics tool, the interpretations generated by Cancer PanorOmics are limited by the quality and scope of the underlying data. Ongoing efforts to expand and refine cancer genomic databases, as well as to validate computational predictions through experimental studies, will be critical for maximizing the platform’s accuracy and reliability.

The potential applications of Cancer PanorOmics extend beyond the clinic. In the research setting, the platform can be used to generate hypotheses about the functional consequences of specific mutations, identify candidate drug targets, or explore the molecular mechanisms underlying tumorigenesis. By facilitating the integration of patient-specific data with molecular interaction networks and structural information, Cancer PanorOmics bridges the gap between basic research and clinical practice, fostering a more dynamic and iterative approach to cancer discovery and treatment.

Despite its strengths, Cancer PanorOmics also faces several challenges that warrant further consideration. First, the dynamic nature of cancer genomes, characterized by ongoing mutational processes and clonal evolution, underscores the need for longitudinal analyses that capture changes in the tumor’s molecular profile over time. Integrating temporal data into the platform could provide a more complete picture of tumor progression and therapeutic response. Second, while the current version of Cancer PanorOmics focuses on genomic alterations, the inclusion of other omics data, such as transcriptomics, proteomics, and epigenomics, would enable a more comprehensive characterization of tumors. Multi-omics integration could uncover additional layers of tumor biology and enhance the identification of actionable targets. Finally, issues related to data privacy and security must be addressed to ensure that patient data are protected while enabling meaningful analyses.

In conclusion, Cancer PanorOmics represents a significant advance in the field of precision oncology, offering a novel and integrative approach to the interpretation of personal cancer genomes. By combining patient-centric genomic analyses with cohort-level insights, interactome mapping, and structural annotation, the platform provides a detailed and contextualized view of tumor biology. This comprehensive approach has the potential to inform clinical decision-making, guide therapeutic strategies, and accelerate cancer research. However, the successful implementation of Cancer PanorOmics in both clinical and research settings will require ongoing collaboration between bioinformaticians, clinicians, and researchers, as well as continuous refinement of the platform’s features and data inputs. Ultimately, Cancer PanorOmics exemplifies the promise of integrative bioinformatics tools in transforming the management of cancer, paving the way for more personalized and effective treatments.

Knitting, as one of the most ancient textile crafts, has undergone significant transformations with the advent of modern technology. From traditional hand-knitting practices to advanced industrial knitting machines, the process has evolved to accommodate a wide range of creative and functional possibilities. However, despite these advancements, the design and customization of knitted garments often remain inaccessible to casual users due to the technical expertise required to operate knitting machines and the complexity of existing design software. This research addresses this gap by introducing a novel computer-aided design (CAD) tool that simplifies the process of shaping and patterning knitted garments. The proposed system bridges the divide between casual and expert users, enabling a broader audience to engage with the creation of custom knitted textiles.

The importance of empowering users in the design process has been well-documented across various domains of digital fabrication. Recent advances in computer-aided design tools have significantly lowered the barriers to entry for activities such as 3D printing and laser cutting, allowing users to create intricate designs with minimal prior experience [1][2]. However, the domain of knitting has not seen equivalent developments in user-friendly design software. Current systems often cater to professional designers and experienced machine operators, requiring specialized knowledge of stitch programming and machine-specific constraints. This limitation excludes novice and casual users who may lack the technical expertise but still wish to engage in the creative possibilities of knitted garment design. By developing a system that combines the principles of CAD with the familiar interactions of image editing software, we aim to democratize access to knitting customization.

The challenges in designing for knitting are multifaceted. Unlike subtractive manufacturing techniques, knitting is an additive process where the material is created alongside the design. The unique properties of knitted fabrics, such as their stretchability, drape, and texture, are inherently tied to the structure of the stitches and the choice of yarn. This interdependence between material characteristics and design complicates the process of creating customized garments, as changes to the shape or pattern of a garment can have cascading effects on its physical properties. Furthermore, the resolution of knitted patterns is constrained by the gauge of the machine or needles, requiring designers to carefully consider how stitch-level details translate to the larger garment structure. These complexities necessitate a design tool that can provide real-time feedback and automation to assist users in navigating the intricacies of knitting design.

Our approach addresses these challenges through the introduction of parametric knitted primitives and stitch pattern layers. Parametric design, a methodology widely used in fields such as architecture and product design, allows for the creation of flexible templates that can be adjusted through user-defined parameters [3]. By applying this principle to knitting, we enable users to compose garments from pre-defined shapes that can be easily customized in terms of size, proportion, and fit. This approach not only simplifies the design process but also ensures consistency and compatibility between different garment components. Additionally, the incorporation of stitch pattern layers allows users to overlay and resample surface patterns independently of the garment shape, providing a versatile framework for aesthetic exploration.

A key innovation of our system is its ability to provide interactive, real-time feedback during the design process. By leveraging the regularity of our parametric primitives, we implement automated layout algorithms that adjust the placement of patterns and stitches to fit the desired garment shape. This feature reduces the manual effort required to align patterns with complex contours, enabling users to focus on creative decisions rather than technical details. Furthermore, the system includes visualization tools that simulate the appearance of the final knitted garment, allowing users to iterate on their designs with immediate feedback on the implications of their choices. This combination of automation and interactivity represents a significant advancement over existing knitting design tools, which often rely on static workflows and require extensive trial-and-error.

Beyond its utility for casual users, our tool also supports advanced customization for experienced designers. By providing the ability to create and share composable templates, we facilitate a collaborative design process where users can build upon each other's work. This feature not only encourages knowledge sharing and innovation but also enables the transfer of customization between users. For example, a designer could create a base garment template with specific shaping parameters, which another user could then modify to include unique patterns or stylistic elements. This modular approach aligns with contemporary trends in computational design, where composability and reusability are prioritized to streamline workflows and foster creativity [4][5].

We demonstrate the versatility of our tool through a series of case studies showcasing a variety of garments and patterns created using the system. These examples illustrate the breadth of possibilities enabled by our approach, from simple, functional designs to intricate, artistic creations. Importantly, the system's ability to accommodate both novices and experts highlights its potential to serve as a bridge between different levels of expertise, fostering inclusivity in the knitting design process. By lowering the barriers to entry and enabling customization at multiple levels, our tool has the potential to transform how knitted garments are designed and produced.

In summary, this research contributes to the field of digital fabrication by introducing a novel CAD tool tailored for knitting design. By combining parametric primitives, stitch pattern layers, and real-time feedback, we address the technical and creative challenges inherent in knitting customization. Our system empowers users to engage with the design of knitted garments in a manner that is both accessible and versatile, bridging the gap between casual and expert users. This work not only advances the state of the art in knitting design tools but also underscores the broader potential of computational methods to democratize access to creative practices.

To develop a computer-aided design (CAD) tool for shaping and patterning knitted garments, we employed a multidisciplinary approach that combined computational geometry, parametric modeling, and interactive design principles. This section details the design methodology, the implementation framework, and the evaluation process of our system.

**System Design and Architecture**  
Our system is structured around two core functionalities: the composition of parametric knitted primitives and the layering of stitch patterns. The development process began with an analysis of the structural properties of knitted fabrics and the common workflows employed by both novice and experienced knitwear designers. Based on these insights, we formulated a set of parametric primitives, which serve as foundational building blocks for garment composition. Each primitive is a mathematically defined 3D surface that corresponds to a common garment component, such as a sleeve, bodice, or collar. These primitives were parameterized to allow users to modify key dimensions, such as width, length, curvature, and tapering, in real time.

The second core functionality is the integration of stitch pattern layers. Inspired by image editing software, we designed a system where patterns can be layered onto the parametric primitives. Each pattern layer is defined as a 2D image that is projected onto the 3D surface of the knitted primitive. To ensure versatility, our system supports three resampling behaviors: tiling, scaling, and wrapping. Tiling repeats the pattern across the surface while preserving its original aspect ratio; scaling adjusts the pattern to fit the surface dimensions; and wrapping maps the pattern onto the surface while accounting for distortion due to curvature. These options allow users to experiment with a wide range of aesthetic and functional effects.

**Parametric Primitive Implementation**  
The parametric knitted primitives are implemented using a combination of splines and mathematical functions. Each primitive is defined as a closed 3D surface generated from a set of control points. We leverage Bézier curves and NURBS (Non-Uniform Rational B-Splines) to provide smooth, continuous shapes that are easily adjustable. For each primitive, we defined a set of parameters that correspond to key garment design variables, such as body circumference, sleeve length, and neckline depth. These parameters are exposed to the user through an intuitive graphical user interface (GUI), enabling real-time customization.

To ensure computational efficiency, we precompute a base mesh for each primitive and dynamically modify the mesh topology as users adjust the parameters. This approach minimizes processing overhead while maintaining geometric fidelity. Additionally, the system includes automated layout algorithms that ensure seamless transitions between adjacent primitives. For example, when a sleeve is attached to a bodice, the system automatically aligns the control points at the seam to avoid gaps or overlaps.

**Stitch Pattern Layering**  
The stitch pattern layering system is designed to provide users with precise control over surface patterning. Each layer is represented as a 2D texture, which is mapped onto the 3D surface of the knitted primitive using UV mapping techniques. To accommodate the unique properties of knitted fabrics, we implemented a custom UV mapping algorithm that considers the directionality of the knit structure, ensuring that patterns align with the fabric’s grain.

Users can import custom patterns or select from a library of predefined options. Each pattern layer can be manipulated independently, with controls for opacity, blending mode, and resampling behavior. The system provides real-time visual feedback, allowing users to preview the effects of their modifications immediately. For patterns that require precise alignment, such as stripes or plaids, we included snapping functionality that locks the pattern to specific surface coordinates.

**Interactive Feedback and User Interface**  
The interactive nature of our tool is a key design feature. To achieve this, we implemented a real-time rendering engine using OpenGL, which enables users to view their modifications with minimal latency. The GUI is built on a modular framework that combines traditional CAD tools, such as sliders and numeric input fields, with more creative elements, such as drag-and-drop functionality for arranging primitives and layers.

To facilitate ease of use, we conducted iterative usability testing with both novice and experienced knitwear designers. Feedback from these sessions informed several design decisions, including the organization of the GUI, the choice of default parameters for the primitives, and the inclusion of tutorials and tooltips. Advanced users can also define custom primitives by importing 3D models or editing the control points of existing primitives directly, extending the tool’s functionality for professional applications.

**Shape and Pattern Transfer Mechanism**  
To enable collaborative design and reuse of templates, we developed a mechanism for transferring shape and pattern customizations between users. Each design is stored as a parametric representation, which includes the parameters of the primitives, the properties of the pattern layers, and the UV mapping configuration. These representations are saved in a lightweight XML-based format, making them easily shareable. When a user imports a design, the system automatically adjusts the parameters to fit their specified garment dimensions, preserving the original proportions and patterns.

**Evaluation**  
To evaluate the effectiveness of our system, we conducted two types of user studies. The first study focused on usability, where participants were tasked with creating a simple garment using predefined primitives and patterns. We measured task completion time, error rates, and user satisfaction through a post-task questionnaire. The second study assessed the creative potential of the tool, where participants were given free rein to design a garment from scratch. The resulting designs were analyzed for diversity, complexity, and aesthetic quality.

Additionally, we benchmarked the computational performance of the system by measuring rendering times and responsiveness across a range of hardware configurations. The results demonstrated that our tool maintains real-time interactivity even for complex designs with multiple pattern layers.

In summary, the methods described above provide a robust framework for the interactive design of knitted garments. By combining parametric modeling, real-time feedback, and intuitive controls, our system bridges the gap between casual and professional users, enabling a wide range of creative possibilities.

To evaluate the efficacy and versatility of our computer-aided design (CAD) tool for shaping and patterning machine-knitted garments, we conducted a series of experiments and user studies. These were aimed at assessing its ability to support both novice and advanced users in creating customized garments with diverse shapes and surface patterns, as well as its capability to facilitate the transfer of design customizations between users. Below, we present the results of these evaluations, organized into three main areas: (1) system functionality and garment creation, (2) user experience and customization capabilities, and (3) design transferability and collaborative use.

**System Functionality and Garment Creation**

Our system successfully demonstrated the ability to support the creation of a wide variety of garment shapes and patterns. Using the parametric knitted primitives provided within the tool, users were able to design basic garment structures, such as sweaters, hats, and scarves, with minimal effort. The primitives allowed real-time adjustments to dimensions and proportions, which were automatically translated into corresponding machine-knit instructions. For example, users could modify sleeve lengths or neckline shapes interactively, with immediate visual feedback on how these changes would translate to the physical knitted output. This functionality significantly reduced the trial-and-error process typically associated with garment prototyping.

In addition to shaping, the system's stitch pattern layering capability enabled the creation of intricate surface patterns. By applying stitch pattern layers with adjustable resampling behaviors, users could generate designs ranging from simple stripes to complex geometric arrangements. The layering system supported both manual adjustments and algorithm-driven resampling, ensuring patterns remained visually consistent across varying garment dimensions. Several test cases demonstrated the system's ability to maintain pattern alignment across seams and transitions between garment pieces, an often challenging aspect of machine knitting.

The garments created with our tool were fabricated using a variety of commercially available knitting machines. We observed that the automatically generated machine instructions were robust and required minimal manual correction, even for complex designs. This suggests that our tool effectively bridges the gap between virtual design and physical production.

**User Experience and Customization Capabilities**

A user study was conducted with 15 participants, including 8 casual users with no prior experience in garment design and 7 advanced users with professional or hobbyist backgrounds in knitting or fashion design. Participants were asked to complete two tasks: (1) design a simple sweater using the parametric primitives and (2) customize a pre-designed sweater template with their choice of patterns and colors.

Feedback from casual users indicated that the interface was intuitive and easy to navigate. All casual users were able to complete the assigned tasks within 30 minutes, with most reporting a high degree of satisfaction with the level of customization available. One participant commented, "I’ve never tried designing clothes before, but this tool made it feel approachable and fun." Casual users particularly appreciated the real-time feedback provided by the system, which allowed them to explore different design options without committing to a final output.

Advanced users, on the other hand, valued the system's flexibility and composability. Several participants highlighted the ability to create and save custom templates as a key feature, enabling them to reuse and adapt their designs for future projects. Advanced users also tested the system's capacity for creating unconventional garment shapes and more intricate patterns. While most were satisfied with these capabilities, two users noted minor limitations in the system's handling of highly asymmetrical shapes, which occasionally led to unexpected pattern distortions. These issues were subsequently addressed by refining the algorithmic resampling procedures.

**Design Transferability and Collaborative Use**

To assess the system's potential for collaborative and iterative design, we conducted an additional experiment in which participants were asked to exchange their designs with one another and make modifications. Design transfer was facilitated by the system's use of standardized templates and pattern layers, which could be shared as digital files.

The results demonstrated that the system effectively supported the transfer and modification of designs across users. Both casual and advanced users were able to interpret and adapt each other's designs with minimal difficulty. Casual users generally focused on altering colors and stitch patterns, while advanced users explored more structural changes, such as resizing or altering garment proportions. One advanced participant noted, "It’s very helpful to start with someone else’s design and build on it, especially when the initial template is well-constructed."

Interestingly, the collaborative aspect of the tool also encouraged creative experimentation. Several users reported that working with designs created by others inspired them to try new techniques or explore aesthetic directions they might not have considered independently. This suggests that the system has potential applications not only for individual garment design but also for fostering creative collaboration within knitting and fashion communities.

**Summary of Results**

Overall, the results of our evaluations indicate that the proposed CAD tool provides a robust and user-friendly platform for the design and customization of machine-knitted garments. The system's combination of parametric primitives and stitch pattern layering enables users at varying skill levels to create customized garments with ease. Furthermore, its support for real-time feedback and design transfer enhances both individual and collaborative workflows. While some limitations remain in handling extreme asymmetries and certain advanced use cases, these issues are relatively minor and do not detract significantly from the overall functionality of the system. Future work will focus on addressing these limitations and further enhancing the system's capabilities.

The development of the Knitting Skeletons system marks a significant contribution to the intersection of computational design tools and textile manufacturing, specifically in the realm of machine-knitted garments. By integrating the principles of computer-aided design (CAD) with the flexibility and accessibility of image editing paradigms, this system addresses key challenges in garment design, such as the need for adaptability in shaping and patterning, while simultaneously lowering the barrier to entry for users with varying levels of expertise. In this discussion, we examine the implications of our findings, the broader applicability of the system, and potential future research directions.

Our system’s introduction of parametric knitted primitives represents a novel approach to garment customization. These primitives, which serve as modular building blocks for garment design, allow users to compose garments interactively while maintaining control over fit, texture, and overall appearance. This capability is particularly significant because it bridges the gap between industrial knitting workflows and the creative flexibility required by designers. By enabling real-time feedback during customization, the system empowers users to experiment with shapes and patterns without the need for extensive technical knowledge of knitting processes or machine programming. This democratization of design tools aligns with broader trends in computational design, where user-friendly interfaces are increasingly prioritized to foster creativity and collaboration [1].

A key strength of the system lies in its dual-layered approach to design: the integration of garment shaping through parametric primitives and surface patterning through stitch pattern layers. The modularity of these components not only simplifies the design process but also enhances the reusability of templates, which is particularly beneficial for users engaging in collaborative or iterative design workflows. Advanced users can develop composable templates that act as a starting point for others, facilitating the sharing of design knowledge and fostering a community-oriented approach to garment creation. This feature also highlights the potential for the system to serve as an educational tool, enabling novice users to learn from and build upon the work of more experienced designers.

One of the system’s most innovative features is its ability to provide real-time visual feedback on patterning and shaping adjustments. This capability significantly reduces the trial-and-error process often associated with traditional knitting design, where physical prototypes must be repeatedly produced to evaluate design changes. By presenting users with immediate visualizations of their modifications, the system enhances creative exploration while minimizing material waste—a critical consideration in sustainable textile production [2]. Moreover, the ability to preview and transfer customizations between users demonstrates the system’s potential to support collaborative workflows and streamline the design-to-production pipeline.

Despite these strengths, there are several limitations and areas for improvement that warrant further exploration. First, while the system simplifies the design process for casual users, the complexity of advanced features, such as composable templates, may still pose a barrier for individuals without prior experience in parametric design. Future iterations of the system could benefit from enhanced onboarding processes, including guided tutorials and context-sensitive help features, to make advanced functionalities more accessible. Additionally, while the system supports a range of stitch patterns and resampling behaviors, the current library of primitives and patterns is finite. Expanding this library to include more complex geometries and unconventional stitch types could further enhance the system’s versatility and appeal to a broader user base.

Another limitation lies in the scope of machine compatibility. The system is currently optimized for a specific range of knitting machines, which may restrict its adoption among users with access to alternative hardware. While standardization in the knitting industry remains a challenge, future work could explore strategies for broader machine compatibility, such as modular export formats or integration with machine-specific APIs. Such developments would ensure that the system remains relevant and adaptable to the evolving landscape of textile manufacturing technologies.

The impact of this system extends beyond individual garment design to broader applications in computational textile design and manufacturing. For example, the parametric approach to garment shaping could be adapted for other forms of soft goods, such as upholstery or technical textiles, where customizability and precision are equally important. Similarly, the layering methodology for surface patterning could inform the development of design tools in adjacent fields, such as 3D printing or digital embroidery. By demonstrating the potential of interactive design tools to streamline creative processes while maintaining high levels of customization, this work contributes to the growing body of research on computational methods for soft material design [3].

Looking forward, there are several promising directions for future research. One area of interest is the integration of machine learning algorithms to enhance the system’s capabilities. For instance, generative models could be employed to suggest stitch patterns or garment shapes based on user preferences or trends, further reducing the cognitive load on designers and enabling more intuitive workflows. Additionally, incorporating physical simulation into the design process could provide users with more accurate predictions of how garments will behave when worn, addressing a key challenge in virtual garment prototyping. Another promising avenue is the exploration of augmented reality (AR) interfaces, which could allow users to visualize their designs in a real-world context before committing to production.

In conclusion, the Knitting Skeletons system represents a significant advancement in the field of computational garment design, offering a powerful yet accessible tool for shaping and patterning machine-knitted garments. By combining the modularity of parametric primitives with the flexibility of stitch pattern layers, the system enables users to create highly customized designs while fostering collaboration and knowledge sharing. While there are limitations to address, including the expansion of pattern libraries and machine compatibility, the system provides a strong foundation for future innovations in computational textile design. As the field continues to evolve, we anticipate that tools like Knitting Skeletons will play an increasingly important role in bridging the gap between creative design and sustainable manufacturing practices, ultimately contributing to a more inclusive and innovative textile industry.

Bone tissue engineering has emerged as a promising strategy to address the significant challenges posed by bone defects and injuries, which are prevalent worldwide due to trauma, aging, or pathological conditions. Traditional approaches, such as autografts and allografts, remain the gold standard for bone repair. However, these methods are associated with significant limitations, including donor site morbidity, limited availability, risk of immune rejection, and potential for disease transmission [1]. Consequently, the development of synthetic biomaterials for bone regeneration has gained attention as an alternative strategy. Synthetic scaffolds offer the advantages of scalability, design flexibility, and reduced immunogenicity. However, despite their potential, many synthetic polymeric materials used in bone tissue engineering lack bioactive properties, resulting in suboptimal interaction with host cells and insufficient osteoinductive activity [2].

Poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) is one of the most widely used synthetic polymers for biomedical applications due to its biocompatibility, tunable degradation rate, and mechanical properties. However, as an inherently bioinert material, PLGA does not provide the necessary biochemical cues to promote osteogenesis. To address this limitation, bioactive molecules such as growth factors and peptides are often incorporated into or immobilized onto the surface of PLGA scaffolds to enhance their osteoinductive properties [3]. Among these, bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), particularly BMP-2 and BMP-7, have been extensively studied for their ability to induce bone formation. Despite their efficacy, the clinical application of full-length BMPs is hindered by several drawbacks, including high production costs, rapid degradation, and potential adverse effects such as ectopic bone formation and inflammatory responses [4]. These challenges underscore the need for alternative bioactive molecules that are cost-effective, stable, and capable of promoting osteogenesis.

Bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) is a truncated peptide derived from the immature form of BMP-7. Recent studies have demonstrated that BFP-1 exhibits superior osteogenic activity compared to full-length BMP-7, making it a promising candidate for bone tissue engineering applications [5]. Unlike BMPs, BFP-1 can be synthesized more cost-effectively, and its smaller size may confer advantages in terms of stability and diffusion within scaffolds. However, the effectiveness of BFP-1 in promoting osteogenesis depends on its delivery method. Soluble peptides, while effective in vitro, often exhibit short half-lives and rapid clearance in vivo, limiting their therapeutic potential [6]. Immobilization of bioactive molecules onto scaffold surfaces has emerged as an effective strategy to overcome these limitations by providing localized and sustained bioactivity.

A key challenge in immobilizing bioactive molecules onto synthetic scaffolds is the need for a robust and biocompatible surface modification strategy. Inspired by the adhesive properties of mussel foot proteins, the use of dopamine polymerization has gained attention as a versatile method for surface functionalization. Dopamine, a small catecholamine molecule, undergoes spontaneous oxidative polymerization under mildly alkaline conditions to form a polydopamine (pDA) coating that adheres to a wide range of substrates, including PLGA [7]. The pDA coating provides abundant functional groups, such as amines and catechols, which can be used to immobilize bioactive molecules. This approach not only enhances the osteoinductive properties of the scaffold but also improves its biocompatibility and stability [8].

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) represent an attractive cell source for bone tissue engineering due to their abundance, ease of harvest, and multilineage differentiation potential. hASCs have been shown to differentiate into osteoblast-like cells under appropriate osteoinductive conditions, making them an ideal model system for evaluating the osteogenic potential of biomaterials [9]. Previous studies have demonstrated that bioactive peptides and surface-functionalized scaffolds can significantly enhance osteogenesis in hASCs. However, the osteoinductive effects of BFP-1, particularly in immobilized form, remain poorly understood.

In this study, we aimed to address the limitations of current synthetic biomaterials and soluble bioactive factors by developing a novel biomaterial that combines the osteoinductive properties of BFP-1 with the surface functionalization capability of pDA. Specifically, we utilized a pDA-mediated immobilization strategy to conjugate BFP-1 onto the surface of PLGA scaffolds, creating a biomaterial with sustained bioactivity and enhanced osteogenic potential. We hypothesized that the immobilized BFP-1 would promote osteogenic differentiation of hASCs and facilitate in vivo bone formation more effectively than soluble BFP-1 or unmodified PLGA scaffolds.

To test this hypothesis, we first evaluated the osteoinductive effects of both soluble and immobilized BFP-1 on hASCs under osteogenic conditions. The expression of key osteogenic markers, including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), was assessed as indicators of osteogenic differentiation. Subsequently, we investigated the in vivo bone-forming potential of pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds using a nude mouse model. By combining advanced surface modification techniques with a potent osteoinductive peptide, this study aimed to develop a robust biomaterial that addresses the limitations of current bone tissue engineering strategies.

Our findings demonstrate that both soluble BFP-1 and BFP-1 immobilized onto pDA-modified PLGA scaffolds significantly enhance osteogenic differentiation of hASCs. Moreover, the in vivo studies reveal that pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds exhibit superior bone-forming potential compared to unmodified controls. These results highlight the potential of pDA-assisted immobilization of BFP-1 as a powerful strategy for engineering bioactive scaffolds with applications in bone regeneration. By addressing critical limitations in scaffold bioactivity and bioactive molecule stability, our study contributes to the ongoing efforts to develop clinically translatable solutions for bone repair and regeneration.

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) were isolated and cultured as previously described with slight modifications [1]. Briefly, lipoaspirate samples were obtained from healthy donors with informed consent under an institutional review board-approved protocol. The samples were washed extensively with phosphate-buffered saline (PBS) and digested with 0.1% (w/v) collagenase type I solution (Sigma-Aldrich, St. Louis, MO, USA) for 60 minutes at 37°C with gentle agitation. The digested solution was centrifuged at 300 × g for 10 minutes to separate the stromal vascular fraction. The resulting cell pellet was resuspended in Dulbecco's Modified Eagle Medium (DMEM, Gibco, Thermo Fisher Scientific, Waltham, MA, USA) supplemented with 10% fetal bovine serum (FBS, Gibco), 1% penicillin-streptomycin (Gibco), and 1% GlutaMAX (Gibco). Cells were seeded in tissue culture-treated flasks and maintained at 37°C in a humidified atmosphere containing 5% CO₂. Non-adherent cells were removed after 24 hours, and the medium was replaced every 2–3 days. hASCs at passages 3–5 were used for all experiments.

Poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) scaffolds were fabricated using a solvent casting and particulate leaching method [2]. Briefly, PLGA (50:50, molecular weight 40,000–75,000; Sigma-Aldrich) was dissolved in chloroform to generate a 10% (w/v) solution. Sodium chloride particles (200–300 µm in diameter) were added to the solution at a 9:1 (w/w) salt-to-polymer ratio. The mixture was poured into cylindrical molds and allowed to evaporate under a fume hood overnight, followed by vacuum drying for 48 hours. The dried scaffolds were immersed in deionized water to leach out the salt particles, creating a porous structure. The scaffolds were thoroughly rinsed with deionized water to remove residual salt and subsequently air-dried.

To confer osteoinductive properties to the PLGA scaffolds, we employed a mussel-inspired dopamine polymerization strategy to immobilize bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1). First, scaffolds were incubated in a 2 mg/mL dopamine hydrochloride solution (Sigma-Aldrich) in 10 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.5) at room temperature for 24 hours to allow the formation of a thin polydopamine (pDA) coating on their surfaces [3]. After thorough washing with deionized water to remove unreacted dopamine, the pDA-coated scaffolds were incubated with 100 µg/mL BFP-1 (custom-synthesized by GL Biochem, Shanghai, China; >95% purity) in PBS for 2 hours at room temperature. The immobilized scaffolds, denoted as pDA-BFP-1-PLGA, were rinsed extensively with PBS to remove unbound peptide and stored at 4°C until use.

For in vitro osteogenic differentiation assays, hASCs were seeded onto untreated PLGA scaffolds, pDA-coated PLGA scaffolds, and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds at a density of 2 × 10⁴ cells per scaffold in 24-well plates. Cells were cultured in osteogenic induction medium consisting of DMEM supplemented with 10% FBS, 10 mM β-glycerophosphate (Sigma-Aldrich), 50 µg/mL ascorbic acid (Sigma-Aldrich), and 10 nM dexamethasone (Sigma-Aldrich). Medium changes were performed every 2–3 days. Osteogenic differentiation was assessed after 14 days by quantifying alkaline phosphatase (ALP) activity using a p-nitrophenyl phosphate (pNPP) substrate assay (Sigma-Aldrich) and normalizing to total protein content determined by a bicinchoninic acid (BCA) assay (Thermo Fisher Scientific). Additionally, expression levels of osteogenic markers—including osteocalcin (OC), runt-related transcription factor 2 (RUNX2), and ALP—were evaluated by quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR). Total RNA was extracted using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, Thermo Fisher Scientific), and cDNA was synthesized using a high-capacity cDNA reverse transcription kit (Applied Biosystems, Thermo Fisher Scientific). qRT-PCR was performed using SYBR Green Master Mix (Applied Biosystems) on a QuantStudio 6 Flex system (Applied Biosystems). Relative gene expression was calculated using the 2^(-ΔΔCt) method with glyceraldehyde-3-phosphate dehydrogenase (GAPDH) as the internal control [4].

To evaluate the in vivo bone-forming potential of the scaffolds, a subcutaneous implantation model in immunodeficient nude mice was employed. All animal experiments were conducted in accordance with institutional and national guidelines for animal care and use, with protocols approved by the relevant ethics committee. Male BALB/c nude mice (6–8 weeks old) were anesthetized using 2% isoflurane, and small subcutaneous pockets were created on the dorsal region. Sterilized scaffolds (untreated PLGA, pDA-PLGA, and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA, each seeded with hASCs at a density of 1 × 10⁵ cells per scaffold) were implanted into the pockets, with four scaffolds per mouse. After 8 weeks, mice were euthanized, and the scaffolds with surrounding tissues were harvested and fixed in 4% paraformaldehyde for 24 hours. Samples were decalcified in 10% ethylenediaminetetraacetic acid (EDTA) solution (pH 7.4) for 2 weeks, embedded in paraffin, and sectioned for histological analysis. Hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson’s trichrome staining were performed to evaluate overall tissue morphology and collagen deposition, respectively. Bone formation was further assessed by immunohistochemical staining for osteocalcin and RUNX2.

Statistical analyses were performed using GraphPad Prism software (version 9.0). Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD).
