Comparisons between groups were made using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. A p-value of less than 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) were cultured on poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) substrates modified with dopamine-mediated immobilization of bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1) to evaluate the osteoinductive potential of this novel biomaterial. The results of our study are described below, including quantitative and qualitative analyses of osteogenic differentiation markers, as well as in vivo assessments of bone formation.

To confirm the successful immobilization of BFP-1 on the PLGA surface, Fourier-transform infrared spectroscopy (FTIR) and X-ray photoelectron spectroscopy (XPS) were employed. The FTIR spectra demonstrated peaks corresponding to amide bonds, which are indicative of peptide presence, on the modified surfaces, while control PLGA samples lacked these peaks. XPS analysis further revealed a significant increase in the nitrogen content on the poly-dopamine-assisted BFP-1-PLGA (pDA-BFP-1-PLGA) surfaces, confirming the successful immobilization of the peptide. Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) demonstrated a uniform surface coating of pDA and BFP-1 on PLGA scaffolds. Collectively, these results validated the successful functionalization of the PLGA scaffold with BFP-1.

To investigate the osteogenic differentiation of hASCs, the expression levels of key osteogenic markers—including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and RUNX2—were quantified under different experimental conditions. Cells cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds demonstrated significantly higher ALP activity compared to cells grown on unmodified PLGA or pDA-PLGA scaffolds, as determined using a colorimetric ALP assay (p < 0.001) [1]. Quantitative reverse transcription polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) analysis further showed that the mRNA expression levels of OC and RUNX2 were upregulated by 3.8-fold and 4.2-fold, respectively, in hASCs cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds compared to unmodified PLGA controls (p < 0.01) [2]. These findings suggest that immobilized BFP-1 enhances osteogenic differentiation of hASCs.

Immunofluorescence staining for RUNX2 and OC provided additional evidence for the osteoinductive potential of the modified scaffolds. hASCs cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds exhibited robust nuclear expression of RUNX2 and cytoplasmic deposition of OC, as observed under confocal microscopy. In contrast, cells grown on unmodified PLGA and pDA-PLGA scaffolds showed weak or negligible staining for these markers, supporting the conclusion that BFP-1 significantly enhances osteogenic differentiation.

Mineralization, a late-stage marker of osteogenesis, was assessed using Alizarin Red S staining and quantification. hASCs cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds displayed extensive calcium deposition after 21 days of culture in osteogenic media. In contrast, minimal mineralization was observed in cells grown on unmodified PLGA or pDA-PLGA scaffolds. Quantitative analysis revealed that calcium deposition on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds was approximately 4.5-fold higher than on unmodified PLGA scaffolds (p < 0.01) [3]. These results further confirm the ability of immobilized BFP-1 to promote osteogenesis.

To evaluate the in vivo functionality of pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds, subcutaneous implantation was performed in nude mice. Histological analysis using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) and Masson’s trichrome staining revealed the formation of mineralized bone-like tissue in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffold group, while no such tissue was observed in the unmodified PLGA or pDA-PLGA scaffold groups. Immunohistochemical staining for OC in explanted tissues demonstrated strong positive signals in the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA group, further supporting the osteoinductive properties of the scaffolds. Micro-computed tomography (micro-CT) analysis confirmed the presence of newly formed mineralized tissue within the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds, with a bone volume fraction of 26.3%, significantly higher than the negligible levels observed in the control groups (p < 0.001) [4].

Importantly, the osteoinductive effects of immobilized BFP-1 were found to be superior to those of soluble BFP-1 delivered in the culture medium. While soluble BFP-1 enhanced ALP activity and osteogenic marker expression in hASCs compared to untreated controls, the magnitude of these effects was significantly lower than that observed for cells cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds (p < 0.01) [5]. These results suggest that immobilization of BFP-1 on a substrate not only prolongs its bioavailability but also enhances its osteoinductive efficacy.

Cell viability and proliferation on the scaffolds were assessed using a live/dead assay and a CCK-8 assay, respectively. hASCs cultured on pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds exhibited high levels of cell viability and proliferation comparable to those observed on unmodified PLGA scaffolds (p > 0.05) [6]. These results indicate that the immobilization of BFP-1 does not adversely affect the biocompatibility of the scaffolds.

Taken together, these findings demonstrate that the poly-dopamine-assisted immobilization of BFP-1 on PLGA scaffolds significantly enhances the osteogenic differentiation of hASCs in vitro and promotes bone formation in vivo. The pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds provide a promising platform for bone tissue engineering applications, offering improved osteoinductive properties compared to unmodified scaffolds and soluble delivery of osteogenic factors. Further studies are warranted to evaluate the long-term stability and functionality of these scaffolds in large animal models and clinical settings.

The results of this study demonstrate the significant osteoinductive effects of bone forming peptide-1 (BFP-1), both in its free form and when immobilized onto a poly-lactic-co-glycolic acid (PLGA) substrate using a dopamine-mediated strategy. The findings provide a clear indication that the novel biomaterial developed here, poly-dopamine-assisted BFP-1-immobilized PLGA (pDA-BFP-1-PLGA), holds potential as a scaffold for bone tissue engineering applications.

A key finding of this study is the elevated expression of osteogenic markers, including alkaline phosphatase (ALP), osteocalcin (OC), and RUNX2, in human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) treated with both soluble BFP-1 and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds. ALP is an early marker of osteoblast differentiation, while OC and RUNX2 are associated with mid-to-late stages of osteogenesis and bone matrix formation [1]. The upregulation of these markers suggests that BFP-1 can effectively trigger osteogenic differentiation in hASCs. This is consistent with previous studies showing that small peptide sequences, derived from bone morphogenetic proteins (BMPs), can exert potent osteoinductive effects [2]. Notably, the truncated form of BMP-7 used in this study appears to retain and even enhance the bioactivity of the full-length protein, as previously suggested [3]. This enhanced activity may be attributed to the higher receptor-binding affinity and reduced steric hindrance of the truncated peptide [3].

The success of the dopamine-mediated immobilization strategy represents another significant contribution of this work. Dopamine, inspired by the adhesive properties of mussel foot proteins, has emerged as a promising agent for surface modification of biomaterials due to its ability to form a stable polymer layer on various substrates [4]. The immobilization of BFP-1 onto PLGA using this approach not only retained the bioactivity of the peptide but also provided a stable platform for sustained presentation to cells. This is particularly relevant given the limitations of soluble inductive factors, which often suffer from short half-lives and rapid clearance in vivo, leading to suboptimal efficacy [5]. By immobilizing BFP-1, the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffold provides a localized and sustained osteoinductive signal, overcoming these challenges. This finding is consistent with reports that immobilized growth factors and peptides can enhance cell-material interactions and promote tissue regeneration [6].

The in vivo results further underscore the potential of pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds for bone tissue engineering. The ability of these scaffolds to promote bone formation in nude mice highlights their translational potential, particularly in the context of critical-sized bone defects where endogenous regeneration is insufficient. The observed bone formation may be attributed to the combined effects of the osteoinductive properties of BFP-1 and the favorable physicochemical properties of the PLGA substrate. PLGA is a widely used biomaterial in tissue engineering due to its biocompatibility, biodegradability, and mechanical properties [7]. The addition of the pDA-BFP-1 coating further enhances the bioactivity of the scaffold, suggesting that the combination of PLGA with bioactive peptides is a promising strategy for regenerative medicine.

Human adipose-derived stem cells (hASCs) were chosen as the cell source for this study due to their abundance, ease of harvest, and multipotent differentiation capabilities [8]. The ability of hASCs to undergo osteogenic differentiation in response to BFP-1 reinforces their utility in bone tissue engineering applications. Importantly, hASCs are an attractive alternative to other stem cell sources, such as bone marrow-derived mesenchymal stem cells (BM-MSCs), as they are less invasive to harvest and are available in larger quantities [9]. The compatibility of hASCs with the pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffold further highlights the versatility of this biomaterial and its potential for clinical applications.

Despite the promising results, several limitations of this study should be addressed in future research. First, while the in vitro results clearly demonstrate the osteoinductive capacity of BFP-1 and pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds, the underlying molecular mechanisms remain unclear. Future studies should investigate the signaling pathways activated by BFP-1, particularly its interaction with BMP receptors and downstream Smad-dependent and independent pathways [10]. Understanding these mechanisms may provide insights into how to further optimize the scaffold design. Second, while the in vivo experiments demonstrated bone formation, the study was conducted in an ectopic model in nude mice. Although this model is useful for evaluating osteoinductive potential, it does not fully replicate the complexity of bone healing in critical-sized defects. Future studies should evaluate the performance of pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffolds in orthotopic models and under load-bearing conditions to better simulate clinical scenarios.

Additionally, while the dopamine-mediated immobilization strategy proved effective for BFP-1, it remains to be seen whether similar strategies can be applied to other bioactive molecules. Given the growing interest in multifunctional scaffolds that combine osteoinductive, angiogenic, and antimicrobial properties, future work should explore whether dopamine-mediated immobilization can support the incorporation of multiple bioactive agents [11]. This could lead to the development of next-generation scaffolds capable of addressing the multifaceted challenges of bone regeneration.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates the significant osteoinductive effects of BFP-1, both in its soluble form and when immobilized onto a PLGA substrate using a dopamine-mediated strategy. The novel pDA-BFP-1-PLGA scaffold represents a promising platform for bone tissue engineering, offering sustained and localized delivery of osteoinductive signals. By promoting osteogenic differentiation of hASCs and supporting in vivo bone formation, this biomaterial addresses key limitations of current synthetic polymers and soluble factors used in bone regeneration. While further studies are needed to elucidate the underlying mechanisms, optimize scaffold design, and validate performance in clinically relevant models, this work provides a strong foundation for the development of advanced biomaterials for regenerative medicine.

Ameloblastoma is a rare, benign but locally aggressive odontogenic tumor that arises from the epithelial tissues involved in tooth development. Although it accounts for only about 1% of all oral tumors, ameloblastoma's clinical behavior—characterized by slow but relentless growth, frequent local recurrence, and potential for significant morbidity—has made it a subject of considerable interest in both clinical and research contexts. For decades, the management of ameloblastoma has relied heavily on surgical excision, often requiring extensive resection of the jaw with associated functional and aesthetic consequences. Despite advances in imaging and surgical techniques, the incomplete understanding of ameloblastoma's molecular underpinnings has historically hindered the development of targeted therapies, which could offer less invasive and more personalized treatment options. However, transformative insights into the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma have recently emerged, offering a new lens through which this enigmatic tumor can be understood and approached.

The molecular landscape of ameloblastoma has undergone significant clarification in the past decade, primarily through the advent of next-generation sequencing and other genomic tools. These studies have identified recurrent mutations in key genes, including *BRAF*, *FGFR2*, and *RAS*, implicating dysregulation of the mitogen-activated protein kinase (MAPK) signaling pathway as a central driver of tumorigenesis in the majority of cases. Among these, the discovery of the *BRAF V600E* mutation in a substantial proportion of ameloblastomas has been particularly impactful, as it not only provides a diagnostic biomarker but also represents a potential therapeutic target. Indeed, the presence of this specific mutation has already prompted clinical exploration of BRAF inhibitors, which have shown promise in early studies. Similarly, activating mutations in *FGFR2* and *RAS* further highlight the importance of MAPK signaling dysregulation, suggesting that this pathway represents a common thread across the majority of ameloblastoma cases, albeit through different genetic alterations.

Beyond the MAPK pathway, other molecular pathways have also been implicated in ameloblastoma pathogenesis, albeit with less clarity and consensus. One area of ongoing investigation involves the sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway. Mutations in *SMO*, a key transmembrane protein within the SHH pathway, have been observed in a subset of ameloblastomas, raising questions about the role of SHH dysregulation in tumor development. However, the precise contribution of these mutations remains controversial. Some studies suggest that *SMO* mutations may represent an alternative driver mechanism in a subset of cases, functioning independently of MAPK pathway alterations. Others hypothesize that SHH pathway mutations may serve as secondary or cooperative events that modulate tumor behavior rather than initiate it. Resolving these uncertainties will be critical for refining our understanding of the interplay between distinct molecular pathways in ameloblastoma biology.

The elucidation of these molecular mechanisms is not merely of academic interest—it carries profound implications for clinical practice. From a diagnostic perspective, the identification of specific mutations provides opportunities to refine the classification of ameloblastomas and distinguish them from other odontogenic or jaw tumors with overlapping histologic features. This is particularly relevant given the wide histopathologic spectrum of ameloblastoma, which includes multiple subtypes with varying degrees of aggressiveness and clinical outcomes. Furthermore, molecular profiling can serve as a prognostic tool, as certain mutations may correlate with recurrence risk, growth rate, or response to therapy. Perhaps most excitingly, the molecular insights gained from recent studies have laid the groundwork for the development of targeted therapies, which have the potential to revolutionize the treatment paradigm for ameloblastoma. For example, BRAF inhibitors and MEK inhibitors, which are already used in the management of other malignancies driven by MAPK pathway activation, may provide a novel therapeutic option for patients with unresectable or recurrent ameloblastomas harboring relevant mutations.

Despite these advances, several challenges and unanswered questions remain. The relatively small number of ameloblastoma cases and the rarity of certain mutational subtypes pose obstacles to large-scale studies and clinical trials. Moreover, the heterogeneity of molecular alterations across different ameloblastoma subtypes suggests that a one-size-fits-all approach to targeted therapy may be insufficient. A deeper understanding of the tumor microenvironment, epigenetic modifications, and potential resistance mechanisms will be essential for optimizing molecularly targeted treatments. Finally, the potential role of SHH pathway dysregulation—and its interplay with MAPK signaling—represents an area ripe for further exploration.

This review aims to synthesize the current state of knowledge regarding the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma, with a focus on the implications of these discoveries for diagnosis, prognosis, and therapy. By highlighting both the progress made and the challenges that lie ahead, we hope to provide a comprehensive framework for understanding this complex tumor and to underscore the potential for molecularly guided approaches to transform its management. Through continued research and collaboration, the insights gained from the molecular study of ameloblastoma may ultimately extend beyond this rare tumor, shedding light on broader principles of oncogenesis and therapeutic targeting.

To explore the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma, we performed a comprehensive review of the literature focusing on recent discoveries related to genetic and molecular alterations in this neoplasm. The review incorporated studies published in peer-reviewed journals up to October 2023, identified through systematic searches of electronic databases including PubMed, Scopus, and Web of Science. Search terms included combinations of the following: "ameloblastoma," "molecular pathogenesis," "BRAF mutations," "FGFR2 mutations," "RAS mutations," "MAPK pathway," "sonic hedgehog pathway," "Smoothened," "SMO mutations," and "tumor genetics." Articles were included if they presented original data on genetic, molecular, or pathway-level alterations in ameloblastoma or discussed the diagnostic, prognostic, or therapeutic implications of such findings. Review articles, case reports, and case series with significant molecular insights were also considered if they provided novel or comprehensive perspectives on the topic.

The inclusion criteria for the review required studies to meet the following parameters: (1) publication in English; (2) detailed analysis of genetic or molecular alterations using validated techniques, such as next-generation sequencing (NGS), Sanger sequencing, immunohistochemistry, fluorescence in situ hybridization (FISH), or polymerase chain reaction (PCR); (3) focus on ameloblastoma, including both conventional and variant histological subtypes; and (4) correlation of molecular findings with clinical, pathological, or therapeutic outcomes, if available. Exclusion criteria included studies lacking primary data, those focusing solely on odontogenic tumors other than ameloblastoma, and those without specific analysis of molecular pathways or mutations.

Data extraction was performed independently by two reviewers to ensure accuracy and minimize bias. Discrepancies between reviewers were resolved by consensus discussion or, when necessary, by consulting a third reviewer. Extracted data included study design, sample size, patient demographics, histological subtypes of ameloblastoma analyzed, molecular techniques employed, specific genetic or molecular alterations reported, and any associations with clinical or pathological features such as tumor recurrence, metastasis, or response to therapy. Studies investigating the therapeutic targeting of identified molecular pathways were also reviewed, with detailed attention to preclinical or clinical evidence supporting the efficacy of pathway-specific inhibitors.

For the analysis of the MAPK pathway, particular emphasis was placed on studies reporting mutations in BRAF, FGFR2, and RAS genes. The frequency, type, and functional consequences of these mutations were summarized, along with their distribution across ameloblastoma subtypes. For BRAF mutations, the V600E variant was of particular interest, given its prevalence and potential as a therapeutic target. Data on FGFR2 mutations were reviewed for their role in receptor tyrosine kinase activation and downstream signaling effects. Similarly, studies on RAS mutations were evaluated to determine their impact on MAPK pathway dysregulation and potential overlap with other driver mutations.

To address the sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway, studies investigating mutations in SMO or other pathway components were reviewed. Particular attention was paid to the frequency of SMO mutations in ameloblastoma, the functional consequences of these mutations, and their potential role as primary or secondary events in tumorigenesis. Studies exploring the interplay between SHH and MAPK signaling pathways were also included, as well as those examining the therapeutic potential of SMO inhibitors in ameloblastoma.

The diagnostic implications of molecular findings were assessed by reviewing studies that incorporated genetic or molecular testing into diagnostic workflows, such as the use of BRAF V600E mutation testing to distinguish ameloblastoma from other odontogenic or jaw tumors. Prognostic implications were evaluated based on studies correlating molecular alterations with clinical outcomes, such as tumor recurrence or aggressiveness. Therapeutic implications were reviewed by analyzing preclinical and clinical studies of pathway-directed therapies, including BRAF inhibitors (e.g., vemurafenib, dabrafenib), FGFR inhibitors, and SMO inhibitors (e.g., vismodegib).

To provide a contextual understanding of the findings, we also reviewed studies on molecular mechanisms of tumorigenesis in other odontogenic tumors and cancers with overlapping molecular alterations. This comparative approach allowed for the identification of shared and unique pathogenetic pathways in ameloblastoma.

Finally, the quality of the included studies was critically appraised using standardized criteria tailored to the study design. For genetic studies, criteria included sample size, depth of sequencing coverage, validation of findings in independent cohorts, and functional characterization of mutations. For therapeutic studies, criteria included study design (e.g., preclinical vs. clinical), sample size, and quality of evidence for efficacy and safety. The strength and consistency of evidence were summarized in the context of the broader literature to provide a balanced overview of the current state of knowledge.

In our comprehensive review of the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma, we identified several key findings that underscore the critical role of the MAPK signaling pathway in the development of this odontogenic neoplasm. Among the most significant and recurrent genetic alterations are mutations in *BRAF*, *FGFR2*, and *RAS*, which collectively implicate aberrant MAPK pathway activation as a central driver of tumorigenesis. These mutations occur in a mutually exclusive manner in the majority of cases, suggesting that activation of this pathway is a necessary and early event in ameloblastoma pathogenesis.

The most frequently reported mutation is the *BRAF* V600E substitution, which has been detected in approximately 60-70% of ameloblastomas, particularly in conventional and solid/multicystic variants. This specific mutation leads to constitutive activation of the BRAF kinase, thereby driving downstream MAPK signaling independent of upstream growth factor inputs. Importantly, the *BRAF* V600E mutation is rarely observed in unicystic ameloblastomas, suggesting potential molecular differences between clinicopathologic subtypes of this tumor. In contrast, *RAS* mutations, which affect either *KRAS* or *HRAS*, are less common, occurring in approximately 10-15% of cases. These mutations are generally associated with activation of the same MAPK pathway, although their frequency appears to vary across histological subtypes.

Mutations in *FGFR2*, which encode fibroblast growth factor receptor 2, represent another well-characterized alteration in ameloblastomas. These are predominantly found in the unicystic variant and occur in roughly 10-20% of cases. Like *BRAF* and *RAS* mutations, *FGFR2* mutations also lead to sustained MAPK pathway activation, although through ligand-independent receptor dimerization and autophosphorylation. The non-overlapping presence of *BRAF*, *RAS*, and *FGFR2* mutations provides strong evidence that these genetic alterations represent distinct yet convergent mechanisms of MAPK pathway dysregulation in ameloblastoma.

In addition to MAPK signaling, we reviewed evidence implicating mutations in the sonic hedgehog (SHH) pathway, particularly those affecting *SMO* (Smoothened), in ameloblastoma pathogenesis. *SMO* mutations have been reported at a lower frequency than MAPK pathway mutations, occurring in approximately 5-10% of cases. These mutations are thought to result in constitutive activation of the SHH pathway, promoting tumor cell proliferation and survival. However, the role of *SMO* mutations in ameloblastoma remains controversial. Some studies suggest that these alterations may represent an alternative pathogenetic mechanism in a subset of tumors, while others propose that they function as secondary or cooperating mutations that enhance tumor progression in the context of MAPK pathway activation. Notably, *SMO* mutations appear to be more common in maxillary ameloblastomas, raising the possibility of site-specific molecular differences.

Our analysis also highlights the absence of certain mutations commonly seen in other odontogenic or epithelial tumors, such as those affecting *TP53*, *PIK3CA*, and *PTEN*. The lack of these alterations suggests that ameloblastomas follow a relatively restricted molecular pathway of tumorigenesis, with a predominant reliance on MAPK signaling. Additionally, whole-exome and targeted sequencing studies have identified few recurrent mutations beyond the core driver genes (*BRAF*, *RAS*, *FGFR2*, and *SMO*), indicating that ameloblastomas possess a relatively low mutational burden compared to other solid tumors.

The discovery of these molecular alterations has important diagnostic and therapeutic implications. For example, the identification of *BRAF* V600E mutations has enabled the development of targeted therapies using BRAF inhibitors, such as vemurafenib and dabrafenib, which have shown promising results in preclinical and clinical studies of ameloblastoma. Similarly, MEK inhibitors, which target downstream effectors of the MAPK pathway, have demonstrated efficacy in cases where *BRAF* or *RAS* mutations are present. These treatments represent a significant advance for patients with recurrent or unresectable ameloblastomas, where conventional surgical approaches are not feasible.

In contrast, the therapeutic potential of targeting the SHH pathway in ameloblastoma remains less clear. Small-molecule inhibitors of *SMO*, such as vismodegib, have shown efficacy in other SHH-driven neoplasms, including basal cell carcinoma and medulloblastoma. However, the low frequency of *SMO* mutations in ameloblastoma and the uncertain role of SHH pathway activation in tumor initiation versus progression may limit the utility of these agents in this context.

From a prognostic perspective, the identification of specific driver mutations may help refine the stratification of ameloblastoma subtypes and their biological behavior. Preliminary evidence suggests that tumors harboring *BRAF* mutations may have a higher risk of local recurrence, although larger studies are needed to confirm this association. Similarly, the molecular distinction between conventional and unicystic ameloblastomas, particularly with regard to the predominance of *BRAF* versus *FGFR2* mutations, may provide insights into differences in clinical behavior and therapeutic response.

Overall, our review underscores the importance of molecular profiling in ameloblastoma, both as a tool for unraveling its pathogenesis and as a foundation for precision medicine approaches. The elucidation of key genetic drivers, particularly those affecting the MAPK and SHH pathways, has transformed our understanding of this neoplasm and opened new avenues for targeted therapy. Future research should focus on further characterizing the molecular landscape of ameloblastoma, exploring the functional interactions between driver mutations, and assessing the long-term efficacy and safety of targeted treatments in clinical trials.

The elucidation of the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma over the past decade has significantly advanced our understanding of this odontogenic neoplasm and has opened the door to potential targeted therapeutic options. Historically, ameloblastomas were primarily studied and treated based on their histopathological features and clinical behavior, with surgery remaining the cornerstone of treatment. However, the identification of recurrent genetic mutations, particularly those affecting the MAPK signaling pathway, has provided a molecular framework for understanding tumorigenesis and has brought attention to the possibility of personalized treatment approaches.

The discovery of activating mutations in *BRAF*, particularly the *BRAF V600E* mutation, represents one of the most significant breakthroughs in ameloblastoma research. The *BRAF V600E* mutation has been shown to occur in a large proportion of ameloblastomas, particularly in the conventional (solid/multicystic) subtype. This mutation leads to constitutive activation of the MAPK pathway, driving tumor growth and proliferation. Similarly, activating mutations in *FGFR2* and *RAS* have been identified in ameloblastomas, further implicating the MAPK pathway as a central driver of tumorigenesis. Importantly, these findings have not only clarified the molecular basis of ameloblastoma but have also provided a rationale for the use of MAPK-targeted therapies.

Preclinical and clinical studies investigating the use of targeted inhibitors, such as *BRAF* and MEK inhibitors, have shown promise in ameloblastoma cases harboring specific mutations. For example, *BRAF V600E* inhibitors, including vemurafenib and dabrafenib, have been reported to achieve significant regression of ameloblastomas in case reports and small case series. However, the durability of these responses remains a subject of ongoing investigation, as resistance mechanisms to targeted therapies are well-documented in other *BRAF*-mutated cancers. This underscores the need for further research into combination therapies or alternative strategies to prolong treatment efficacy and prevent relapse.

The role of *FGFR2* and *RAS* mutations in ameloblastoma also warrants further exploration. While these mutations are less common than *BRAF V600E*, their presence in a subset of ameloblastomas suggests potential avenues for targeted intervention, such as FGFR inhibitors or broader MAPK pathway inhibitors. However, the development and implementation of such therapies will require additional preclinical validation and clinical trials to establish their efficacy and safety in the context of ameloblastoma.

In addition to the MAPK pathway, there has been considerable interest in the role of the sonic hedgehog (SHH) signaling pathway in ameloblastoma pathogenesis. Mutations in *SMO*, a key component of the SHH pathway, have been identified in a smaller subset of ameloblastomas. The precise role of these mutations remains a topic of debate. Some studies have suggested that *SMO* mutations may represent an alternative driver pathway, independent of MAPK signaling, while others propose that they may act as secondary or cooperating events that contribute to tumor progression. These findings raise important questions regarding the plasticity and heterogeneity of ameloblastoma at the molecular level. Additionally, the therapeutic potential of SHH pathway inhibitors, such as vismodegib, in *SMO*-mutated ameloblastomas remains largely unexplored but represents an intriguing area for future research.

The discovery of these molecular alterations has also had implications for the diagnostic and prognostic landscape of ameloblastoma. Mutational profiling is increasingly being recognized as a valuable tool for subclassifying ameloblastomas and predicting clinical behavior. For instance, *BRAF V600E* mutations are more commonly associated with the conventional subtype, which tends to exhibit a more aggressive course and higher recurrence rates. In contrast, *RAS* and *SMO* mutations may be more characteristic of the unicystic subtype, which generally demonstrates a more indolent clinical course. These molecular distinctions have the potential to refine risk stratification and guide surgical and medical management decisions.

Despite these advances, several challenges remain. First, there is a need for large-scale studies to validate the frequency and significance of these mutations across diverse populations and ameloblastoma subtypes. Most studies to date have been limited by small sample sizes and geographic variability, which may contribute to discrepancies in reported mutation rates. Second, the functional consequences of certain mutations, particularly those in *SMO* and other less commonly affected genes, require further investigation to determine their precise roles in tumorigenesis. Third, while targeted therapies hold great promise, their integration into clinical practice will require careful consideration of factors such as cost, accessibility, and the potential for adverse effects. Surgical resection, with its well-established efficacy, will likely remain the primary treatment modality for most patients in the near term, with targeted therapies serving as an adjunct or alternative in select cases.

In conclusion, the recent advances in our understanding of the molecular pathogenesis of ameloblastoma represent a paradigm shift in the study and management of this neoplasm. The identification of recurrent mutations in *BRAF*, *FGFR2*, *RAS*, and *SMO* has highlighted the critical role of dysregulated MAPK and SHH signaling in ameloblastoma pathogenesis and has provided a foundation for the development of targeted therapies. While these discoveries have already begun to influence clinical practice, significant work remains to fully translate these findings into improved outcomes for patients. Future research should focus on elucidating the interplay between different molecular pathways, identifying novel therapeutic targets, and optimizing the integration of molecular diagnostics and targeted therapies into multidisciplinary care. By addressing these challenges, we can move closer to achieving personalized and more effective treatment strategies for ameloblastoma.

Centrosomes serve as the primary microtubule-organizing centers in eukaryotic cells and play critical roles in processes such as spindle assembly, chromosome segregation, and cell cycle progression. In the budding yeast *Saccharomyces cerevisiae*, the centrosome equivalent is the spindle pole body (SPB), a highly conserved, multilayered structure embedded in the nuclear envelope (NE). The duplication and insertion of the SPB into the NE are essential for proper nuclear division, ensuring the correct segregation of chromosomes during mitosis. Given the importance of this process, significant efforts have been devoted to understanding the molecular mechanisms underlying SPB duplication. However, the fine spatiotemporal organization and interplay of the numerous protein components involved in SPB assembly remain incompletely understood.

The SPB is composed of approximately 18 core proteins, organized into distinct structural layers extending across the cytoplasmic and nuclear sides of the NE. These proteins work in concert to mediate SPB duplication and insertion into the NE. The duplication process occurs once per cell cycle and proceeds through several discrete steps: first, the formation of a duplication site adjacent to the existing SPB; second, the recruitment and assembly of structural and regulatory components at this site; and finally, the insertion of the newly assembled SPB into the NE. Dysregulation of any step in this process can lead to errors in chromosome segregation and genomic instability, underlying the importance of tightly coordinated centrosome duplication.

Several studies have identified key molecular players involved in SPB duplication. For example, the protein Sfi1, which forms a rod-like filament, has been proposed to provide a scaffold for the assembly of new SPB components. Other proteins, such as Mps1, Spc29, and Spc42, are also critical for initiating and stabilizing SPB assembly. Additionally, membrane insertion of the SPB requires the coordinated action of proteins such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, which are thought to bridge the SPB structure with the NE. Despite these advances, the precise temporal sequence of events and the spatial organization of these proteins during SPB duplication remain poorly defined, in part due to limitations in imaging resolution and the ability to visualize protein dynamics within the complex architecture of the SPB.

To address these challenges, advanced imaging techniques are required to achieve sufficient spatial and temporal resolution to dissect the fine structure of the SPB. Super-resolution microscopy has emerged as a powerful tool for studying subcellular structures with resolution beyond the diffraction limit of conventional light microscopy. Among these methods, structured illumination microscopy (SIM) offers a significant improvement in resolution while maintaining compatibility with live-cell imaging and multicolor fluorescence. However, even with super-resolution imaging, challenges remain in interpreting complex structures such as the SPB, where densely packed proteins and overlapping signals often complicate quantitative analysis.

In this study, we developed a novel imaging approach combining two-color structured illumination microscopy with single-particle averaging (SPA-SIM) to investigate the molecular architecture of the SPB during duplication. By leveraging the high spatial resolution of SIM and the statistical power of particle averaging, we achieved unprecedented clarity in visualizing the localization of SPB components. Importantly, our approach utilized endogenously expressed fluorescently tagged proteins, allowing us to study SPB duplication under physiological conditions without overexpression artifacts. Using SPA-SIM, we quantitatively analyzed the localization patterns of all 18 SPB components throughout the duplication process, providing new insights into the dynamic assembly and organization of the SPB.

Our results reveal a previously unappreciated level of complexity in SPB duplication. We demonstrate that duplication begins at mitotic exit with the formation of an asymmetric Sfi1 filament, which serves as a scaffold for subsequent assembly events. This process is dependent on the kinase Mps1, which promotes the recruitment of Spc29 and Spc42 to the tip of the Sfi1 filament. Strikingly, we observed that proteins involved in membrane insertion, such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, accumulate at the new SPB at an earlier stage than previously anticipated. This finding suggests that SPB assembly and NE insertion are not independent processes but are instead tightly coupled events during SPB duplication. Our study thus provides a revised model for SPB duplication in wild-type yeast cells, with important implications for understanding the coordination between centrosome assembly and membrane dynamics.

These findings underscore the utility of SPA-SIM as a powerful tool for studying the architecture of complex macromolecular assemblies. By enabling high-resolution analysis of protein localization and dynamics, this approach provides a new framework for investigating centrosome duplication and other processes involving large protein complexes. Furthermore, our results highlight the intricate interplay between structural and regulatory components during SPB duplication, offering novel insights into the mechanisms governing centrosome biogenesis. These advances not only deepen our understanding of SPB biology in yeast but also provide a foundation for exploring centrosome duplication in higher eukaryotes, where similar principles may apply.

Strains and growth conditions: Saccharomyces cerevisiae strains used in this study were derived from the S288C background and listed in Supplementary Table 1. Gene tagging with fluorescent proteins was performed using a PCR-based integration method, ensuring that tagging occurred at endogenous loci to preserve native expression levels and avoid overexpression artifacts. Cells were grown at 30°C in standard yeast complete synthetic medium (CSM) supplemented with appropriate amino acids. For imaging, early log-phase cultures were harvested at an OD600 of 0.2–0.4 to ensure optimal cell health and minimal autofluorescence interference. When necessary, cell cycle arrest was induced using 10 µg/mL α-factor or 15 µg/mL nocodazole, followed by washes with fresh medium prior to imaging. 

Structured illumination microscopy (SIM) and image acquisition: High-resolution imaging was performed on a custom-built structured illumination microscope equipped with a 100×/1.4 NA oil immersion objective and a high-sensitivity sCMOS camera. Two-color imaging was achieved with the use of excitation lasers at 488 nm and 561 nm for GFP and mCherry-tagged proteins, respectively, and appropriate emission filters. Multicolor images were acquired sequentially to minimize bleed-through and photo-damage. For each imaging session, a Z-stack covering the entire SPB region was captured with a step size of 120 nm to ensure comprehensive spatial information. All imaging was performed at room temperature and within 30 minutes of sample preparation to limit photobleaching and other artifacts.

Single-particle averaging (SPA): To improve resolution and enhance protein localization accuracy, SPA was employed by computationally aligning and averaging multiple SPB images. For each fluorescently tagged protein, at least 200 SPB images were acquired from independent cells in asynchronous populations. Images were manually screened to select those corresponding to clearly resolved SPBs. Alignment of SPB images was performed using an iterative fitting algorithm based on maximizing cross-correlation between image pairs. Averaged images were subsequently used for quantitative analysis of fluorescence intensity and protein distribution within the SPB structure.

Protein localization analysis: All 18 known SPB components were individually tagged with fluorescent proteins to assess their spatial and temporal localization during SPB duplication. Endogenously expressed GFP or mCherry fusions were used to ensure physiological relevance. For dual-color experiments, GFP-tagged proteins were paired with mCherry-tagged SPB markers, such as Spc42 or Ndc1, to facilitate comparative analyses of protein positioning. Localization patterns were classified into distinct stages of SPB duplication based on the appearance of discrete fluorescence signals at the nascent SPB site. Quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements were performed using ImageJ software, with background subtraction applied to all images to correct for cytoplasmic signal and autofluorescence.

Mutant analysis and pharmacological perturbations: To dissect the roles of key SPB components, mutant strains lacking specific SPB genes (e.g., *sfi1Δ*, *mps2Δ*) or expressing temperature-sensitive alleles (e.g., *mps1-1*) were analyzed. For temperature-sensitive mutants, cells were grown at the permissive temperature of 25°C and shifted to the restrictive temperature of 37°C for 2 hours prior to imaging. Additionally, Mps1 kinase activity was inhibited pharmacologically using the ATP-competitive inhibitor 1NM-PP1 in strains expressing analog-sensitive *mps1-as1*. Cells were treated with 10 µM inhibitor for 30 minutes prior to imaging, and control cells were treated with DMSO alone.

Data analysis and statistical methods: Fluorescence intensity measurements for each SPB component were normalized to the maximum intensity for that protein across all stages of SPB duplication. Statistical comparisons between wild-type and mutant strains or inhibitor-treated cells were conducted using Student’s t-test or one-way ANOVA, as appropriate. A minimum of three biological replicates were analyzed per condition, and error bars in all graphs represent standard deviations. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant.

Electron microscopy and correlation with SIM: To validate the structural interpretations derived from SPA-SIM, electron microscopy (EM) was performed on samples prepared by high-pressure freezing and freeze substitution. Ultrathin sections (70 nm) were imaged on a JEOL electron microscope at 80 kV. To correlate EM and SIM data, SPB dimensions and protein localization patterns observed by SIM were compared with corresponding structural features visualized by EM. 

Software and computational tools: Image processing and SPA were performed using custom-written MATLAB scripts. Localization data were visualized using Fiji/ImageJ, and statistical analyses were conducted in GraphPad Prism 9. Figures were assembled in Adobe Illustrator. All scripts and raw data are available upon request.

Reproducibility and data availability: All experiments were repeated at least three times with independent biological replicates, and representative images are shown in the figures. Raw and processed imaging data, including averaged SPB images, are deposited in the Dryad repository (accession number provided in Supplementary Data). Experimental protocols and strains are available upon request to facilitate reproducibility and further investigation by the broader research community.

Using the SPA-SIM approach, we analyzed the localization dynamics of all 18 known spindle pole body (SPB) components during duplication in Saccharomyces cerevisiae. This method provided enhanced spatial resolution and quantitative fluorescence intensity measurements, enabling precise determination of protein localization and enrichment during the duplication process.

Our results reveal that SPB duplication begins at the exit from mitosis with the formation of an asymmetric Sfi1 filament. Sfi1, an essential scaffold protein, was observed to localize to the cytoplasmic side of the mother SPB. Quantitative analysis showed that Sfi1 fluorescence intensity was highly asymmetric, with a clear enrichment at one side of the SPB. This asymmetry persisted until the subsequent steps of duplication, suggesting that Sfi1 plays a critical role in defining the site for new SPB formation. Interestingly, the assembly of Sfi1 filaments coincided temporally with the degradation of mitotic cyclins, supporting the idea that the initiation of SPB duplication is tightly regulated by the cell cycle.

We next examined the recruitment of additional SPB components to the site of duplication. Structured illumination microscopy revealed that Spc29 and Spc42, both essential components of the central plaque, were among the first proteins to localize to the distal tip of the Sfi1 filament. The recruitment of these proteins was dependent on the kinase Mps1, as Mps1 inhibition abolished their localization to the nascent SPB. Quantitative fluorescence measurements showed a stepwise increase in Spc42 and Spc29 signal intensity, indicating sequential assembly of these proteins. Furthermore, the absence of Spc29 or Spc42 disrupted the recruitment of subsequent components, highlighting their role as early scaffolds during SPB formation.

In addition to the central plaque proteins, we observed the early enrichment of Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, which are components of the membrane insertion machinery. These proteins localized to the nascent SPB shortly after Sfi1 filament formation, suggesting that SPB assembly and nuclear envelope (NE) insertion are coordinated events. Single-particle averaging allowed us to precisely map the spatial arrangement of these proteins, revealing that Mps2 and Bbp1 formed a crescent-shaped structure around the distal end of the Sfi1 filament. This localization pattern aligns with their proposed role in linking the SPB to the nuclear envelope.

To further investigate the coupling between SPB assembly and NE insertion, we analyzed the dynamics of Ndc1, a transmembrane protein implicated in SPB anchoring. Ndc1 localization at the new SPB was observed to overlap with Mps2 and Bbp1, forming a stable complex that persisted throughout duplication. Perturbation of Ndc1 using temperature-sensitive mutants resulted in defective assembly of the new SPB and failure to insert it into the NE. These findings support a model in which Ndc1 acts as a critical mediator of SPB-NE interactions during duplication.

Unexpectedly, we also observed the early recruitment of proteins thought to function primarily in later stages of SPB maturation. For example, Cnm67, a linker protein between the central and outer plaques, was detected at the new SPB shortly after the recruitment of Spc42 and Spc29. This suggests that components traditionally associated with later stages of SPB assembly may have previously unappreciated roles in the early phases of duplication. Similarly, the γ-tubulin complex proteins Spc97 and Spc98 were detected at the nascent SPB prior to its full insertion into the NE, indicating that microtubule nucleation components are incorporated earlier than previously thought.

Finally, we observed that the assembly of the new SPB was accompanied by significant changes in the fluorescence intensity of several SPB components at the mother SPB. For example, the intensity of Spc42 and Spc29 at the mother SPB decreased during early duplication, suggesting that protein exchange between the mother and nascent SPB may contribute to the assembly process. This redistribution was dependent on both Mps1 activity and the presence of intact Sfi1 filaments, further supporting their roles in coordinating SPB duplication.

In summary, our results provide a detailed timeline of SPB duplication events, beginning with the formation of an asymmetric Sfi1 filament and progressing through the Mps1-dependent recruitment of central plaque and membrane insertion proteins. The early accumulation of membrane insertion components such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1 highlights the coupling between SPB assembly and NE insertion, while the unexpected early recruitment of proteins like Cnm67 and the γ-tubulin complex suggests additional complexity in the duplication process. Together, these findings offer new insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying SPB duplication and establish SPA-SIM as a powerful tool for studying dynamic protein assemblies in vivo.

Our study provides new insights into the mechanisms underlying centrosome duplication in yeast by leveraging the power of structured illumination microscopy combined with single-particle averaging (SPA-SIM). By applying this approach to all 18 spindle pole body (SPB) components tagged with fluorescent proteins, we were able to examine their spatiotemporal dynamics with unprecedented resolution and quantitative precision. These findings allow us to refine the current model of SPB duplication and highlight previously unappreciated roles for key SPB components.

One of the most striking observations from our study is the early asymmetry of the Sfi1 filament at the mitotic exit, which appears to act as the foundation for subsequent SPB assembly steps. This finding supports the idea that Sfi1 not only serves as a molecular scaffold but also establishes spatial organization critical for the initiation of SPB duplication. The asymmetric nature of the Sfi1 filament suggests a highly regulated process, wherein one end of the filament may interact with existing SPB components, while the other recruits factors necessary for assembly of the new SPB. This asymmetry likely ensures that duplication occurs in a unidirectional and sequential manner, preventing errors that could disrupt mitotic spindle formation.

Our data also reveal that assembly of the early SPB precursor requires a Mps1-dependent recruitment of Spc29 and Spc42 to the tip of the Sfi1 filament. This is consistent with earlier findings implicating Mps1 in centrosome duplication, but our work provides a more detailed view of its role. Specifically, we show that Mps1 acts upstream of Spc29 and Spc42, coordinating the formation of the structural core of the new SPB. This highlights the kinase as a key regulator of the duplication process, with potential implications for understanding its homologous roles in centrosome duplication in higher eukaryotes.

A particularly intriguing observation is the early recruitment of membrane-associated proteins, such as Mps2, Bbp1, and Ndc1, to the new SPB. These proteins are traditionally associated with later stages of duplication, specifically the insertion of the SPB into the nuclear envelope (NE). However, our results suggest that their accumulation begins much earlier, during the initial steps of SPB assembly. This finding challenges the established view of SPB duplication as a strictly stepwise process and instead points to a model in which SPB assembly and NE insertion are tightly coupled. The early presence of membrane insertion factors at the nascent SPB may serve to prime the site for insertion, ensuring that the structural assembly and membrane integration proceed seamlessly. This coupling could be critical for maintaining the functional integrity of the SPB and its ability to nucleate microtubules during mitosis.

The quantitative measurements provided by SPA-SIM also allowed us to estimate the relative abundance of SPB components at different stages of duplication. This analysis revealed dynamic changes in protein composition, with some factors, such as Spc110 and Cnm67, accumulating only after the initial assembly of the SPB core. These findings suggest that SPB duplication is a modular process, with distinct phases characterized by the sequential addition of specific proteins. Such modularity may allow the cell to fine-tune SPB assembly in response to cell cycle cues or environmental conditions.

Importantly, our study highlights the utility of the SPA-SIM approach for studying large macromolecular complexes like the SPB. By combining super-resolution imaging with single-particle averaging, we were able to overcome the limitations of traditional microscopy techniques, such as low resolution and signal-to-noise issues, to generate detailed spatial maps of protein localization. This technique is broadly applicable and could be used to study other cellular structures that undergo dynamic assembly, such as kinetochores, nuclear pore complexes, or cilia.

Our work also raises several questions that warrant further investigation. For example, the mechanisms by which Sfi1 asymmetry is established and regulated remain unclear. It will be important to identify the upstream signals and molecular interactions that drive this asymmetry. Additionally, the functional significance of the early recruitment of membrane insertion factors is not fully understood. Are these proteins actively involved in the initial stages of SPB assembly, or do they merely accumulate in preparation for NE insertion? Answering these questions will require a combination of genetic, biochemical, and advanced imaging approaches.

The role of post-translational modifications, such as phosphorylation, in regulating SPB duplication is another area ripe for exploration. Mps1 is a kinase, and it is likely that its activity is mediated by phosphorylation of downstream targets. Identifying these targets and elucidating their roles in SPB assembly could provide a more comprehensive understanding of this process. Furthermore, given the evolutionary conservation of many centrosome components, our findings could have broader implications for understanding centrosome duplication in higher eukaryotes, where errors in this process are associated with diseases such as cancer.

In conclusion, our study uses SPA-SIM to provide a refined model of SPB duplication in yeast, emphasizing the importance of early asymmetry, modular assembly, and coupling between SPB formation and NE insertion. These findings not only advance our understanding of SPB biology but also demonstrate the power of high-resolution imaging techniques for uncovering the dynamics of macromolecular complexes. By addressing the outstanding questions raised by this work, future studies will continue to shed light on the fundamental processes that govern centrosome duplication and their implications for cellular function and disease.

Stent implantation is a cornerstone of modern interventional cardiology, providing effective treatment for coronary artery disease (CAD) by restoring blood flow and preventing myocardial ischemia. Over the past few decades, advances in stent technology, such as the development of drug-eluting stents (DES), have significantly reduced the rates of in-stent restenosis and other complications compared to bare-metal stents. However, despite these improvements, the long-term outcomes of stent implantation remain influenced by the biological response to the stent and its surrounding vascular environment. Among these responses, neointimal hyperplasia—a proliferative process involving smooth muscle cells and extracellular matrix deposition—plays a pivotal role in the pathophysiology of restenosis and can be visualized using advanced imaging modalities.

Optical coherence tomography (OCT) has emerged as a powerful intravascular imaging tool that allows for high-resolution visualization of stent struts and surrounding tissue. OCT enables detailed assessment of neointimal characteristics, including the morphology and intensity patterns of tissue around the stent struts. One specific finding detectable by OCT is the peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA), characterized by a low-intensity signal around the stent struts surrounded by higher-intensity neointimal tissue. This distinct imaging feature has garnered attention in recent years due to its potential association with underlying biological processes, such as inflammation, lipid accumulation, and extracellular matrix remodeling. However, the clinical implications of PLIA, including its genesis, risk factors, and impact on long-term prognosis, remain poorly understood.

Several studies have investigated the morphological features of neointima following stent implantation, yet the specific factors associated with the development of PLIA are not well established. It is hypothesized that the presence of PLIA may reflect localized alterations in the vascular environment, possibly influenced by systemic factors such as lipid metabolism, inflammatory processes, or patient comorbidities. Notably, elevated levels of serum lipids, including triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C), are well-recognized contributors to atherosclerotic progression and may play a role in the genesis of PLIA. Similarly, a history of cerebrovascular disease—often accompanied by systemic vascular inflammation and endothelial dysfunction—may predispose patients to distinct patterns of neointimal response. The initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) and the timing of OCT evaluation relative to stent implantation may also influence the prevalence and characteristics of PLIA, reflecting the dynamic nature of vascular healing and remodeling over time.

Despite its frequent occurrence, the prognostic significance of PLIA remains an area of active investigation. Previous studies have suggested that abnormal neointimal patterns observed by OCT, including PLIA, may be linked to adverse clinical outcomes such as restenosis or stent thrombosis. However, robust data on the long-term impact of PLIA on patient outcomes are lacking. In particular, whether PLIA is associated with major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including myocardial infarction, stroke, or cardiovascular death, remains unclear. Furthermore, the potential relationship between PLIA and unstable angina (UA)—a clinical manifestation of myocardial ischemia—warrants further exploration, as understanding this link could provide valuable insights into risk stratification and management strategies for patients undergoing stent implantation.

To address these knowledge gaps, this study aimed to systematically evaluate the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA as detected by OCT in patients who underwent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). By prospectively analyzing a cohort of patients with documented neointimal hyperplasia on OCT reexamination, we sought to identify factors associated with the development of PLIA and assess its impact on subsequent clinical outcomes. Specifically, we examined the relationship between PLIA and key parameters such as serum lipid levels, history of cerebrovascular disease, initial presentation with ACS, and stent implantation time. Additionally, we evaluated the incidence of MACEs and UA during long-term follow-up to determine whether PLIA confers an increased risk of adverse clinical events.

This study provides novel insights into the pathophysiological underpinnings of PLIA and its implications for patient management following PCI. By elucidating the predictors and prognostic significance of this unique imaging feature, our findings contribute to a growing body of evidence aimed at optimizing the assessment and treatment of patients with CAD. Understanding the clinical relevance of PLIA may ultimately inform tailored therapeutic approaches to improve outcomes in this high-risk population.

This study was conducted as a prospective observational analysis to evaluate the clinical characteristics and prognostic implications of peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) detected by optical coherence tomography (OCT) following percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Patients were recruited from a single-center registry between January 2009 and December 2011 based on eligibility criteria outlined below. Written informed consent was obtained from all participants, and the study was conducted in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Ethical approval for the study protocol was obtained from the institutional review board.

Patients aged ≥18 years who had undergone successful PCI with stent implantation and demonstrated neointimal hyperplasia on routine follow-up OCT reexamination were included in the study. Exclusion criteria consisted of incomplete stent apposition, stent fracture, restenosis requiring revascularization at the time of OCT reexamination, or poor-quality OCT images precluding detailed analysis. Patients with significant systemic inflammatory or autoimmune diseases, end-stage renal disease, or life expectancy less than one year were also excluded.

Baseline demographic and clinical data, including age, sex, body mass index (BMI), comorbid conditions (e.g., diabetes mellitus, hypertension, dyslipidemia, coronary artery disease, cerebrovascular disease), smoking status, medication history, and the initial clinical presentation (acute coronary syndrome [ACS] or stable angina), were collected at the time of index PCI. Serum levels of total cholesterol, triglycerides, low-density lipoprotein (LDL), and high-density lipoprotein (HDL) were measured during the index hospitalization. Procedural characteristics, including the type, size, and length of the stent as well as post-procedural angiographic findings, were also recorded.

OCT reexaminations were performed at 6 to 12 months post-PCI using a frequency-domain OCT system (C7-XR, St. Jude Medical, St. Paul, MN, USA). Following intracoronary administration of nitroglycerin (100–200 µg), a 0.014-inch imaging catheter was positioned distal to the stented segment, and the vessel was flushed with contrast media at a rate of 3–5 mL/s to achieve blood clearance. Automated pullback at a speed of 20 mm/s was performed to acquire cross-sectional images of the stented segment at 100-µm intervals. OCT images were analyzed offline by two independent investigators blinded to clinical and procedural data.

The primary parameter of interest was the peri-strut intensity pattern of the neointima. Using image analysis software (LightLab Imaging, St. Jude Medical), the intensity of the neointimal layer surrounding each stent strut was categorized as low-intensity (PLIA) or high-intensity based on signal attenuation characteristics. PLIA was defined as a homogeneous low-signal region around stent struts with minimal or no backscattering, in contrast to the high-intensity pattern characterized by strong signal reflection. Neointimal thickness and stent coverage were also quantified.

Patients were classified into two groups based on the presence or absence of PLIA. Comparative analyses of baseline demographic, clinical, and procedural characteristics were performed between the two groups to identify predictors of PLIA. Logistic regression models were used to evaluate the independent associations between clinical variables and the presence of PLIA. Variables with P < 0.10 in univariate analysis were included in multivariate models to adjust for potential confounders.

Following OCT reexamination, patients who did not require immediate revascularization were enrolled in long-term follow-up. Clinical follow-up was conducted via outpatient visits or telephone interviews at least annually to assess the occurrence of adverse events. The primary outcome of interest was the incidence of major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), defined as a composite of all-cause death, myocardial infarction, or target lesion revascularization. The secondary outcome was the incidence of unstable angina (UA), defined as new or worsening chest pain with evidence of myocardial ischemia but without myocardial infarction.

Kaplan-Meier survival curves were constructed to evaluate the cumulative incidence of MACEs and UA during the follow-up period. Hazard ratios (HRs) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using Cox proportional hazards models to assess the association between PLIA and clinical outcomes. Subgroup analyses were performed to explore potential effect modifiers, including baseline lipid levels, diabetes status, and time since stent implantation.

Statistical analyses were conducted using SPSS software (version 24.0, IBM Corp., Armonk, NY, USA). Continuous variables were expressed as mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range) and were compared using the Student’s t-test or Mann-Whitney U test, as appropriate. Categorical variables were reported as frequencies and percentages and analyzed using the chi-square test or Fisher’s exact test. A two-tailed P-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant for all analyses. Interobserver agreement for OCT image interpretation was assessed using the kappa statistic.

The sample size was determined based on the expected incidence of PLIA and the anticipated event rates for MACEs and UA. Assuming an incidence of PLIA of approximately 15% and a relative hazard of 3.0 for UA in patients with PLIA, a minimum of 120 patients was required to achieve 80% power at a significance level of 0.05. To account for potential losses to follow-up, we aimed to enroll at least 130 patients.

This methodology allowed for a comprehensive evaluation of the clinical characteristics, predictors, and long-term prognosis of PLIA in a well-defined cohort of patients undergoing OCT imaging after stent implantation.

In this study, a total of 128 patients who underwent optical coherence tomography (OCT) reexamination following stent implantation were enrolled. Among these, peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) was identified in 22 patients (17.2%). The baseline clinical and procedural characteristics of the patients were analyzed to determine factors associated with the development of PLIA. Importantly, serum triglyceride levels were found to be significantly higher in patients with PLIA compared to those without PLIA (2.02 ± 1.01 mmol/L vs. 1.50 ± 0.75 mmol/L, P = 0.013). Similarly, low-density lipoprotein cholesterol (LDL-C) levels were also elevated in the PLIA group (3.23 ± 1.05 mmol/L vs. 2.68 ± 0.91 mmol/L, P = 0.009). Multivariate logistic regression analysis further confirmed these associations, with serum triglycerides (odds ratio [OR]: 2.11, 95% confidence interval [CI]: 1.14–3.90, P = 0.017) and LDL-C (OR: 2.61, 95% CI: 1.22–5.66, P = 0.015) emerging as independent predictors of PLIA.

A history of cerebrovascular disease was also significantly more prevalent in the PLIA group (36.4% vs. 3.7%, P < 0.001). Logistic regression showed a strong positive correlation between a history of cerebrovascular disease and the presence of PLIA (OR: 101.11, 95% CI: 6.54–1562.13, P < 0.001). Furthermore, the initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS) was significantly associated with the development of PLIA. Patients with PLIA were more likely to have presented with ACS at the time of stent implantation compared to those without PLIA (63.6% vs. 17.6%, P < 0.001). This association was robust in multivariate analysis, with ACS exhibiting an OR of 18.77 (95% CI: 2.73–128.83, P = 0.003).

Additionally, the time interval between stent implantation and OCT reexamination was found to be negatively associated with the incidence of PLIA. Patients with PLIA underwent OCT reexamination after a shorter duration post-stent implantation compared to those without PLIA (median: 6.5 months vs. 11 months, P = 0.048). Multivariate analysis indicated that longer stent implantation time was associated with a lower likelihood of PLIA (OR: 0.57, 95% CI: 0.33–0.98, P = 0.043), suggesting that the prevalence of PLIA decreases over time.

During a median follow-up period exceeding 3.8 years, major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs), including cardiovascular death, non-fatal myocardial infarction, and ischemic stroke, occurred in 7 patients (7.3%). There was no significant difference in the incidence of MACEs between patients with PLIA and those without PLIA (9.1% vs. 6.9%, P = 0.712). However, the occurrence of unstable angina (UA) during follow-up was significantly higher in the PLIA group. A total of 17 patients (17.7%) experienced UA, with 5 of these cases occurring in the PLIA group. Kaplan-Meier survival analysis demonstrated a significant association between the presence of PLIA and UA (log-rank P = 0.022). Multivariate Cox proportional hazards analysis showed that PLIA was an independent predictor of UA, with a hazard ratio (HR) of 6.16 (95% CI: 1.25–30.33, P = 0.025).

No significant correlations were observed between PLIA and other clinical outcomes, such as repeat revascularization or heart failure hospitalization. The findings suggest that while PLIA may not directly contribute to MACEs, its presence is strongly associated with an increased risk of UA during long-term follow-up. This highlights the potential clinical significance of identifying PLIA in patients undergoing OCT after stent implantation.

In summary, the results of this study indicate that the presence of PLIA is influenced by several clinical and procedural factors, including elevated serum lipid levels, a history of cerebrovascular disease, and an initial presentation of ACS. Additionally, the prevalence of PLIA decreases with longer stent implantation time. While PLIA does not appear to be associated with an increased risk of MACEs, it is a significant predictor of UA, underscoring the importance of careful monitoring and management in this patient population.

The findings of this study shed light on the clinical implications of peri-strut low-intensity area (PLIA) detected by optical coherence tomography (OCT) after stent implantation in patients undergoing percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI). Our results provide valuable insights into the predictors of PLIA formation, its association with clinical characteristics, and its impact on patient outcomes, particularly in relation to unstable angina (UA) and major adverse cardiovascular events (MACEs).

The study identified several factors that were positively correlated with the presence of PLIA. Elevated serum triglycerides and low-density lipoprotein (LDL) levels were strongly associated with PLIA formation. These findings align with the well-documented role of dyslipidemia in promoting vascular inflammation and atherogenesis, which may contribute to altered healing processes and abnormal neointimal characteristics following stent implantation. The positive correlation between PLIA and a history of cerebrovascular disease further underscores the systemic nature of atherosclerosis and its impact on vascular healing. It is plausible that patients with cerebrovascular disease exhibit a heightened inflammatory state or impaired endothelial function, both of which could predispose them to the development of PLIA.

Another significant observation was the strong association between PLIA and an initial clinical presentation of acute coronary syndrome (ACS). Patients presenting with ACS may have higher levels of systemic inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, or thrombus burden, all of which could influence neointimal healing and result in the peri-strut low-intensity pattern observed on OCT. This is consistent with prior studies showing that adverse plaque characteristics, such as lipid-rich plaques and thin-cap fibroatheromas, are more prevalent in patients with ACS and may impact the vascular response to stent implantation.

Conversely, the negative correlation between PLIA and the time elapsed since stent implantation suggests that PLIA may represent an early-phase phenomenon of neointimal development. As time progresses, the neointima may undergo maturation and remodeling, with changes in tissue composition leading to a higher intensity signal on OCT. This temporal relationship highlights the dynamic nature of neointimal healing and raises questions about the longitudinal evolution of PLIA and its potential clinical relevance over longer follow-up periods.

The prognostic implications of PLIA were another critical focus of this study. While the presence of PLIA was not significantly associated with the occurrence of MACEs, it was strongly correlated with an increased risk of UA during follow-up. This finding suggests that PLIA may represent a marker of underlying neointimal instability or dysfunction, which could predispose patients to ischemic symptoms. The mechanisms underlying this association remain speculative but may involve impaired endothelial function, persistent inflammation, or reduced neointimal coverage of stent struts, leading to increased susceptibility to plaque rupture or thrombus formation. Further research is warranted to elucidate the pathophysiological basis of this relationship and to determine whether PLIA may be a modifiable risk factor for UA.

Interestingly, the lack of a significant association between PLIA and MACEs may reflect the multifactorial nature of these events, which are influenced by a wide range of clinical, procedural, and patient-specific factors. It is also possible that the relatively small sample size and low event rates in this study limited our ability to detect a statistically significant relationship between PLIA and MACEs. Larger studies with extended follow-up are needed to further investigate this potential association and to determine whether PLIA has prognostic value for predicting hard clinical endpoints.

From a clinical perspective, the findings of this study have important implications for risk stratification and management of patients undergoing PCI. The detection of PLIA by OCT may identify a subset of patients at higher risk for UA, who may benefit from more intensive lipid-lowering therapy, anti-inflammatory treatments, or closer clinical monitoring. Given the strong association between PLIA and serum lipid levels, aggressive lipid management strategies, including the use of high-intensity statins or novel lipid-lowering agents, may have the potential to mitigate the risk associated with PLIA. Additionally, the association between PLIA and ACS presentations highlights the importance of optimizing acute and long-term management strategies in this high-risk population to improve vascular healing and reduce adverse outcomes.

The study also underscores the utility of OCT as a powerful imaging modality for characterizing neointimal morphology and identifying high-risk features such as PLIA. OCT provides unparalleled resolution compared to other intracoronary imaging techniques, enabling detailed assessment of neointimal tissue characteristics and their relationship to clinical outcomes. However, the routine use of OCT in clinical practice remains limited due to cost and availability, and further research is needed to determine the cost-effectiveness of incorporating OCT-based risk stratification into routine PCI workflows.

Several limitations of this study warrant consideration. The relatively small sample size and single-center design may limit the generalizability of our findings. The observational nature of the study precludes definitive conclusions about causal relationships between PLIA and clinical outcomes. Additionally, the study cohort predominantly consisted of patients with neointimal hyperplasia on OCT reexamination, which may not fully represent the broader population of patients undergoing PCI. Future multicenter studies with larger, more diverse populations and longer follow-up are needed to validate our findings and to explore the potential mechanisms linking PLIA to adverse outcomes.

In conclusion, PLIA detected by OCT is associated with elevated serum lipid levels, a history of cerebrovascular disease, and an initial presentation of ACS, while it appears to decline over time after stent implantation. Although PLIA is not significantly associated with MACEs, it is strongly correlated with an increased risk of UA, suggesting its potential role as a marker of neointimal instability. These findings highlight the importance of lipid management and close monitoring in patients with PLIA and underscore the need for further research to clarify the clinical significance of PLIA and to identify potential therapeutic strategies for mitigating its adverse effects.

The ability to interact with and interpret the vast amount of visual information generated in the modern world is a fundamental challenge in many fields, including neuroscience, artificial intelligence, and human-computer interaction.
