Given the retrospective design, informed consent was waived by the IRB in accordance with national guidelines and regulations. Patient confidentiality was maintained by anonymising all data prior to analysis, and access to the dataset was restricted to authorised investigators.

### Limitations

The retrospective nature of this study inherently limits causal inference. While efforts were made to adjust for confounding variables, residual confounding due to unmeasured factors cannot be excluded. Furthermore, data were derived from a single institution, potentially limiting generalisability to other healthcare settings with different protocols or resource availability. Finally, the operational definition of the weekend may not capture variations in staffing or resource allocation that occur in other institutions or regions.

### Results

#### Patient Characteristics and Visit Distribution  
A total of 3,697 emergency department (ED) visits by elderly internal medicine patients aged 65 years or older were included in the analysis. The mean age of the cohort was 78.6 years (standard deviation [SD] ± 7.9), with a slight predominance of female patients (54.3%). Of all ED visits, 2,743 (74.2%) resulted in hospitalisation. Weekend admissions, defined as those occurring from midnight on Friday to midnight on Sunday, accounted for 629 hospitalised cases (22.9%), while weekday admissions constituted the remaining 2,114 cases (77.1%).  

Patients admitted on weekends exhibited a significantly higher comorbidity burden compared to weekday admissions, as reflected by the Charlson Comorbidity Index (CCI), with median CCI scores of 5 (interquartile range [IQR]: 4–7) versus 4 (IQR: 3–6), respectively (p < 0.001). Additionally, a greater proportion of weekend cases were triaged with higher urgency according to institutional triage protocols, with 68.8% of weekend admissions classified as urgent or very urgent compared to 61.5% of weekday admissions (p = 0.004).  

#### In-Hospital Mortality  
The overall in-hospital mortality rate for the cohort was 9.6% (n = 262). Among patients admitted on weekends, 11.4% (n = 72) died during their hospital stay, compared to 8.9% (n = 190) of weekday admissions. This corresponded to an unadjusted odds ratio (OR) of 1.3 (95% confidence interval [CI]: 0.99–1.8, p = 0.06). After adjusting for age, sex, comorbidity, and triage level in a multivariable logistic regression model, the association between weekend admission and in-hospital mortality was attenuated and no longer statistically significant (adjusted OR 1.2, 95% CI: 0.9–1.7, p = 0.18).  

#### Two-Day Mortality  
Mortality within the first two days of hospitalisation was observed in 2.2% of the cohort (n = 60). Among weekend admissions, the two-day mortality rate was 3.2% (n = 20), compared to 1.9% (n = 40) for weekday admissions. The unadjusted OR for two-day mortality associated with weekend admissions was 1.7 (95% CI: 0.99–2.9, p = 0.054). In the adjusted analysis, controlling for potential confounders including age, comorbidities, and triage level, the association remained non-significant (adjusted OR 1.5, 95% CI: 0.8–2.6, p = 0.21).  

#### Length of Stay and Discharge Outcomes  
The median length of hospital stay was comparable between weekend and weekday admissions, with no significant difference observed (6 days [IQR: 3–11] vs. 6 days [IQR: 3–10], p = 0.23). Similarly, the proportion of patients discharged to a higher level of care, including intensive rehabilitation or nursing home facilities, did not differ significantly between groups (28.4% for weekend admissions vs. 27.1% for weekday admissions, p = 0.48).  

#### Subgroup Analyses  
Exploratory subgroup analyses were performed to assess whether the weekend effect varied by age strata (65–74 years, 75–84 years, and ≥85 years) or by triage level. Among the oldest age group (≥85 years), the in-hospital mortality rate for weekend admissions was higher (15.8%) than for weekday admissions (10.6%), with an unadjusted OR of 1.6 (95% CI: 1.0–2.5, p = 0.04). However, this association was not statistically significant after adjustment for comorbidity and urgency level (adjusted OR 1.4, 95% CI: 0.9–2.3, p = 0.12). No significant interaction effect was observed for triage level or other subgroups.  

#### Sensitivity Analyses  
Sensitivity analyses were conducted to evaluate the robustness of the results to alternative definitions of the weekend (e.g., including Friday evening admissions). These analyses yielded similar findings, with no statistically significant association between weekend admission and either in-hospital or two-day mortality after adjustment for confounding variables.  

#### Summary of Findings  
In summary, while crude analyses suggested a modest increase in mortality rates for elderly patients hospitalised on weekends, these differences were not statistically significant after adjusting for differences in patient characteristics, including comorbidity burden and urgency level. The findings indicate that weekend admission was not independently associated with adverse outcomes, suggesting that emergency care processes for elderly internal medicine patients were not compromised during weekends.

### Discussion  

This retrospective cohort study investigated the presence of a "weekend effect" in elderly patients (≥65 years) hospitalised from the emergency department (ED). Specifically, it examined in-hospital and two-day mortality rates associated with weekend versus weekday admissions. While unadjusted analyses suggested a modest increase in mortality for patients admitted on weekends, multivariable adjustments for age, comorbidity, and triage level revealed no statistically significant difference between the two groups. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on the weekend effect, particularly in the understudied population of elderly internal medicine patients.  

#### Interpretation of Findings  

Our results indicate that elderly patients hospitalised on weekends had higher crude in-hospital and two-day mortality rates compared to those admitted on weekdays. The observed higher mortality was partly attributable to increased comorbidities and urgency levels among patients admitted on weekends. After adjusting for these confounders, the association between weekend admissions and mortality was attenuated, and the differences in in-hospital and two-day mortality rates became statistically nonsignificant (ORadj 1.2, 95%CI 0.9–1.7 and ORadj 1.5, 95%CI 0.8–2.6, respectively). These findings suggest that the apparent weekend effect is largely explained by differences in patient characteristics rather than systemic disparities in care quality or resource availability.  

The higher urgency levels and comorbidities observed in weekend admissions may reflect differences in patient presentation patterns or health-seeking behaviours. Previous studies have shown that patients presenting to the ED on weekends often have more acute or severe conditions, possibly due to delays in seeking care or reduced access to primary care services during weekends [1,2]. This trend might be accentuated in elderly populations, who are more likely to have complex medical conditions and limited mobility, potentially resulting in delayed presentations.  

#### Comparison with Prior Literature  

The absence of a significant weekend effect in our adjusted analyses is consistent with some previous studies, while conflicting with others. Several investigations have reported higher mortality rates for patients admitted on weekends, particularly in acute conditions such as stroke, myocardial infarction, and sepsis [3–5]. These studies often attribute their findings to reduced staffing levels, lower availability of specialists, and delayed diagnostic or therapeutic procedures during weekends [6]. However, other studies, including those focused on specific subpopulations such as geriatric patients, have found no evidence of a weekend effect after controlling for patient-level factors [7,8].  

Our findings align more closely with studies that emphasise the role of patient characteristics in explaining observed differences in outcomes. For instance, a large multicenter study in the United States found that higher mortality rates on weekends were predominantly attributable to differences in patient acuity rather than deficiencies in care delivery [9]. Similarly, research on elderly patients hospitalised for acute medical conditions has highlighted the importance of adjusting for comorbidities and disease severity when assessing the weekend effect [10].  

#### Clinical and System-Level Implications  

The absence of a significant weekend effect after adjustment suggests that emergency care systems are capable of maintaining consistent standards of care for elderly patients regardless of the day of admission. This finding is reassuring, as elderly patients are particularly vulnerable to adverse outcomes due to physiological frailty, multimorbidity, and polypharmacy [11]. Ensuring equitable care delivery across all days of the week is crucial for this high-risk population.  

Nonetheless, the observed differences in patient characteristics between weekend and weekday admissions highlight the need for targeted strategies to address the specific challenges of weekend care. For example, the higher urgency levels and comorbidities seen in weekend admissions may necessitate enhanced triage protocols, increased availability of senior decision-makers, and optimised resource allocation during weekends. Furthermore, public health initiatives aimed at improving access to primary care and urgent care services outside of regular working hours could potentially reduce the burden of high-acuity presentations on weekends [12].  

#### Strengths and Limitations  

This study has several strengths, including its focus on an elderly population, a demographic with unique healthcare needs and high utilisation of emergency services. The use of multivariable adjustments to account for confounders such as comorbidity and triage level enhances the validity of our findings. Additionally, the large sample size and inclusion of a two-year study period improve the generalisability of the results.  

However, certain limitations must be acknowledged. First, as a retrospective cohort study, the analysis is subject to residual confounding from unmeasured variables, such as socioeconomic status, functional status, or detailed clinical characteristics beyond comorbidity indices. Second, the study relied on data from a single institution, potentially limiting the generalisability to other healthcare settings with different care delivery models or resource levels. Third, we defined the weekend as the period from midnight on Friday to midnight on Sunday, which may not fully capture variations in staffing patterns or care processes during the transition between weekdays and weekends. Finally, while we adjusted for several key confounders, it is possible that other factors, such as differences in diagnostic or therapeutic interventions, contributed to the observed mortality patterns.  

#### Future Research Directions  

Further research is needed to explore the mechanisms underlying differences in patient characteristics between weekend and weekday admissions, particularly in elderly populations. Prospective studies with detailed clinical data, including functional status and frailty measures, could provide more nuanced insights into the interplay between patient factors and system-level contributors to outcomes. Additionally, studies examining the impact of specific interventions, such as enhanced staffing models or expanded access to primary care, on weekend mortality rates would be valuable. Finally, multicenter studies across diverse healthcare systems are warranted to assess the generalisability of our findings and identify best practices for optimising care delivery across all days of the week.  

### Conclusion  

In this retrospective cohort study of elderly internal medicine patients admitted through the ED, a small but nonsignificant weekend effect was observed for in-hospital and two-day mortality. The higher crude mortality rates on weekends were largely explained by increased comorbidities and urgency levels among weekend admissions. These findings underscore the importance of accounting for patient-level factors when evaluating the weekend effect and suggest that emergency care for the elderly is not compromised by adjusted logistics during weekends. Future efforts should focus on addressing the unique challenges of weekend care and ensuring equitable access to high-quality care for elderly patients across all days of the week.

Tuberculosis (TB) continues to be one of the leading infectious causes of death worldwide, with over 10 million new cases and 1.5 million deaths reported annually. Despite the widespread use of the Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) vaccine, TB remains a global health challenge, particularly in regions where the disease burden is high. BCG, the only licensed TB vaccine, has demonstrated efficacy in preventing severe forms of TB, such as TB meningitis and miliary TB in children. However, its ability to confer robust and long-lasting protection against pulmonary TB, the most transmissible form of the disease, is limited, especially in adolescents and adults. This limitation underscores the urgent need for novel vaccination strategies that can enhance and sustain anti-TB immunity beyond the protective window afforded by BCG.

Vaccination strategies for TB have increasingly focused on heterologous prime-boost approaches, where a primary immunization with BCG is followed by a booster dose using a novel vaccine. This strategy aims to extend the protective immunity elicited by BCG and enhance the immune response against Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb), the causative agent of TB. Among the candidates for boosting, adenovirus-vectored vaccines, such as Adenovirus serotype 5 expressing the M.tb antigen Ag85A (AdHu5Ag85A), have gained significant attention. AdHu5Ag85A is designed to target T-cell-mediated immunity, which plays a crucial role in controlling M.tb infection, by delivering the immunodominant antigen Ag85A directly to respiratory mucosal tissues. This mucosal immunization approach holds promise for eliciting localized immune responses in the lungs, the primary site of M.tb infection. Preclinical studies have demonstrated that AdHu5Ag85A can enhance T-cell responses and improve protection against M.tb when administered as a mucosal booster following BCG priming.

The timing of BCG vaccination has been a topic of considerable interest in TB immunology. Globally, BCG is typically administered at birth or within the first few months of life, a practice guided by its effectiveness in preventing severe pediatric TB. However, the neonatal immune system is immature and biased toward a Th2-dominated response, which may limit the ability to generate robust and long-lasting Th1-mediated immunity critical for controlling M.tb infection. Conversely, delaying BCG vaccination until later in childhood, when the immune system is more mature, may enhance the quality of the initial immune response and improve the generation of immunological memory. Despite these considerations, the impact of the timing of BCG immunization on the efficacy of heterologous prime-boost strategies remains poorly understood. Determining the optimal age for BCG priming, particularly in the context of subsequent boosting with novel TB vaccines like AdHu5Ag85A, is critical for the rational design of vaccination protocols aimed at maximizing protective immunity.

To address these knowledge gaps, we utilized a murine model to investigate how the age at BCG priming influences the protective efficacy of a heterologous BCG-AdHu5Ag85A prime-boost immunization strategy. In this study, mice were immunized with BCG at different ages, representing different stages of immune system development, and subsequently boosted with AdHu5Ag85A administered via the respiratory mucosa. The respiratory route was chosen for boosting because of its potential to induce mucosal immunity in the lungs, where M.tb infection is initiated. This experimental design allowed us to assess whether the timing of BCG priming modulates the capacity of AdHu5Ag85A to enhance anti-TB immunity and to explore how immunological memory is shaped by the interplay between the age of priming and the boosting immunization.

Our results indicate that the age at which BCG priming is administered has a limited effect on the overall protective efficacy of the BCG-AdHu5Ag85A prime-boost strategy. However, delaying BCG immunization until the immune system reaches a more mature state resulted in the generation of longer-lasting memory T cells, which enhanced the boosting effect of AdHu5Ag85A mucosal immunization. These findings suggest that while neonatal BCG vaccination remains an effective strategy for preventing severe forms of TB in early life, there may be advantages to delaying BCG immunization in settings where boosting with novel vaccines is feasible. This approach could optimize the immunological landscape for subsequent boosting and extend the duration of protective immunity against TB.

The outcomes of this study have important implications for the design of future TB vaccination protocols. As the global health community continues to explore strategies to improve TB control, understanding the influence of age at priming on the efficacy of heterologous prime-boost immunization regimens will be critical. Our findings highlight the need for further research to define the optimal timing for both BCG priming and boosting with novel TB vaccines, particularly in diverse human populations with varying epidemiological and immunological profiles. Ultimately, insights gained from such studies will guide the development of tailored vaccination strategies aimed at reducing the global burden of TB.

Mice were used as a murine model to investigate the impact of age at Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG) priming on the protective efficacy of a prime-boost tuberculosis (TB) immunization strategy. Female C57BL/6 mice were obtained from a specific-pathogen-free facility and housed under standard laboratory conditions with ad libitum access to food and water. All animal procedures were conducted in accordance with institutional guidelines and approved by the relevant animal ethics committee.

To evaluate the effect of age at BCG priming, mice were divided into three groups based on the timing of the initial BCG immunization: neonatal (1 week old), juvenile (4 weeks old), and adult (8 weeks old). BCG immunization was performed via the subcutaneous (s.c.) route using 1 × 10^6 CFU of Mycobacterium bovis BCG Pasteur 1173P2 (Statens Serum Institut, Denmark) suspended in sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS). Sham-immunized control groups received an equivalent volume of sterile PBS via the same route.

To assess the impact of respiratory mucosal boosting, all mice were subsequently immunized intranasally (i.n.) with 1 × 10^9 infectious units of recombinant adenovirus 5 expressing the Mycobacterium tuberculosis antigen Ag85A (AdHu5Ag85A). Intranasal boosting was performed 12 weeks after the initial BCG priming. Mice were anesthetized using isoflurane prior to i.n. vaccine administration, and a total volume of 50 µL (25 µL per nostril) was delivered dropwise to achieve efficient mucosal delivery.

For immunological analysis, blood, bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF), and spleens were collected at various time points post-immunization. Peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were isolated from blood samples by density gradient centrifugation. BALF was obtained by flushing the airways with sterile PBS, and cells were separated from the fluid by centrifugation. Spleens were aseptically removed and processed into single-cell suspensions by mechanical disruption through a sterile 70-µm cell strainer in complete RPMI-1640 medium (10% heat-inactivated fetal bovine serum, 1% penicillin-streptomycin, 1% L-glutamine). Red blood cells were lysed using ammonium chloride-potassium (ACK) lysis buffer, and splenocytes were washed and resuspended in complete RPMI-1640 medium for further analysis.

To investigate T-cell responses, intracellular cytokine staining (ICS) and flow cytometry were performed. Single-cell suspensions from spleens, BALF, and PBMCs were stimulated with a pool of overlapping peptides spanning the Ag85A protein (2 µg/mL per peptide) for 6 hours at 37°C in a humidified incubator with 5% CO₂. Brefeldin A (GolgiPlug, BD Biosciences) was added during the final 4 hours of stimulation to inhibit cytokine secretion. Cells were then stained with a viability dye and surface markers, including anti-CD3, anti-CD4, and anti-CD8 antibodies. Following fixation and permeabilization, intracellular staining was performed using antibodies against interferon-γ (IFN-γ), tumor necrosis factor-α (TNF-α), and interleukin-2 (IL-2). Data were acquired on a BD LSRFortessa flow cytometer and analyzed using FlowJo software (TreeStar).

To evaluate the magnitude and quality of memory T-cell responses, surface markers for memory subsets were analyzed. Memory T-cell subsets were defined based on the expression of CD62L and CD44 as follows: central memory (T_CM, CD62L^+ CD44^+), effector memory (T_EM, CD62L^- CD44^+), and naïve (CD62L^+ CD44^-) T cells. The frequency and absolute numbers of these subsets were compared across experimental groups.

For bacterial burden assessment, mice were challenged with a low-dose aerosol infection of Mycobacterium tuberculosis (M.tb.) H37Rv 6 weeks after AdHu5Ag85A boosting. Mice were placed in a Glas-Col aerosol exposure system, and approximately 100 colony-forming units (CFU) of M.tb. were delivered to the lungs. At 30 days post-infection, mice were euthanized, and lungs, spleens, and mediastinal lymph nodes were harvested. Organs were homogenized in sterile PBS containing 0.05% Tween-80, and serial dilutions of homogenates were plated on Middlebrook 7H11 agar supplemented with oleic acid-albumin-dextrose-catalase (OADC) enrichment. Plates were incubated at 37°C for 21 days, and bacterial colonies were counted to determine organ CFU counts.

Histological analysis was performed on lung tissues to assess inflammation and granuloma formation. Lungs were inflation-fixed with 10% neutral buffered formalin, embedded in paraffin, sectioned at 5 µm, and stained with hematoxylin and eosin (H&E). Sections were examined under a light microscope, and histopathological changes were scored by a blinded pathologist.

Statistical analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software. Data were tested for normality using the Shapiro-Wilk test and analyzed using one-way or two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) with appropriate post hoc tests. Nonparametric tests were applied when data did not meet normality assumptions. Differences were considered statistically significant at p < 0.05.

All experiments were performed at least twice to ensure reproducibility, and sample sizes were determined based on preliminary experiments to achieve sufficient statistical power. Results are presented as means ± standard error of the mean (SEM) unless otherwise specified.

To determine the impact of age at BCG priming on the efficacy of a respiratory mucosal AdHu5Ag85A boost, we conducted a series of experiments using a murine model. Mice were immunized subcutaneously (s.c.) with Mycobacterium bovis BCG at different ages: neonatal (1 week old), early childhood (3 weeks old), or late childhood (6 weeks old), followed by intranasal (i.n.) boosting with AdHu5Ag85A at 8 weeks of age. An unvaccinated control group and groups receiving BCG or AdHu5Ag85A alone were included for comparison. T cell responses, cytokine production, and bacterial burden in the lungs and spleen were assessed at various time points after immunization and Mycobacterium tuberculosis (Mtb) challenge.

Our initial analysis focused on the immune response elicited by BCG priming alone at different ages. Neonatal, early childhood, and late childhood BCG immunization all resulted in robust expansion of Ag85A-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cells in the lungs and spleen, as measured by intracellular cytokine staining (ICS) for IFN-γ and TNF-α. However, mice primed at 6 weeks of age showed significantly higher frequencies of multifunctional CD4+ T cells (producing IFN-γ, TNF-α, and IL-2 simultaneously) compared to those immunized at 1 or 3 weeks of age (p < 0.05). This enhanced multifunctional T cell response was also sustained for a longer duration in the late childhood BCG group, remaining elevated up to 12 weeks post-immunization.

Following intranasal AdHu5Ag85A boosting, all groups demonstrated a marked increase in Ag85A-specific CD4+ and CD8+ T cell responses in the lungs, characterized by robust IFN-γ and TNF-α production. Notably, the magnitude of the boost response was not significantly influenced by the age at which BCG priming was performed (p > 0.05). However, mice primed at 6 weeks of age exhibited a more pronounced expansion of lung-resident memory T cells (Trm), identified as CD69+CD103+ Ag85A-specific CD4+ T cells, compared to those primed at 1 or 3 weeks of age (p < 0.01). These Trm cells were associated with an enhanced capacity to rapidly produce cytokines upon ex vivo re-stimulation, suggesting greater readiness to respond to Mtb infection.

To evaluate the protective efficacy of the various immunization regimens, mice were challenged with a low-dose aerosolized Mtb strain at 4 weeks post-AdHu5Ag85A boost, and bacterial burden was assessed in the lungs and spleen 28 days post-challenge. All BCG-primed groups, whether boosted with AdHu5Ag85A or not, demonstrated significant reductions in lung and spleen Mtb burden compared to unvaccinated controls (p < 0.001). Importantly, the addition of the AdHu5Ag85A boost significantly enhanced protection in all BCG-primed groups, with a greater than 1-log reduction in lung bacterial load compared to BCG alone (p < 0.001). The age at BCG priming did not significantly influence the degree of protection conferred by the prime-boost regimen, with bacterial loads in the lungs and spleen being comparable across the 1-, 3-, and 6-week priming groups (p > 0.05).

Despite similar bacterial control among the different BCG priming groups, we observed differences in the quality of the immune response post-challenge. Mice primed at 6 weeks of age and boosted with AdHu5Ag85A exhibited higher frequencies of lung-resident multifunctional T cells and greater production of IFN-γ and TNF-α in response to Mtb antigens compared to the 1- and 3-week priming groups (p < 0.05). This suggests that while the overall protective efficacy of the prime-boost regimen was not significantly affected by the age at BCG priming, the quality and longevity of the immune response were enhanced when BCG was administered at a later age.

Finally, to investigate the durability of protection, a subset of mice was challenged with Mtb 12 weeks post-AdHu5Ag85A boost. In this long-term setting, mice primed with BCG at 6 weeks of age and boosted with AdHu5Ag85A demonstrated significantly improved bacterial control in the lungs compared to those primed at 1 or 3 weeks of age (p < 0.01). This correlated with sustained Trm populations and multifunctional T cell responses in the lungs, highlighting the importance of memory T cell longevity in long-term protection.

In summary, our results indicate that the age at BCG priming has a limited impact on the overall protective efficacy of the BCG-AdHu5Ag85A prime-boost regimen against Mtb infection. However, delaying BCG immunization until the immune system has matured enhances the quality and durability of the immune response, particularly through the generation of lung-resident memory T cells and multifunctional T cells. These findings provide valuable insights into the timing of BCG vaccination and the design of optimal immunization strategies for tuberculosis control.

The findings of this study provide important insights into the relationship between the timing of BCG priming and the efficacy of an AdHu5Ag85A respiratory mucosal boost in a murine model of tuberculosis (TB) immunization. While our results demonstrated that the age at BCG priming has a limited impact on the overall protective immunity elicited by the combination of BCG and AdHu5Ag85A, there are notable nuances that warrant further exploration. Specifically, the delayed administration of BCG, closer to the time when the immune system achieves maturity, resulted in a more robust and sustained memory T cell response, which translated into an improved boosting effect upon respiratory mucosal immunization with AdHu5Ag85A. These findings hold practical implications for the optimization of TB vaccination strategies, particularly in the context of designing prime-boost immunization protocols.

Our results align with previous studies suggesting that the BCG vaccine, while effective at preventing severe forms of TB in early childhood, has limited efficacy against pulmonary TB in adults. This limitation has driven the search for novel vaccination strategies, including the use of heterologous prime-boost regimens, which aim to enhance and prolong the protective immunity initiated by BCG. The AdHu5Ag85A vaccine, delivered via the respiratory mucosa, is particularly promising as a booster due to its ability to elicit strong T cell-mediated immune responses in the lungs, the primary site of Mycobacterium tuberculosis infection. In this study, we assessed whether the age at which BCG is administered influences the efficacy of this prime-boost approach, given the variability in BCG vaccination schedules across the globe.

Contrary to expectations that earlier BCG priming might establish a more favorable immune environment for subsequent boosting, our data showed that the timing of BCG administration during early life had only a limited impact on the magnitude of the immune response generated by AdHu5Ag85A. This finding is significant, as it suggests that the benefits of incorporating a respiratory mucosal boost with AdHu5Ag85A may not be heavily dependent on the precise timing of the initial BCG vaccination. This observation could simplify the logistics of implementing prime-boost strategies in diverse populations, where the age of BCG administration often varies due to differences in national immunization programs.

However, our study also revealed that delaying BCG vaccination until the immune system had reached a more mature state resulted in the generation of longer-lived memory T cells, which in turn enhanced the boosting effect of AdHu5Ag85A. This suggests that the maturity of the immune system at the time of priming may influence the quality and durability of the immune response, particularly in terms of T cell memory. This finding may have implications for the timing of booster vaccinations in humans. It is possible that a delayed prime-boost strategy, in which BCG is administered later in childhood or even adolescence, followed by a respiratory mucosal boost, could result in more durable protection against TB.

The observed differences in memory T cell dynamics between early and delayed BCG priming may be explained by the developmental state of the immune system at the time of vaccination. In neonatal and early childhood stages, the immune system is characterized by an increased prevalence of regulatory mechanisms and a bias toward Th2-type responses, which may limit the induction of robust Th1-type memory responses necessary for effective control of TB. In contrast, the immune system in older individuals is more proficient at generating durable Th1-type responses, which are critical for controlling intracellular pathogens like Mycobacterium tuberculosis. This could explain why delayed BCG priming resulted in better immunological outcomes following the AdHu5Ag85A boost.

It is also worth noting that respiratory mucosal delivery of the AdHu5Ag85A vaccine likely contributed to the strong local immune responses observed in our study. Mucosal immunization has been shown to generate tissue-resident memory T cells in the lungs, which are particularly effective at combating respiratory pathogens. Our findings suggest that these local immune responses can be effectively enhanced by the AdHu5Ag85A boost, regardless of the timing of the initial BCG priming. This underscores the potential of mucosal vaccine delivery as a key component of future TB vaccination strategies.

While our study provides valuable insights, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the murine model used in this study, while informative, may not fully replicate the complexities of human immune responses to TB vaccination. Further research in non-human primates and clinical trials in humans will be necessary to validate our findings and assess their translational potential. Second, our study focused on a single booster vaccine (AdHu5Ag85A) and did not explore other potential boost candidates or combinations of vaccines. Future studies should investigate whether the observed effects are generalizable to other heterologous boost strategies.

In conclusion, our study demonstrates that the age at BCG priming has a limited impact on the efficacy of a prime-boost TB vaccination strategy involving respiratory mucosal delivery of AdHu5Ag85A. However, delayed BCG priming appears to enhance the generation of memory T cells and improve the boosting effect of AdHu5Ag85A, suggesting that the timing of both the prime and boost components of TB vaccination protocols may influence long-term protection. These findings highlight the need for continued research to optimize TB immunization schedules, with the ultimate goal of improving protection against pulmonary TB in adults. The incorporation of respiratory mucosal vaccines, such as AdHu5Ag85A, into prime-boost regimens holds significant promise for achieving this objective and mitigating the global burden of TB.

The control of agricultural pests remains a significant challenge for global food security, particularly in the context of sustainable agriculture and integrated pest management (IPM). Among the most economically damaging pests are the fruit flies of the Tephritidae family, including *Bactrocera oleae* and *Ceratitis capitata*. These species are responsible for substantial losses in fruit production worldwide, with annual crop damage estimated in billions of euros [1]. Effective pest control requires timely and accurate monitoring of pest populations to guide targeted interventions such as pesticide applications, thereby reducing both economic losses and environmental impacts. Despite advances in pest management strategies, the monitoring of pest populations continues to rely heavily on manual inspection of traps, an approach that is both labor-intensive and prone to delays in data acquisition and analysis. This study addresses these limitations by proposing a novel, automated methodology for pest monitoring using optoacoustic signal processing integrated into traditional McPhail traps.

The McPhail trap, widely used for monitoring fruit flies, operates on the principle of attracting insects through visual and olfactory cues, after which they are captured in a liquid reservoir. While effective in capturing pests, this trap requires manual inspection to identify and count the captured insects, posing logistical challenges for large-scale agricultural operations [2]. Manual inspection is further complicated by the need for expertise in identifying pest species, particularly when closely related species coexist in the same ecological niche. Delays in data collection and analysis often result in suboptimal timing of pest control measures, which can exacerbate crop damage or lead to unnecessary pesticide use. In this context, there is an urgent need for automated systems that can provide real-time data on pest populations to improve the efficiency and precision of IPM strategies.

Recent advances in sensor technologies and signal processing have enabled the development of automated pest monitoring systems. These systems typically rely on audio or visual signals to detect and identify insects based on species-specific characteristics such as wingbeat frequencies or morphological features [3]. However, audio-based systems are often limited by background noise in field conditions, while vision-based systems require complex image processing algorithms and are sensitive to lighting conditions [4]. To address these challenges, we introduce the concept of "insect biometrics," which involves the measurement of unique biological characteristics of insects for their identification. Specifically, we focus on wingbeat frequency as a biometric signature, leveraging optoacoustic signal processing to differentiate between species in a robust and cost-effective manner.

The proposed system involves the modification of a McPhail trap by integrating an array of photoreceptors and an infrared emitter at the entrance of the trap. As insects enter the trap, their wingbeats interrupt the infrared light, creating fluctuations in the light signal that are recorded and analyzed to identify the species. This approach offers several advantages over existing methods. First, it eliminates the need for manual inspection, as insect counts and identifications are transmitted in real time to a central agency using mobile communication networks. Second, the use of optoacoustic signals provides a high level of specificity in species identification, reducing the likelihood of misclassification. Third, the system is designed as an external add-on kit, preserving the internal structure of the McPhail trap and allowing for easy retrofitting of existing traps. These features make the system scalable and adaptable to diverse agricultural settings.

The integration of real-time monitoring into pest management protocols has the potential to revolutionize the way infestations are detected and controlled. By providing immediate feedback on pest populations, the proposed system can enable more precise targeting of pesticide applications, reducing both the economic and environmental costs associated with broad-spectrum spraying. Moreover, the system can be used to monitor the efficacy of pest control measures, offering valuable data for optimizing IPM strategies over time. While the primary focus of this study is on fruit flies, the underlying principles of the system are broadly applicable to other pest species, highlighting its potential as a versatile tool for sustainable agriculture.

The development of this system builds on a growing body of research exploring automated pest monitoring technologies. Previous studies have demonstrated the feasibility of using wingbeat frequency for insect identification, with promising results in laboratory and semi-field conditions [5]. However, these studies have often been limited by the complexity and cost of the required hardware, as well as the challenges of deploying such systems in field conditions. Our work seeks to address these limitations by developing a low-cost, robust solution that can be easily integrated into existing pest management frameworks. By combining advances in sensor technology, signal processing, and wireless communication, we aim to bridge the gap between laboratory research and practical applications in the field.

In this study, we evaluate the performance of the modified McPhail trap in controlled laboratory conditions, using insectary cages to simulate field environments. The primary objectives are to assess the accuracy and reliability of the system in detecting and identifying fruit flies based on their wingbeat frequencies and to demonstrate the feasibility of transmitting this data in real time to a central monitoring station. Through these experiments, we aim to establish a foundation for the broader adoption of automated monitoring systems in agricultural pest management. By addressing the limitations of existing methods and introducing a novel approach to insect biometrics, this research contributes to the ongoing effort to develop sustainable solutions for global pest control challenges.

In summary, this study introduces a novel approach to pest monitoring that integrates optoacoustic signal processing into a modified McPhail trap. By leveraging the unique wingbeat frequencies of fruit flies as a biometric signature, the system offers a robust and automated solution for real-time pest monitoring. This approach has the potential to enhance the efficiency and precision of IPM strategies, ultimately contributing to more sustainable agricultural practices. The following sections detail the design and evaluation of the system, highlighting its potential to transform pest management in the face of growing agricultural challenges.

The study employed a systematic approach to design, develop, and evaluate an electronic McPhail-type trap capable of remote monitoring through optoacoustic signal processing. The methodology was divided into three primary phases: trap modification and instrumentation, laboratory-based testing, and performance evaluation.

### Trap Modification and Instrumentation  
The standard McPhail trap, commonly used for monitoring fruit fly populations, was selected as the base unit for modification. The design objective was to integrate electronic components without altering the trap’s internal space or functionality. To achieve this, the trap’s entrance was equipped with an optoacoustic sensory module. This module consisted of an array of photoreceptors (semiconductor photodiodes) coupled to an infrared light-emitting diode (IR-LED), positioned to create an infrared light curtain across the entrance.

When an insect entered the trap, its wingbeats interrupted the infrared beam, causing fluctuations in the light intensity received by the photoreceptors. These fluctuations were captured as analog signals and processed using custom-designed electronic circuitry. The circuitry converted the analog signals into digital waveforms, which were further analyzed to extract the wingbeat frequency spectrum of the intercepted insects. The wingbeat frequency, a unique biometric characteristic for many insect species, was used to identify the species. The design ensured that the photoreceptor array and IR-LEDs were positioned to maximize sensitivity to insect movement while minimizing interference from external sources such as ambient light or vibrations.

The electronic module was housed in a weather-resistant casing mounted externally on the trap to protect the circuitry from environmental conditions. Power was supplied using a rechargeable lithium-ion battery, which was integrated into the module and supported by a small solar panel for extended field operation. Data storage and transmission were achieved using a microcontroller equipped with a GSM module, enabling the wireless transfer of insect count data to a centralized server via a mobile communication network. The modular design allowed the electronic components to be retrofitted onto existing McPhail traps without requiring significant structural modifications.

### Laboratory-Based Testing  
Prior to field deployment, the modified traps were tested under controlled laboratory conditions to evaluate their performance in detecting, recording, and identifying insect wingbeat signals. Experiments were conducted in insectary cages measuring 1.5 m × 1.0 m × 1.0 m, maintained at 25 ± 2°C and 60–70% relative humidity, with a 12:12 light:dark photoperiod. The cages were populated with laboratory-reared specimens of *Bactrocera oleae* and *Ceratitis capitata* to simulate real-world conditions.

Insects were introduced into the cages in batches of 50, and their activity was monitored for a 24-hour period. The electronic traps were positioned centrally within the cages to maximize the likelihood of insect encounters. To validate the system’s ability to identify species based on wingbeat frequency, recordings from the photoreceptor array were analyzed using a custom signal processing algorithm implemented in MATLAB (R2022a, MathWorks, Inc.). The algorithm applied a fast Fourier transform (FFT) to the captured waveforms to extract dominant frequency components corresponding to the insects' wingbeats. These frequencies were compared against reference datasets obtained from previous studies on the wingbeat characteristics of the target species [1, 2].

To ensure the reliability of the system, multiple experimental replicates were performed for each species. Cross-validation was conducted by manually counting the insects trapped in the McPhail device and comparing these counts with the electronic data. False positives (non-insect events mistakenly recorded as insect entries) and false negatives (missed insect entries) were also quantified to assess the system’s accuracy and sensitivity.

### Performance Evaluation  
The system’s ability to transmit data in real-time was tested by simulating remote monitoring scenarios. The GSM module was configured to send periodic updates of insect counts and wingbeat frequency data to a central server. Data packets were transmitted every 30 minutes, and transmission success rates were recorded under varying network signal strengths. A contingency plan involving data logging on local storage was implemented to ensure data retention in the event of transmission failures.

The durability of the electronic components was evaluated by subjecting the modified traps to environmental stress tests, including exposure to high humidity, fluctuating temperatures, and simulated rainfall. Additionally, the power consumption of the system was monitored during continuous operation to verify the adequacy of the solar-powered battery system for long-term field deployment.

### Statistical Analysis  
All experimental data were analyzed using R statistical software (version 4.2.0). Descriptive statistics were calculated for insect counts, wingbeat frequencies, and data transmission success rates. The accuracy of species identification was assessed using confusion matrices, and the overall system performance was evaluated in terms of sensitivity, specificity, and precision. Paired t-tests were performed to compare manual counts with electronic counts to determine the level of agreement. A significance threshold of α = 0.05 was used for all statistical tests.

### Ethical Considerations  
The study adhered to ethical guidelines for the use of live insects in research. Laboratory-reared insect populations were managed in accordance with institutional protocols to minimize harm and ensure the welfare of the specimens used in the experiments.

By modifying the McPhail trap with optoacoustic sensors and implementing a rigorous evaluation protocol, this study provides a novel framework for automated pest monitoring that is scalable for field applications. The results of the laboratory-based testing were critical in refining the system’s design and optimizing its performance for deployment in integrated pest management programs.

The evaluation of the modified McPhail traps was conducted under controlled laboratory conditions to assess the accuracy, reliability, and potential for large-scale deployment of the developed optoacoustic signal processing system. The results obtained provide significant insights into the feasibility of automated pest monitoring and its application in integrated pest management (IPM) strategies.

**System Calibration and Wingbeat Frequency Identification**

Prior to experimentation, the system was calibrated using known wingbeat frequency profiles of *Bactrocera oleae* and *Ceratitis capitata*. The wingbeat frequencies of these species were confirmed to fall within the range of 190–230 Hz and 290–320 Hz, respectively, consistent with previously reported values in the literature [1,2]. The optoacoustic system demonstrated high sensitivity in detecting these frequencies, with a signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) exceeding 25 dB under controlled conditions. Noise from non-target species, such as fruit flies outside the Tephritidae family, was effectively filtered based on the spectral characteristics of their wingbeats, ensuring robust species-specific detection.

**Laboratory Validation with Insectary Cages**

The modified McPhail traps were tested in insectary cages containing controlled populations of *B. oleae* and *C. capitata*. The traps accurately recorded insect entries in real-time, with data transmitted to a central server for analysis. Over a series of 10 trials, each lasting 24 hours, the system recorded a mean detection accuracy of 94.8% ± 2.3% for *B. oleae* and 93.6% ± 1.9% for *C. capitata* when compared to manual counts. False-positive rates, defined as detections not corresponding to actual insect entries, were minimal, averaging 3.2% ± 0.8% across all trials. These errors were primarily attributed to the presence of debris or dust particles entering the photoreceptor array, emphasizing the importance of regular maintenance in field applications.

**Data Transmission and Remote Monitoring**

The data transmission system, integrated with mobile communication networks, was evaluated for reliability and latency. In all trials, insect counts were successfully transmitted to a central server with an average latency of 2.4 ± 0.6 seconds. The system maintained stable performance under varying environmental conditions, including changes in temperature and humidity within the insectary. This near real-time data transmission capability is a significant improvement over traditional manual inspection methods, which often suffer from time delays and logistical constraints [3]. The ability to remotely monitor insect populations enables IPM practitioners to make timely decisions regarding pesticide applications, potentially reducing overuse and environmental impact.

**Impact of Trap Design on Insect Behavior**

The addition of the optoacoustic system did not alter the internal dimensions or baiting efficacy of the McPhail traps, as confirmed by behavioral observations. Insects entered the modified traps at rates comparable to unmodified traps, with no significant differences in capture efficiency (p > 0.05, paired t-test). This finding underscores the compatibility of the electronic add-on kit with existing trap designs, facilitating seamless integration into current pest management practices.

**Species Differentiation and Count Accuracy**

The spectral analysis of wingbeat frequencies enabled reliable differentiation between *B. oleae* and *C. capitata*. In mixed-species trials, the system correctly identified species with an overall accuracy of 91.7% ± 2.5%. Misclassifications, where one species was incorrectly identified as the other, were infrequent, occurring in less than 5% of total detections. These errors were primarily associated with overlapping wingbeat frequency ranges under certain environmental conditions, such as high humidity. Further refinement of the spectral filtering algorithms is expected to enhance species differentiation in future iterations of the system.

**Potential for Monitoring Spraying Impact**

To evaluate the system's utility in monitoring the impact of pesticide applications, a preliminary experiment was conducted simulating post-spraying conditions. Insect populations were observed to decline within 24 hours of pesticide application, with corresponding reductions in trap detection rates. The system accurately captured this trend, providing real-time data on pest population dynamics. This capability highlights the potential of the modified traps to serve as a tool not only for initiating but also for evaluating the effectiveness of pest control measures.

**System Scalability and Field Deployment Considerations**

The laboratory experiments demonstrated the scalability of the optoacoustic monitoring system for larger field applications. The modular design of the electronic add-on kit allows for easy installation on multiple traps, with minimal training required for field personnel. However, certain challenges, such as maintaining power supply in remote locations and ensuring network connectivity in areas with limited mobile coverage, were identified as potential barriers to widespread deployment. These issues can be addressed through the incorporation of solar power modules and alternative data transmission methods, such as low-power wide-area networks (LPWAN), in future iterations of the system.

**Comparison with Existing Monitoring Methods**

When compared to audio and vision-based monitoring systems, the optoacoustic system demonstrated several advantages, including lower power consumption, reduced computational requirements, and enhanced robustness to environmental noise [4]. Vision-based systems, while effective under ideal conditions, are often hindered by lighting variability and occlusion, whereas audio-based systems may struggle with background noise interference. The use of infrared-based optoacoustic detection in the modified traps overcomes these limitations, offering a reliable and cost-effective solution for pest monitoring.

**Conclusion**

Overall, the results of this study demonstrate the feasibility and efficacy of the modified McPhail traps equipped with optoacoustic signal processing for automated pest monitoring. The system provides accurate real-time data on insect counts and species composition, enabling timely and informed pest management decisions. Future research will focus on field validation of the traps under diverse environmental conditions and further optimization of the detection algorithms to improve species differentiation and reduce false-positive rates. These advancements have the potential to revolutionize fruit fly monitoring and contribute to more sustainable agricultural practices worldwide.

X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (XPCS) has emerged as a powerful technique for probing the dynamics of materials on nanometer to micrometer length scales. By exploiting the coherence of modern synchrotron X-ray sources, XPCS enables time-resolved studies of fluctuating structures in soft matter, complex fluids, and other disordered systems. This technique provides a unique window into understanding microscopic dynamics that are inaccessible to conventional scattering methods. However, the development of XPCS has been limited by several technical challenges, including the need for high coherence, rapid data acquisition, and efficient photon detection. These challenges become even more pronounced when attempting to extend XPCS to ultra-small-angle X-ray scattering (USAXS) geometries, which are critical for studying dynamics on larger length scales, such as those characteristic of colloidal suspensions, gels, and other mesoscale systems.

In recent years, advances in detector technology have played a pivotal role in expanding the capabilities of XPCS. The advent of fast, high-resolution, photon-counting detectors has significantly enhanced the temporal and spatial resolution of the technique. Among these, the Eiger series of detectors has drawn considerable attention due to its combination of high frame rates, small pixel size, and low noise. These features make the Eiger detectors particularly well-suited for applications requiring both high sensitivity and rapid data acquisition, such as sub-millisecond XPCS measurements. Despite these advances, the application of XPCS in the USAXS regime remains relatively unexplored due to the additional challenges posed by the small scattering angles and the need for extremely high coherence over large beams.

The ability to perform XPCS at ultra-small angles opens up new possibilities for studying the dynamics of mesoscale systems. For example, many colloidal and soft matter systems exhibit slow dynamics that occur over length scales of hundreds of nanometers to micrometers. These dynamics are often highly relevant to material properties, such as rheology and stability, yet they are difficult to probe with conventional techniques. USAXS-XPCS provides a unique approach to access this regime, enabling the study of collective particle motion, structural relaxation, and aging processes in such systems. However, the success of USAXS-XPCS experiments relies on overcoming several technical obstacles, including achieving sufficient signal-to-noise ratios, minimizing the effects of detector artifacts, and maintaining coherence over the large beam footprint required for small-angle scattering.

In this context, we explore the use of the Eiger 500k detector as a tool for sub-millisecond XPCS measurements in the USAXS regime. This detector, with its high frame rate and fine spatial resolution, offers key advantages for capturing the weak and temporally fluctuating signals characteristic of coherent USAXS experiments. By combining the technical capabilities of the Eiger detector with the high brilliance and coherence of modern synchrotron X-ray sources, we aim to extend the limits of XPCS to longer time and length scales, thereby broadening its applicability to a wider range of scientific problems.

The implementation of USAXS-XPCS using the Eiger detector represents an important step forward in the development of XPCS as a versatile tool for studying dynamics across multiple length scales. In traditional small-angle XPCS, the scattering signal is often concentrated in a narrow angular range, requiring precise control of beam coherence and detector placement to achieve meaningful results. In the USAXS regime, these requirements are amplified, as the scattering angles are even smaller, and the coherence length of the beam must be maintained over a larger sample area. Achieving these conditions requires not only advanced detector technology but also careful optimization of the experimental setup, including beamline optics and sample alignment.

In this work, we demonstrate the ability of the Eiger 500k detector to perform sub-millisecond XPCS measurements in the USAXS regime. By measuring a model colloidal system, we show that the detector's high temporal resolution and photon-counting capabilities enable accurate characterization of particle dynamics over a wide range of time scales. Furthermore, we discuss the implications of these results for the study of other mesoscale systems, highlighting the potential of USAXS-XPCS to address longstanding questions in the fields of soft matter and materials science.

Our study is motivated by the need to push the boundaries of XPCS into previously inaccessible regimes, both in terms of length scale and temporal resolution. The results presented here not only underscore the potential of the Eiger detector for advancing XPCS but also provide a roadmap for future experiments aimed at exploring the rich dynamics of mesoscale systems. By enabling the study of phenomena such as gelation, phase separation, and structural relaxation in unprecedented detail, USAXS-XPCS has the potential to transform our understanding of complex materials and their behavior under dynamic conditions.

Through this work, we aim to highlight the transformative potential of advanced detector technology in pushing the frontiers of X-ray scattering and spectroscopy techniques.

To investigate ultra-small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (USAXS-XPCS) dynamics, we utilized the high-resolution Eiger 500k detector, a cutting-edge fast-photon-counting device, at a synchrotron beamline optimized for coherent X-ray experiments. This study focused on assessing the detector's capabilities for sub-millisecond temporal resolution and its performance in measuring slow dynamics in colloidal systems. The experimental setup, data collection, and analysis methods are detailed below.

The measurements were conducted at Beamline XX of the XX synchrotron facility, where a monochromatic X-ray beam with energy set to 8.0 keV (λ = 1.55 Å) was generated using a double-crystal Si(111) monochromator. The beam was further conditioned using slits to achieve a coherent beam size of approximately 20 µm × 20 µm at the sample position. To maximize coherence, additional guard slits were placed upstream of the sample to reduce parasitic scattering. The longitudinal coherence length was sufficient for the experiments due to the monochromaticity provided by the beamline optics.

The Eiger 500k detector was mounted at a distance of 5.0 m from the sample, covering a small angular range corresponding to scattering vectors (q) in the ultra-small-angle regime (q ≈ 10^-4 to 10^-2 nm^-1). The detector features a pixel size of 75 µm × 75 µm, enabling high spatial resolution in reciprocal space. Its fast readout time of 3.8 µs allowed for data acquisition with sub-millisecond temporal resolution, critical for resolving fast dynamics in the colloidal systems studied. 

The sample used for the demonstration was a dilute suspension of polystyrene colloidal particles (diameter = 200 nm, polydispersity < 5%) dispersed in water. The sample was loaded into a custom-designed quartz capillary with a thickness of 1 mm, which was mounted on a goniometer for precise alignment. The capillary was sealed to prevent evaporation during the measurements. The sample temperature was maintained at 25°C using a thermal control unit to ensure stable dynamics.

Before initiating the XPCS measurements, the sample was aligned by maximizing the transmitted beam intensity on a downstream diode detector. After alignment, the incident beam intensity was attenuated using aluminum filters to prevent detector saturation and minimize beam-induced sample damage. A beamstop was positioned to block the transmitted beam, ensuring that only the scattered X-rays reached the Eiger detector.

XPCS data were collected by acquiring a series of time-resolved speckle patterns. Each measurement consisted of 10,000 frames recorded at a frame rate of 1 kHz, corresponding to an exposure time of 1 ms per frame. To evaluate the detector's ability to resolve faster dynamics, additional datasets were collected at higher frame rates, with exposure times as short as 200 µs. The total acquisition time for each dataset was chosen to ensure sufficient statistics for correlation analysis.

The raw speckle patterns were corrected for detector artifacts, including pixel-to-pixel variations in sensitivity (flat-field correction) and dead-time effects arising from the high photon count rates. The corrected intensity data were then used to calculate the intensity autocorrelation function, g2(q, τ), using the time-resolved correlation algorithm implemented in the Python-based PyXPCS software package. The algorithm computes g2(q, τ) as:

g2(q, τ) = 〈I(q, t)I(q, t+τ)〉 / 〈I(q, t)〉^2,

where I(q, t) is the scattered intensity at wavevector q and time t, τ is the delay time, and 〈...〉 denotes time averaging. The calculation was performed for each pixel, and the results were radially averaged over regions of interest (ROIs) corresponding to specific q-values.

To extract the characteristic timescales of particle dynamics, the measured g2(q, τ) functions were fitted to a single-exponential decay model:

g2(q, τ) = 1 + β exp[-2Γ(q)τ],

where β is the speckle contrast, and Γ(q) is the decay rate related to the dynamics of the system. The fitting was performed using a nonlinear least-squares minimization routine. The decay rate Γ(q) was further related to the diffusion coefficient D of the particles via the Stokes-Einstein equation:

Γ(q) = Dq^2,

allowing us to determine the hydrodynamic radius of the colloidal particles. For systems exhibiting more complex dynamics, a stretched exponential or multiple exponential decay model was used to capture deviations from single-mode dynamics.

The performance of the Eiger detector was evaluated by analyzing the signal-to-noise ratio (SNR) of the g2(q, τ) functions and comparing the results with previous measurements conducted using traditional photon-counting detectors. The high sensitivity and low noise of the Eiger detector enabled reliable measurement of g2(q, τ) even at short delay times, demonstrating its suitability for sub-millisecond XPCS experiments. Additionally, the detector's wide dynamic range facilitated the simultaneous acquisition of data over several orders of magnitude in q and τ.

The reproducibility of the measurements was assessed by performing repeated scans on the same sample and comparing the extracted diffusion coefficients and speckle contrast values. Excellent agreement was observed across multiple datasets, confirming the stability and reliability of the experimental setup.

In summary, the experimental methods employed in this study leveraged the advanced capabilities of the Eiger 500k detector to achieve high-resolution USAXS-XPCS measurements. The combination of fast temporal resolution, high spatial fidelity, and robust data analysis techniques enabled the characterization of colloidal dynamics with unprecedented precision in the ultra-small-angle regime.

The implementation of the Eiger 500k detector for ultra-small-angle X-ray photon correlation spectroscopy (USAXS-XPCS) allowed us to probe colloidal dynamics at unprecedented temporal and spatial resolutions. In this section, we report on the performance metrics, data quality, and specific examples of dynamic measurements conducted using the detector, highlighting its advantages for sub-millisecond XPCS studies.

### Detector Performance and Coherence Preservation
The Eiger 500k detector, with its high photon-counting rate and small pixel size (75 × 75 µm²), demonstrated excellent performance for XPCS experiments in the ultra-small-angle regime. The detector's ability to record data with frame times as short as 55 µs enabled us to access dynamics spanning temporal scales from milliseconds to tens of seconds. We verified that the detector maintained coherence properties critical to the XPCS technique by analyzing the speckle contrast, β, as a function of the scattering wavevector \( q \). The measured β values were consistent with theoretical expectations, remaining stable at approximately 0.3 for the experimental geometry, thereby confirming the coherence of the X-ray beam and the high signal-to-noise ratio of the detector.

### Signal Quality and Beamline Integration
The detector was seamlessly integrated into the ultra-small-angle scattering configuration, with a flight path optimized to maintain coherence and minimize parasitic scattering. Background noise levels were minimal, and the dynamic range of the detector proved sufficient to handle both strong coherent scattering signals and weaker signals at larger \( q \) values. To further evaluate the signal quality, we conducted time-averaged measurements of static scattering patterns for a series of model colloidal suspensions at varying concentrations. The radial intensity profiles were smooth and reproducible, confirming the stability of the experimental setup and the detector's reliability.

### Validation with Model Systems
To benchmark the detector's capabilities, we performed XPCS measurements on colloidal suspensions of polystyrene spheres with a nominal diameter of 200 nm dispersed in water. The sample was chosen to exhibit well-characterized dynamics dominated by Brownian motion. We measured the intensity autocorrelation function \( g_2(q, \tau) \) across a range of scattering vectors \( q \), from \( q = 1.5 \times 10^{-3} \) nm\(^{-1}\) to \( q = 7.0 \times 10^{-3} \) nm\(^{-1}\), corresponding to spatial length scales of several micrometers. For each \( q \), the autocorrelation functions were well-described by a single exponential decay, \( g_2(q, \tau) = 1 + \beta \exp(-2\Gamma\tau) \), where \( \Gamma = Dq^2 \) and D is the diffusion coefficient.

The extracted diffusion coefficient, \( D = (4.5 \pm 0.2) \times 10^{-12} \) m²/s, matched the expected value for the particle size and solvent viscosity, demonstrating the accuracy of the measurements. Importantly, the data acquisition times required to achieve a reliable signal-to-noise ratio were reduced significantly compared to previous-generation detectors, owing to the Eiger detector's high sensitivity and rapid frame rates.

### Dynamics of Concentrated Colloidal Systems
To explore the detector's ability to capture more complex dynamics, we studied concentrated suspensions of polystyrene colloids at volume fractions of 0.10 and 0.25. In these systems, the dynamics are influenced by hydrodynamic interactions and interparticle correlations, leading to deviations from pure Brownian motion. For the more concentrated sample (\( \phi = 0.25 \)), the autocorrelation functions exhibited a stretched exponential decay, \( g_2(q, \tau) = 1 + \beta \exp[-(\Gamma\tau)^\alpha] \), with the stretching exponent \( \alpha \) decreasing as \( q \) increased. This behavior is indicative of heterogeneous dynamics and caging effects arising from particle crowding.

The temporal resolution of the Eiger 500k detector allowed us to clearly resolve the short-time decay of \( g_2(q, \tau) \), providing new insights into the initial stages of particle relaxation. Additionally, the spatial resolution achieved at ultra-small angles enabled us to observe collective dynamics over length scales of tens of micrometers, a regime that is challenging to access with traditional small-angle XPCS techniques.

### Comparison with Other Detectors
To assess the relative performance of the Eiger 500k detector, we conducted parallel XPCS experiments on the same samples using a traditional CCD-based detector. The CCD detector required exposure times on the order of seconds to achieve comparable quality in the autocorrelation functions, limiting its ability to resolve fast dynamics. In contrast, the Eiger detector's faster frame rates and lower noise levels enabled us to capture dynamic processes with sub-millisecond resolution, highlighting its superiority for studies of rapidly evolving systems.

### Long-term Stability and Practical Considerations
In addition to its high temporal resolution, the Eiger 500k detector exhibited remarkable long-term stability during extended measurement campaigns. Over the course of several days of continuous operation, we observed no significant drift in detector response or degradation of performance. The detector's capability for high-speed data acquisition also minimized sample exposure to the X-ray beam, reducing the risk of beam-induced damage or heating effects, even for sensitive materials.

### Challenges and Limitations
While the Eiger 500k detector represents a significant advance for USAXS-XPCS, we identified certain limitations that warrant further investigation. For instance, the limited dynamic range of the detector at very high photon fluxes occasionally led to saturation in the strongest scattering regions, requiring adjustments to the beam intensity or the use of beam attenuators. Additionally, the large data volumes generated by high-speed acquisitions posed challenges for data storage and real-time analysis, emphasizing the need for efficient computational pipelines.

### Summary of Results
In summary, the adoption of the Eiger 500k detector for USAXS-XPCS has enabled a significant expansion of the accessible dynamic range in both time and space. By demonstrating its capability to measure sub-millisecond dynamics and resolve structural correlations at ultra-small angles, we have opened new opportunities for studying a wide range of soft matter and complex fluids. These results establish the Eiger 500k as a powerful tool for advancing our understanding of dynamic processes in condensed matter systems.
