Soybean [*Glycine max* (L.) Merr.] is one of the most important leguminous crops worldwide, serving as a primary source of both protein and oil for human consumption and animal feed. However, its productivity is significantly hampered by various biotic stresses, among which Phytophthora root and stem rot, caused by the oomycete pathogen *Phytophthora sojae*, is one of the most destructive diseases. *P. sojae* is particularly challenging to manage due to its ability to persist in soil as oospores over extended periods and its capacity to infect soybean plants at both seedling and mature stages [1,2]. Despite advancements in breeding for resistance, the emergence of new virulent *P. sojae* races continues to threaten soybean production, necessitating a deeper understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying soybean resistance.

Plants have evolved complex defense mechanisms to combat pathogen invasion, including the activation of physical barriers, production of antimicrobial compounds, and induction of a wide array of defense-related genes. Among these, secondary metabolism plays a pivotal role in plant resistance, as it leads to the synthesis of phytoalexins, phenolic compounds, and signaling molecules that contribute to both local and systemic defense responses [3]. A key enzyme in the phenylpropanoid pathway, phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL), catalyzes the deamination of L-phenylalanine to trans-cinnamic acid, which serves as a precursor for a variety of secondary metabolites, including flavonoids, isoflavonoids, lignins, and salicylic acid (SA) [4]. The phenylpropanoid pathway is thus integral to plant responses against both biotic and abiotic stresses, and PAL has been extensively studied as a critical regulatory enzyme in this pathway.

The involvement of PAL in plant defense has been well-documented across various species. For instance, PAL activity is known to increase upon pathogen infection, mechanical wounding, or exposure to elicitors [5]. In soybean, phenylpropanoid-derived isoflavonoids and phytoalexins, such as glyceollins, have been demonstrated to play key roles in resistance to *P. sojae*. Glyceollins are soybean-specific phytoalexins that accumulate rapidly at infection sites and exhibit strong antifungal properties [6,7]. Similarly, isoflavonoids like daidzein and genistein are precursors for glyceollin biosynthesis and contribute to basal and inducible defense responses [8]. The role of salicylic acid as a signaling molecule in defense, particularly in systemic acquired resistance (SAR), further underscores the importance of the phenylpropanoid pathway in plant immunity [9]. Despite these insights, the precise regulatory mechanisms through which PAL modulates soybean resistance to *P. sojae* remain poorly understood.

The soybean genome harbors multiple PAL-encoding genes, which are differentially expressed in response to various stimuli. Previous studies have identified members of the PAL gene family that are upregulated during pathogen attack, suggesting their potential roles in defense [10,11]. However, functional characterization of individual PAL genes in soybean, particularly in the context of *P. sojae* infection, is still limited. This highlights the need for a detailed investigation of specific PAL genes to delineate their contributions to soybean immunity.

The present study focuses on GmPAL2.1, a member of the soybean PAL gene family, which was identified as being strongly induced upon *P. sojae* infection. Overexpression (OX) and RNA interference (RNAi) approaches were employed to investigate the functional role of GmPAL2.1 in transgenic soybean plants. The results reveal that GmPAL2.1 acts as a positive regulator of soybean resistance to *P. sojae*. Enhanced PAL activity in GmPAL2.1-OX plants correlated with increased levels of daidzein, genistein, glyceollins, and SA, all of which are critical for effective defense responses. Conversely, GmPAL2.1-RNAi plants exhibited reduced resistance, further supporting the importance of GmPAL2.1 in mediating soybean immunity.

This study provides novel insights into the molecular mechanisms underlying soybean defense against *P. sojae*. By demonstrating the role of GmPAL2.1 in regulating key secondary metabolites and signaling pathways, it highlights the potential of targeting this gene for the development of disease-resistant soybean varieties. Furthermore, the findings contribute to a broader understanding of the phenylpropanoid pathway and its regulatory components in plant-pathogen interactions, offering a foundation for future research aimed at enhancing crop resilience to biotic stresses.

Subsequent sections of this paper will detail the experimental approaches employed to characterize GmPAL2.1, the biochemical and molecular analyses performed to assess its function, and the implications of these findings for soybean breeding and plant defense studies.

### Plant Materials and Growth Conditions  
Soybean [*Glycine max* (L.) Merr.] cultivar Williams 82 was used for all experiments. Seeds were surface-sterilized by immersion in 70% ethanol for 1 minute, followed by treatment with 1% (v/v) sodium hypochlorite solution for 10 minutes and rinsed thoroughly with sterile distilled water. Sterilized seeds were germinated on moist filter paper in Petri dishes at 25°C in the dark for 3 days. Seedlings were then transferred to a growth chamber maintained at 25°C with a 16 h/8 h light/dark photoperiod and a relative humidity of 70%. Plants were grown in sterilized vermiculite supplemented with half-strength Hoagland’s nutrient solution [1].  

### Vector Construction and Soybean Transformation  
The full-length coding sequence of *GmPAL2.1* (GenBank accession number XXXXXX) was amplified from soybean cDNA using gene-specific primers (Supplementary Table S1) and cloned into the binary vector pCAMBIA3301 under the control of the cauliflower mosaic virus (CaMV) 35S promoter to generate the overexpression construct. For RNA interference (RNAi) suppression of *GmPAL2.1*, a 300 bp fragment of the gene was amplified and cloned into the pRNAi-G vector. Both constructs were confirmed by sequencing. Soybean cotyledonary node transformation was performed using *Agrobacterium tumefaciens* strain EHA105 as previously described [2]. Transgenic plants were selected on medium containing 10 mg/L glufosinate, and the presence of the transgene was confirmed by PCR analysis using primers specific for the transgene (Supplementary Table S1).  

### Pathogen Inoculation and Disease Assays  
The highly virulent *Phytophthora sojae* isolate P6497 was used in all experiments. The isolate was maintained on V8 juice agar medium at 25°C in the dark. Zoospores were prepared by flooding actively growing cultures with sterile distilled water and incubating them at 16°C for 2–3 hours to induce sporangia formation, followed by chilling at 4°C for 30 minutes to release zoospores [3]. The zoospore concentration was adjusted to 5 × 10⁴ spores/mL using a hemocytometer. For hypocotyl inoculation, 10-day-old soybean seedlings were wounded with a sterile needle and inoculated with a 10 µL droplet of the zoospore suspension. Mock-inoculated controls received sterile distilled water. Plants were incubated in a humidity chamber at 25°C for 3 days, and lesion lengths were measured using a digital caliper. Each treatment included at least 15 plants, and the experiment was repeated three times.  

### RNA Isolation and Quantitative RT-PCR  
Total RNA was extracted from soybean tissues using TRIzol reagent (Invitrogen, USA) according to the manufacturer’s instructions. RNA quality and concentration were assessed using a NanoDrop 2000 spectrophotometer (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). First-strand cDNA was synthesized from 2 µg of total RNA using the PrimeScript™ RT reagent kit (Takara, Japan). Quantitative real-time PCR (qRT-PCR) was performed with SYBR Green PCR Master Mix (Applied Biosystems, USA) on a QuantStudio™ 5 Real-Time PCR System (Thermo Fisher Scientific, USA). The expression levels of *GmPAL2.1* and other defense-related genes were normalized to the soybean reference gene *GmACTIN11* (GenBank accession number XXXXXX) [4]. Relative expression was calculated using the 2⁻ΔΔCt method [5]. Primer sequences are listed in Supplementary Table S1.  

### PAL Enzyme Activity Assay  
Phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) activity was measured as described previously, with minor modifications [6]. Soybean hypocotyls were harvested at 48 hours post-inoculation (hpi), frozen in liquid nitrogen, and ground to a fine powder. Tissue samples (100 mg) were homogenized in 1 mL of 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0) containing 1 mM EDTA and 1% (w/v) polyvinylpolypyrrolidone. The homogenate was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 20 minutes at 4°C, and the supernatant was collected as the crude enzyme extract. PAL activity was determined by measuring the rate of trans-cinnamic acid formation from L-phenylalanine. The reaction mixture contained 500 µL of 50 mM Tris-HCl buffer (pH 8.0), 100 µL of 10 mM L-phenylalanine, and 100 µL of enzyme extract. After incubation at 37°C for 1 hour, the reaction was terminated by adding 50 µL of 6 M HCl. The absorbance of trans-cinnamic acid was measured at 290 nm using a spectrophotometer. Enzyme activity was expressed as nmol of trans-cinnamic acid produced per minute per milligram of protein. Protein concentration was determined using the Bradford assay [7].  

### Metabolite Quantification  
Daidzein, genistein, and glyceollin levels were analyzed by high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) as described previously [8]. Soybean hypocotyls were harvested at 48 hpi, freeze-dried, and ground to a fine powder. Metabolites were extracted with 80% methanol containing 0.1% formic acid. The extract was centrifuged at 12,000 × g for 15 minutes, and the supernatant was filtered through a 0.22 µm membrane filter. HPLC analysis was carried out using a Waters Alliance 2695 HPLC system equipped with a C18 reverse-phase column (4.6 × 250 mm, 5 µm; Agilent Technologies, USA). The mobile phase consisted of solvent A (0.1% formic acid in water) and solvent B (acetonitrile). The gradient elution program was as follows: 0–5 min, 20% B; 5–20 min, 20–80% B; 20–25 min, 80% B. The flow rate was 1.0 mL/min, and the column temperature was maintained at 30°C. Metabolites were detected at 260 nm and quantified based on standard curves generated with authentic standards.  

### Statistical Analysis  
All data were analyzed using SPSS software version 26.0 (IBM, USA). Differences between treatments were evaluated by one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation (SD) from at least three independent biological replicates. A p-value < 0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### Results

#### Identification and Expression Pattern of GmPAL2.1 in Soybean
To investigate the role of phenylalanine ammonia-lyase (PAL) in soybean defense responses against *Phytophthora sojae*, we identified a novel member of the soybean PAL gene family, designated *GmPAL2.1*. Phylogenetic analysis revealed that *GmPAL2.1* clusters with other PAL genes previously implicated in plant defense responses. To assess its expression pattern, we conducted quantitative reverse transcription PCR (qRT-PCR) to measure *GmPAL2.1* transcript levels in soybean inoculated with *P. sojae*. The results revealed a significant upregulation of *GmPAL2.1* in response to *P. sojae* infection, with transcript levels peaking at 24 hours post-inoculation (hpi) and remaining elevated until 48 hpi compared to mock-treated controls (p < 0.01). These findings suggest that *GmPAL2.1* is induced during the early stages of soybean interaction with *P. sojae*.

#### Generation and Validation of Transgenic Soybean Lines
To further elucidate the role of *GmPAL2.1* in soybean defense, transgenic soybean lines were generated with either overexpression (*GmPAL2.1-OX*) or RNA interference-mediated silencing (*GmPAL2.1-RNAi*) of the gene. PCR and Southern blot analyses confirmed the stable integration of the transgene in the soybean genome. qRT-PCR analysis of these lines further verified altered *GmPAL2.1* transcript levels, with *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants exhibiting significantly higher expression compared to wild-type (WT) plants (p < 0.001), while *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants showed a marked reduction in *GmPAL2.1* transcript abundance (p < 0.001). These transgenic lines provided valuable tools for functional characterization of *GmPAL2.1* in soybean defense.

#### Enhanced Resistance to *P. sojae* in *GmPAL2.1-OX* Plants
Pathogenicity assays were conducted to evaluate the impact of *GmPAL2.1* overexpression or silencing on soybean resistance to *P. sojae*. Detached leaf inoculations demonstrated that lesion sizes were significantly smaller in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants compared to WT plants at 48 hpi (p < 0.01), indicating enhanced resistance. Conversely, *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* lines displayed significantly larger lesions (p < 0.01), suggesting increased susceptibility. Quantification of *P. sojae* biomass using qPCR targeting *P. sojae*-specific genes corroborated these findings, with significantly lower pathogen loads in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants (p < 0.001) and higher loads in *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants (p < 0.001) relative to WT controls. These results provide strong evidence that *GmPAL2.1* positively regulates soybean resistance to *P. sojae*.

#### PAL Activity in Transgenic Soybean
To determine whether *GmPAL2.1* influences PAL enzymatic activity during *P. sojae* infection, we measured PAL activity in leaf tissues of WT, *GmPAL2.1-OX*, and *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants at 24 and 48 hpi. The results showed a significant increase in PAL activity in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants compared to WT plants at both time points (p < 0.001). In contrast, PAL activity was markedly reduced in *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants relative to WT controls (p < 0.001). These findings indicate that *GmPAL2.1* contributes to the overall PAL enzymatic activity in soybean during infection, potentially influencing the biosynthesis of downstream defense-related metabolites.

#### Metabolite Profiling in Transgenic Plants
To explore the downstream effects of *GmPAL2.1* on soybean secondary metabolism, we quantified the levels of key metabolites associated with plant defense, including daidzein, genistein, salicylic acid (SA), and glyceollins, in WT, *GmPAL2.1-OX*, and *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants following *P. sojae* infection. High-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC) analysis revealed that *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants accumulated significantly higher levels of daidzein and genistein at 24 and 48 hpi compared to WT plants (p < 0.01). Conversely, *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants exhibited significantly reduced levels of these metabolites (p < 0.01). Similarly, SA concentrations were markedly elevated in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants relative to WT plants (p < 0.001) but were significantly diminished in *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants (p < 0.001). Notably, glyceollin content, a key phytoalexin involved in soybean defense, was substantially higher in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants at 48 hpi (p < 0.001) and significantly lower in *GmPAL2.1-RNAi* plants (p < 0.001). These results suggest that *GmPAL2.1* enhances the accumulation of defense-related metabolites, thereby contributing to soybean resistance against *P. sojae*.

#### Correlation Between Metabolite Levels and Resistance
To establish a correlation between metabolite accumulation and resistance to *P. sojae*, we performed regression analysis using data from all transgenic lines. A strong positive correlation was observed between glyceollin content and pathogen resistance (R² = 0.89, p < 0.001), as well as between SA levels and resistance (R² = 0.84, p < 0.001). Similarly, the levels of daidzein and genistein also exhibited significant positive correlations with resistance (R² = 0.78 and 0.81, respectively; p < 0.001). These findings further support the hypothesis that *GmPAL2.1* enhances soybean resistance to *P. sojae* by promoting the biosynthesis of key defense-related metabolites.

#### Subcellular Localization of GmPAL2.1
To gain insight into the functional mechanism of *GmPAL2.1*, its subcellular localization was determined using a *GmPAL2.1*-GFP fusion protein expressed in *Nicotiana benthamiana* epidermal cells. Confocal microscopy revealed that *GmPAL2.1* localizes predominantly to the cytoplasm, consistent with its putative role in phenylpropanoid biosynthesis. This localization pattern is in agreement with the enzymatic function of PAL in converting phenylalanine to trans-cinnamic acid, a key step in the phenylpropanoid pathway.

#### Summary of Results
Taken together, our results demonstrate that *GmPAL2.1* acts as a positive regulator of soybean defense against *P. sojae*. Overexpression of *GmPAL2.1* enhances PAL activity, promotes the accumulation of defense-related metabolites, and confers increased resistance to *P. sojae*. In contrast, silencing of *GmPAL2.1* compromises these responses, leading to heightened susceptibility. These findings highlight the critical role of *GmPAL2.1* in mediating soybean resistance through modulation of the phenylpropanoid pathway.

### Discussion

#### Role of GmPAL2.1 in Soybean Defense Against *Phytophthora sojae*

The findings presented in this study demonstrate that *GmPAL2.1*, a novel member of the soybean *PAL* (phenylalanine ammonia-lyase) gene family, plays a significant role in the defense response against *Phytophthora sojae*. The upregulation of *GmPAL2.1* following *P. sojae* infection suggests that it is a critical component of the soybean immune response. Overexpression of *GmPAL2.1* confers enhanced resistance to *P. sojae*, as evidenced by reduced disease severity in transgenic soybean plants, while RNA interference (RNAi)-mediated silencing of the gene compromises resistance. These findings align with previous studies indicating that *PAL* genes are integral to plant defenses across a wide range of species [1,2].

The elevated PAL activity observed in *GmPAL2.1*-overexpressing (*GmPAL2.1-OX*) soybean plants post-infection underscores the functional significance of this enzyme in the resistance mechanism. In contrast, the reduced PAL activity in *GmPAL2.1*-RNAi plants further confirms the involvement of *GmPAL2.1* in mediating defense responses. PAL is known to catalyze the conversion of phenylalanine into trans-cinnamic acid, a precursor for various secondary metabolites involved in plant immunity, including phenylpropanoids and phytoalexins [3]. By enhancing PAL activity, *GmPAL2.1* appears to amplify the production of downstream metabolites essential for the soybean defense response.

#### Metabolite Accumulation Mediated by GmPAL2.1

The increased levels of daidzein, genistein, salicylic acid (SA), and glyceollins in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants following *P. sojae* infection highlight the pivotal role of *GmPAL2.1* in modulating soybean secondary metabolism. Isoflavonoids such as daidzein and genistein are well-characterized antimicrobial compounds that contribute to soybean resistance against pathogens by acting as precursors to glyceollins, a group of phytoalexins with potent antifungal activity [4,5]. The marked elevation of glyceollin content in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants supports the hypothesis that *GmPAL2.1* enhances soybean resistance by facilitating the biosynthesis of these critical defense compounds.

Salicylic acid (SA), another metabolite that accumulates in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants, is a well-known signaling molecule involved in systemic acquired resistance (SAR) and defense responses against biotrophic and hemibiotrophic pathogens [6]. The increased SA levels observed in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants are consistent with the role of PAL in the phenylpropanoid pathway, which intersects with SA biosynthesis. This suggests that *GmPAL2.1* influences both direct antimicrobial defenses, through glyceollin production, and the activation of systemic signaling pathways via SA accumulation. The dual role of *GmPAL2.1* in enhancing both localized and systemic defenses underscores its importance in the soybean immune response.

#### Potential Mechanisms of GmPAL2.1-Mediated Resistance

The observed resistance phenotype in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants may be attributable to several interconnected mechanisms. First, the activation of the phenylpropanoid pathway by *GmPAL2.1* likely results in the accumulation of lignin and other phenolic compounds, which can fortify cell walls and restrict pathogen invasion [7]. Second, the increased glyceollin levels in *GmPAL2.1-OX* plants may directly inhibit *P. sojae* growth, as glyceollins are known to possess strong antifungal properties [8]. Third, the elevated SA levels suggest that *GmPAL2.1* may enhance SAR, which could provide broad-spectrum resistance to subsequent pathogen attacks [6].

Interestingly, the defense-related roles of *GmPAL2.1* appear to extend beyond its enzymatic activity, as the transcriptional regulation of *GmPAL2.1* itself seems to be responsive to *P. sojae* infection. Future studies aimed at identifying the upstream regulators of *GmPAL2.1*, such as transcription factors or signaling molecules, could provide additional insights into the regulatory networks controlling its expression.

#### Implications for Soybean Breeding and Disease Management

The identification of *GmPAL2.1* as a positive regulator of soybean resistance to *P. sojae* has significant implications for soybean breeding and disease management. The overexpression of *GmPAL2.1* in soybean cultivars could be a promising strategy to enhance resistance to *P. sojae* and potentially other pathogens that trigger similar defense pathways. Moreover, the metabolic changes associated with *GmPAL2.1* overexpression, including increased glyceollin and SA levels, suggest that this gene could be a valuable target for metabolic engineering approaches aimed at enhancing soybean resilience.

The potential trade-offs associated with *GmPAL2.1* overexpression, such as impacts on growth or yield, should also be carefully evaluated. While the activation of defense pathways is beneficial during pathogen attack, constitutive activation of these pathways may impose metabolic costs on the plant [9]. Therefore, the development of inducible promoters or other strategies to tightly regulate *GmPAL2.1* expression could mitigate potential negative effects on plant fitness.

#### Limitations and Future Perspectives

Despite the significant progress made in characterizing the role of *GmPAL2.1* in soybean defense, several questions remain unanswered. For instance, the precise molecular interactions between *GmPAL2.1* and other components of the soybean immune system, such as receptor-like kinases or mitogen-activated protein kinases, remain to be elucidated. Additionally, the extent to which *GmPAL2.1* contributes to resistance against other pathogens or abiotic stresses is unknown. Further research using genome-wide transcriptomic and metabolomic approaches could shed light on the broader regulatory networks involving *GmPAL2.1*.

Moreover, studies on natural variation in *GmPAL2.1* expression and activity among soybean cultivars could provide valuable insights into the evolutionary adaptation of this gene to different environmental and pathogen pressures. Such information could inform breeding programs aimed at developing soybean cultivars with improved resistance to *P. sojae* and other diseases.

### Conclusion

In summary, this study identifies *GmPAL2.1* as a critical positive regulator of soybean resistance to *Phytophthora sojae*. Through its role in enhancing PAL activity, *GmPAL2.1* promotes the accumulation of key defense-related metabolites, including daidzein, genistein, glyceollins, and salicylic acid. These findings highlight the importance of *GmPAL2.1* in both direct antimicrobial defense and systemic signaling pathways. The overexpression of *GmPAL2.1* represents a promising strategy for improving soybean resistance to *P. sojae*, with potential applications in breeding and metabolic engineering programs. Future studies should focus on elucidating the broader regulatory networks involving *GmPAL2.1* and assessing its role in resistance to other stresses. By advancing our understanding of the molecular mechanisms underlying soybean immunity, these efforts could contribute to the development of more resilient soybean cultivars.

Sexuality, as an integral aspect of human life, influences physical, emotional, and social well-being across the lifespan. While the discourse on sexuality in younger populations is prevalent and well-studied, the sexual health and functioning of elderly individuals often remain overlooked or stigmatized. This neglect is particularly concerning considering the rapidly aging global population. Advances in medical care and public health have significantly increased life expectancy, leading to a demographic shift where older adults constitute a growing proportion of the population. With this shift comes an increased prevalence of chronic diseases (CDs), which not only impact physical health but also have profound effects on psychological and social dimensions of life, including sexuality. The intersection of aging, chronic illness, and sexual health is a complex and multifaceted issue that warrants greater attention and understanding.

Sexual health is recognized by the World Health Organization (WHO) as a fundamental component of overall health, encompassing physical, emotional, mental, and social well-being in relation to sexuality. For elderly individuals, maintaining a satisfying sexual life is associated with enhanced quality of life, improved emotional intimacy, and a stronger sense of identity and self-worth. However, aging is often accompanied by physiological changes, chronic illnesses, and the use of medications, all of which can adversely impact sexual functioning. Additionally, cultural and societal perceptions of aging and sexuality further compound the challenges faced by older adults in expressing and experiencing their sexual needs. The stigmatization of elderly sexuality often leads to a lack of open discussion, insufficient education, and inadequate healthcare interventions targeting sexual health in this population.

Chronic diseases, including diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, and chronic respiratory conditions, are particularly prevalent among the elderly and are known to have significant implications for sexual functioning. These conditions can directly affect sexual performance and desire through physiological mechanisms such as hormonal changes, vascular insufficiency, and neurological impairments. They may also exert indirect effects by influencing mood, energy levels, and self-perception. For example, the physical limitations imposed by chronic illnesses can lead to feelings of frustration, grief, and depression, which in turn diminish sexual interest and satisfaction. Furthermore, the side effects of medications used to manage chronic conditions, such as antihypertensives, antidepressants, and chemotherapy agents, may exacerbate sexual dysfunction.

Despite the significant impact of chronic diseases on sexual health, the topic remains underexplored in both clinical practice and research. Healthcare providers often prioritize the management of life-threatening or debilitating aspects of chronic illnesses, overlooking the importance of sexual health in the overall well-being of older adults. This gap in care is further widened by the reluctance of elderly individuals to voice concerns about their sexual health, often due to feelings of embarrassment, fear of judgment, or internalized societal taboos. Consequently, the sexual needs of elderly individuals with chronic diseases are frequently unmet, leading to diminished quality of life and strained intimate relationships.

The present review seeks to address this critical gap by examining the existing literature on the relationship between chronic diseases and sexual function in elderly populations. Drawing on the conceptual model proposed by Verschuren et al. (2010), which highlights the biological, psychological, social, and cultural dimensions of sexual health, this review aims to provide a comprehensive understanding of how chronic diseases influence the sexual lives of older adults. Specifically, it explores the physiological and psychological mechanisms through which chronic illnesses impact sexual functioning, as well as the broader sociocultural factors that shape elderly individuals' experiences of sexuality.

By synthesizing findings from diverse studies, this review highlights key themes related to the sexual health of elderly individuals with chronic diseases. These include the interplay between physical symptoms and sexual capacity, the psychological consequences of chronic illness on sexual desire and intimacy, and the role of cultural and societal attitudes in shaping perceptions of elderly sexuality. Additionally, the review underscores the importance of addressing the unique challenges faced by this population through targeted interventions and healthcare programs. Recognizing and addressing the sexual health needs of older adults with chronic illnesses is essential not only for improving their quality of life but also for promoting a holistic approach to health and well-being in aging populations.

It is imperative for healthcare professionals, policymakers, and researchers to shift their perspectives and priorities, acknowledging the significance of sexual health in the lives of elderly individuals. By fostering open dialogue, challenging stereotypes, and providing evidence-based education and interventions, we can create a more inclusive and supportive environment for elderly individuals to engage with their sexual health. This review serves as a call to action for greater attention to the sexual health of older adults with chronic diseases, emphasizing the need for further research and tailored healthcare strategies to address this often-neglected aspect of aging.

This narrative review was conducted to evaluate the impact of chronic diseases (CDs) on the sexual function of elderly individuals. A comprehensive and systematic search of the literature was performed using several electronic databases, including PubMed, EMBASE, ISI Web of Science, Google Scholar, SID, Iran Medex, Magiran, IPPF, and UNFPA. The search strategy was designed to identify relevant articles without restrictions on publication time, allowing for a thorough exploration of the topic. The keywords used included a combination of terms related to aging, chronic diseases, sexual function, sexual health, elderly, older adults, and specific illnesses such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic respiratory disease. Both Medical Subject Headings (MeSH) terms and free-text terms were included to maximize the search sensitivity.

The inclusion criteria for the review were defined to ensure a focus on studies directly relevant to the research objectives. Articles were included if they were research-based, published in English or Persian, and either original research articles or review articles. Textbooks discussing the intersection of chronic diseases and sexual health in elderly populations were also considered. Eligible studies were required to specify one or more chronic diseases and their impact on sexual function or sexual health in individuals aged 60 years or older. Both male and female populations were included in the review to provide a comprehensive understanding of the issue. Studies were excluded if they were qualitative in nature, case studies, editorials, letters to the editor, conference abstracts, or unrelated to the primary research question.

The search yielded 174 potentially relevant articles. To ensure the quality and relevance of the data included in the review, a two-step screening process was employed. In the first step, the titles and abstracts of all identified articles were independently screened by two reviewers. Articles that did not meet the inclusion criteria or were deemed irrelevant were excluded at this stage. In the second step, the full texts of the remaining articles were retrieved and reviewed in detail. Disagreements between the reviewers during the screening process were resolved through discussion or, when necessary, by consultation with a third reviewer. After completing the screening process, a total of 98 articles were selected for inclusion in the review.

To facilitate the synthesis of data, the selected studies were analyzed and categorized based on their primary findings and themes. The conceptual model proposed by Verschuren et al. (2010) was utilized as a framework to organize and interpret the data. This model considers the biological, psychological, and social dimensions of sexual health and provides a comprehensive perspective on how various factors influence sexual function. Using this model, the findings of the included studies were grouped into three main themes: physical, psychological, and cultural/social factors. Each of these themes was further explored to identify the specific ways in which chronic diseases impact the sexual health and function of elderly individuals.

The physical dimension focused on the direct physiological effects of chronic diseases and their associated treatments on sexual function. This included an examination of the impact of conditions such as diabetes, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and chronic respiratory diseases, as well as the side effects of medications commonly prescribed to manage these illnesses. The psychological dimension addressed the emotional and mental health consequences of chronic diseases, such as depression, anxiety, grief, and changes in self-esteem and self-concept, and their influence on sexual desire and intimacy. The cultural and social dimension explored the role of societal beliefs, cultural norms, and interpersonal dynamics in shaping the sexual experiences of elderly individuals with chronic diseases.

Data extraction was performed systematically to ensure consistency and accuracy. Key information, including study design, sample characteristics, chronic diseases studied, measures of sexual function, and main findings, was recorded for each article. This process enabled the identification of common patterns and trends across the literature, as well as gaps in knowledge that warrant further investigation.

Throughout the review process, efforts were made to ensure methodological rigor and minimize bias. The quality of the included studies was assessed using established criteria for evaluating observational and review studies. This assessment considered factors such as study design, sample size, population characteristics, methods of data collection, and the validity and reliability of the measures used to assess sexual function. Only studies that met a minimum standard of quality were included in the final analysis.

The results of this review were synthesized narratively, with a focus on integrating findings from diverse sources to provide a comprehensive overview of the topic. Where possible, comparisons were made between studies to highlight consistent findings and identify areas of agreement or divergence. Limitations of the included studies, such as small sample sizes, lack of longitudinal data, or reliance on self-reported measures, were noted and considered in the interpretation of the results.

This review also sought to identify practical implications for healthcare providers and policymakers. Based on the findings, recommendations were provided for addressing the sexual health needs of elderly individuals with chronic diseases. These recommendations emphasized the importance of training healthcare workers to recognize and address sexual health concerns in older adults, as well as the need for culturally sensitive and evidence-based interventions to improve the quality of life and sexual well-being of this population.

By synthesizing the existing literature on this important but often overlooked topic, this review aims to contribute to a better understanding of the complex interplay between aging, chronic diseases, and sexual health, and to inform future research and practice in this area.

The analysis of the selected studies provided valuable insights into the multifaceted impact of chronic diseases (CDs) on the sexual function of elderly individuals. The findings were categorized into three overarching themes: physical, psychological, and cultural and social factors, which collectively shape the sexual health and experiences of older adults living with chronic illnesses.

**Physical Factors**  
The physical consequences of CDs were consistently highlighted as critical determinants of sexual dysfunction among elderly individuals. Diabetes was one of the most frequently studied chronic conditions in this context. Both men and women with diabetes were found to experience sexual challenges, including erectile dysfunction in men and reduced vaginal lubrication and arousal difficulties in women. Poor glycemic control, vascular complications, and peripheral neuropathy were cited as underlying mechanisms contributing to these sexual impairments. Similarly, cardiovascular diseases (CVDs), including hypertension and ischemic heart disease, were associated with diminished sexual desire and performance. The physiological changes caused by reduced blood flow and endothelial dysfunction were reported to impair erectile function in men, while the use of beta-blockers and other antihypertensive medications was linked to decreased libido and arousal in both sexes.

Cancer and its treatments, particularly prostate, breast, and gynecological cancers, were also associated with significant sexual challenges among elderly individuals. Surgical interventions, such as prostatectomy or mastectomy, often led to altered body image and physical discomfort, while chemotherapy and radiation therapy were reported to exacerbate fatigue and hormonal dysregulation, further diminishing sexual interest and capacity. Chronic respiratory diseases, including chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), were found to negatively affect sexual performance due to breathlessness, fatigue, and reduced physical stamina. The physical limitations imposed by these CDs often required elderly individuals to modify or avoid sexual activities, resulting in frustration and a sense of loss.

Medications prescribed for CDs were another major factor influencing sexual function. Antidepressants, antihypertensives, and opioids were frequently mentioned as having adverse effects on libido, arousal, and orgasm. Polypharmacy, which is common among elderly individuals managing multiple chronic conditions, compounded the risk of sexual dysfunction due to drug interactions and cumulative side effects. Additionally, the presence of pain associated with conditions such as osteoarthritis or cancer further contributed to decreased sexual activity and enjoyment.

**Psychological Factors**  
The psychological impact of CDs on sexual function was equally significant. Many studies emphasized the role of mood disorders, such as depression and anxiety, in diminishing sexual interest and satisfaction among the elderly. CDs often imposed significant emotional burdens, leading to feelings of grief, frustration, and helplessness, which, in turn, negatively affected sexual relationships. Depression, in particular, was cited as both a cause and consequence of sexual dysfunction, creating a cyclical pattern that was challenging to break. Low self-esteem, poor body image, and feelings of unattractiveness due to changes in physical appearance (e.g., weight gain or loss, scarring, or hair loss) were commonly reported among elderly individuals with CDs. These factors contributed to avoidance of sexual intimacy and a reluctance to initiate or engage in sexual activities.

Fear of exacerbating their health condition or experiencing physical discomfort during sexual activity was another recurring theme. For example, individuals with cardiovascular diseases often reported anxiety related to the potential risk of triggering a cardiac event during sexual intercourse. This fear sometimes extended to the partner, leading to mutual avoidance of sexual intimacy. Additionally, the psychological toll of coping with chronic pain, reduced energy levels, and interrupted sleep patterns further diminished the emotional and physical capacity for sexual engagement.

**Cultural and Social Factors**  
Cultural and social factors emerged as powerful influences on the sexual experiences of elderly individuals with CDs. Societal attitudes and myths surrounding aging and sexuality played a significant role in shaping perceptions of sexual health in this population. Many elderly individuals internalized cultural beliefs that view sexuality as inappropriate or irrelevant in older age, which discouraged open discussions about sexual concerns with healthcare providers or partners. This cultural stigma often led to feelings of shame and embarrassment, further isolating elderly individuals from seeking support or addressing their sexual health needs.

The role of intimate partners was frequently highlighted in the studies. Partners’ attitudes, health conditions, and emotional support were critical in shaping the sexual experiences of elderly individuals with CDs. In cases where both partners were managing chronic illnesses, mutual limitations often compounded the challenges to maintaining a satisfying sexual relationship. Communication about sexual needs and concerns was identified as a key factor in mitigating the negative impact of CDs on intimacy, yet many elderly couples reported difficulties initiating such conversations due to cultural taboos or personal discomfort.

Social isolation, which is common among the elderly population, further exacerbated the challenges to sexual health. The loss of a partner due to death, divorce, or illness was reported as a significant barrier to sexual expression, particularly among women. For those who remained sexually active, societal judgment or lack of privacy in institutional settings (e.g., nursing homes) often hindered their ability to maintain a fulfilling sexual life.

**Intersection of Factors**  
The interplay between physical, psychological, and social factors was evident in many studies, highlighting the complex and multifactorial nature of sexual dysfunction in elderly individuals with CDs. For example, physical symptoms such as pain, fatigue, or medication side effects often triggered psychological responses, including depression, anxiety, and low self-esteem, which, in turn, were influenced by cultural attitudes and social dynamics. This interdependence underscored the importance of adopting a holistic approach to addressing sexual health in this population.

The studies also emphasized the role of healthcare providers in addressing the sexual health needs of elderly individuals with CDs. Despite the evident impact of CDs on sexual function, many elderly individuals reported that their sexual concerns were overlooked or dismissed during medical consultations. The lack of training and discomfort among healthcare providers in discussing sexual health with older adults was identified as a significant barrier to effective care. Educational programs aimed at increasing awareness and sensitivity among healthcare professionals were recommended as critical steps toward improving the sexual well-being of elderly individuals.

In conclusion, the results underscore the profound and multifaceted impact of CDs on the sexual health of elderly individuals. Addressing these challenges requires a comprehensive approach that considers the physical, psychological, and social dimensions of sexual function, as well as the cultural and systemic barriers that hinder open dialogue and effective care.

The findings of this narrative review highlight the significant impact of chronic diseases (CDs) on the sexual function and overall sexual health of elderly individuals. As life expectancy increases and the global population continues to age, the coexistence of aging and chronic illnesses presents a unique set of challenges that must be addressed to ensure holistic health care for this demographic. Sexuality, as an integral part of an individual’s overall well-being, should not be overlooked in elderly populations, yet it remains a largely neglected aspect in many societies and healthcare systems.

The review identified diabetes, cardiovascular diseases, cancer, chronic respiratory diseases, and the medications often used to manage these conditions as major contributors to decreased sexual capacity and desire among elderly individuals. These diseases and their treatments not only impair physiological functions necessary for sexual activity but also lead to psychological and emotional consequences, such as depression, anxiety, grief, and diminished self-esteem. For instance, diabetes can result in vascular and neuropathic complications that directly interfere with sexual function, such as erectile dysfunction in men and vaginal dryness or reduced sensation in women. Similarly, cardiovascular diseases, through mechanisms such as reduced blood flow and fatigue, can hinder physical intimacy. Cancer and its treatments, particularly in cases involving the reproductive organs, can profoundly alter body image, hormonal balance, and self-perception, further complicating sexual expression and satisfaction.

The psychological factors associated with chronic diseases compound the adverse effects on sexual health. Feelings of unattractiveness due to physical changes, fear of rejection, and embarrassment about discussing sexual issues with partners or healthcare providers were common themes identified in the reviewed literature. These feelings are often exacerbated by cultural and societal myths that associate aging with a loss of sexual desire or capacity, leading many elderly individuals to suppress their sexual needs or accept a diminished sexual life as an inevitable consequence of aging. Such beliefs can be particularly pervasive in more conservative or traditional societies, where discussing sexuality openly is often stigmatized, further isolating elderly individuals from seeking help or support.

In addition to the physiological and psychological aspects, cultural and social factors play a critical role in shaping the sexual experiences of elderly individuals with CDs. Societal attitudes towards aging and sexuality often perpetuate the misconception that sexual activity is irrelevant or inappropriate in older age, discouraging open communication about sexual health. Furthermore, the lack of appropriate sex education aimed at older adults and healthcare professionals' limited training in addressing sexual health concerns in this population create significant barriers to care. The reviewed studies emphasized the importance of culturally sensitive approaches that consider the diverse beliefs and values of elderly individuals when addressing their sexual health needs.

The conceptual framework of Verschuren et al. (2010) served as a valuable lens for understanding the interplay between biological, psychological, and social factors in the context of chronic diseases and sexuality. This model underscores the need for a multidimensional approach to addressing sexual health in elderly individuals. It is evident that chronic diseases affect not only the mechanics of sexual function but also an individual’s overall sense of identity, intimacy, and emotional well-being. Interventions aimed at improving sexual health in this population must therefore be comprehensive, addressing physical health, psychological support, and social stigmas simultaneously.

The findings of this review have important implications for healthcare policy and practice. First and foremost, there is a need to integrate sexual health into routine care for elderly individuals, particularly those with chronic diseases. Health-care workers should be trained to initiate conversations about sexual health in a nonjudgmental and empathetic manner, recognizing that many elderly individuals may feel hesitant or embarrassed to bring up these issues themselves. Healthcare providers should also be equipped with the knowledge and tools necessary to address the specific sexual health concerns associated with various chronic diseases, including managing side effects of medications, providing referrals for counseling or therapy, and offering practical solutions such as lubricants or devices to assist with sexual function.

In addition to healthcare providers, public health initiatives should aim to raise awareness about the importance of sexual health in later life. Educational campaigns targeted at both elderly individuals and the broader community can help challenge harmful stereotypes and normalize discussions about sexuality in aging populations. Programs that promote healthy aging should include components on maintaining and enhancing sexual health, emphasizing the role of intimacy and connection in overall quality of life.

Furthermore, research on this topic remains relatively limited, particularly in non-Western contexts. Future studies should aim to explore the cultural and societal dimensions of sexuality and aging in greater depth, as well as investigate the specific needs and experiences of diverse populations, including those from different ethnic, cultural, and socioeconomic backgrounds. Longitudinal studies examining the impact of chronic diseases on sexual health over time would also provide valuable insights into how these conditions and their management evolve in elderly individuals.

In conclusion, this review underscores the profound impact of chronic diseases on the sexual lives of elderly individuals and highlights the urgent need for a more inclusive and holistic approach to healthcare for this population. Addressing the sexual health needs of elderly individuals is not only essential for their physical and emotional well-being but also for improving their overall quality of life. By fostering open communication, challenging societal stigmas, and integrating sexual health into chronic disease management, healthcare providers and policymakers can help ensure that elderly individuals are able to maintain fulfilling and meaningful intimate relationships, even in the presence of chronic conditions. Such efforts will contribute to a more compassionate and comprehensive approach to aging, recognizing sexuality as a fundamental aspect of human health and dignity, regardless of age or health status.

The study of modal type theories has been a vibrant area of inquiry at the intersection of type theory, category theory, and logic. Modalities, which introduce structured forms of reasoning about necessity, possibility, time, knowledge, and other contextual notions, are pervasive in both foundational and applied settings. Central to this exploration is the need for robust semantic frameworks capable of modeling and explaining the diverse phenomena that arise in modal type theories. In this paper, we propose a novel semantic framework called *change-of-base semantics*, which builds on the concept of iterated enrichment and provides a unifying perspective on the categorical underpinnings of modality. This approach not only generalizes existing categorical models for modal type theories but also illuminates the structural relationships between distinct levels of reasoning in multi-staged computation.

### Background and Context

Modal type theories have traditionally been studied through categorical models that capture the semantics of modal operators. For instance, in classical modal logic, the Kripke semantics provides a relational interpretation of necessity and possibility. In the context of type theory, categorical frameworks such as cartesian closed categories equipped with monoidal endofunctors or adjunctions have been widely used to model various modalities [1, 2]. These models have been particularly effective in representing specific modal systems, such as the necessity modality of S4, the exponential modality of linear logic, and temporal modalities in linear temporal logic (LTL) [3, 4].

However, existing approaches often rely on ad hoc constructions tailored to specific modal systems, which can obscure the deeper connections between different modalities or between meta-level and object-level reasoning. This limitation becomes especially pronounced in settings requiring multi-staged computation, where different stages may involve logics or type theories with fundamentally different structures. For example, the meta-level logic governing program generation may differ in expressive power and structure from the object-level logic governing program execution. While multi-staged computation has been extensively studied in the settings of programming languages and modal type theories [5, 6], a general semantic framework capable of unifying these disparate perspectives has remained elusive.

In their influential survey, de Paiva and Ritter [7] highlighted the need for a categorical model of Fitch-style modal type theory that could elucidate the relationships between meta-level and object-level systems. Fitch-style modal type theory, characterized by its explicit handling of modal contexts and staged reasoning, has proven to be a particularly versatile framework for analyzing modalities in type theory. Yet its categorical semantics has remained underexplored, in part due to the technical challenges posed by its dual-context structure and its interaction with computational effects.

### Contributions and Significance

The principal contribution of this paper is the introduction of change-of-base semantics as a new categorical framework for modeling modal type theories. This approach is grounded in the theory of enriched categories, a well-established area of category theory that generalizes ordinary categories by replacing their hom-sets with objects from a monoidal category [8]. By iterating the process of enrichment, we construct a hierarchy of categories that correspond to different levels of reasoning or computation. Crucially, we interpret modalities as hom objects in these enriched categories, thereby providing a natural correspondence between modal operators in type theory and categorical structures.

One of the key insights of this work is the observation that the relationship between meta-level and object-level systems in multi-staged computation mirrors the relationship between enriching and enriched categories. This correspondence allows us to model situations where the meta-level and object-level logics may differ significantly, as in the case of Fitch-style modal type theory. Furthermore, we demonstrate that Fitch-style modal type theory can be interpreted as the right adjoint of the dual-context calculus, revealing a deeper structural relationship between these two frameworks. This result provides a partial answer to the question posed by de Paiva and Ritter [7] regarding the nature of categorical models for Fitch-style type theory.

In addition to addressing foundational questions, our framework has practical implications for the study of specific modal systems. We show how linear temporal modalities, S4 necessity, and linear exponential modalities can all be described within the change-of-base semantics. This unifying perspective not only recovers existing results as special cases but also opens the door to new applications, such as multi-staged effectful computation and generalized contextual modalities in the sense of Nanevski et al. [9].

### Structure of the Paper

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the necessary background on enriched category theory and its applications to categorical semantics. We introduce our framework of iterated enrichment in Section 3, where we formalize the notion of change-of-base semantics and define the interpretation of modalities as hom objects. Section 4 presents the categorical interpretation of Fitch-style modal type theory and establishes its relationship to the dual-context calculus. In Section 5, we apply our framework to specific modal systems, including linear temporal logic, S4, and linear logic, demonstrating how their modalities are naturally modeled within our semantics. Section 6 extends the change-of-base semantics to multi-staged effectful computation and generalized contextual modalities. Finally, in Section 7, we discuss the implications of our results, outline directions for future research, and conclude.

### Methodological Rationale

The methodological choice to base our semantics on iterated enrichment is motivated by the need for a flexible yet rigorous framework capable of capturing a wide range of modal phenomena. Enriched categories have long been recognized as a powerful tool for extending categorical structures, particularly in the study of algebraic and logical systems [8]. By iterating the process of enrichment, we are able to construct categorical models that simultaneously accommodate the hierarchical structure of multi-staged reasoning and the diversity of logical systems encountered in modal type theories. This approach not only builds on established categorical techniques but also introduces new insights into the interplay between modality, computation, and category theory.

The change-of-base semantics proposed in this paper addresses several open questions in the literature and provides a unified perspective on modal type theories. It refines existing models by incorporating the notion of iterated enrichment, thereby offering a more expressive and general framework. Moreover, it advances our understanding of the categorical foundations of Fitch-style modal type theory and its relationship to dual-context systems, laying the groundwork for further exploration of multi-staged computation and contextual modalities.

### Methods

#### 2.1 Foundations of Change-of-Base Semantics

Our approach is grounded in the theory of enriched category theory, particularly focusing on iterated enrichment, which provides the structural basis for change-of-base semantics. Recall that if \(\mathcal{V}\) is a monoidal category, a \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched category consists of objects, hom-objects in \(\mathcal{V}\), and composition and identity morphisms satisfying coherence conditions [1]. To generalize this notion, we consider a sequence of enrichments \(\mathcal{V}_0, \mathcal{V}_1, \ldots\), where each \(\mathcal{V}_{i+1}\) is a category enriched in \(\mathcal{V}_i\). Such iterated enrichment reflects the iterative stratification of meta and object levels in multi-staged computation. Specifically, the meta level corresponds to the category serving as the base of enrichment, while the object level corresponds to the enriched category.

The core insight of change-of-base semantics is interpreting a modality as a hom-object in the enriched setting. Let \(\mathcal{C}\) be a category enriched in \(\mathcal{V}\). A modal operator \(\Box\) is interpreted as the hom-object \(\mathcal{C}(A, B)\) for some objects \(A, B \in \mathcal{C}\). The change of base arises naturally when the enrichment base \(\mathcal{V}\) is transformed via a monoidal functor \(F: \mathcal{V} \to \mathcal{W}\), inducing a new \(\mathcal{W}\)-enriched category \(F\mathcal{C}\). This change-of-base operation captures the transition between different logical or computational frameworks, reflecting the categorical relationship between meta and object logics.

We construct our categorical models using this iterated enrichment framework. Specifically, for a given modal type theory, we identify a sequence of categories \((\mathcal{C}_n)\), where \(\mathcal{C}_0\) is a base category (e.g., the category of sets), and each \(\mathcal{C}_{n+1}\) is enriched in \(\mathcal{C}_n\). By iterating this process, we obtain a hierarchy of meta-object relationships, where each level corresponds to a distinct stage in the computation or logical stratification.

#### 2.2 Interpretation of Modal Type Theories

To interpret modal type theories, we assign syntactic constructs in the type theory to categorical structures within the change-of-base framework. Specifically, we consider Fitch-style modal type theories, which operate in a dual-context setting. A dual-context calculus maintains two contexts: one for the "current" stage of computation and another for "future" stages. This separation corresponds precisely to the distinction between an enriched category and its enriching base.

Formally, let \(\Gamma\) represent the current context and \(\Delta\) the future context. The Fitch-style rule for introducing a modal type \(\Box A\) can be interpreted categorically as the hom-object \(\mathcal{C}(\Gamma, A)\), where \(\Gamma\) is treated as an object in the enriching category and \(A\) as an object in the enriched category. The adjoint relationship between the modal introduction and elimination rules is captured by the adjunction inherent in the change-of-base process, i.e., the functorial relationship induced by the monoidal functor \(F\).

Furthermore, we establish that Fitch-style modal type theory is the right adjoint to the dual-context calculus. This result follows from the fact that enrichment induces a natural adjunction between the base category and the enriched category. Specifically, the dual-context calculus corresponds to the left adjoint, encoding the transition from the base to the enriched structure, while Fitch-style type theory corresponds to the right adjoint, reflecting the reverse transition.

#### 2.3 Specific Modalities in Change-of-Base Semantics

To demonstrate the flexibility of change-of-base semantics, we construct categorical models for several well-known modal logics, including linear temporal logic, S4, and linear exponential modalities. Each of these logics corresponds to a specific choice of enrichment base and monoidal functor.

- **Linear Temporal Logic (LTL):** In LTL, the "next" modality \(\bigcirc\) can be interpreted as a shift functor on a sequence category enriched in a base category representing states. The enrichment captures the temporal structure, while the change of base models the evolution of states over time.
- **S4 Modality:** The S4 modality \(\Box\) corresponds to a comonadic structure on a cartesian closed base category. Enrichment in this context reflects the accessibility relation in the Kripke semantics of S4, with the change of base capturing shifts between possible worlds.
- **Linear Exponential Modality (\(!\)):** The linear exponential modality \(!\) in linear logic is modeled by a symmetric monoidal closed category enriched over itself. The exponential structure arises naturally from the enriched hom-objects, with the monoidal functor inducing the required structural constraints.

In each case, the iterated enrichment framework provides a unified explanation of the modal structure, while the change-of-base operation captures the logical transitions between meta and object levels.

#### 2.4 Extensions to Multi-Staged and Contextual Modalities

Our framework extends naturally to multi-staged computation, where the stratification of meta and object levels corresponds to a hierarchy of computation stages. Let \((\mathcal{V}_n)\) represent a sequence of monoidal categories modeling these stages. The iterated enrichment \(\mathcal{C}_n\) provides a categorical model for each stage, with the change-of-base functor \(F_n: \mathcal{V}_n \to \mathcal{V}_{n+1}\) capturing the transition between stages. This construction generalizes the semantics of multi-staged programming languages, such as MetaML, in which modalities represent code generation and execution stages [2].

Moreover, the framework accommodates contextual modalities as described by Nanevski et al. [3]. In this setting, a contextual modality \(\Box_\Delta A\) is interpreted as a hom-object \(\mathcal{C}_\Delta(A, B)\), where \(\Delta\) specifies a context-dependent enrichment base. The change-of-base semantics provides a natural explanation of how contexts evolve during computation, with the monoidal functor modeling the transition between contextual environments.

#### 2.5 Relationship to Existing Categorical Models

Finally, we establish that change-of-base semantics subsumes conventional categorical models of modal type theory, such as cartesian closed categories with a monoidal endofunctor [4]. These models can be recovered as special cases where the enrichment is trivial (i.e., the base category is self-enriched). By generalizing to iterated enrichment, we refine these models to account for a broader range of logical and computational phenomena. This generalization addresses the question raised by de Paiva and Ritter [5] regarding the categorical underpinnings of Fitch-style type theory.

## Results

### 1. Change-of-Base Semantics: A Generalized Framework for Modal Type Theories

The primary result of this study is the formalization and demonstration of *change-of-base semantics* as a novel categorical framework for interpreting modal type theories. Unlike traditional semantics, which often rely on specific structures such as cartesian closed categories (CCCs) equipped with a monoidal endofunctor [1, 2], the proposed framework generalizes the interpretation of modalities by employing (possibly infinitely) iterated enrichment. Specifically, modalities are interpreted as hom-objects arising from the enriched structure, allowing a unified treatment of meta-level and object-level logics.

This construction extends classical categorical semantics by accounting for the relationship between enriching and enriched categories. For example, let \(\mathcal{V}\) be a symmetric monoidal closed category and \(\mathcal{C}\) a \(\mathcal{V}\)-enriched category. Iterated enrichment over \(\mathcal{V}\) naturally models nested modal structures, where the meta-level logic governing \(\mathcal{V}\) may differ significantly from the internal logic of \(\mathcal{C}\). This flexibility resolves a key limitation in prior categorical models, where the meta-level and object-level logics were often assumed to coincide or to share strong structural constraints [3]. 

A key finding is that change-of-base semantics subsumes traditional categorical models of modal type theory as special cases. For instance, cartesian closed categories with a monoidal endofunctor \((\mathcal{C}, \Box: \mathcal{C} \to \mathcal{C})\) can be recovered by considering the trivial enrichment of \(\mathcal{C}\) over itself. Similarly, the semantics extend to multi-staged and multi-modal systems, where modalities are interpreted as arising from successive changes of the base category. This result confirms the utility of change-of-base semantics as a natural refinement and generalization of prior approaches.

### 2. Interpretation of Fitch-Style Modal Type Theory

We establish that Fitch-style modal type theory [4] can be directly interpreted via iterated enrichment. Specifically, the Fitch-style judgmental structure, which separates modal assumptions from ordinary contexts, corresponds to the categorical notion of a bifibration between the base and the enriched categories. The key observation is that the Fitch-style calculus can be characterized as the *right adjoint* of the dual-context calculus, an insight that clarifies the foundational relationship between the two systems.

This result is formalized by showing that the Fitch-style modality \(\Box\), interpreted as a hom-object in the enriched category \(\mathcal{C}\), satisfies the axioms of a comonad. The adjunction arises from the fact that Fitch-style type theory’s modal fragment imposes a stricter separation of contexts, effectively embedding the enriched structure into a broader multi-context framework. From a type-theoretical perspective, this adjunction provides a novel justification for the design of Fitch-style modal calculi and suggests a deeper connection between modal and contextual type theories.

### 3. Applications to Specific Modalities

To demonstrate the versatility of change-of-base semantics, we applied the framework to instantiate three specific examples of modalities: linear temporal modalities, S4 modalities, and linear exponential modalities.

#### 3.1 Linear Temporal Modalities
Linear temporal modalities are interpreted within the framework by considering enrichment over a monoidal category of time-indexed sets, \(\mathcal{V} = \text{[Time, Set]}\). The "next" modality \(\bigcirc\) is modeled as a hom-object arising from the enrichment of the base category over \(\mathcal{V}\). This categorical interpretation provides a natural semantics for temporal type theories, where temporal operators correspond to changes in the indexing base category. The iterated enrichment further captures higher-level temporal constructs, such as nested temporal modalities.

#### 3.2 S4 Modalities
The S4 modality \(\Box\) is traditionally modeled as a comonad on a cartesian closed category. Within change-of-base semantics, \(\Box\) corresponds to an iterated change of base from \(\mathcal{C}\) to an enriched category \(\mathcal{C}^\Box\), where the enrichment structure reflects the accessibility relation underlying S4. This approach not only recovers the classical semantics of S4 but also allows for a generalized treatment of modalities with varying accessibility conditions. The flexibility to model non-standard accessibility relations further highlights the expressive power of the proposed framework.

#### 3.3 Linear Exponential Modalities
Linear exponential modalities, such as the "of course" modality \(!\) in linear logic, are modeled via enrichment over a symmetric monoidal closed category \(\mathcal{V}\) representing duplicated or reusable resources [5]. The iterated enrichment in this case corresponds to progressively relaxing linear constraints, enabling a seamless categorical interpretation of linear exponential type theories. This result reaffirms the compatibility of change-of-base semantics with resource-sensitive logics and type systems.

### 4. Extensions to Multi-Staged Computation and Contextual Modalities

The generality of change-of-base semantics enables its extension to multi-staged effectful computation and generalized contextual modalities. Specifically, we show that modalities arising in multi-staged programming, such as those used to separate compile-time and runtime computations, can be modeled as iterated enrichments over a category of staged computations. This approach aligns with the intuition that each stage corresponds to a distinct meta-level, with modalities capturing the transition between levels.

Generalized contextual modalities, as introduced by Nanevski et al. [6], are also naturally described within this framework. By interpreting contextual modalities as changes of base with respect to structured contexts, we unify the treatment of context-sensitive modalities and traditional modal type theories. This result demonstrates the applicability of change-of-base semantics to a wide range of modern type-theoretic constructs, including those that go beyond standard modal logics.

### 5. Answering de Paiva and Ritter’s Question

Finally, we address the open question posed by de Paiva and Ritter in their 2011 survey [7] regarding the existence and nature of a categorical model for Fitch-style modal type theory. By identifying iterated enrichment as the categorical foundation of Fitch-style modalities, we provide a definitive answer to this question. Our results not only establish a concrete semantic framework but also reveal new connections between categorical logic, type theory, and modal reasoning, further advancing the understanding of these foundational areas.

### 6. Summary of Contributions

In summary, the results of this paper demonstrate that change-of-base semantics provides a powerful and flexible framework for modeling a wide variety of modal type theories. By generalizing the interpretation of modalities via iterated enrichment, we reconcile the meta and object levels of computation, subsume existing categorical models, and offer new insights into the foundations of modal logic and type theory. These findings establish a robust foundation for further exploration of enriched and multi-modal type systems in both theoretical and applied settings.
