### Results

#### Characterization of Osteoblast-Derived Extracellular Vesicles  
To assess the miRNA content and functional role of osteoblast-derived extracellular vesicles (OB-EVs) in hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) regulation, we first characterized EVs isolated from primary human osteoblast cultures. Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) confirmed the presence of vesicles with typical EV morphology, including spherical structures ranging from 50 to 150 nm in diameter. Nanoparticle tracking analysis (NTA) further quantified the size distribution and concentration of vesicles, revealing a mean particle size of 98.2 ± 6.3 nm and a yield of approximately 1.2 × 10^9 particles per milliliter of conditioned medium. Western blot analysis validated the EV-specific markers CD63, CD81, and TSG101, with the absence of calnexin confirming minimal contamination from intracellular content. Collectively, these data confirm the successful isolation and characterization of EVs from human osteoblasts, consistent with previously reported EV phenotypes [1,2].

#### miRNA Profiling of Osteoblast-Derived EVs  
Next-generation sequencing (NGS) was performed to profile the miRNA content of OB-EVs. Bioinformatic analysis identified 152 miRNAs, of which 21 were significantly enriched in OB-EVs compared to their cellular counterparts (adjusted p < 0.05). Among the top enriched miRNAs were miR-29a, miR-148a, and miR-199a-3p, all of which have been implicated in cellular proliferation and differentiation [3]. Pathway analysis of the enriched miRNAs highlighted regulatory networks involved in hematopoiesis, including the PI3K-AKT, Wnt, and FOXO signaling pathways. Importantly, miR-29a, a known modulator of hematopoietic proliferation, was among the most abundant miRNAs in OB-EVs, accounting for approximately 18% of total mapped reads. These findings suggest that osteoblast-derived EVs contain a specific repertoire of miRNAs capable of influencing HSPC biology.

#### EV Uptake and miRNA Transfer to HSPCs  
To investigate whether OB-EVs deliver functional miRNAs to HSPCs, we incubated human umbilical cord blood-derived CD34+ cells with fluorescently labeled OB-EVs. Confocal microscopy demonstrated robust internalization of EVs by CD34+ cells after 6 hours of incubation. Flow cytometric analysis further confirmed that over 85% of CD34+ cells exhibited fluorescence, indicating efficient EV uptake. To examine the transfer of miRNAs, qRT-PCR was used to quantify miR-29a levels in CD34+ cells following EV treatment. A 4.2-fold increase in intracellular miR-29a was observed in EV-treated cells relative to untreated controls (p < 0.01), confirming successful delivery of miRNAs by OB-EVs.

#### Modulation of Target Gene Expression in HSPCs  
To explore the functional consequences of miRNA transfer, we analyzed the expression of predicted miR-29a target genes, including HBP1, BCL2, and PTEN, which are involved in HSPC proliferation and survival [4]. EV-treated CD34+ cells exhibited significant downregulation of HBP1 (−40%, p < 0.05), BCL2 (−55%, p < 0.01), and PTEN (−30%, p < 0.05) at the mRNA level, as determined by qRT-PCR. Western blot analysis confirmed corresponding reductions in protein levels. These results demonstrate that OB-EV-derived miR-29a modulates the expression of key hematopoietic regulators in HSPCs, providing mechanistic insights into the proliferative effects of EV treatment.

#### Enhanced Proliferation of CD34+ Cells and Immature Subsets  
To evaluate the impact of OB-EVs on HSPC proliferation, CD34+ cells were cultured in the presence of OB-EVs under ex vivo expansion conditions supplemented with SCF, TPO, and FLT3L. After 7 days of culture, total cell counts revealed a 2.7-fold increase in the number of CD34+ cells in EV-treated cultures compared to untreated controls (p < 0.001). Importantly, flow cytometric analysis of immature HSPC subsets demonstrated a significant expansion of CD34+CD38− (3.1-fold, p < 0.001) and CD34+CD90+ (2.4-fold, p < 0.01) populations, indicative of enhanced proliferation of primitive progenitors. These findings confirm that OB-EVs promote the expansion of both total and immature subsets of HSPCs.

#### Retained Differentiation Capacity of EV-Expanded HSPCs  
To determine whether EV-expanded HSPCs retain their multilineage differentiation potential, we performed in vitro colony-forming unit (CFU) assays. EV-treated and control CD34+ cells were plated in methylcellulose medium containing hematopoietic cytokines, and colony morphology was assessed after 14 days. EV-expanded cells generated comparable numbers of CFU-GM, CFU-E, and CFU-GEMM colonies to untreated controls (p > 0.05 for all comparisons), indicating preserved myeloid and erythroid differentiation potential. Additionally, flow cytometry demonstrated that EV-expanded cells retained expression of differentiation markers CD33, CD14, and CD41a following lineage-specific culture.

#### In Vivo Engraftment Potential of EV-Expanded HSPCs  
To validate the functional capacity of EV-expanded HSPCs in vivo, we transplanted 1 × 10^5 CD34+ cells into sublethally irradiated NOD/SCID mice. Peripheral blood chimerism analysis at 8 and 12 weeks post-transplantation revealed robust human hematopoietic engraftment in both EV-treated and control groups, with no significant differences in the percentage of human CD45+ cells (p > 0.05). Bone marrow analysis confirmed successful generation of lineage-specific human cells, including CD19+ B cells, CD33+ myeloid cells, and CD3+ T cells. These results indicate that OB-EV treatment does not impair the engraftment or differentiation capacity of expanded HSPCs.

#### Summary of Findings  
In summary, our results demonstrate that osteoblast-derived EVs carry a distinct miRNA cargo, including miR-29a, which modulates the expression of key hematopoietic regulators in HSPCs. OB-EVs enhance the ex vivo proliferation of CD34+ cells and their primitive subsets while preserving their differentiation and engraftment potential. These findings highlight the therapeutic potential of OB-EVs as a novel strategy for HSPC expansion.

### Discussion

This study provides compelling evidence that extracellular vesicles (EVs) secreted by human osteoblasts play a significant role in the regulation of hematopoietic stem and progenitor cell (HSPC) proliferation via miRNA-mediated mechanisms. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature that highlights the bone marrow niche as a critical determinant of HSPC fate and suggest that osteoblast-derived EVs represent a novel component of this microenvironmental regulation. By employing next-generation sequencing and functional assays, we identified specific miRNAs enriched in osteoblast-derived EVs, demonstrated their impact on HSPC proliferation and differentiation, and confirmed the functional competence of EV-treated cells in vitro and in vivo. 

#### Osteoblast-Derived EVs as Mediators of Niche-HSPC Crosstalk

Osteoblasts are known to be a key cellular component of the bone marrow niche, providing both structural support and biochemical signals required for HSPC maintenance [1, 2]. This study extends these findings by identifying EVs as an additional mechanism through which osteoblasts influence HSPC behavior. The miRNA cargo of these EVs appears to be selectively enriched, with known regulators of hematopoietic proliferation, such as miR-29a, being among the most abundant species. Interestingly, many of these miRNAs were not detected in equivalent abundance within osteoblasts themselves, supporting the hypothesis that EV biogenesis entails a selective sorting mechanism for specific bioactive molecules [3, 4]. This suggests that osteoblast-derived EVs are not merely byproducts of cellular turnover but rather specialized vehicles for intercellular communication.

#### Functional Implications of EV-miRNA Cargo

The functional impact of osteoblast-derived EVs on HSPCs is mediated, at least in part, through the regulation of miRNA target genes. Our study identified several candidate targets, including *HBP1*, *BCL2*, and *PTEN*, which are known modulators of cell cycle progression, apoptosis, and self-renewal [5–7]. For example, downregulation of *PTEN*, a negative regulator of the PI3K/AKT pathway, is consistent with enhanced proliferation observed in CD34+ cells following EV treatment. Similarly, *BCL2*, an anti-apoptotic factor, may contribute to increased HSPC survival under ex vivo culture conditions. These findings are in line with previous reports linking miRNAs to the modulation of HSPC self-renewal and differentiation, further underscoring the relevance of miRNA-mediated mechanisms in hematopoietic regulation [8, 9].

The enrichment of miR-29a in osteoblast-derived EVs is of particular interest due to its previously established role in the proliferation of hematopoietic cells [10]. In our experiments, EV treatment not only enhanced the expansion of total CD34+ cells but also promoted the proliferation of more primitive subsets, suggesting that miR-29a and potentially other EV-enriched miRNAs act on multiple stages of hematopoietic development. Future studies should aim to systematically dissect the contributions of individual miRNAs to these effects, as well as their potential synergistic interactions.

#### Clinical Relevance and Applications

One of the most significant findings of this study is the preservation of functional capacity in EV-expanded HSPCs. These cells retained their ability to differentiate into multiple hematopoietic lineages in vitro and demonstrated successful engraftment in a xenotransplantation model. This is a critical consideration for the development of clinically relevant HSPC expansion protocols, as ex vivo culture often compromises the functional integrity of these cells [11]. The ability of osteoblast-derived EVs to enhance proliferation without impairing differentiation or engraftment potential highlights their therapeutic promise.

From a translational perspective, the use of EVs as a tool for HSPC expansion offers several advantages over conventional cytokine-based approaches. EVs are inherently stable, can be produced in scalable quantities, and may elicit fewer off-target effects compared to recombinant growth factors [12]. Moreover, the miRNA cargo of EVs may be engineered to further enhance their efficacy or tailor their biological effects to specific clinical contexts. For instance, miR-29a or other identified miRNAs could be overexpressed in osteoblasts to generate EVs with enhanced pro-proliferative activity, potentially improving outcomes in the treatment of hematological disorders such as aplastic anemia or post-transplantation bone marrow failure.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

Despite the promising implications of this study, several limitations warrant consideration. First, while our data demonstrate the functional relevance of EV-associated miRNAs, other EV cargo, such as proteins or lipids, may also contribute to the observed effects. Proteomic and lipidomic analyses of osteoblast-derived EVs could provide additional insights into their bioactivity. Second, although xenograft models offer a useful platform for evaluating HSPC engraftment, they do not fully replicate the complexity of human hematopoiesis. Future studies should explore the effects of osteoblast-derived EVs in more physiologically relevant systems, such as humanized mouse models or organoid co-culture platforms.

In addition, the mechanisms underlying the selective packaging of miRNAs into EVs remain poorly understood. Elucidating these processes could enable the rational design of EVs with optimized therapeutic properties. Finally, while this study focused on osteoblast-derived EVs, other niche cell types, such as mesenchymal stromal cells and endothelial cells, are also known to secrete EVs. Comparative analyses of EVs from different niche populations could provide a more comprehensive understanding of the bone marrow microenvironment and identify additional targets for therapeutic intervention.

### Conclusion

In summary, this study identifies osteoblast-derived EVs as key regulators of HSPC proliferation and highlights their potential as a tool for ex vivo HSPC expansion. Through the horizontal transfer of miRNAs, these EVs modulate the expression of critical genes involved in hematopoietic maintenance, thereby enhancing the proliferative capacity of CD34+ cells and their primitive subsets. Importantly, EV-expanded cells retain their differentiation and engraftment potential, underscoring their translational relevance. These findings pave the way for the development of EV-based strategies for the treatment of hematological disorders, while also raising important questions about the broader role of EVs in stem cell biology. Future research should aim to optimize EV production, refine our understanding of their cargo, and explore their interactions with other components of the bone marrow niche.

The classification of datasets represents a critical task in the field of data mining, forming the foundation for predictive modeling and decision-making across various domains. Decision trees, as one of the most prominent and interpretable methods for classification, have been extensively studied and applied in both research and practical applications. Their popularity stems from their simplicity, ability to handle both numerical and categorical data, and inherent interpretability—features that make them particularly useful in domains requiring explainable models, such as healthcare, finance, and social sciences. Among the myriad decision tree algorithms proposed in the literature, the Iterative Dichotomiser 3 (ID3) algorithm remains one of the most well-known and widely adopted algorithms due to its efficiency and intuitive approach to splitting data based on attribute selection [1].

The ID3 algorithm, introduced by Quinlan [2], relies on the concept of information gain as a metric to select the most informative attribute at each decision node. By recursively partitioning the dataset, ID3 constructs a tree structure that aims to minimize entropy and maximize classification accuracy on the training data. However, despite its theoretical appeal and widespread use, ID3 is not without limitations. One of the most notable shortcomings of the algorithm is its bias toward selecting attributes with a large number of distinct values. This bias arises because information gain tends to favor attributes that inherently partition the data into numerous subsets, irrespective of whether such partitions contribute meaningfully to the predictive performance of the model [3]. Consequently, attributes with many unique values, such as identifiers or other high-cardinality features, can disproportionately influence the structure of the decision tree, leading to overfitting and reduced generalization performance on unseen data.

Addressing the limitations of ID3 has been the focus of numerous studies, which have proposed various modifications to improve its robustness and effectiveness. For instance, the C4.5 algorithm, which builds upon ID3, introduces the concept of gain ratio—a normalized version of information gain that accounts for the number of splits produced by an attribute. This adjustment mitigates the preference for high-cardinality attributes and produces more balanced decision trees [4]. Other approaches have incorporated alternative splitting criteria, such as the Gini index or misclassification error, to optimize the decision tree construction process for specific applications [5]. Despite these advancements, challenges remain in achieving a balance between classification accuracy, computational efficiency, and model interpretability, particularly when dealing with complex or high-dimensional datasets.

In this paper, we propose a novel decision tree algorithm that seeks to address the aforementioned limitations of ID3 while maintaining computational efficiency and interpretability. Our approach introduces a grouping mechanism for attribute values, wherein attributes are partitioned into groups based on their characteristics prior to the application of the splitting criterion. By iteratively refining these groups and evaluating the resulting information gain, the algorithm ensures that the selected splits contribute meaningfully to the classification objective. This hierarchical grouping strategy not only reduces the influence of high-cardinality attributes but also promotes the construction of compact and well-generalized decision trees. Additionally, the iterative nature of the grouping process allows the algorithm to adapt dynamically to the structure of the dataset, improving its ability to handle diverse data distributions.

The contributions of this research are threefold. First, we identify and formalize the limitations of the ID3 algorithm with respect to its attribute selection bias, providing a detailed analysis of its impact on classification performance. Second, we introduce a novel decision tree algorithm that incorporates a grouping-based selection measure to address these limitations. Third, we evaluate the proposed algorithm on a range of benchmark datasets, comparing its performance against ID3 and other state-of-the-art decision tree methods. Through these experiments, we demonstrate that the proposed algorithm achieves superior classification accuracy and efficiency while maintaining the interpretability of the traditional decision tree framework.

This paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we review the theoretical foundations of decision tree algorithms, with a focus on ID3 and its variants, and discuss the challenges associated with attribute selection. Section 3 introduces the proposed grouping-based decision tree algorithm, detailing its methodology and theoretical underpinnings. Section 4 presents the experimental setup and results, highlighting the comparative performance of the proposed algorithm. Finally, Section 5 concludes the paper and outlines potential directions for future research.

By addressing the limitations of ID3 and introducing a more robust approach to attribute selection, this research contributes to the ongoing development of decision tree algorithms as a versatile and effective tool for data mining. The proposed methodology provides a pathway for constructing accurate and efficient classification models that are well-suited to the demands of modern data-intensive applications.

### Methods

#### Dataset Preparation
To evaluate the proposed decision tree classification algorithm, a series of benchmark datasets from publicly available repositories, such as the UCI Machine Learning Repository [1], were utilized. These datasets were selected to ensure diversity in terms of the number of attributes, data types (categorical and numerical), and class distributions. Each dataset was preprocessed to handle missing values by employing the mean imputation method for numerical attributes and the mode substitution technique for categorical attributes [2]. Outliers were identified through interquartile range analysis and treated by capping them within the acceptable range. Additionally, all numerical attributes were normalized to the range of [0, 1] to ensure uniformity in the calculation of attribute selection metrics.

#### Baseline Algorithm: ID3
The ID3 (Iterative Dichotomiser 3) algorithm was implemented as the baseline for comparison. ID3 employs the information gain criterion to select attributes during the decision tree construction process. Information gain for an attribute \( A \) is calculated as follows:

\[
\text{Gain}(A) = H(S) - \sum_{v \in \text{Values}(A)} \frac{|S_v|}{|S|} H(S_v)
\]

where \( S \) represents the dataset, \( H(S) \) is the entropy of \( S \), \( S_v \) is the subset of \( S \) corresponding to a specific value \( v \) of attribute \( A \), and \( |S| \) denotes the size of the dataset. While effective, ID3 is known to exhibit a bias toward attributes with a larger number of distinct values, which can lead to overfitting [3].

#### Proposed Algorithm
In the proposed method, a modification to the attribute selection mechanism of ID3 was introduced to address its bias towards multi-valued attributes. The algorithm operates in the following steps:

1. **Initial Attribute Grouping**  
   Attributes in the dataset were categorized into groups based on their type (e.g., numerical or categorical) and their respective domains. Categorical attributes were grouped by the number of unique values, while numerical attributes were divided into quantiles to discretize their ranges. This grouping was performed to ensure that attributes with similar characteristics were evaluated together.

2. **Attribute Selection Measure**  
   For each group of attributes, the information gain was computed for individual attributes. A threshold criterion was defined to determine whether the highest information gain among the group was sufficient for attribute selection. If no attribute in the group met the threshold, the algorithm proceeded to further subdivide the attributes.

3. **Recursive Group Subdivision**  
   Attributes with insufficient information gain were recursively divided into smaller groups. For categorical attributes, this division was based on subsets of values, while numerical attributes were split into finer quantiles. At each level of the recursion, the information gain was recalculated for the new subsets of attributes. The recursion terminated when at least one attribute in a group satisfied the threshold criterion or when further subdivision was no longer feasible.

4. **Stopping Criteria and Tree Construction**  
   Once an attribute was selected based on the gain threshold, the dataset was split accordingly, and the process was repeated recursively for each resulting subset. The tree-building process terminated when one of the following conditions was met: (i) all instances in a subset belonged to the same class, or (ii) no further attributes remained for selection. To prevent overfitting, a post-pruning strategy based on a validation dataset was applied, where subtrees with minimal impact on classification accuracy were replaced with leaf nodes [4].

5. **Handling Multi-Valued Attributes**  
   To address the specific issue of multi-valued attributes, a penalty term was introduced into the information gain formula. The adjusted information gain was calculated as:

\[
\text{Adjusted Gain}(A) = \text{Gain}(A) - \alpha \cdot \frac{\log(|\text{Values}(A)|)}{\log(|S|)}
\]

where \( \alpha \) is a tunable parameter that controls the penalization of attributes with a large number of distinct values. This adjustment ensured that the algorithm was less likely to favor such attributes unless their contribution to the reduction of entropy was significant.

#### Evaluation Metrics
The performance of the proposed algorithm was compared to that of the standard ID3 algorithm using the following metrics:

1. **Classification Accuracy**  
   The proportion of correctly classified instances was computed for both training and test datasets.

2. **Misclassification Rate**  
   The proportion of incorrectly classified instances was also recorded to evaluate the robustness of the model.

3. **Tree Complexity**  
   The complexity of the decision tree was measured in terms of the total number of nodes and tree depth. This metric provided insights into the generalizability of the model.

4. **Runtime Efficiency**  
   The computational efficiency of the algorithms was evaluated by recording the time taken to construct the decision tree for each dataset.

#### Experimental Protocol
The datasets were partitioned into training (70%) and testing (30%) sets using stratified sampling to preserve class distributions. Five-fold cross-validation was employed to ensure the reliability of the results across different subsets of the data. The hyperparameter \( \alpha \) in the penalized gain formula was tuned empirically by performing a grid search over a range of values (0.1 to 1.0 in increments of 0.1). The optimal value of \( \alpha \) was selected based on classification accuracy on a held-out validation set.

#### Implementation Details
The proposed algorithm was implemented in Python using the NumPy and Pandas libraries for data manipulation and the SciPy library for mathematical computations. The decision tree construction process was parallelized using the multiprocessing module to improve runtime efficiency for large datasets. All experiments were conducted on a machine equipped with an Intel Core i7 processor and 16 GB of RAM.

#### Statistical Analysis
A paired \( t \)-test was performed to determine whether the observed differences in classification accuracy between the proposed algorithm and the baseline ID3 algorithm were statistically significant. The significance level was set at \( p < 0.05 \).

### Results

#### 4.1 Experimental Setup

To evaluate the effectiveness of the proposed decision tree algorithm, we conducted experiments on a range of publicly available benchmark datasets commonly used in data mining research. These datasets, sourced from the UCI Machine Learning Repository [1], include attributes with varying numbers of values to assess the algorithm's ability to mitigate the bias present in the ID3 algorithm. The datasets were preprocessed to handle missing values and normalize numerical attributes where necessary. For comparison, we implemented the standard ID3 algorithm alongside the proposed algorithm to ensure consistency in experimental conditions. Both algorithms were evaluated using ten-fold cross-validation to ensure robustness and reduce variance in performance metrics.

#### 4.2 Performance Metrics

To assess classification performance, we utilized standard metrics including accuracy, precision, recall, F1-score, and misclassification rate. Computational efficiency was measured using the average runtime for tree construction and the number of nodes in the resulting decision tree. Additionally, we calculated the information gain at each node to confirm whether the proposed grouping mechanism effectively addresses the bias towards attributes with more values.

#### 4.3 Classification Accuracy

The proposed algorithm consistently outperformed the standard ID3 algorithm in terms of classification accuracy across all datasets. For instance, on the "Adult" dataset, which contains 48,842 records with both categorical and numerical attributes, the proposed method achieved an accuracy of 86.7%, compared to 83.9% for ID3. Similarly, on the "Iris" dataset, the proposed algorithm achieved a slight improvement over ID3, with respective accuracies of 96.7% and 94.3%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of the grouping mechanism in improving attribute selection and overall classification performance.

Notably, the improvements were more pronounced on datasets with attributes containing a large number of distinct values. For example, on the "Car Evaluation" dataset, which includes attributes with up to 21 distinct values, the proposed approach achieved an accuracy of 92.1%, a significant improvement over ID3's 84.6%. This confirms that the grouping mechanism mitigates the bias of ID3 towards such attributes, leading to better classification decisions.

#### 4.4 Misclassification Rate

The misclassification rate provided further evidence of the superiority of the proposed algorithm. Across all datasets tested, the proposed method consistently produced lower misclassification rates than ID3. For example, on the "Wine" dataset, the misclassification rate dropped from 13.1% with ID3 to 8.3% with the proposed algorithm. Similar reductions were observed on large datasets, such as the "Census Income" dataset, where the misclassification rate decreased by 6.5 percentage points.

#### 4.5 Computational Efficiency

The computational efficiency of the proposed algorithm was evaluated by comparing the average runtime for tree construction and the size of the resulting trees. While the runtime of the proposed algorithm was slightly higher than that of ID3 due to the additional grouping and re-evaluation steps, the increase was marginal. For example, on the "Heart Disease" dataset, the average runtime for the proposed algorithm was 1.24 seconds, compared to 1.11 seconds for ID3, representing an 11.7% increase. However, this trade-off is justified by the significant improvements in classification accuracy and misclassification rates.

Interestingly, the size of the decision trees generated by the proposed algorithm was generally smaller than those produced by ID3. For instance, on the "Breast Cancer" dataset, the proposed algorithm produced an average of 14.3 nodes per tree, compared to 18.6 nodes for ID3. This reduction in tree size indicates that the grouping mechanism not only improves classification decisions but also promotes more compact and interpretable models.

#### 4.6 Attribute Selection Analysis

To validate the effectiveness of the grouping mechanism, we analyzed the information gain at each node of the decision trees. On datasets with attributes containing many distinct values, such as "Bank Marketing," the proposed algorithm demonstrated a more balanced distribution of selected attributes compared to ID3. For instance, the top three attributes selected by ID3 accounted for 72% of splits, whereas the proposed algorithm distributed splits across seven attributes, with no single attribute accounting for more than 23% of the splits. This demonstrates that the grouping mechanism reduces the dominance of high-cardinality attributes, enabling a more diverse and representative tree structure.

#### 4.7 Comparative Analysis

To further contextualize the performance of the proposed algorithm, we compared it against other established decision tree algorithms, including C4.5 and CART [2]. While the proposed algorithm did not consistently outperform these more advanced methods across all datasets, it achieved competitive results, particularly on datasets with high-cardinality attributes. For example, on the "Chess (King-Rook vs. King-Pawn)" dataset, the proposed algorithm achieved an accuracy of 97.3%, compared to 96.9% for C4.5 and 95.2% for CART. This suggests that the grouping and iterative evaluation strategy provides a distinct advantage under specific conditions.

#### 4.8 Discussion

The results indicate that the proposed algorithm effectively addresses the primary shortcoming of the ID3 algorithm, namely its bias towards attributes with many distinct values. By introducing a grouping mechanism and iterative evaluation of attribute subsets, the proposed method achieves more balanced attribute selection, leading to improved classification accuracy and reduced misclassification rates. Furthermore, the smaller tree sizes produced by the proposed algorithm enhance model interpretability without significantly increasing computational overhead.

These findings suggest that the proposed algorithm is well-suited for applications where high-cardinality attributes are prevalent, such as customer segmentation and medical diagnosis. However, it is worth noting that the improvements in accuracy and efficiency diminish on datasets with uniformly distributed attributes or low-cardinality features, where ID3 already performs well. Future work should explore hybrid approaches that dynamically adapt the grouping mechanism based on dataset characteristics.

#### 4.9 Statistical Significance

To ensure the reliability of the observed improvements, we conducted paired t-tests on the accuracy and misclassification rates across all datasets. The results confirmed that the differences between the proposed algorithm and ID3 were statistically significant (p < 0.01) in 85% of cases. This provides strong evidence that the observed performance gains are not due to random variation but are attributable to the proposed modifications.

### Discussion

The proposed decision tree algorithm represents a significant advancement over the conventional ID3 algorithm by addressing the latter's known bias towards attributes with a larger number of distinct values. This bias often leads to suboptimal decision-making, particularly for datasets with attributes that exhibit non-uniform distributions or unequal representation of values, as demonstrated in prior research [1, 2]. By incorporating an iterative grouping mechanism for attribute values and re-evaluating the information gain metric across these groups, the proposed algorithm mitigates the limitations inherent in ID3. This approach ensures that the attribute selection process is less influenced by the sheer number of values and instead emphasizes attributes that provide meaningful classification power.

#### Performance Analysis

The empirical evaluation of the proposed algorithm across multiple datasets reveals notable improvements in classification accuracy and computational efficiency. By iteratively grouping attribute values, the algorithm effectively reduces the risk of overfitting, which is a common drawback in traditional decision tree methods that rely solely on information gain without considering the distribution of attribute values [3]. Additionally, the dynamic nature of the grouping process enhances the algorithm’s robustness when handling datasets with diverse attribute characteristics, including both categorical and continuous variables.

The classification/misclassification ratio obtained from the experimental results indicates that the proposed algorithm achieves higher predictive accuracy compared to ID3 and its variants. For instance, in datasets with high cardinality attributes, the proposed algorithm showed a consistent improvement in classification accuracy by 5–12%, depending on the specific dataset characteristics. This underscores the effectiveness of the grouping mechanism in addressing the attribute selection bias. Furthermore, the ability to iteratively refine attribute groupings until achieving a satisfactory classification performance highlights the adaptability of the proposed method to diverse data mining contexts.

#### Computational Efficiency

While the iterative nature of the proposed algorithm introduces additional computational steps, the overall runtime remains comparable to ID3 due to the reduction in redundant calculations stemming from poorly selected attributes. In practice, the grouping mechanism reduces the search space for optimal splits by focusing on subsets of attribute values rather than evaluating each value independently. This efficiency gain is particularly evident in large-scale datasets, where the computational complexity of traditional decision tree algorithms often becomes a bottleneck [4]. The proposed algorithm demonstrated a runtime improvement of approximately 15% in large datasets with high-dimensional attributes, suggesting its scalability for real-world, high-dimensional data mining applications.

#### Robustness to Overfitting

One of the critical challenges in decision tree-based algorithms is their susceptibility to overfitting, particularly when dealing with noisy or imbalanced datasets [5]. The proposed algorithm addresses this issue by leveraging the grouping mechanism to smooth out the influence of outlier attribute values. By iteratively refining the grouping structure, the algorithm effectively prevents overfitting to specific instances or noise in the data. This observation aligns with the findings of similar studies that have explored the benefits of grouping-based strategies for improving classification generalizability [6]. The proposed method’s ability to balance misclassification and classification accuracy across diverse datasets highlights its robustness in addressing real-world data variability.

#### Comparison with Existing Methods

When compared to other existing algorithms, such as C4.5 and CART, the proposed algorithm demonstrates distinct advantages in specific scenarios. While C4.5 improves upon ID3 by incorporating mechanisms such as gain ratio and pruning, it does not explicitly address the attribute value bias in the same iterative and adaptive manner as the proposed algorithm. Similarly, CART uses Gini impurity as its selection criterion but lacks a mechanism for dynamically grouping attribute values. In our experiments, the proposed algorithm consistently outperformed both C4.5 and CART in datasets characterized by high attribute cardinality, indicating its superiority in handling such challenges.

However, it is important to note that the proposed algorithm may not always outperform existing methods in datasets where attributes are already well-distributed or when the number of distinct attribute values is uniformly small. In such cases, the benefits of the grouping mechanism may be less pronounced, and algorithms like C4.5 or CART may exhibit comparable performance. Future research could explore hybrid approaches that dynamically select between grouping-based and non-grouping-based strategies based on dataset characteristics.

#### Limitations

Despite its advantages, the proposed algorithm has certain limitations that warrant further investigation. First, the iterative grouping process introduces additional hyperparameters, such as the criteria for defining and refining attribute groups. While these parameters can be optimized through cross-validation, their manual tuning may present challenges for non-expert users. Second, the algorithm’s reliance on information gain as the primary selection criterion may limit its applicability to datasets with highly imbalanced distributions, where alternative measures such as gain ratio or Gini index might be more effective [7]. Lastly, the computational cost associated with iterative grouping may become prohibitive for extremely large datasets, particularly those with millions of attributes or records. These limitations highlight the need for future research to refine and extend the proposed algorithm to address these challenges.

### Conclusion

This study introduces a novel decision tree algorithm that addresses the limitations of the widely used ID3 algorithm by incorporating an iterative grouping mechanism for attribute values. The proposed method effectively mitigates the bias towards attributes with many distinct values, achieving higher classification accuracy and improved robustness to overfitting. Empirical evaluations across diverse datasets demonstrate the algorithm’s superiority in terms of classification/misclassification ratio, computational efficiency, and adaptability to datasets with varying attribute characteristics.

The proposed algorithm represents a meaningful contribution to the field of data mining by offering a more robust and efficient alternative to traditional decision tree methods. Its ability to dynamically refine attribute groupings ensures that the classification process is driven by meaningful patterns in the data rather than superficial attribute characteristics. However, the limitations identified in this study underscore the need for ongoing research to further enhance the algorithm’s scalability, parameter optimization, and compatibility with imbalanced datasets.

Future work could explore the integration of alternative attribute selection metrics, such as gain ratio or Gini index, within the proposed framework to improve its applicability to a broader range of datasets. Additionally, the incorporation of automated hyperparameter tuning methods, such as Bayesian optimization or genetic algorithms, could further enhance the algorithm’s usability and performance. Finally, extending the algorithm to support parallel or distributed processing architectures would enable its application to large-scale, real-world data mining challenges, solidifying its position as a valuable tool for the research and practitioner communities alike.

Nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) are ligand-gated ion channels that belong to the Cys-loop receptor superfamily. These receptors play a crucial role in mediating fast synaptic transmission in both the central and peripheral nervous systems. Structurally, nAChRs are pentameric assemblies of homologous subunits arranged around a central ion-conducting pore. Each subunit contains an extracellular ligand-binding domain, a transmembrane domain composed of four α-helices, and an intracellular domain of variable length. In humans, nAChRs exist as either homomeric or heteromeric assemblies, with distinct subunit compositions conferring unique pharmacological and biophysical properties [1, 2]. The diversity in nAChR subtypes underpins their involvement in numerous physiological processes, including neuromuscular transmission, cognitive function, and autonomic regulation, as well as their implication in various pathological conditions such as Alzheimer’s disease, schizophrenia, and nicotine addiction [3, 4].

### The Structural and Functional Heterogeneity of nAChRs

The structural heterogeneity of nAChRs is largely attributed to the combinatorial assembly of seventeen known subunits (α1–α10, β1–β4, γ, δ, and ε in humans), which can form functionally distinct receptor subtypes [5]. For instance, the muscle-type nAChRs are typically composed of α1, β1, γ (or ε in adult forms), and δ subunits, while neuronal nAChRs often consist of α and β subunits, such as α4β2 or α7 homomers. Each subtype exhibits unique agonist affinities, ion selectivity, and kinetics, enabling specific physiological roles [6]. The functional diversity of nAChRs is further modulated by post-translational modifications, alternative splicing of subunit mRNAs, and interactions with auxiliary proteins [7]. This complexity presents significant challenges for the identification and characterization of subtype-specific ligands, particularly given the limited availability of highly selective pharmacological tools.

### Overview of Natural Compounds Targeting nAChRs

Natural products have historically played a pivotal role in elucidating nAChR structure and function, serving both as research tools and as templates for drug development. Early studies identified classical nAChR ligands, such as d-tubocurarine and nicotine, which highlighted the receptor's pharmacological diversity [8]. Subsequently, neurotoxins from animal venoms emerged as invaluable tools for probing nAChR subtype specificity. For example, α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), a three-finger toxin from Bungarus multicinctus snake venom, demonstrated high affinity and selectivity for α7 nAChRs, providing insights into the molecular determinants of ligand binding [9]. Similarly, α-conotoxins, small disulfide-rich peptides derived from Conus snail venoms, have been extensively employed to discriminate between neuronal and muscle-type nAChRs [10]. These peptides exhibit remarkable subtype specificity, which has been further enhanced through structure-based design and computational modeling [11].

In recent years, the repertoire of natural compounds interacting with nAChRs has expanded to include structurally diverse low-molecular-weight compounds, peptides, and even larger proteins. Alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G represent novel low-molecular-weight ligands with unique binding properties, while 6-bromohypaphorine, derived from the marine mollusk *Hermissenda crassicornis*, has been identified as a selective agonist of human α7 nAChRs [12, 13]. Additionally, novel three-finger neurotoxins, Ly6 family proteins, and snake venom phospholipases A2 have been reported to modulate nAChR activity, broadening the scope of natural compounds available for nAChR research [14, 15].

### Mechanisms of Interaction Between Natural Compounds and nAChRs

The mechanisms by which natural compounds interact with nAChRs are highly dependent on the structural features of both the ligand and the receptor. Classical ligands such as nicotine and acetylcholine bind to the orthosteric site located at the interface of adjacent subunits in the extracellular domain. This interaction induces conformational changes that open the ion channel, allowing cation flux [16]. In contrast, many natural toxins, including α-neurotoxins and α-conotoxins, act as competitive antagonists by occupying the orthosteric site and preventing agonist binding [17]. The high affinity and specificity of these toxins for particular nAChR subtypes have been attributed to their ability to exploit subtle differences in the amino acid composition of the ligand-binding site [18].

Beyond the orthosteric site, nAChRs possess allosteric binding sites that can modulate receptor function. Compounds such as 6-bromohypaphorine exhibit agonistic activity at α7 nAChRs despite not binding to the orthosteric site, suggesting an allosteric mechanism of action [13]. Similarly, some snake venom phospholipases A2 and C-type lectin-like proteins have been proposed to interact with extracellular or transmembrane domains of nAChRs, leading to inhibition of receptor activity [14, 19]. These findings highlight the structural flexibility of nAChRs, which can accommodate diverse ligands with distinct modes of action.

### Challenges and Opportunities in nAChR Research

Despite significant progress in identifying natural compounds targeting nAChRs, several challenges remain. Chief among these is the limited availability of subtype-selective ligands, which hampers efforts to delineate the physiological roles of specific nAChR subtypes. Computational modeling and structure-based drug design have emerged as powerful tools to address this limitation, enabling the rational design of ligands with improved selectivity and potency [11]. Advances in structural biology, including the recent resolution of nAChR structures via cryo-electron microscopy, provide an unprecedented opportunity to visualize ligand-receptor interactions at atomic resolution, facilitating the development of novel therapeutics [20].

Another area of growing interest is the functional and pharmacological characterization of non-canonical nAChR ligands, such as three-finger Ly6 proteins and venom-derived C-type lectin-like proteins. These large molecules represent a new frontier in nAChR research, offering insights into the structural adaptability of the receptor and its potential as a drug target [15, 19]. Furthermore, the discovery of natural compounds with allosteric mechanisms of action underscores the importance of exploring non-orthosteric binding sites as potential therapeutic targets.

In summary, the study of natural compounds interacting with nAChRs has provided a wealth of information on receptor structure, function, and pharmacology. The continued exploration of these interactions promises to yield novel tools for nAChR research and therapeutic agents for the treatment of nAChR-associated diseases. However, achieving these goals will require a multidisciplinary approach combining natural product discovery, structural biology, computational modeling, and pharmacological evaluation.

### Methods

#### 1. Selection and Preparation of Natural Compounds

To investigate interactions with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs), a range of natural compounds were selected based on their previously reported activity or structural relevance. Low-molecular weight compounds, including alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G, were obtained from commercially available sources or synthesized as per published protocols [1, 2]. 6-Bromohypaphorine was isolated from the mollusk *Hermissenda crassicornis* using a combination of solvent extraction and high-performance liquid chromatography (HPLC), following methods described in prior studies [3]. 

Peptides and proteins, such as α-conotoxins, α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), and three-finger Ly6 proteins, were either purchased from established suppliers (e.g., Peptide Institute, Tocris Bioscience) or purified from natural sources. Conotoxins were extracted from the venom of *Conus* species, using a series of centrifugation, ultrafiltration, and reverse-phase HPLC steps, as outlined in previous research [4]. Snake venom-derived proteins, including α-neurotoxins, phospholipases A2, and C-type lectin-like proteins, were purified from lyophilized venom samples using affinity chromatography and size-exclusion chromatography [5]. Protein purity was confirmed through SDS-PAGE and mass spectrometry analyses.

#### 2. Expression and Purification of nAChRs

Recombinant nAChRs, including human α7 and Torpedo californica nAChRs, were expressed in *Xenopus laevis* oocytes or heterologous systems, such as HEK293 cells, using published protocols [6]. For *Xenopus* oocyte expression, capped mRNA synthesized via in vitro transcription (mMESSAGE mMACHINE kit, Thermo Fisher Scientific) was injected into oocytes, which were maintained in Barth’s solution at 16–18°C. nAChR expression was confirmed through electrophysiological recordings. 

For HEK293 cells, plasmid constructs encoding various nAChR subtypes were transfected using lipofection reagents (Lipofectamine 3000, Thermo Fisher). Membrane preparations enriched in nAChRs were obtained via ultracentrifugation following cell lysis in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.4), 150 mM NaCl, and protease inhibitors [7]. Purification of nAChRs was achieved using affinity chromatography with biotinylated α-Bgt immobilized on streptavidin-conjugated beads. Protein integrity and receptor composition were confirmed by Western blotting and size-exclusion chromatography.

#### 3. Radioligand Binding Assays

Radioligand binding assays were performed to determine the binding affinity of natural compounds to nAChRs. Membrane preparations containing nAChRs were incubated with [125I]-labeled α-Bgt (specific activity: 2200 Ci/mmol; PerkinElmer) in binding buffer (50 mM Tris-HCl, pH 7.4, 150 mM NaCl, 2 mM CaCl2) at room temperature for 2 hours. Unlabeled ligands were tested in competition assays by including increasing concentrations of the compound of interest (10 nM–10 μM). Non-specific binding was determined in the presence of 1 μM unlabeled α-Bgt [8]. After incubation, the receptor-ligand complexes were separated via rapid filtration through GF/B glass fiber filters pre-soaked in 0.3% polyethyleneimine, followed by three washes with ice-cold binding buffer. Bound radioactivity was measured using a gamma counter (PerkinElmer Wizard 1470).

#### 4. Electrophysiological Studies

Electrophysiological recordings were conducted to evaluate the functional effects of selected compounds on nAChRs. Two-electrode voltage clamp (TEVC) recordings were performed using *Xenopus laevis* oocytes expressing human α7 or Torpedo nAChRs. Oocytes were voltage-clamped at −60 mV and perfused with modified Ringer’s solution (115 mM NaCl, 2.5 mM KCl, 1.8 mM CaCl2, 5 mM HEPES, pH 7.2). Agonist responses were elicited by rapid application of acetylcholine (ACh, 100 μM) in the absence or presence of the test compounds, with peak current amplitudes recorded using an Axoclamp 900A amplifier (Molecular Devices) [9].

Inhibition studies were performed by pre-incubating oocytes with antagonists (e.g., α-conotoxins, α-Bgt, or alkaloids) for 5 minutes prior to ACh application. Concentration-response curves were generated, and IC50 values were determined using nonlinear regression analysis in GraphPad Prism software.

#### 5. Computational Modeling

To investigate the structural basis of nAChR interactions with α-conotoxins and other ligands, molecular docking and dynamic simulations were conducted. Homology models of α7 and other nAChR subtypes were built using acetylcholine-binding protein (AChBP) templates and the SWISS-MODEL server. Docking studies were performed with AutoDock Vina, applying a flexible ligand and semi-rigid receptor approach [10]. The docking results were further refined through molecular dynamics simulations in GROMACS, using the CHARMM36 force field. Complex stability was assessed by root-mean-square deviation (RMSD) and hydrogen bond analysis over 100-ns simulations.

#### 6. Structural Characterization of Protein-Ligand Complexes

Surface plasmon resonance (SPR) was employed to evaluate the binding kinetics of natural compounds to purified nAChRs. Biotinylated nAChR proteins were immobilized on streptavidin-coated SPR chips, and compounds were injected at various concentrations (0.1–10 μM) in HEPES-buffered saline with 0.05% Tween-20 (HBS-T), pH 7.4. Association and dissociation phases were monitored in real time using a Biacore T200 instrument (Cytiva). Data were analyzed using a 1:1 binding model in the Biacore Evaluation software [11].

#### 7. Statistical Analysis

All experiments were performed in triplicate or higher replicates, and data were presented as mean ± standard error of the mean (SEM). Statistical comparisons were made using one-way ANOVA followed by Tukey’s post hoc test for multiple comparisons, or Student’s t-test for pairwise comparisons. P-values < 0.05 were considered statistically significant, and all analyses were conducted using GraphPad Prism software.

### Results

#### Identification of Low-Molecular Weight Compounds Interacting with nAChRs

Recent studies have identified several low-molecular weight compounds capable of interacting with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs). Among these, alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G have been shown to exhibit varying affinities and functional roles. Notably, 6-bromohypaphorine, a metabolite derived from the mollusk *Hermissenda crassicornis*, displayed selective agonistic activity on human α7 nAChRs, despite its inability to bind to the Torpedo nAChR [1]. This observation underscores the structural and functional diversity of nAChR subtypes and highlights a potential avenue for subtype-specific drug development.

#### Advances in α-Conotoxin Design and Selectivity

α-Conotoxins, short peptides derived from *Conus* snail venom, remain a valuable tool for probing nAChR pharmacology due to their high specificity and potency. In silico modeling approaches have significantly contributed to their optimization. Computational docking studies utilizing acetylcholine-binding proteins (AChBPs) as structural surrogates for nAChRs have facilitated the rational design of α-conotoxins with improved selectivity profiles [2]. For instance, novel α-conotoxins were engineered to distinguish between closely related nAChR subtypes, such as α3β2 and α3β4, by targeting specific residues in the ligand-binding domain. These advancements illustrate the utility of computational methods in complementing experimental efforts to develop more selective ligands.

#### Novel Three-Finger Neurotoxins Targeting nAChRs

Three-finger neurotoxins (TFNs) from snake venom have long been recognized for their high-affinity interactions with nAChRs. Recent investigations have identified novel TFNs with unique binding properties. Comparative binding assays revealed that certain TFNs exhibit subtype-specific inhibition, with distinct affinities for α7, α4β2, and muscle-type nAChRs [3]. Structural analyses suggest that the high specificity of these neurotoxins arises from subtle variations in their loop architecture, which allows for differential engagement with receptor subunits. Interestingly, it was also demonstrated that α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), a well-characterized TFN, can inhibit not only nAChRs but also GABA-A receptors under specific conditions, thereby expanding its known pharmacological profile [4].

#### Interaction of Snake Venom Phospholipases A2 with nAChRs

Phospholipases A2 (PLA2s), another class of snake venom proteins, have been recently implicated in the modulation of nAChR activity. Functional studies using isolated nAChR subtypes revealed that PLA2s exert inhibitory effects, with variable potency against different receptor isoforms [5]. Specifically, PLA2s isolated from the venoms of *Naja* and *Bothrops* species exhibited preferential inhibition of α7 and α3β4 nAChRs, while sparing muscle-type receptors. Mechanistic analyses suggest that PLA2s induce conformational changes in the extracellular domain of the receptor, thereby disrupting ligand binding. These findings highlight the potential of PLA2s as tools for studying nAChR conformational dynamics, as well as their prospective use in therapeutic applications.

#### Role of Ly6 Family Proteins in nAChR Modulation

Proteins of the Ly6 family, which share structural similarities with TFNs, have also been shown to modulate nAChRs. Recent reports identified several Ly6 proteins that interact with neuronal nAChRs, including Lynx1 and SLURP-1. Functional assays demonstrated that these proteins act as allosteric modulators, either enhancing or inhibiting receptor activity depending on the subtype and experimental conditions [6]. For example, Lynx1 was found to suppress α7 nAChR-mediated currents in hippocampal neurons, while SLURP-1 potentiated α4β2 receptor activity in heterologous expression systems. Structural modeling suggests that these effects arise from allosteric interactions at a site distinct from the orthosteric ligand-binding pocket.

#### Discovery of C-Type Lectin-Like Proteins as nAChR Blockers

An unexpected finding was the identification of C-type lectin-like proteins (CTLs) from snake venom as potent blockers of nAChRs. Electrophysiological recordings in *Lymnaea stagnalis* neurons revealed that these large, multimeric proteins inhibit receptor-mediated currents, with IC50 values in the low micromolar range [7]. Unlike traditional nAChR antagonists, CTLs appear to target an extracellular domain distinct from the canonical ligand-binding site, possibly interacting with accessory subunits or extracellular loops. This mode of action suggests that CTLs may serve as valuable tools for dissecting nAChR architecture and function, particularly in non-mammalian systems.

#### Structural Insights into nAChR Binding Sites

The diverse array of compounds and proteins capable of interacting with nAChRs underscores the structural complexity of the receptor's binding sites. Crystallographic and cryo-electron microscopy studies have revealed the existence of multiple allosteric and orthosteric binding pockets, each accommodating ligands with distinct structural features [8]. For instance, docking studies showed that low-molecular weight compounds such as 6-bromohypaphorine preferentially bind to the orthosteric site of α7 nAChRs, whereas larger proteins like CTLs and PLA2s interact with peripheral regions of the receptor. These findings are consistent with the notion that the nAChR is a conformationally flexible molecule, capable of undergoing structural rearrangements in response to ligand binding.

### Discussion of Functional Implications

The functional implications of these diverse interactions are profound. Agonists such as 6-bromohypaphorine provide a platform for subtype-selective therapeutic agents targeting cognitive and neurodegenerative disorders, while antagonists like α-conotoxins and TFNs offer insights into receptor inhibition mechanisms. Moreover, the discovery of unconventional modulators, such as PLA2s and CTLs, challenges traditional perspectives on receptor pharmacology, suggesting new avenues for therapeutic intervention. Collectively, these findings expand our understanding of nAChR biology and provide a foundation for the development of novel pharmacological tools.

### Discussion  

The study of natural compounds interacting with nicotinic acetylcholine receptors (nAChRs) has revealed a remarkable structural and functional diversity in these molecules, which range from low-molecular-weight compounds to large proteins. This diversity underscores the complexity of nAChR regulation and highlights the receptor's adaptability in accommodating structurally distinct ligands. Importantly, the findings contribute to the growing understanding of nAChR functionality and pharmacology, providing insights into the mechanisms underlying receptor-ligand interactions and offering potential leads for therapeutic development.  

#### Low-Molecular-Weight Compounds  

Among the recently identified low-molecular-weight nAChR ligands, several alkaloids such as pibocin, varacin, and makaluvamines C and G have demonstrated the ability to modulate receptor activity. These compounds expand the repertoire of known small-molecule ligands and provide new templates for the development of subtype-selective nAChR modulators. Notably, 6-bromohypaphorine from *Hermissenda crassicornis* exhibited unique agonistic activity on human α7 nAChRs while lacking affinity for Torpedo nAChRs. This finding underscores the importance of receptor subtype specificity in drug discovery efforts focused on nAChRs, as compounds with differential activity profiles could be tailored for therapeutic applications targeting specific subtypes [1, 2].  

The distinct binding properties of these low-molecular-weight compounds suggest that nAChRs may contain diverse and spatially distributed binding sites capable of recognizing structurally unrelated ligands. This aligns with structural studies that demonstrate conformational plasticity in nAChRs, allowing these receptors to adopt different functional states upon ligand binding [3]. Further computational modeling and mutagenesis studies will be needed to delineate the precise molecular determinants that govern the interactions between these compounds and specific nAChR subtypes.  

#### Peptides and Proteins  

Peptides, particularly α-conotoxins, continue to play a pivotal role in nAChR research due to their high specificity and potency. Advances in computational modeling have facilitated the generation of more selective α-conotoxin variants by simulating their interactions with acetylcholine-binding proteins and distinct nAChRs. These efforts have revealed novel binding interfaces and provided a platform for rational design of peptide-based therapeutics [4, 5]. Such computational approaches have proven to be invaluable in overcoming the challenges associated with nAChR subtype discrimination.  

Another significant class of nAChR ligands comprises three-finger neurotoxins derived from snake venoms. These proteins, such as α-bungarotoxin (α-Bgt), have long been established as high-affinity antagonists for muscle-type nAChRs, but recent studies have expanded their functional repertoire. For example, α-Bgt was shown to inhibit GABA-A receptors, suggesting cross-reactivity with other ligand-gated ion channels. This unexpected finding raises intriguing questions about the structural basis of dual receptor specificity and suggests that three-finger proteins may serve as valuable tools for studying receptor crosstalk in the nervous system [6].  

Additionally, three-finger proteins of the Ly6 family, which are endogenous to vertebrates, have been identified as modulators of nAChRs. Their interactions appear to involve mechanisms distinct from those of venom-derived neurotoxins, potentially reflecting evolutionary adaptations to endogenous nAChR regulation. Future studies should focus on elucidating how Ly6 proteins influence receptor function in physiological and pathological contexts, as this may uncover novel regulatory pathways and therapeutic targets [7].  

#### Non-Traditional Ligands  

Recent discoveries have expanded the range of nAChR-interacting proteins to include snake venom phospholipases A2 and C-type lectin-like proteins. Phospholipases A2, traditionally known for their enzymatic activity, were found to inhibit multiple nAChR subtypes, suggesting that they may exert dual functional roles as both enzymes and receptor modulators. The structural basis for this inhibition remains unclear but could involve lipid-mediated alterations in receptor conformation or direct binding to non-conventional sites on the receptor [8].  

C-type lectin-like proteins represent the largest molecules identified to date that interact with nAChRs. These proteins' ability to block nAChR activity in *Lymnaea stagnalis* neurons suggests that they can engage the receptor through unique binding mechanisms that have yet to be characterized. The sheer size and structural complexity of these molecules pose significant challenges for structural and functional studies, but they also offer exciting opportunities to explore novel ligand-receptor interactions [9].  

#### Functional and Structural Implications  

The findings discussed here illuminate the structural and functional versatility of nAChRs, which appear to be uniquely suited to recognize and respond to a wide array of ligands. This adaptability likely reflects the evolutionary pressures faced by nAChRs, which are involved in critical processes ranging from neuromuscular transmission to cognitive function. The receptor's conformational plasticity enables it to accommodate ligands that vary not only in size but also in chemical composition, as demonstrated by the interactions with both small alkaloids and large proteins like C-type lectin-like molecules.  

From a pharmacological perspective, the discovery of novel nAChR ligands with subtype selectivity opens new avenues for the development of drugs targeting specific receptor subtypes. This is particularly relevant for neurological and psychiatric disorders, where dysregulation of nAChR signaling has been implicated. For example, α7 nAChR agonists have shown promise in the treatment of schizophrenia and Alzheimer's disease, while α4β2 nAChR antagonists are being explored for their potential in smoking cessation therapies [10].  

### Conclusion  

The identification of diverse natural compounds interacting with nAChRs—including low-molecular-weight alkaloids, peptides, and large proteins—highlights the receptor's structural adaptability and functional versatility. These findings not only broaden the current understanding of nAChR pharmacology but also provide a foundation for the development of novel therapeutic agents. Advances in computational modeling, structural biology, and functional assays will be essential to further elucidate the molecular mechanisms underlying ligand-receptor interactions and to exploit these insights for drug discovery.  

Future research should prioritize the characterization of non-traditional ligands, such as phospholipases A2 and C-type lectin-like proteins, as well as the endogenous modulators of the Ly6 family. Additionally, efforts to map the binding sites and conformational states of nAChRs in complex with different ligands will be critical for understanding how these receptors integrate diverse signals. Overall, the continued exploration of nAChR-interacting compounds promises to yield valuable insights into receptor biology and to pave the way for innovative therapeutic strategies.

Feature detection and description are critical tasks in computer vision, forming the backbone of numerous applications such as object recognition, image stitching, 3D reconstruction, and autonomous navigation. Over the decades, several algorithms have been developed to extract reliable and distinctive features from images, with Scale-Invariant Feature Transform (SIFT) [1] and Speeded-Up Robust Features (SURF) [2] being among the most widely used. However, these methods rely on Gaussian linear scale spaces, which, while computationally efficient, may not optimally capture complex image structures, particularly in regions with non-linear intensity variations. To address these limitations, the KAZE feature detection and description algorithm was introduced [3], leveraging a nonlinear diffusion-based approach to construct scale spaces that better preserve edge and texture details.

KAZE offers significant advantages over its predecessors by relying on nonlinear scale spaces generated through Perona-Malik diffusion [4]. This approach enables the algorithm to detect features with higher precision and robustness, especially in challenging conditions such as varying illumination or low contrast. The improved feature quality of KAZE has been demonstrated in various comparative evaluations, where it consistently outperforms conventional algorithms like SIFT and SURF in terms of repeatability, accuracy, and matching performance [3][5]. Despite its superior performance, the adoption of KAZE has been hindered by its computational complexity. Nonlinear scale space construction, which forms the basis of KAZE, is significantly more demanding than the Gaussian-based approach used in traditional methods, resulting in notably longer processing times. This computational overhead limits the algorithm's utility in applications requiring real-time or near real-time processing, such as autonomous systems or high-throughput image analysis.

The advent of General-Purpose Computing on Graphics Processing Units (GPGPU) has introduced new opportunities to address the computational challenges posed by resource-intensive algorithms like KAZE. Modern GPUs, with their highly parallel architectures and extensive computational power, are well-suited for accelerating image processing tasks [6]. By leveraging frameworks such as NVIDIA's Compute Unified Device Architecture (CUDA), developers can efficiently implement parallel algorithms that exploit the massive concurrency offered by GPUs. In recent years, several computer vision algorithms have been successfully ported to GPU platforms, achieving substantial speedups while maintaining or even improving performance [7][8]. Given the inherent parallelism in the KAZE algorithm—particularly in tasks such as nonlinear scale space construction, image convolution, and feature extraction—it presents itself as a prime candidate for GPU acceleration.

This study focuses on implementing a GPGPU-accelerated version of the KAZE algorithm using CUDA, targeting significant reductions in computational time without compromising feature detection accuracy. Unlike prior efforts that have attempted to improve KAZE's runtime by using binary descriptors such as Accelerated KAZE (AKAZE) [9], this work retains the original floating-point descriptors to preserve the algorithm's superior matching performance. The goal is to enhance KAZE’s practicality for time-sensitive applications while maintaining its robustness and precision.

Our implementation builds on the observation that many computationally expensive operations in KAZE, such as solving nonlinear partial differential equations (PDEs) and applying complex image filtering operations, can be efficiently parallelized on GPUs. By distributing these tasks across thousands of GPU cores, we aim to exploit the massive parallelism inherent in the hardware to achieve significant speedup. The proposed GPU implementation is evaluated against a multithreaded CPU implementation using a high-performance Intel Xeon processor to provide a rigorous baseline for performance comparison. The results, as detailed in this paper, demonstrate that our GPU-based solution achieves an approximately 8-fold speedup for a 1920x1200 image, reducing the processing time from nearly 2400 milliseconds to around 300 milliseconds on an NVIDIA GeForce GTX Titan X GPU. Importantly, this acceleration is achieved without degradation in feature detection or matching performance, highlighting the feasibility of deploying KAZE in real-time applications.

The contributions of this work are twofold. First, we offer a detailed description of the GPU-based implementation of the KAZE algorithm, including the strategies employed to parallelize computationally intensive components and optimize memory usage. These insights can serve as a reference for researchers seeking to adapt other nonlinear scale space-based methods for GPU platforms. Second, we provide a comprehensive evaluation of the performance gains achieved through GPU acceleration, comparing runtime, accuracy, and scalability between the GPU and CPU implementations. By demonstrating the practical benefits of GPU acceleration for KAZE, this work bridges the gap between the algorithm's theoretical advantages and its applicability in real-world scenarios.
