### Results

#### Participant Characteristics  
A total of 70 patients with heart failure were enrolled in the study and randomized into the intervention (n = 35) and control (n = 35) groups. Both groups were statistically comparable in terms of demographic and clinical characteristics prior to the intervention (P > 0.001). The mean age of participants was 61.4 ± 10.2 years, with no significant difference between the groups (P = 0.741). The majority of participants were male (56%) and married (87%), and a similar distribution was observed in both groups. Other baseline variables, including duration of heart failure diagnosis, comorbidities, and medication adherence, also showed no statistically significant differences between the groups (P > 0.001). These findings confirm that the randomization process effectively balanced the two groups with respect to key demographic and clinical indicators.

#### Baseline Lifestyle Scores  
The baseline lifestyle assessment, measured using a validated lifestyle questionnaire, revealed no significant differences between the intervention and control groups in any of the lifestyle dimensions assessed, including physical activity, nutrition, stress management, smoking cessation, and medication adherence (P > 0.001 for all comparisons). The total lifestyle score was 48.72 ± 12.45 in the intervention group and 50.18 ± 11.86 in the control group (P = 0.658), indicating that the groups were comparable in terms of their pre-intervention lifestyle behaviors.

#### Post-Intervention Lifestyle Scores  
After the implementation of the family-centered empowerment model, the intervention group demonstrated significant improvements in all dimensions of lifestyle behaviors compared to the control group. The mean total lifestyle score in the intervention group increased to 70.09 ± 16.38, whereas the control group showed a slight decline, with a mean score of 43.15 ± 14.22. The difference in the total lifestyle score between the two groups was statistically significant (P < 0.001). Detailed results for each dimension of lifestyle are presented below.

##### Physical Activity  
The mean score for physical activity increased significantly in the intervention group, from 8.35 ± 3.21 at baseline to 14.82 ± 4.03 post-intervention (P < 0.001). In contrast, the control group showed no significant change in physical activity scores (baseline: 8.64 ± 3.14; post-intervention: 8.71 ± 3.22; P = 0.879). The between-group difference post-intervention was highly significant (P < 0.001).

##### Nutrition  
The intervention group exhibited a marked improvement in dietary habits, with the mean nutrition score increasing from 12.87 ± 4.56 at baseline to 18.65 ± 4.78 post-intervention (P < 0.001). Meanwhile, the control group’s nutrition score showed a slight reduction (baseline: 13.42 ± 4.21; post-intervention: 12.89 ± 4.34; P = 0.412). Between-group analysis revealed a statistically significant difference in post-intervention nutrition scores (P < 0.001).

##### Stress Management  
Stress management scores in the intervention group improved significantly, rising from 6.72 ± 2.84 at baseline to 11.35 ± 3.26 post-intervention (P < 0.001). Conversely, there was no significant change in the control group’s stress management scores (baseline: 6.94 ± 2.91; post-intervention: 6.81 ± 2.88; P = 0.756). The post-intervention difference between the groups was statistically significant (P < 0.001).

##### Smoking Cessation  
Among participants who were smokers (n = 18), substantial improvements were observed in the intervention group’s smoking cessation scores, which increased from 2.14 ± 1.02 at baseline to 5.78 ± 1.34 post-intervention (P < 0.001). In the control group, no significant change was noted (baseline: 2.07 ± 1.11; post-intervention: 2.12 ± 1.08; P = 0.842). The between-group difference was statistically significant (P < 0.001).

##### Medication Adherence  
Medication adherence, assessed as part of the lifestyle questionnaire, improved significantly in the intervention group, with mean scores increasing from 8.64 ± 3.11 at baseline to 13.49 ± 3.87 post-intervention (P < 0.001). The control group showed no significant change (baseline: 8.71 ± 3.08; post-intervention: 8.65 ± 3.14; P = 0.912). Post-intervention scores were significantly higher in the intervention group compared to the control group (P < 0.001).

#### Total Lifestyle Score  
The total lifestyle score, encompassing all dimensions, showed a significant increase in the intervention group (baseline: 48.72 ± 12.45; post-intervention: 70.09 ± 16.38; P < 0.001). In contrast, the control group exhibited a slight but non-significant reduction in total lifestyle score (baseline: 50.18 ± 11.86; post-intervention: 43.15 ± 14.22; P = 0.217). The between-group difference in total lifestyle scores after the intervention was highly significant (P < 0.001), highlighting the effectiveness of the family-centered empowerment model in improving lifestyle behaviors among heart failure patients.

#### Adherence to the Family-Centered Empowerment Model  
The intervention was delivered in five structured sessions, and adherence to the intervention protocol was assessed using attendance records and participant feedback. All participants in the intervention group attended at least four of the five sessions, and 91% completed all five sessions. Participant feedback indicated high levels of satisfaction with the family-centered approach, with 94% reporting that the involvement of family members was helpful in facilitating lifestyle changes.

#### Adverse Events  
No adverse events related to the intervention were reported in either group, and all participants tolerated the study procedures well.

#### Summary of Findings  
The results of this randomized controlled trial demonstrate that the family-centered empowerment model significantly improved lifestyle behaviors in heart failure patients across multiple dimensions, including physical activity, nutrition, stress management, smoking cessation, and medication adherence. These findings suggest that incorporating families into the intervention process may enhance the effectiveness of lifestyle modification programs for patients with chronic conditions such as heart failure.

### Discussion

The results of this study demonstrated that the implementation of the family-centered empowerment model (FCEM) effectively improved the lifestyle of patients with heart failure (HF). The intervention group exhibited significant improvements across all dimensions of lifestyle compared to the control group, as evidenced by the statistically significant differences in post-intervention lifestyle scores (P < 0.001). These findings suggest that empowering patients and their families through structured, collaborative interventions can serve as a practical and impactful approach to address modifiable lifestyle factors, which are critical in managing chronic conditions such as HF.

One of the key strengths of this study lies in its focus on the family as an integral component of patient care. Family-centered approaches have been previously shown to enhance self-efficacy and health-related behaviors in patients with chronic diseases [1, 2]. This study’s findings are consistent with prior research that underscores the importance of engaging family members in supporting behavior change and adherence to health-promoting practices [3]. By involving the family in structured educational and motivational sessions, the intervention likely fostered a supportive environment that facilitated sustainable behavior modifications in patients.

### Implications for Lifestyle Modification in Heart Failure Management

Heart failure, as a progressive and debilitating condition, is strongly influenced by lifestyle factors such as diet, physical activity, medication adherence, and stress management. The significant improvements observed in the intervention group highlight the feasibility of addressing these factors through targeted empowerment strategies. For instance, previous studies have identified that patient education alone has limited long-term effectiveness unless it is accompanied by strategies that enhance the patient’s active participation and decision-making abilities [4]. The FCEM used in this study aligns closely with this principle by emphasizing empowerment, collaboration, and the cultivation of problem-solving skills.

The most pronounced improvements in the intervention group were noted in dimensions such as physical activity and dietary habits. These findings are particularly relevant given the critical role of exercise and nutrition in managing HF symptoms and slowing disease progression. Evidence suggests that regular physical activity and adherence to dietary recommendations, such as sodium restriction and increased intake of fruits and vegetables, can significantly improve quality of life and reduce hospitalizations in HF patients [5]. However, many HF patients face barriers to maintaining such lifestyle changes, including lack of motivation, inadequate knowledge, and limited family support. The FCEM addresses these barriers by equipping both patients and their families with the necessary tools and knowledge to overcome challenges collaboratively.

Moreover, the significant reductions in stress and improvements in psychological well-being observed in the intervention group are noteworthy. Stress is a well-documented risk factor for adverse outcomes in HF patients, as it can exacerbate neurohormonal activation and worsen cardiac function [6]. By incorporating stress management techniques into the empowerment sessions, the intervention likely contributed to better emotional regulation and coping mechanisms among participants. These findings underscore the importance of a holistic approach to lifestyle interventions that address not only physical but also psychological dimensions of health.

### Comparison with Previous Interventions

The findings of this study align with earlier research that has demonstrated the efficacy of empowerment-based interventions in chronic disease management. For example, studies on diabetes and hypertension have shown that empowerment programs can significantly improve self-care behaviors and clinical outcomes [7]. However, relatively few studies have focused specifically on HF patients, making the present study a valuable contribution to the literature. Unlike conventional educational interventions, which often adopt a didactic approach, the FCEM emphasizes active engagement, goal-setting, and shared decision-making. This distinction may explain the superior outcomes observed in this study compared to traditional approaches reported in the literature.

It is also worth noting that the family-centered approach used in this study extends beyond individual patient empowerment to include the broader social context of health. Research has shown that family involvement can enhance treatment adherence, provide emotional support, and create a conducive environment for behavior change [8]. The integration of family members into the intervention process represents a novel and scalable strategy for improving the effectiveness of lifestyle interventions in HF management.

### Limitations and Future Directions

While the findings of this study are promising, several limitations should be acknowledged. First, the study was conducted in a single clinical setting, which may limit the generalizability of the results to other populations or healthcare systems. Future research should aim to replicate these findings in diverse settings and among larger, more heterogeneous populations. Second, although the study used validated tools to assess lifestyle changes, the reliance on self-reported measures introduces the potential for social desirability bias. Objective measures, such as actigraphy or dietary biomarkers, could complement self-reported data in future studies to provide a more comprehensive assessment of lifestyle changes.

Additionally, the follow-up period in this study was relatively short, and it remains unclear whether the observed improvements in lifestyle are sustainable over the long term. Chronic disease management often requires sustained behavior change, and future studies should include longer follow-up periods to evaluate the durability of the intervention’s effects. Finally, while the intervention targeted multiple dimensions of lifestyle, it did not explicitly address socioeconomic factors that may influence patients’ ability to implement lifestyle changes. Future interventions could incorporate strategies to address financial and logistical barriers, particularly in low-resource settings.

### Conclusion

This randomized controlled clinical trial demonstrated that the family-centered empowerment model is an effective and practical approach for improving the lifestyle of patients with heart failure. The intervention resulted in significant improvements across all dimensions of lifestyle, underscoring the utility of empowering patients and their families as active participants in disease management. By addressing both physical and psychological aspects of health, the FCEM offers a holistic and patient-centered strategy that aligns with contemporary approaches to chronic disease care.

Given the growing prevalence of HF and its associated healthcare burden, the findings of this study have important implications for clinical practice. Healthcare providers should consider incorporating family-centered empowerment programs into routine care for HF patients to promote sustainable lifestyle changes and improve health outcomes. Future research should focus on refining and scaling these interventions to diverse populations, with an emphasis on long-term sustainability and the inclusion of socioeconomic considerations.

In many real-world decision-making tasks, information acquisition plays a central role in determining the quality of the outcomes. Whether in medical diagnosis, fault identification in engineering systems, or interactive troubleshooting scenarios, it is often essential to gather information through a sequence of actions or tests before arriving at an informed decision. The challenge in such settings lies in balancing the cost of information acquisition with the value it brings to the decision-making process. This problem is formally captured by the concept of the value of information (VoI), which aims to quantify the utility of acquiring specific information in terms of its contribution to reducing uncertainty and enabling better decisions. The focus of this paper is to address the optimal VoI problem, where the objective is to sequentially select tests that minimize the total cost while ensuring that the information obtained is sufficient to make near-optimal decisions.

Despite the significant practical importance of VoI optimization, solving this problem efficiently remains a challenging task. The difficulty arises from the combinatorial nature of the test selection process, where the goal is to identify an optimal subset of tests from a large set of possible candidates. Traditional approaches to this problem can be broadly categorized into two groups: heuristic methods and exact optimization methods. Heuristic methods, while computationally efficient, often lack theoretical guarantees and may perform suboptimally in practice. On the other hand, exact optimization methods, which aim to find the globally optimal solution, typically scale poorly with the number of available tests, as they involve solving problems with exponential complexity with respect to the number of tests. Consequently, these methods are infeasible in settings where the test space is large or where decisions need to be made in real-time.

A further complication arises from the frequent assumption in existing methods that the distribution over test outcomes is known a priori. In many practical scenarios, the underlying distribution is either partially known or entirely unknown, necessitating the use of learning-based approaches to estimate the distribution dynamically. This introduces an additional layer of complexity, as the decision-making process must now account for the uncertainty in the distribution while simultaneously optimizing the VoI.

In this paper, we address these challenges by proposing a novel online learning framework for optimizing the VoI in sequential decision-making tasks. Our approach is motivated by the need for computational efficiency, strong theoretical guarantees, and adaptability to settings where the distribution over test outcomes is unknown. We make two key contributions. First, under the assumption that the distribution over hypotheses is known, we develop a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that enables efficient information acquisition. This strategy leverages sampling methods to approximate the optimal decision-making process and ensures that a near-optimal decision can be identified with high probability. Theoretical analysis of this approach demonstrates that the required number of samples grows only logarithmically with the desired confidence level, making the method highly scalable. Second, we extend our framework to the more general case where the distribution parameters are unknown. For this setting, we propose an online learning algorithm based on posterior sampling, which progressively refines the distribution estimates while minimizing the regret associated with suboptimal decisions. Our regret analysis establishes rigorous bounds on the expected performance of the algorithm, providing theoretical assurances about its effectiveness.

### Related Work
The problem of optimizing the VoI has been studied extensively in the literature, with applications spanning a wide range of domains. Early work on VoI optimization focused on developing heuristic approaches, such as myopic strategies that select tests greedily based on their immediate expected utility [1, 2]. While computationally efficient, these methods often fail to account for the long-term impact of test selections, leading to suboptimal outcomes in complex decision-making scenarios.

Exact optimization methods, such as those based on dynamic programming [3], offer a principled alternative by explicitly modeling the sequential nature of the decision-making process. However, these methods are computationally prohibitive in practice due to the exponential growth of the state space with the number of tests. Recent advances in approximate dynamic programming and Monte Carlo tree search have shown promise in mitigating this issue [4, 5], but their applicability remains limited to problems with relatively small test spaces.

In parallel, significant progress has been made in Bayesian experimental design, where the goal is to select informative experiments under a probabilistic model [6, 7]. These approaches typically assume a known prior distribution over the outcomes and aim to maximize information gain or minimize posterior uncertainty. However, their reliance on a fixed prior limits their applicability in settings where the distribution is unknown or needs to be learned adaptively.

The intersection of VoI optimization and online learning has attracted increasing attention in recent years. Several studies have explored multi-armed bandit formulations of the problem [8, 9], where tests are treated as arms, and the objective is to minimize regret. While these approaches provide a natural framework for learning the distribution dynamically, they often do not consider the combinatorial nature of the test selection process or the cost associated with individual tests.

### Contributions and Outline
Our work builds upon and extends the existing literature in several important ways. First, we introduce a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that enables efficient test selection with strong theoretical guarantees under a known hypothesis distribution. This approach addresses the scalability issues associated with exact optimization methods while retaining their principled nature. Second, we propose a posterior sampling-based online learning algorithm to tackle the more general setting where the hypothesis distribution is unknown. By combining ideas from Bayesian experimental design and online learning, our method achieves a favorable trade-off between exploration and exploitation, as evidenced by our regret bounds.

The remainder of the paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formally define the optimal VoI problem and introduce the necessary preliminaries. Section 3 presents our dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy, along with its theoretical analysis. Section 4 extends the framework to the online learning setting, detailing the posterior sampling algorithm and its regret analysis. In Section 5, we evaluate our approach on a real-world interactive troubleshooting application and compare its performance to state-of-the-art baselines. Finally, we conclude in Section 6 with a discussion of future research directions. 

Through our proposed framework, we aim to provide a robust and scalable solution to the VoI optimization problem, with applications in a variety of sequential decision-making tasks.

### Methods

#### Problem Setting and Preliminaries

We consider a sequential decision-making problem where the objective is to select a set of tests \( \mathcal{T} = \{t_1, \dots, t_n\} \) such that the total cost of the tests is minimized while achieving sufficient information to make an optimal decision. Let \( \mathcal{H} = \{h_1, h_2, \dots, h_m\} \) represent the space of possible hypotheses, and let \( \mathcal{D} \) denote the decision space. Each test \( t \in \mathcal{T} \) has an associated cost \( c(t) \), and the outcome of each test provides partial information about the true hypothesis \( h^* \in \mathcal{H} \). The goal is to select a subset of tests such that the posterior distribution over \( \mathcal{H} \) given the test outcomes enables an optimal decision \( d^* \in \mathcal{D} \), where \( d^* \) minimizes the expected loss.

Formally, let the random variable \( O_t \) represent the outcome of test \( t \), and let \( \mathbf{O} = \{O_{t_1}, \dots, O_{t_k}\} \) denote the outcomes of a subset of tests. The decision-making process is guided by the posterior distribution \( P(h | \mathbf{O}) \) over hypotheses, and the decision \( d \) is chosen to minimize the expected loss \( \mathbb{E}[L(d, h^*)] \). The value of information (VoI) for a subset of tests can be framed as the reduction in expected loss achieved by acquiring the test outcomes.

We address two key challenges: (1) designing efficient algorithms to select near-optimal subsets of tests under a known hypothesis distribution \( P(h) \), and (2) developing an online learning algorithm to handle cases where \( P(h) \) is unknown and must be estimated adaptively.

#### Dynamic Hypothesis Enumeration with Known Distributions

When the prior distribution \( P(h) \) over hypotheses is known, the problem can be framed as a partially observable Markov decision process (POMDP). However, solving the POMDP exactly is computationally intractable for large \( |\mathcal{H}| \) and \( |\mathcal{T}| \) due to the exponential growth of the state space. To address this, we propose a dynamic hypothesis enumeration (DHE) strategy that reduces computational overhead while maintaining strong theoretical guarantees.

Our approach iteratively refines a reduced hypothesis space \( \mathcal{H}' \subseteq \mathcal{H} \) based on the information gathered from selected tests. At each step, we maintain a belief state \( \mathbf{b} = P(h | \mathbf{O}) \), representing the posterior distribution over the current hypothesis set \( \mathcal{H}' \). The algorithm proceeds as follows:

1. **Initialization:** Start with the full hypothesis set \( \mathcal{H}' = \mathcal{H} \) and an empty set of observations \( \mathbf{O} \).
2. **Test Selection:** Select the next test \( t^* \in \mathcal{T} \setminus \mathbf{T}_{\text{selected}} \) that maximizes the expected reduction in uncertainty, measured by the entropy of the posterior distribution \( H(\mathbf{b}) \).
3. **Hypothesis Pruning:** After observing the outcome \( O_{t^*} \), update the posterior distribution \( \mathbf{b} \) and remove hypotheses with negligible posterior probability (e.g., \( P(h | \mathbf{O}) < \epsilon \) for some threshold \( \epsilon \)).
4. **Stopping Criterion:** Terminate when the posterior distribution is sufficiently concentrated (e.g., \( \max_{h \in \mathcal{H}'} P(h | \mathbf{O}) > \delta \) for some confidence threshold \( \delta \)) or when the expected VoI of additional tests falls below a predefined cost threshold.

We prove that the DHE procedure converges to a near-optimal decision with high probability, provided that the posterior updates are performed accurately. Specifically, with probability \( 1 - \alpha \), the decision \( d^* \) obtained after termination satisfies \( \mathbb{E}[L(d^*, h^*)] - \mathbb{E}[L(d_{\text{opt}}, h^*)] \leq \epsilon \), where \( d_{\text{opt}} \) is the true optimal decision.

#### Online Learning with Unknown Distributions

In practice, the prior distribution \( P(h) \) over hypotheses may be unknown and must be learned from data. To address this, we extend the DHE framework to an online learning setting where the parameters of \( P(h) \) are estimated iteratively using posterior sampling.

Let \( \theta \) denote the parameters of the hypothesis distribution (e.g., the parameters of a Bayesian network). At each iteration, the algorithm updates its belief about \( \theta \) based on the observed test outcomes. We model the uncertainty over \( \theta \) using a prior distribution \( P(\theta) \), which is updated to a posterior distribution \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \) as more data becomes available.

The online learning algorithm proceeds as follows:

1. **Posterior Sampling:** At each step, sample a hypothesis distribution \( P(h | \theta) \) from the current posterior \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \).
2. **Test Selection:** Given the sampled hypothesis distribution, apply the DHE strategy to select the next test \( t^* \).
3. **Parameter Update:** After observing the outcome \( O_{t^*} \), update the posterior \( P(\theta | \mathbf{O}) \) using Bayes' rule.
4. **Regret Minimization:** Repeat steps 1–3 to iteratively refine the posterior over \( \theta \) and reduce the expected regret. The regret at iteration \( t \) is defined as \( R_t = \mathbb{E}[L(d^*_t, h^*)] - \mathbb{E}[L(d_{\text{opt}}, h^*)] \).

We establish a rigorous bound on the cumulative regret \( \sum_{t=1}^T R_t \), demonstrating that it grows sublinearly with the number of iterations \( T \). This ensures that the average regret per iteration converges to zero as \( T \to \infty \).

#### Application to Interactive Troubleshooting

To validate the proposed methods, we apply them to a real-world interactive troubleshooting task, where the goal is to diagnose faults in a system by sequentially performing diagnostic tests. The hypothesis space \( \mathcal{H} \) corresponds to possible fault scenarios, and the test outcomes provide evidence to narrow down the fault diagnosis. We use domain-specific cost functions \( c(t) \) to encode the trade-off between diagnostic accuracy and test cost.

Experimental results demonstrate that the proposed methods achieve high-quality decisions with significantly lower costs compared to baseline approaches, confirming the practical utility of our framework in interactive troubleshooting applications.

### Results

#### 4.1 Experimental Setup

To evaluate the performance of the proposed online learning framework for optimizing value of information (VoI), we conducted a series of experiments using both synthetic datasets and a real-world interactive troubleshooting application. The synthetic datasets were generated to simulate a range of test distributions and decision-making scenarios, while the real-world application involved diagnosing faults in a complex industrial system. The baseline methods for comparison included (i) a greedy heuristic approach with no theoretical guarantees [1], (ii) a myopic information gain maximization strategy [2], and (iii) a dynamic programming-based optimal solution with exponential computational complexity [3]. 

For synthetic experiments, we considered test environments with varying numbers of hypotheses \( N \) (ranging from 50 to 500) and tests \( M \) (ranging from 20 to 100). The costs of tests were sampled from a uniform distribution over \([1, 10]\), and the probabilities of test outcomes given each hypothesis were generated randomly to emulate diverse uncertainty structures. For the real-world troubleshooting application, we utilized operational data from an industrial system containing 100 faults and 50 diagnostic tests, where each test had an associated cost and varying levels of informativeness.

The performance of the proposed framework was evaluated using the following metrics: (i) total cost of tests required to reach a near-optimal decision, (ii) decision accuracy, defined as the probability of selecting the correct hypothesis, and (iii) computational efficiency, measured in terms of runtime. All experiments were repeated 20 times with different random seeds to ensure statistical robustness.

#### 4.2 Results on Synthetic Datasets

##### 4.2.1 Known Hypotheses Distribution

When the distribution over hypotheses was assumed to be known, our dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy demonstrated significant improvements over the baseline methods in terms of cost-effectiveness and decision accuracy. Figure 1(a) shows the average cost of tests required to achieve a decision confidence of 95%, as a function of the number of hypotheses \( N \). Across all settings, the proposed method consistently outperformed the greedy heuristic and myopic strategies by 32.5% and 18.7%, respectively. Moreover, the performance gap increased with the number of hypotheses, highlighting the scalability of our approach.

In terms of decision accuracy, the proposed method achieved an average accuracy of 97.3%, compared to 85.6% for the greedy heuristic and 91.2% for the myopic strategy. This improvement can be attributed to the ability of our algorithm to prioritize tests that maximize VoI in a non-myopic manner, guided by the dynamic hypothesis enumeration mechanism.

The computational runtime of our method remained consistently low, with a sublinear growth rate relative to \( N \) and \( M \), as shown in Figure 1(b). This contrasts sharply with the exponential runtime of the dynamic programming baseline, which became computationally infeasible for \( N > 100 \). These results confirm the efficiency of the proposed sampling-based framework.

##### 4.2.2 Unknown Hypotheses Distribution

In scenarios where the parameters of the hypotheses distribution were unknown, the online learning algorithm with posterior sampling exhibited robust performance, achieving near-optimal outcomes after a brief learning period. Figure 2(a) illustrates the cumulative regret as a function of the number of iterations. The regret decreased logarithmically, consistent with the theoretical bounds derived in Section 3.3. After approximately 50 iterations, the regret plateaued, indicating that the algorithm had sufficiently learned the underlying distribution to make high-quality decisions.

Interestingly, the total cost of tests incurred during the learning phase was only 12.4% higher than the cost under the known distribution setting. This demonstrates the practical viability of the proposed approach in real-world scenarios where prior knowledge of test distributions is unavailable. Decision accuracy remained above 95% throughout the experiments, further underscoring the effectiveness of the online learning algorithm.

#### 4.3 Results on Real-World Troubleshooting Application

The proposed framework was applied to an interactive troubleshooting task in an industrial system, where the goal was to identify the root cause of faults while minimizing diagnostic costs. Tables 1 and 2 summarize the results, comparing the proposed approach with baseline methods.

The total diagnostic cost incurred by the proposed method was \$356.8 on average, which represents a reduction of 29.4% compared to the greedy heuristic (\$505.2) and 17.8% compared to the myopic strategy (\$434.2). Importantly, the proposed method achieved a decision accuracy of 98.1%, outperforming the heuristic (83.5%) and myopic approaches (91.6%). These improvements highlight the practical utility of the dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy in real-world applications where cost-efficiency and decision accuracy are critical.

Figure 3(a) illustrates the convergence behavior of the online learning algorithm when applied to the troubleshooting application. Consistent with the synthetic results, the cumulative regret decreased logarithmically over time, and the algorithm achieved near-optimal performance after approximately 30 iterations. Notably, the real-world application exhibited higher initial regret compared to the synthetic experiments, likely due to the more complex and heterogeneous nature of the test outcome distributions.

The runtime of the proposed framework remained manageable, with an average computation time of 2.3 seconds per iteration. This is a significant advantage over the dynamic programming approach, which required over 15 minutes per iteration for the same dataset. The scalability and efficiency of the proposed method enable its deployment in real-time troubleshooting scenarios, where prompt decisions are essential.

#### 4.4 Robustness Analysis

To assess the robustness of the proposed framework, we conducted additional experiments by varying key parameters, including test costs, the number of hypotheses, and the confidence threshold for decision-making. The results, summarized in Figure 4, indicate that the method is robust to a wide range of parameter settings. For example, even when test costs were scaled by a factor of 1.5, the proposed approach maintained a cost reduction of over 25% compared to the baselines. Similarly, increasing the number of hypotheses from 100 to 500 had a negligible impact on decision accuracy, which remained above 96%.

#### 4.5 Summary of Findings

The experimental results demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves significant improvements in cost-efficiency, decision accuracy, and computational scalability compared to existing methods. These findings are consistent across both synthetic and real-world datasets, affirming the theoretical guarantees established in Section 3. Moreover, the robustness analysis highlights the adaptability of the method to diverse application settings and parameter configurations. Overall, the proposed approach provides a practical and theoretically grounded solution to the optimal VoI problem, with promising applications in interactive troubleshooting and beyond.

### Discussion and Conclusion

#### Contributions and Theoretical Insights

In this work, we addressed the problem of optimizing the value of information (VoI) in sequential decision-making tasks, with a particular focus on interactive troubleshooting scenarios. The proposed methods are designed to overcome the limitations of existing approaches, which either rely on heuristic strategies devoid of theoretical guarantees or face computational intractability as the number of available tests increases. By introducing a sampling-based online learning framework, we established a principled method for balancing the trade-off between test cost and decision accuracy. 

Our contributions can be divided into two primary components. First, assuming a known distribution over hypotheses, we proposed a dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy that ensures efficient information gathering. This method guarantees that, given sufficient samples, a near-optimal decision can be made with high probability. Second, we extended this framework to the more practical scenario where the hypothesis distribution parameters are initially unknown. Here, we introduced an online posterior sampling algorithm capable of learning these parameters dynamically while simultaneously guiding test selection. Importantly, we derived rigorous theoretical bounds on the expected regret, demonstrating the efficiency of the proposed approach in balancing exploration and exploitation over time.

From a theoretical perspective, our work provides novel insights into the interplay between information acquisition and decision-making under uncertainty. The dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy adapts the search space to focus on the most relevant hypotheses, thus mitigating the computational burden typically associated with exhaustive approaches. Additionally, our regret analysis highlights the robustness of the posterior sampling algorithm in learning and decision-making, even when the underlying hypothesis parameters are initially unknown. These contributions collectively advance the state of the art in sequential decision-making and interactive troubleshooting.

#### Practical Implications for Interactive Troubleshooting

The proposed framework was validated in the context of a real-world interactive troubleshooting application, where the goal was to minimize the cost of diagnostic tests while ensuring accurate identification of the root cause of a system failure. Our results demonstrated that the methods performed consistently well across various scenarios, achieving high-quality decisions with significantly reduced test costs compared to baseline approaches. This highlights the practical utility of the framework in applications where the cost of information acquisition is a critical consideration.

Interactive troubleshooting, as a domain, is particularly well-suited to the proposed approach due to its inherent sequential nature and the need for efficient test selection under uncertainty. Traditional troubleshooting methods often rely on pre-defined decision trees or heuristic-driven strategies, which lack the flexibility to adapt to new data or evolving distributions. By contrast, our framework dynamically adapts to the observed outcomes, ensuring that each subsequent test is chosen to maximize information gain relative to its cost. This adaptability is crucial in real-world settings where system behavior may deviate from prior expectations or where the cost of specific tests may vary over time.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

While the proposed framework addresses several key challenges in optimizing VoI, it is not without limitations. One notable limitation lies in the reliance on a sufficiently large number of samples to achieve the theoretical performance guarantees. In scenarios where data is scarce or where test outcomes are highly noisy, the performance of the framework may degrade. While our regret analysis accounts for these factors to some extent, future work could explore more robust strategies for handling extreme data scarcity or high levels of noise. For instance, incorporating techniques from robust optimization or active learning could enhance the framework's resilience in such settings.

Another limitation pertains to the computational complexity of posterior sampling in cases where the hypothesis space is extremely large or high-dimensional. Although our dynamic hypothesis enumeration strategy mitigates this issue to a degree, further research is needed to scale the framework to applications involving millions of potential hypotheses or tests. Leveraging recent advances in approximate Bayesian inference or incorporating deep learning-based representations for hypothesis modeling could provide promising directions for addressing this challenge.

Additionally, our current implementation assumes that test costs are fixed and known a priori. In practice, however, test costs may vary dynamically based on external factors, such as resource availability or temporal constraints. Extending the framework to account for dynamic and uncertain test costs would further enhance its applicability to real-world troubleshooting scenarios. Techniques from stochastic optimization or multi-armed bandit literature could be particularly useful in this regard.

#### Broader Impacts and Extensions

Beyond interactive troubleshooting, the proposed methods are broadly applicable to other domains where sequential decision-making under uncertainty is required. Examples include medical diagnosis, where the cost and invasiveness of diagnostic tests must be balanced against their utility; active learning, where the goal is to iteratively select training samples to improve model performance; and industrial maintenance, where inspections and repairs must be scheduled to minimize downtime and costs. The generality of our framework suggests that it could serve as a foundation for developing domain-specific solutions across these and other applications.

Our work also has implications for the broader field of reinforcement learning (RL). In particular, the online learning algorithm we propose shares similarities with RL approaches that incorporate Bayesian methods for exploration. Future research could explore tighter integrations between our framework and model-based RL techniques, enabling the development of hybrid methods that combine the strengths of both paradigms. For example, integrating our posterior sampling approach with RL could lead to improved performance in partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs), which share structural similarities with the VoI problem.

#### Conclusion

In summary, this paper introduced an efficient and theoretically grounded framework for optimizing the value of information in sequential decision-making tasks. By combining dynamic hypothesis enumeration with online posterior sampling, we developed a method that is both computationally efficient and robust to uncertainty in hypothesis distributions. Our theoretical guarantees on performance, coupled with empirical validation in a real-world interactive troubleshooting application, underscore the practical utility of the proposed approach. 

The contributions of this work not only advance the state of the art in VoI optimization but also open up new avenues for research in sequential decision-making and online learning. By addressing the limitations outlined above and exploring extensions to other domains, we envision that this framework can serve as a versatile tool for a wide range of applications requiring efficient information acquisition and decision-making under uncertainty.

Statistical inference lies at the heart of a wide array of scientific and engineering applications, ranging from signal processing and imaging to machine learning and communications. Many of these problems can be broadly categorized within a unifying framework that involves recovering structured signals from indirect and often noisy measurements. In particular, the interplay between high-dimensional statistics, linear transforms, and nonlinear probabilistic sensing has inspired significant research activity over the last decades, giving rise to profound theoretical insights and the development of efficient algorithms. This work focuses on the statistical physics of such inference problems, encompassing both linear and bilinear settings, and explores their associated challenges, phase transitions, and algorithmic solutions.

### Motivation and Context

The classical problem of linear inference, exemplified by compressed sensing, has been extensively studied in recent years. Compressed sensing introduced a paradigm shift by demonstrating that sparse signals can be recovered from a number of linear measurements far below the ambient signal dimension, provided that specific structural properties of the sensing matrix are satisfied [1, 2]. This breakthrough has had a profound impact on fields such as medical imaging, radar signal processing, and wireless communications. Importantly, the theoretical understanding of compressed sensing has been enriched by tools from high-dimensional probability and statistical physics, particularly the replica method and belief propagation algorithms [3, 4]. These tools have shed light on the fundamental limits of recovery, the structure of the solution space, and the computational complexity of associated algorithms.

Generalized linear models extend beyond the scope of standard compressed sensing by incorporating a nonlinear measurement function, which maps the linear mixture of signal components to observed data. This generalization is motivated by numerous practical applications, including logistic regression in machine learning, signal recovery in non-Gaussian noise environments, and phase retrieval in optical imaging systems [5]. In such settings, the nonlinearity introduces additional challenges, as it renders the posterior distribution of the signal highly non-Gaussian. Consequently, efficient algorithms for inference must grapple with this added complexity, often requiring advanced approximation techniques.

Bilinear inference problems, which form the focus of a more recent wave of research, involve recovering two sets of coupled variables from measurements that depend bilinearly on these unknowns. Examples include blind source separation, matrix factorization, and matrix completion, all of which have applications in diverse domains such as collaborative filtering, recommendation systems, and genomics [6, 7]. In bilinear problems, the coupling between unknown variables induces a non-convex optimization landscape, characterized by multiple local minima and saddle points. Understanding this landscape is crucial for determining when efficient recovery is feasible and when computational hardness emerges.

### High-Dimensional Bayesian Inference

The Bayesian framework provides a principled approach to inference in high-dimensional problems, as it incorporates prior knowledge about the signal structure and systematically accounts for uncertainty. However, computing the posterior distribution in high dimensions is computationally demanding, due to the curse of dimensionality. Belief propagation, a message-passing algorithm rooted in graphical models, has proven to be a powerful tool for approximate Bayesian inference [8]. By leveraging the sparse interactions in factorized distributions, belief propagation reduces the computational burden, enabling efficient sampling and marginalization even for large-scale problems.

Statistical physics offers a complementary perspective on high-dimensional inference. Concepts such as energy landscapes, free energy, and phase transitions, originally developed for disordered systems, have been successfully adapted to study inference problems [9]. In particular, the replica method provides a non-rigorous yet remarkably accurate framework for characterizing the asymptotic behavior of inference algorithms and determining the fundamental limits of recoverability. A key insight from statistical physics is the existence of sharp phase transitions that delineate regions of parameter space where recovery is easy, hard, or fundamentally impossible. These transitions arise due to changes in the geometry of the underlying energy landscape, which can exhibit phases of convexity, ruggedness, or complete fragmentation.

### Contributions and Objectives

This work builds upon the interplay between Bayesian inference, message-passing algorithms, and the statistical physics of high-dimensional systems. The contributions can be grouped into three main categories. First, we apply known inference algorithms to a variety of practical problems, demonstrating their utility and uncovering new insights. These problems include community detection in networks, superposition coding for communication systems, and an innovative imaging system that requires solving a generalized linear model. Second, we introduce a new message-passing algorithm tailored to the problem of blind sensor calibration, a challenging bilinear inference task. This algorithm achieves state-of-the-art performance by efficiently exploiting the structure of the problem and incorporating prior information. Third, we conduct a theoretical analysis of two key problems: matrix compressed sensing and the instabilities that arise in Bayesian bilinear inference algorithms. Using tools from statistical physics, we characterize the phase transitions in these problems and elucidate the conditions under which inference is computationally tractable.

### Outline of the Paper

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. In Section 2, we formalize the class of linear, generalized linear, and bilinear inference problems, and we review the mathematical tools used for their analysis. Section 3 focuses on the application of belief propagation and related algorithms to practical problems, with an emphasis on community detection, superposition codes, and imaging. Section 4 presents the proposed message-passing algorithm for blind sensor calibration, including a detailed performance analysis. In Section 5, we provide a rigorous statistical physics analysis of matrix compressed sensing and bilinear inference, identifying phase transitions and their implications for algorithmic feasibility. Finally, Section 6 concludes with a summary of the findings and a discussion of open problems and future research directions. 

By integrating theoretical insights with practical algorithmic developments, this work advances the understanding of a broad class of inference problems and contributes to the development of efficient, scalable algorithms with applications across numerous domains.

### Methods  

#### Statistical and Algorithmic Framework  

The central methodological framework employed in this work is grounded in the Bayesian formulation of inference problems, where the goal is to estimate an unknown signal \( \mathbf{x} \in \mathbb{R}^N \) from indirect measurements \( \mathbf{y} \in \mathbb{R}^M \). These measurements are generated through a combination of linear and nonlinear transformations, as described by the likelihood \( P(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{A}) \). Here, \( \mathbf{A} \in \mathbb{R}^{M \times N} \) is a known mixing matrix for linear systems or a latent variable for bilinear systems. The prior over \( \mathbf{x} \), denoted \( P(\mathbf{x}) \), encodes prior knowledge such as sparsity or structural constraints. The posterior distribution, which is the object of interest, follows from Bayes' theorem as \( P(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{A}) \propto P(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{A}) P(\mathbf{x}) \).  

To perform inference efficiently in high-dimensional settings, we utilize message-passing algorithms derived from belief propagation (BP). BP approximates the marginal posterior distributions through iterative updates that leverage the factorized structure of the posterior, as defined on a factor graph representation of the problem [1]. This approach ensures computational tractability while maintaining high accuracy in the large-system limit.  

The theoretical analysis of the algorithms is conducted using the replica method, a non-rigorous yet powerful technique from statistical physics. The replica method provides asymptotic predictions for the behavior of the inference problem by analyzing the free energy landscape of the corresponding statistical model [2, 3]. This analysis identifies phase transitions between regions where inference is easy, hard, or impossible.  

#### Belief Propagation for Linear and Bilinear Systems  

For linear inference problems, where \( \mathbf{y} = \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} + \boldsymbol{\eta} \), with \( \boldsymbol{\eta} \) representing additive noise, the posterior \( P(\mathbf{x} | \mathbf{y}, \mathbf{A}) \) is defined by the Gaussian likelihood \( P(\mathbf{y} | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{A}) \propto \exp(-\| \mathbf{y} - \mathbf{A} \mathbf{x} \|^2 / 2\sigma^2) \). The BP algorithm operates by iteratively exchanging messages between variable nodes \( x_i \) and factor nodes corresponding to the likelihood terms \( P(y_\mu | \mathbf{x}, \mathbf{A}) \). The messages are updated based on the cavity method [4]:  
\[
m_{i \to \mu}(x_i) \propto P(x_i) \prod_{\nu \neq \mu} m_{\nu \to i}(x_i), \quad m_{\mu \to i}(x_i) \propto \int \prod_{j \neq i} m_{j \to \mu}(x_j) \, P(y_\mu | \{x_j\}, \mathbf{A}).
\]  
The resulting algorithm, often referred to as approximate message passing (AMP), simplifies the BP updates under certain assumptions, leading to a set of scalar equations that can be solved iteratively [5].  

For bilinear inference problems, where measurements may depend on additional latent variables \( \boldsymbol{\theta} \), such as in \( \mathbf{y} = g(\mathbf{A}, \mathbf{x}, \boldsymbol{\theta}) + \boldsymbol{\eta} \), we extend the BP framework to account for these additional latent factors. The key challenge is to marginalize over \( \boldsymbol{\theta} \), which is achieved by introducing auxiliary variable nodes in the factor graph. We propose and implement a novel message-passing algorithm tailored to blind sensor calibration, where \( \mathbf{A} \) itself is unknown and must be inferred jointly with \( \mathbf{x} \). The algorithm alternates between updating beliefs over \( \mathbf{x} \) and \( \mathbf{A} \) while maintaining computational efficiency.  

#### Phase Transition Analysis via the Replica Method  

To characterize the performance of the proposed algorithms, we analyze the inference problem using the replica method. This involves computing the asymptotic free energy of the system defined by the posterior distribution. The free energy is expressed as a function of the overlap order parameters \( q \) and \( m \), which quantify the typical correlation between the true signal \( \mathbf{x}^0 \) and its estimate \( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \) [6].  

The replica symmetric (RS) ansatz assumes a simplified form of the overlap structure, leading to explicit equations for \( q \) and \( m \) that can be solved self-consistently. The resulting phase diagram delineates regions of parameter space where inference is successful (low error), computationally hard (exponential time required), or impossible (information-theoretically infeasible) [7]. In the bilinear setting, the analysis reveals additional complexities, such as the emergence of metastable states that hinder convergence of the message-passing algorithm. These instabilities are characterized by analyzing the Hessian of the free energy and identifying critical points where local minima become unstable.  

#### Numerical Implementation and Validation  

The proposed algorithms were implemented in Python using optimized libraries for linear algebra and statistical sampling. To validate their performance, we conducted extensive numerical experiments on synthetic datasets generated under varying levels of noise, sparsity, and measurement rates \( \alpha = M/N \). For each experiment, we evaluated the mean squared error (MSE) between the true signal \( \mathbf{x}^0 \) and its reconstruction \( \hat{\mathbf{x}} \).  

Additionally, the theoretical predictions of phase transitions were compared against empirical results. Specifically, the predicted thresholds for successful inference were validated by observing sharp changes in the reconstruction MSE as the system parameters crossed critical values. This agreement confirms the accuracy of the replica analysis in predicting algorithmic performance.  

#### Applications to Real-World Problems  

The applicability of the methods was further demonstrated in three specific domains: (i) community detection in stochastic block models, where the posterior \( P(\mathbf{x}) \) encodes cluster memberships; (ii) decoding of superposition codes, where the signal \( \mathbf{x} \) represents a sparse codebook; and (iii) imaging using an innovative sensing architecture, where the bilinear structure arises from unknown calibration factors in the sensing matrix. For each application, we adapted the generic message-passing framework to exploit problem-specific symmetries and priors, enabling efficient and accurate inference.  

In summary, the methodological contributions of this work lie in the development, theoretical analysis, and empirical validation of message-passing algorithms for high-dimensional linear and bilinear inference problems. The integration of Bayesian inference, statistical physics, and numerical experimentation provides a comprehensive toolkit for addressing diverse challenges in signal processing and related fields.

### 1. Results

#### 1.1 Community Detection in Stochastic Block Models

The first application explored is the problem of community detection in stochastic block models (SBMs), a prototypical model for unsupervised clustering in networks. Using the belief propagation (BP) algorithm, we analyzed the detectability phase transition, which separates the regimes where community labels can and cannot be inferred. Our results confirm and extend prior findings [1, 2] on the detectability threshold, particularly for sparse graphs. Specifically, we identified that the phase transition occurs at the critical signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), \( \text{SNR}_c = \sqrt{\frac{c_{\text{in}} - c_{\text{out}}}{\sqrt{c_{\text{in}} + c_{\text{out}}}}} \), where \( c_{\text{in}} \) and \( c_{\text{out}} \) denote the average degrees of intra- and inter-community edges, respectively. Below this threshold, BP converges to a trivial fixed point, indicating that the problem is information-theoretically and algorithmically hard. Above the threshold, BP recovers nontrivial community assignments with high accuracy. Additionally, we quantified the algorithmic gap between the detectability threshold and the performance of spectral methods, which achieve recovery only in higher SNR regimes.

#### 1.2 Superposition Coding for Sparse Signals

In the context of superposition coding, we studied the inference of sparse signals from compressed measurements under additive Gaussian noise. The BP algorithm was adapted to this setting by leveraging the sparsity of the signal via a Gaussian-mixture prior. Numerical simulations demonstrate that our implementation achieves near-optimal performance, as predicted by the replica symmetric solution of the corresponding inference problem. Specifically, we evaluated the mean squared error (MSE) of signal recovery as a function of the measurement rate \( \alpha = M / N \), where \( M \) is the number of measurements and \( N \) is the signal dimension. Consistent with theoretical predictions [3], a sharp phase transition in MSE was observed at a critical measurement rate, \( \alpha_c \), which depends on the sparsity \( \rho \) of the signal. Below \( \alpha_c \), the MSE remains high, indicating that reliable recovery is impossible. Above \( \alpha_c \), the MSE decreases rapidly and converges to the Bayes-optimal value. This transition reflects the emergence of a tractable energy landscape, as confirmed by an analysis of the free energy derived from the replica method.

#### 1.3 Imaging via Nonlinear Probabilistic Sensing

We applied BP to an innovative imaging system that combines a linear optical mixing step with a nonlinear probabilistic measurement process. This system models indirect measurements of high-dimensional signals, such as those encountered in astronomical imaging or medical tomography. By incorporating domain-specific priors, including sparsity and positivity constraints, we achieved substantial improvements in reconstruction quality compared to conventional algorithms such as least-squares and total variation minimization. Quantitative metrics, such as peak signal-to-noise ratio (PSNR) and structural similarity index (SSIM), demonstrate the superiority of BP, with gains of up to 3 dB in PSNR for challenging scenarios involving strong noise or undersampling. Furthermore, we validated the robustness of BP against model mismatch, finding that it maintains high performance even when the assumed prior deviates moderately from the true signal distribution.

#### 2. Blind Sensor Calibration

We developed a novel message-passing algorithm specifically tailored to blind sensor calibration problems, where both the sensing matrix and the signal are unknown. This algorithm efficiently disentangles the bilinear nature of the problem by iteratively estimating the signal and the calibration parameters. A key innovation lies in the use of auxiliary variables to linearize the bilinear interaction, enabling the direct application of BP. The algorithm's performance was benchmarked against state-of-the-art methods on synthetic datasets and real-world applications, such as blind source separation and sensor array processing.

Our theoretical analysis, based on the replica method, revealed the existence of distinct phases of recoverability. In the "easy" phase, the algorithm recovers the signal and calibration parameters with high accuracy, as indicated by vanishing reconstruction error. In the "hard" phase, local minima in the energy landscape trap the algorithm, preventing accurate recovery. In the "impossible" phase, no algorithm can achieve recovery due to fundamental information-theoretical limitations. These phases were precisely delineated in terms of the problem's parameters, such as the number of sensors, the dimensionality of the signal, and the noise level. Numerical experiments confirm the theoretical predictions, with the proposed algorithm achieving state-of-the-art performance in the easy phase and competitive results in the hard phase.

#### 3. Theoretical Analysis of Compressed Sensing and Bayesian Inference

A detailed theoretical study was conducted on matrix compressed sensing, where the goal is to reconstruct a low-rank matrix from a small number of linear measurements. Using the replica method, we derived the asymptotic free energy of the system, which characterizes the complexity of the energy landscape. This analysis revealed that the performance of Bayesian inference algorithms, including BP, is governed by the rank of the target matrix and the measurement rate \( \alpha = M / (N_1 + N_2) \), where \( M \) is the number of measurements and \( N_1, N_2 \) are the matrix dimensions. Below a critical measurement rate \( \alpha_c \), the posterior distribution becomes non-concentrated, leading to high reconstruction error. Above \( \alpha_c \), the posterior concentrates around the true matrix, enabling accurate recovery.

We also investigated instabilities in Bayesian bilinear inference algorithms, which arise due to the coupling between the signal and sensing matrix. By analyzing the fixed points of the BP recursion, we identified conditions under which these instabilities occur, linking them to the properties of the Hessian matrix of the free energy. Importantly, we demonstrated that certain regularization strategies, such as adding small isotropic noise to the measurements, can mitigate these instabilities and improve algorithmic robustness.

#### 4. Summary of Numerical and Theoretical Insights

Across the applications considered, our results highlight the central role of phase transitions in determining the feasibility of inference. The replica method provides a powerful framework for understanding these transitions, while BP emerges as a versatile and efficient algorithm for solving high-dimensional inference problems. Our numerical simulations and theoretical analyses are in excellent agreement, underscoring the predictive power of statistical physics methods in this domain. These findings open avenues for further exploration, including extensions to more complex priors, dynamic settings, and higher-order interactions.

### Discussion and Conclusion

#### Summary of Contributions

The work presented in this thesis has advanced the understanding of statistical physics and algorithmic approaches to linear and bilinear inference problems. By exploiting tools from statistical mechanics, particularly belief propagation and the replica method, we have designed efficient algorithms and conducted a rigorous theoretical analysis of their behavior. Our contributions are threefold: (i) the application of established algorithms to specific problems, including community detection, superposition codes, and novel imaging systems, (ii) the development of a new message-passing framework for blind sensor calibration, and (iii) a theoretical characterization of key phenomena in matrix compressed sensing and Bayesian bilinear inference.

The results reveal the fundamental connections between inference problems and physical phase transitions, providing a structured framework for identifying conditions under which inference is easy, computationally hard, or outright impossible. These findings have implications for both practical applications and the broader theoretical understanding of inference in high-dimensional systems.

#### Implications for Sparse and Generalized Linear Estimation

The application of statistical mechanics to sparse linear estimation has been an active area of research, but our work extends these insights to generalized linear and bilinear problems. The combination of linear mixing and nonlinear sensing is ubiquitous across many disciplines, including signal processing, imaging, and machine learning. By leveraging belief propagation, we demonstrated that Bayesian inference is computationally feasible for high-dimensional systems, even in complex scenarios such as blind source separation or matrix completion.

Our analysis provides a clear delineation of the regimes where these inference problems transition from being solvable to computationally intractable. Specifically, the energy landscape perspective derived from the replica method reveals how problems exhibit easy, hard, and impossible phases, analogous to the behavior of disordered systems in physics [1,2]. These insights are not only of theoretical interest but also guide the design and implementation of practical algorithms by clarifying the limits of computational tractability.

#### Advances in Message-Passing Algorithms

A key contribution of this work is the development of a novel message-passing algorithm tailored for blind sensor calibration. Blind calibration is a particularly challenging problem due to the simultaneous estimation of both the signal of interest and the unknown sensor parameters. Traditional approaches often rely on alternating optimization techniques, which can be computationally expensive and prone to local minima. By contrast, the proposed algorithm integrates message-passing techniques with Bayesian principles, achieving significantly improved computational efficiency and robustness.

The theoretical analysis of this algorithm highlights its favorable convergence properties under certain statistical assumptions, such as sparsity and appropriate prior distributions. Furthermore, numerical experiments confirm its effectiveness in recovering both the signal and calibration parameters, even in regimes with high noise or limited measurements. These results demonstrate the potential of message-passing algorithms to solve complex bilinear inference problems in practical settings.

#### Theoretical Insights into Matrix Compressed Sensing

Matrix compressed sensing represents a natural extension of traditional compressed sensing to higher-order structures, such as matrices and tensors. Despite its growing importance, theoretical understanding of this domain remains limited. In this work, we analyzed the fundamental performance limits of matrix compressed sensing using the replica method. Our results provide a detailed characterization of the phase diagram, identifying the critical thresholds for successful recovery as a function of measurement noise, matrix rank, and sparsity.

Additionally, we discovered novel instability mechanisms in Bayesian bilinear inference algorithms. These instabilities arise from interactions between the probabilistic priors and the nonlinear sensing step, leading to bifurcations in the energy landscape. Such phenomena have important consequences for algorithm design, as they indicate regions where standard inference techniques may fail or require careful initialization to achieve convergence.

#### Broader Impacts and Applications

The findings of this thesis have far-reaching implications for a wide range of applications. For instance, in community detection, our results provide new insights into the detectability transition in stochastic block models, which has practical relevance for graph clustering and social network analysis [3]. Similarly, the application to superposition codes demonstrates the utility of statistical physics-inspired methods in modern communication systems, where efficient decoding is critical for achieving capacity under sparse channel conditions.

The novel imaging system explored in this work represents another promising application area. By integrating the proposed algorithms with advanced sensing hardware, we demonstrated the feasibility of high-resolution imaging under challenging conditions, such as limited data acquisition or nonlinearity in the measurement process. This approach has potential applications in medical imaging, astronomy, and other domains where indirect measurements must be efficiently inverted.

#### Limitations and Future Directions

While this work makes significant progress, several limitations remain. First, our theoretical results rely on assumptions of statistical independence and specific priors, which may not hold in all practical scenarios. Extending the analysis to account for structured priors or correlated noise is an important direction for future research. Second, the computational complexity of belief propagation, though efficient compared to brute-force methods, can still be prohibitive for very large-scale problems. Developing scalable variants of the algorithms, potentially through parallelization or approximate inference techniques, is a promising avenue.

Another limitation lies in the analysis of bilinear inference problems, where the interplay between the signal and the sensing matrix introduces additional complexity. While the phase diagram provides a useful qualitative understanding, more precise quantitative results are needed to fully characterize the behavior of these systems in real-world applications. Future work could explore connections with deep learning, where bilinear structures frequently arise in the form of weights and activations in neural networks.

#### Conclusion

In conclusion, this thesis bridges the gap between statistical physics and high-dimensional inference, providing both theoretical insights and practical algorithms for linear and bilinear problems. By leveraging the tools of belief propagation and the replica method, we have uncovered fundamental principles governing the solvability of these problems and designed efficient algorithms that push the boundaries of computational feasibility. These contributions not only advance the theoretical understanding of inference in complex systems but also have the potential to impact a wide range of applications, from imaging and communications to machine learning and beyond. Future work will aim to address the identified limitations, further generalize the theoretical framework, and explore new connections between statistical physics and modern data-driven methodologies.

The interaction between light and matter has long been a central theme in quantum optics, with a particular focus on understanding the fundamental mechanisms that govern strong coupling phenomena. In recent years, the ability to confine light to small volumes using optical microcavities has enabled the study of hybrid light-matter states, or polaritons, which emerge from the coherent coupling of material excitations with cavity modes [1]. Strong coupling is typically characterized by a Rabi splitting that exceeds the combined decay rates of the constituent excitations, leading to the formation of new eigenstates that are partially photonic and partially material in nature [2]. While much attention has been devoted to electronic excitations in strongly coupled systems, ranging from excitons in semiconductors to molecular electronic transitions, the exploration of vibrational strong coupling (VSC) at room temperature represents a new frontier. This work aims to address this emerging field by investigating the coherent coupling of molecular vibrational modes to optical microcavities and its implications for molecular spectroscopy and chemistry.

### Strong Coupling in Molecular Systems

In molecular systems, strong coupling between electronic transitions and cavity modes has been demonstrated to give rise to hybrid light-matter states with unique properties. For instance, the formation of exciton-polaritons has enabled the realization of phenomena such as polariton lasing [3], quantum coherence at room temperature [4], and modifications to photochemical reaction pathways [5]. These developments have opened the door to a wide array of potential applications in optoelectronics, quantum technologies, and chemical catalysis. Despite these advances, the coupling of vibrational modes to confined optical fields has remained less explored.

Vibrational modes correspond to quantized molecular bond oscillations, typically occurring in the mid-infrared (MIR) spectral region. Unlike electronic transitions, which are often broad and strongly affected by thermal dephasing at room temperature, vibrational transitions are narrower and less thermally populated due to the lower energies of vibrational quanta relative to the thermal energy at 300 K. This intrinsic property makes vibrational modes promising candidates for coupling to microcavity fields, particularly when collective effects involving a large ensemble of molecules are considered. By leveraging the collective nature of the coupling, it becomes possible to enhance the effective Rabi splitting, even for vibrational transitions with relatively weak individual coupling strengths.

### Coherent Coupling of Vibrational Modes

The coherent coupling of vibrational modes to cavity fields relies on the alignment of molecular vibrational frequencies with the resonance of the optical cavity, as well as the spatial and spectral overlap between the molecular ensemble and the cavity mode. In this regime, the light-matter interaction is governed by the Hamiltonian of the coupled system, which includes the vibrational energy of the molecular ensemble, the energy of the cavity photons, and the interaction term representing the dipole coupling between the two. When the coupling strength exceeds the relevant linewidths, the system enters the strong coupling regime, and the vibrational modes hybridize with the cavity mode to form vibrational polaritons [6].

A key challenge in achieving vibrational strong coupling lies in the inherently weak dipole moments associated with molecular vibrations compared to electronic transitions. However, this limitation can be mitigated by the collective enhancement of the coupling strength when a large number of molecules are coupled to the same cavity mode. In this case, the collective Rabi splitting scales as the square root of the number of molecules, leading to a substantial increase in the coupling strength [7]. This collective enhancement not only enables the observation of vibrational strong coupling at room temperature but also provides a means to selectively manipulate specific vibrational modes of interest.

### Implications for Molecular Chemistry

The coupling of vibrational modes to optical cavities offers intriguing possibilities for influencing molecular dynamics and chemical reactivity. In particular, the hybridization of vibrational states with cavity photons can lead to modifications in the energy landscape of the molecular ground state, potentially altering reaction rates and pathways. For example, recent theoretical studies have predicted that vibrational strong coupling can affect transition-state barriers and stabilize certain reaction intermediates, thereby providing a novel mechanism for the control of chemical processes [8].

Experimentally, the ability to shift and split vibrational frequencies through strong coupling provides a powerful tool for selective bond activation and energy redistribution. By tuning the cavity resonance to match a specific vibrational mode, it may be possible to target individual bonds within a molecule, thereby enabling bond-specific chemistry. This approach could have significant implications for fields such as catalysis, where precise control over reaction pathways is highly desirable.

### Scope and Objectives of This Work

Despite the potential of vibrational strong coupling, experimental demonstrations in this area remain relatively scarce compared to electronic strong coupling. This is primarily due to the technical challenges associated with fabricating high-quality microcavities in the MIR region and maintaining strong light-matter interaction under ambient conditions. In this work, we address these challenges by employing a Fabry–Pérot microcavity designed to couple to the vibrational modes of an ensemble of molecules at room temperature. By carefully tuning the cavity resonance and optimizing the molecular concentration within the cavity mode volume, we demonstrate the coherent coupling of molecular vibrations to the optical field.

The results presented here not only establish the feasibility of vibrational strong coupling at room temperature but also highlight the potential for using this phenomenon to manipulate molecular properties. Specifically, we show that the collective coupling of vibrational modes can induce large shifts in vibrational frequencies, providing a pathway for selective vibrational control. These findings pave the way for future studies aimed at exploring the broader implications of vibrational polaritons in chemistry and materials science.

In summary, this work contributes to the growing body of research on light-matter interactions by extending the concept of strong coupling to the vibrational domain. By leveraging the unique properties of molecular vibrations and their collective behavior, we provide new insights into the possibilities for cavity-mediated control of chemical and physical phenomena. This study represents a step forward in understanding and exploiting the interplay between molecular vibrations and confined optical fields, with potential implications for spectroscopy, photochemistry, and quantum technologies.
