To address these knowledge gaps, the present study investigates the interplay between water systems, diet composition, and GIT microbiota in rainbow trout. Specifically, it examines the effects of balanced and unbalanced alternative protein diets on fish performance and GIT bacterial communities under recirculating and flow-through water systems. The use of balanced diets, supplemented with crystalline amino acids such as lysine, methionine, and threonine, is hypothesized to improve nutrient utilization and growth performance compared to unbalanced diets. Furthermore, the study evaluates whether rearing water serves as a primary source of microbial colonization in the GIT and how this varies between luminal and mucosal compartments. By employing 16S rRNA gene sequencing, the study characterizes the bacterial diversity and composition in both luminal and mucosal samples from the GIT, as well as in the rearing water.

The experimental design incorporates a two-phase feeding trial to further elucidate the effects of water systems and diet on fish performance and microbiota. In the first phase, fish were reared exclusively in either a recirculating or flow-through system and fed one of four experimental diets. In the second phase, fish were transferred between systems to assess the adaptability of their GIT microbiota to a new water environment while continuing on the same diet. This approach provides a unique opportunity to disentangle the effects of diet, water system, and their interaction on GIT microbial dynamics and fish performance. The findings from this study aim to advance our understanding of how environmental and dietary factors shape microbial communities in aquaculture systems, with implications for improving fish health, feed efficiency, and sustainable production practices.

In summary, this study explores the hypothesis that the water system is a controlling variable in modulating the diversity and function of the GIT microbiota in rainbow trout, with significant implications for fish performance. By integrating dietary and environmental factors, it seeks to elucidate the mechanisms by which water systems influence microbial colonization and function in the GIT, thereby contributing to the development of optimized feeding strategies and rearing practices for sustainable aquaculture.

The study was conducted using a two-phase feeding trial to evaluate the effects of diet quality and rearing water systems on the growth performance and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) bacterial composition of rainbow trout (*Oncorhynchus mykiss*). The experimental protocol consisted of two alternative protein diets fed under two distinct water systems (recirculating (RR) and flow-through (FF)) with a crossover design implemented for the second phase.

Rainbow trout with an initial mean weight of 12.02 ± 0.61 g were obtained from a commercial hatchery and acclimated to the experimental facilities for two weeks prior to the start of the experiment. Fish were sorted and stocked at a density of 30 fish per tank into 48 experimental tanks, with 12 replicate tanks per dietary treatment. Each tank had a volume of 200 L and was supplied with either recirculating or flow-through water based on the assigned rearing system. Water temperature was maintained at 15 ± 1°C with dissolved oxygen levels above 7 mg/L throughout the experimental period.

The two alternative protein diets were formulated to contain 38% digestible protein and 20% fat. One diet was based on animal protein as the primary protein source, and the other was based on plant protein. Each diet was further subdivided into two formulations: one balanced with crystalline amino acids (lysine, methionine, and threonine) to meet the essential amino acid requirements of rainbow trout, and one unbalanced to serve as a suboptimal control. The feeds were produced as sinking pellets using a cold extrusion method and stored under vacuum-sealed conditions until use. Feed intake was monitored, and fish were hand-fed to apparent satiation three times daily.

Phase 1 of the study lasted for 8 weeks, during which fish in each tank were maintained in their assigned water system and fed one of the four dietary treatments. At the end of Phase 1, fish from each tank were randomly split into two groups. One group was transferred to a new tank with the opposing water system (i.e., fish from RR were moved to FF and vice versa), while the other group remained in their original tank and system. Both groups continued to receive their assigned diets for an additional 8 weeks during Phase 2 of the study, bringing the total duration of the experiment to 16 weeks.

At the end of the trial, three fish per tank were randomly selected for sampling. Fish were euthanized with an overdose of tricaine methanesulfonate (MS-222) buffered with sodium bicarbonate (at a concentration of 200 mg/L), and body weight, length, and body indexes (hepatosomatic index (HSI) and viscerosomatic index (VSI)) were recorded. Whole-body proximate composition was determined by standard analytical methods. Crude protein was measured using the Kjeldahl method, crude fat by ether extraction, and moisture by drying at 105°C to constant weight. Gross energy content was analyzed using a bomb calorimeter.

For microbiota analysis, both luminal and mucosal samples were collected from the anterior intestine. Luminal samples were obtained by gently flushing the intestinal contents with sterile phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), while mucosal samples were collected by scraping the intestinal mucosa with sterile scalpel blades. Samples were immediately frozen on dry ice and stored at −80°C until DNA extraction. In addition, 500 mL of water was collected from each tank at the time of sampling for analysis of the bacterial community composition in the rearing water. Feed samples from each dietary treatment were also collected to assess the microbial composition of the feed.

Total genomic DNA was extracted from luminal, mucosal, water, and feed samples using a commercial DNA extraction kit (e.g., Qiagen DNeasy PowerSoil Kit) following the manufacturer’s protocol with minor modifications to enhance yield and quality. The concentration and purity of extracted DNA were assessed using a NanoDrop spectrophotometer and agarose gel electrophoresis. The V4 region of the 16S rRNA gene was amplified using universal primers (e.g., 515F and 806R) with Illumina adapter overhangs. PCR amplification was performed in triplicate for each sample to minimize amplification bias. Amplicons were pooled, purified using AMPure XP beads, and quantified using a Qubit fluorometer. Sequencing libraries were prepared and sequenced on an Illumina MiSeq platform with a 2 × 250 bp paired-end configuration.

Raw sequencing data were processed using the QIIME2 pipeline. Reads were quality-filtered, trimmed, and denoised, and operational taxonomic units (OTUs) were assigned based on 97% sequence similarity using the SILVA database as the reference. Alpha diversity metrics, including Shannon and Simpson indices, were calculated to assess within-sample diversity, while beta diversity was evaluated using Bray-Curtis dissimilarity and visualized through non-metric multidimensional scaling (NMDS). Statistical analyses of microbial community composition were conducted using analysis of similarity (ANOSIM) and permutational multivariate analysis of variance (PERMANOVA).

Growth performance and body composition data were analyzed using a two-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) to evaluate the effects of diet, rearing system, and their interactions. Microbial composition data were analyzed using multivariate techniques, with tank serving as the experimental unit. All statistical analyses were performed using R software, with significance set at P < 0.05.

Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the institutional animal care and use committee, and all procedures were conducted in accordance with relevant guidelines for the care and use of aquatic animals in research.

The results of this study highlight the complex interplay between diet composition, water system type, and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) bacterial diversity in rainbow trout. Key findings are presented below, focusing on fish performance metrics, bacterial community composition, and the influence of rearing water.

Fish performance was significantly influenced by diet, diet quality, and water system. Fish weight was affected by all three factors, showing significant differences based on diet (P = 0.0008), diet quality (P = 0.0030), and water system (P < 0.0010). Fish fed balanced diets exhibited higher growth rates compared to those fed unbalanced diets, regardless of the specific source of dietary protein. Similarly, fish reared in the flow-through (FF) system performed better in terms of growth than those reared in the recirculating (RR) system. Body fat content was also significantly impacted by diet (P = 0.0008), diet quality (P = 0.0041), and water system (P = 0.0177). Fish fed balanced diets and those in the FF system exhibited higher body fat percentages compared to their counterparts. Feed intake, however, was primarily influenced by the water system (P = 0.0008), with fish in the FF system consuming more feed than those in the RR system. Body energy content followed a similar trend, being significantly higher in fish from the FF system (P < 0.0010). Despite these differences in weight, fat, and energy, body indexes (e.g., hepatosomatic and viscerosomatic indexes) were not significantly affected by dietary treatment or water system, suggesting that systemic physiological changes were not observed under these conditions.

The bacterial community composition within the GIT exhibited substantial variability based on both sample location (luminal versus mucosal) and rearing system. Compositional dissimilarities were evident between samples from the rearing water and the different GIT locations. Statistical analyses using ANOSIM (R = 0.29, P = 0.0010) and PERMANOVA (R = 0.39, P = 0.0010) confirmed significant differences between these groups, underscoring the importance of rearing water as a potential environmental determinant of GIT microbiota. However, no significant differences were observed in the bacterial composition of dietary samples (ANOSIM: R = 0.004, P = 0.3140; PERMANOVA: R = 0.008, P = 0.4540), suggesting that diet itself did not serve as a primary source of microbial colonization.

Taxonomic analysis revealed that the GIT microbiota was dominated by three major bacterial phyla: Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes. These phyla were consistently present across all treatments, although their relative abundances varied depending on both sample location and water system. Luminal samples exhibited greater compositional dissimilarity compared to mucosal samples (ANOSIM: R = 0.40, P = 0.0010; PERMANOVA: R = 0.56, P = 0.0010), indicating a more dynamic and variable microbial community in the GIT lumen. In contrast, mucosal-associated bacterial communities were more stable, with lower levels of variability (ANOSIM: R = 0.37, P = 0.0010; PERMANOVA: R = 0.41, P = 0.0010). This suggests that the mucosal microbiota might play a more specialized role in host-microbe interactions, potentially linked to nutrient absorption and immune modulation.

Further investigation into the functional potential of the bacterial communities revealed distinct metabolic profiles between mucosal and luminal samples. Bacteria associated with carbohydrate metabolism and certain amino acid pathways were predominantly observed in mucosal samples, indicating their putative role in processing dietary components at the interface of the host and microbiota. In contrast, luminal samples were characterized by a higher abundance of bacteria linked to general nutrient degradation, reflecting the transient and variable nature of the lumen environment.

Rearing water was identified as a significant factor mediating bacterial colonization of the GIT. Aeromonas and Acinetobacter, two genera commonly associated with aquatic environments, were more prevalent in fish reared in the RR system compared to the FF system. These genera were also frequently detected in rearing water samples, supporting the hypothesis that water serves as a primary route for the introduction of these bacteria into the GIT. The higher prevalence of these genera in the RR system may be due to differences in water treatment and microbial load between the two systems. The FF system, characterized by continuous water exchange, likely limited the buildup of these bacteria, whereas the RR system, with its recirculated water, provided a more stable environment for their proliferation and subsequent colonization of the fish.

In summary, this study demonstrates that water system type acts as a controlling variable modulating both fish performance and GIT bacterial diversity in rainbow trout. The FF system was associated with improved growth and energy deposition, likely due to its influence on feed intake and microbiota composition. The GIT microbiota was shaped by both environmental factors (e.g., rearing water) and host-associated factors (e.g., mucosal versus luminal location), with significant implications for fish health and nutrient utilization. These findings underscore the importance of considering water system design and management in aquaculture to optimize fish performance and promote a beneficial microbial environment.

The findings of this study underscore the intricate relationship between rearing water systems, dietary composition, and gastrointestinal tract (GIT) microbiota in rainbow trout. The results clearly indicate that the water system is a key modulating factor influencing bacterial diversity in the GIT, as well as fish performance metrics such as body weight, feed intake, and body fat content. These findings have important implications for aquaculture practices, particularly in optimizing water systems and dietary formulations to improve fish health and productivity.

The significant effects of the water system on fish weight, feed intake, and body energy highlight the critical role of environmental conditions in shaping fish growth and metabolism. The recirculating (RR) and flow-through (FF) systems provide distinct environmental conditions, including differences in water exchange rates, microbial communities in the water, and the accumulation of metabolic waste. These factors likely explain the observed variations in fish performance. Specifically, the RR system may promote a more stable environment that supports efficient nutrient utilization and growth, as evidenced by the higher body energy levels and feed intake in fish reared in this system. Conversely, the FF system, with its continuous water exchange, may have different microbial dynamics that could influence nutrient availability and energy metabolism. These findings highlight the need to consider rearing system design when developing feeding strategies and management practices for rainbow trout.

The diet also played a significant role in modulating fish performance. The use of balanced and unbalanced alternative protein diets showed clear effects on weight gain and body fat content, demonstrating the importance of dietary amino acid balance in fish nutrition. The supplementation of crystalline amino acids, such as lysine, methionine, and threonine, likely contributed to improved protein utilization and growth in fish fed balanced diets. This supports previous findings that amino acid supplementation can effectively enhance the nutritional quality of alternative protein diets, allowing for the partial replacement of fishmeal with animal or plant protein sources. However, the lack of significant effects of diet and water system on body indexes suggests that other factors, such as genetic variation or initial fish size, may also contribute to these parameters.

The compositional differences in bacterial communities between the rearing water and the GIT, as well as between the luminal and mucosal compartments of the intestine, underscore the complex interactions between the external environment and the host's internal microbiota. The rearing water appeared to be a major source of colonization for certain bacterial genera, such as *Aeromonas* and *Acinetobacter*, which were prevalent in the GIT. These genera are known for their metabolic versatility and ability to thrive in aquatic environments, suggesting that waterborne bacteria play a critical role in shaping the GIT microbiome of rainbow trout. This finding is consistent with previous studies that have identified water as a key reservoir of microbial diversity in fish.

The higher dissimilarity observed in luminal bacterial communities compared to mucosal communities suggests that luminal microbiota may be more influenced by external factors, such as diet and waterborne microbial populations, while mucosal communities are likely more stable and host-associated. The predominance of bacteria from the phyla Proteobacteria, Firmicutes, and Bacteroidetes in both luminal and mucosal samples highlights their importance in the rainbow trout GIT. These phyla are well-known for their roles in nutrient metabolism, including carbohydrate and amino acid degradation, which are essential for fish health and growth. The observation of bacteria associated with carbohydrate and amino acid metabolism in the mucosal intestine further supports the hypothesis that the mucosal microbiota plays a critical role in nutrient absorption and host metabolism.

Interestingly, the dietary treatments did not significantly influence the overall bacterial composition in the GIT. This suggests that the water system exerts a stronger influence on microbial communities than diet, at least within the context of this study. However, subtle changes in microbial composition or functional potential that were not detected at the community level may still have implications for fish health and performance. Future studies employing metagenomic or transcriptomic approaches could provide deeper insights into the functional roles of specific microbial taxa and their interactions with the host.

The significant compositional dissimilarities between rearing water and GIT samples, as evidenced by ANOSIM and PERMANOVA analyses, highlight the selective pressures exerted by the fish intestine on microbial colonization. While waterborne microbes serve as an initial source of colonization, only certain taxa are likely able to persist and establish within the GIT. Understanding these selective pressures and identifying key microbial taxa that contribute to fish health could inform strategies for microbiome manipulation, such as the use of probiotics or prebiotics in aquaculture.

Overall, this study demonstrates that the water system is a critical variable modulating both fish performance and GIT microbiota in rainbow trout. By influencing microbial colonization and nutrient availability, the water system has a profound impact on the health and productivity of farmed fish. These findings emphasize the need for holistic approaches to aquaculture management that integrate water quality, microbial dynamics, and dietary strategies to optimize fish performance and sustainability.

In conclusion, this study provides new insights into the interactions between water systems, diet, and GIT microbiota in rainbow trout. The results highlight the importance of considering water system design and dietary formulations in aquaculture to promote optimal fish growth and health. Future research should focus on elucidating the functional roles of specific microbial taxa in the fish GIT and exploring strategies to enhance beneficial microbial communities through targeted interventions. By advancing our understanding of these complex interactions, we can develop more sustainable and efficient aquaculture practices that meet the growing demand for high-quality fish products.

Schizophrenia is a chronic and debilitating mental health disorder that significantly impacts individuals’ functioning and quality of life. Characterized by a combination of positive symptoms such as hallucinations and delusions, negative symptoms including social withdrawal and lack of motivation, and general psychopathology symptoms like anxiety and depression, schizophrenia requires long-term management and care. This disorder not only imposes a substantial burden on patients and their families but also generates significant economic costs for healthcare systems globally. Consequently, understanding the impact of schizophrenia on patients’ health-related quality of life (HRQoL) is crucial for informing clinical decision-making and resource allocation.

Health utility scores, which quantify individuals’ preferences for different health states, are essential for conducting cost–utility analyses—a common type of economic evaluation used to assess healthcare interventions. These scores are typically derived from generic, preference-based measures of HRQoL, such as the five-level EuroQol five-dimensional (EQ-5D-5L) instrument and the Short Form six-dimensional (SF-6D) instrument. Both tools are widely used to generate quality-adjusted life years (QALYs), a standard metric for evaluating the cost-effectiveness of medical treatments. The EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments are particularly valuable because they provide utility scores on a single index scale, enabling comparisons across different diseases and interventions.

Despite their utility, direct collection of EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D data is not always feasible in clinical or research settings due to time, cost, or logistical constraints. In such cases, mapping—also referred to as cross-walking—offers a viable alternative. Mapping involves using statistical models to estimate utility scores based on other commonly collected clinical or disease-specific measures. This approach is especially relevant in the context of schizophrenia, where disease-specific instruments such as the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) are routinely used to assess symptom severity.

The PANSS is a clinician-administered tool designed to evaluate the severity of positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms in individuals with schizophrenia. Given its widespread use in both clinical practice and research, the PANSS provides a rich source of data that can potentially be leveraged to estimate utility scores. However, there is limited evidence on how PANSS scores can be mapped onto generic utility instruments like the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D. Furthermore, existing studies on this topic have predominantly been conducted in Western populations, leaving a significant gap in understanding how these mapping algorithms perform in non-Western contexts such as Asia.

Singapore, a multicultural city-state in Southeast Asia, provides a unique setting for studying the relationship between schizophrenia symptoms and HRQoL. The country’s healthcare system is characterized by a mix of public and private funding, and there is growing interest in conducting cost–utility analyses to guide resource allocation. However, the availability of utility data for individuals with schizophrenia remains limited. Developing reliable mapping algorithms for this population would not only address this gap but also support the broader application of economic evaluations in mental health care.

The current study aims to address these gaps by mapping PANSS scores onto EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores in a sample of patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder in Singapore. Specifically, we sought to develop and validate statistical models for predicting utility scores based on PANSS subscales and patient demographics, such as age and gender. To ensure the robustness of our findings, we employed three different regression methods—ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations, and Tobit regression—and evaluated multiple model specifications.

By providing a practical method for estimating utility scores from PANSS data, this study has the potential to benefit both clinicians and researchers. For clinicians, the mapping algorithms can serve as a tool for assessing the broader impact of schizophrenia symptoms on patients’ HRQoL, facilitating more informed treatment decisions. For researchers, the ability to estimate utility scores in the absence of direct EQ-5D-5L or SF-6D data can enhance the feasibility of conducting cost–utility analyses, ultimately supporting evidence-based policy-making in mental health care.

In this paper, we present the results of our mapping study, highlighting the best-performing models for predicting EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores. We also discuss the implications of our findings for clinical practice and research, as well as the challenges and limitations associated with mapping approaches. By bridging the gap between disease-specific and generic HRQoL measures, this study contributes to the growing body of evidence on the economic evaluation of mental health interventions and underscores the importance of integrating HRQoL considerations into the care of individuals with schizophrenia.

This study focused on developing mapping algorithms to predict utility scores derived from the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments using the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder. The study was conducted in a tertiary psychiatric hospital in Singapore, and the methodology is described in detail below.

### Study Design and Participants

A cross-sectional design was employed, and participants were recruited from adult inpatients and outpatients diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorders according to the Diagnostic and Statistical Manual of Mental Disorders, 5th edition (DSM-5). Inclusion criteria included being between 18 and 65 years of age, having a confirmed diagnosis of schizophrenia spectrum disorder, and being able to provide informed consent. Patients with severe cognitive impairments or comorbid neurological disorders that could interfere with their ability to complete study assessments were excluded.

A total of 239 participants were recruited for this study. Sociodemographic and clinical data, including age, gender, and illness duration, were collected. The PANSS was administered to assess symptom severity, while utility scores were obtained using the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments. Ethical approval for the study was obtained from the relevant institutional review board, and all participants provided written informed consent before participation.

### Instruments and Measures

#### Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS)
The PANSS is a clinician-rated instrument used to evaluate the severity of schizophrenia symptoms. It consists of 30 items grouped into three subscales: positive symptoms (7 items), negative symptoms (7 items), and general psychopathology (16 items). Each item is rated on a scale from 1 (absent) to 7 (extreme), with higher scores indicating greater symptom severity. For this study, the PANSS subscales were further divided into five factors based on prior literature: positive symptoms, negative symptoms, excitement, depression, and cognitive symptoms.

#### EQ-5D-5L
The EQ-5D-5L is a preference-based measure of health-related quality of life (HRQoL) developed by the EuroQol Group. It assesses five dimensions of health (mobility, self-care, usual activities, pain/discomfort, and anxiety/depression), each rated on five levels of severity. Utility scores were derived using the Singapore-specific value set, which ranges from -0.769 to 1, with higher scores indicating better health-related quality of life.

#### SF-6D
The SF-6D is another preference-based HRQoL instrument derived from the Short Form-36 Health Survey (SF-36). It consists of six dimensions (physical functioning, role limitations, social functioning, pain, mental health, and vitality), each with 4–6 response levels. Utility scores range from 0.296 to 1, with higher scores indicating better HRQoL. In this study, the SF-6D utility scores were calculated based on an algorithm developed for the Singapore population.

### Statistical Analysis

#### Mapping Approach
The primary objective of this study was to develop mapping algorithms to predict EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores from PANSS scores. Three regression methods were used to model the relationship between PANSS subscales and utility scores: ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations (CLAD), and Tobit regression. These methods were chosen to account for the properties of utility data, which are often bounded and skewed.

#### Model Specifications
Six model specifications were tested for each regression method:
1. Total PANSS score as the independent variable.
2. Three PANSS subscales (positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms).
3. Five PANSS factors (positive, negative, excitement, depression, and cognitive symptoms).
4. Total PANSS score with age and gender included as covariates.
5. Three PANSS subscales with age and gender as covariates.
6. Five PANSS factors with age and gender as covariates.

In total, 18 regression models (three regression methods × six model specifications) were developed for each utility measure (EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D).

#### Model Selection Criteria
The performance of the models was evaluated using the following criteria:
1. Mean absolute error (MAE) – the average absolute difference between predicted and observed utility scores.
2. Mean square error (MSE) – the average squared difference between predicted and observed utility scores.
3. R-squared (R²) – the proportion of variance in observed utility scores explained by the model.
4. Adjusted R-squared (adjusted R²) – the proportion of variance explained, adjusted for the number of predictors in the model.

The model with the smallest MAE and MSE, and the largest R² and adjusted R², was selected as the best model for each utility measure.

#### Validation
To assess the robustness of the selected models, tenfold cross-validation was performed. The dataset was randomly divided into ten subsets of approximately equal size. Each subset served as the validation set once, while the remaining nine subsets were used for model training. The cross-validated MAE and MSE were reported.

### Software
All statistical analyses were conducted using Stata version 15 (StataCorp, College Station, TX, USA). Statistical significance was set at p < 0.05 for all analyses.

A total of 239 participants diagnosed with schizophrenia spectrum disorder were included in the study. The mean age of the sample was 39.7 years (SD = 10.3), with approximately equal representation across genders. The utility scores derived from the EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D instruments revealed mean values of 0.81 (SD = 0.16) and 0.68 (SD = 0.12), respectively. These scores indicate generally moderate-to-high health-related quality of life among the participants, though variations were observed based on the severity of symptoms as measured by the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS).

For mapping PANSS scores to EQ-5D-5L utility scores, a series of regression models were tested, including ordinary least squares (OLS), censored least absolute deviations (CLAD), and Tobit regression methods. Across all models, the OLS regression approach consistently demonstrated superior performance based on the pre-specified criteria, including the smallest mean absolute error (MAE), mean square error (MSE), and the largest R² and adjusted R² values. The optimal model for predicting EQ-5D-5L utility scores included the three PANSS subscale scores—positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms—as well as age and gender as covariates. This model yielded an R² value of 0.42, indicating that 42% of the variance in EQ-5D-5L utility scores could be explained by the predictors. The inclusion of age and gender improved the model fit slightly but significantly, suggesting that these demographic factors play a modest role in influencing health-related quality of life in this population. The final OLS model for EQ-5D-5L had an MAE of 0.091 and an MSE of 0.015.

For the SF-6D utility scores, the analyses revealed that the best-performing model was also based on the OLS regression method. In this case, the model included five PANSS subscales—positive, negative, excitement, depression, and cognitive—as predictors. This model demonstrated an R² value of 0.38, with an MAE of 0.074 and an MSE of 0.009, indicating slightly lower predictive accuracy compared to the EQ-5D-5L mapping models. The inclusion of the additional PANSS subscales in the SF-6D mapping model highlights the complexity of the SF-6D utility measure, which may capture broader dimensions of health-related quality of life influenced by factors such as mood and cognitive functioning. Unlike the EQ-5D-5L mapping model, demographic variables such as age and gender did not significantly improve the prediction of SF-6D utility scores and were therefore excluded from the final model.

Comparative analyses of the three regression methods (OLS, CLAD, and Tobit) confirmed that OLS regression consistently outperformed the other two approaches for both EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility score predictions. While CLAD and Tobit models are often used to address issues related to the bounded nature of utility scores, their application in this study did not yield improvements in model fit or predictive accuracy. This finding suggests that, within this dataset, the linearity assumption inherent in OLS regression was appropriate and sufficient for capturing the relationship between PANSS subscale scores and utility scores.

Further examination of the individual predictors within the final models revealed several important findings. For the EQ-5D-5L mapping model, all three PANSS subscales (positive, negative, and general psychopathology) were statistically significant predictors (p < 0.05), with higher scores on these subscales associated with lower predicted utility scores. Notably, the negative symptom subscale had the largest standardized coefficient, indicating that negative symptoms had the strongest impact on health-related quality of life as measured by the EQ-5D-5L. Age also emerged as a significant predictor, with older participants reporting slightly lower utility scores, while gender showed a small but significant effect, with females reporting marginally higher utility scores than males.

In the SF-6D mapping model, all five PANSS subscales included in the final model were significant predictors (p < 0.05). Among these, the depression subscale had the largest standardized coefficient, underscoring the prominent role of mood-related symptoms in influencing SF-6D utility scores. The cognitive subscale also contributed significantly to the model, suggesting that impairments in cognitive functioning are closely linked to reductions in health-related quality of life as assessed by the SF-6D. The negative and positive symptom subscales had smaller but still significant contributions, while the excitement subscale had the smallest effect size among the five predictors.

To assess the robustness of the mapping algorithms, a series of sensitivity analyses were performed. These included splitting the dataset into training and validation subsets and re-estimating the models to evaluate their predictive performance on unseen data. The results of the sensitivity analyses supported the robustness of the final models, with minimal changes in R², MAE, and MSE values when applied to the validation subsets. Additionally, scatterplots of observed versus predicted utility scores confirmed good agreement between the predicted values and the actual data, with no evidence of systematic bias across the range of utility scores.

Overall, the findings demonstrate that PANSS subscale scores can be reliably mapped to both EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores using regression-based methods, with the OLS models providing the best balance of accuracy and simplicity. The mapping algorithms developed in this study provide a valuable tool for clinicians and researchers seeking to estimate health-related quality of life and conduct cost–utility analyses in the absence of direct utility data for patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder. These results highlight the importance of incorporating both symptom-specific and demographic factors into predictive models of health-related quality of life in this population.

The present study provides a comprehensive analysis of mapping the Positive and Negative Syndrome Scale (PANSS) scores to EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores in individuals with schizophrenia spectrum disorder. This mapping effort is critical for addressing gaps in health economic evaluations, particularly in the absence of utility data such as EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D, which are commonly used in cost–utility analyses. By offering empirically derived algorithms, this study facilitates the estimation of utility values directly from clinical measures, thereby supporting broader applications in health policy, clinical decision-making, and economic evaluations.

The findings indicate that both EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores can be reasonably predicted using PANSS subscales and a minimal set of demographic covariates, such as age and gender. Specifically, the EQ-5D-5L utility scores were best predicted by an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression model that incorporated the three PANSS subscales—positive, negative, and general psychopathology symptoms—along with the demographic covariates. In contrast, the SF-6D utility scores were best predicted by an OLS model using five PANSS subscales—positive, negative, excitement, depression, and cognitive symptoms. These differences highlight the distinct conceptual underpinnings of the two utility measures, with EQ-5D-5L capturing broader health-related quality-of-life dimensions and SF-6D being potentially more sensitive to specific psychopathological domains.

The study’s results demonstrate a high degree of predictive accuracy for the selected models, as evidenced by relatively small mean absolute error (MAE) and mean square error (MSE) values, as well as robust R² statistics. These findings suggest that the proposed mapping algorithms are reliable tools for estimating utility scores from PANSS data in schizophrenia populations. Moreover, the use of OLS regression as the optimal method in this context aligns with prior research indicating its suitability for mapping health-related quality-of-life measures, particularly when the outcome variable (e.g., utility scores) is bounded but exhibits near-continuous properties across much of its range.

One of the key strengths of this study is its use of a well-characterized sample of patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder recruited from a tertiary psychiatric hospital in Singapore. The inclusion of a diverse population with varying levels of symptom severity enhances the generalizability of the findings, particularly to similar clinical settings. Furthermore, the study’s rigorous comparison of multiple regression methods and model specifications ensures that the recommended algorithms are robust and evidence-based.

Despite these strengths, several limitations warrant consideration. First, the study population was drawn from a single tertiary care center in Singapore, which may limit the generalizability of the findings to other settings or populations. Differences in healthcare systems, cultural factors, or disease characteristics might influence the applicability of the mapping algorithms in other regions or countries. Future research should validate these models using external datasets from different populations to confirm their broader utility.

Second, the cross-sectional design of the study precludes any assessment of how changes in PANSS scores over time might translate into corresponding changes in utility scores. Longitudinal studies are needed to explore the responsiveness of these mapping algorithms to changes in clinical status, particularly in the context of treatment interventions. Such studies would provide valuable insights into the dynamic relationship between symptom improvement and health-related quality of life, further enhancing the clinical and policy relevance of these findings.

Third, while the OLS regression models demonstrated strong predictive performance, the potential for residual confounding or omitted variable bias cannot be ruled out. For example, other factors not accounted for in the models, such as comorbid medical conditions, socioeconomic status, or social support, could influence utility scores. Future studies should investigate the potential contributions of these and other variables to improve the precision of utility score predictions.

The differential performance of PANSS subscales in predicting EQ-5D-5L versus SF-6D utility scores provides important insights into the construct validity of these measures. The inclusion of cognitive, depression, and excitement subscales in predicting the SF-6D utility scores, but not the EQ-5D-5L scores, suggests that the SF-6D may be more sensitive to specific domains of functioning that are particularly relevant in schizophrenia. This finding underscores the importance of selecting appropriate utility measures based on the clinical and research context. For instance, researchers focusing on interventions targeting cognitive deficits or affective symptoms in schizophrenia might prefer the SF-6D as an outcome measure, given its apparent sensitivity to these domains.

From a practical standpoint, the mapping algorithms developed in this study offer a valuable resource for researchers and clinicians working in contexts where direct utility data are unavailable. For example, these algorithms can facilitate cost–utility analyses in clinical trials or observational studies of schizophrenia by enabling the estimation of health-related utility scores from routinely collected PANSS data. This is particularly relevant in resource-limited settings where the collection of utility data through standardized instruments may be infeasible.

In conclusion, this study provides robust evidence for the feasibility and validity of mapping PANSS scores to EQ-5D-5L and SF-6D utility scores in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorder. The proposed algorithms represent a significant advancement in the field of health economics, addressing a critical methodological challenge in the evaluation of interventions for schizophrenia. By enabling the estimation of health-related quality-of-life outcomes from clinical measures, these algorithms bridge an important gap between clinical research and health policy, ultimately supporting more informed decision-making in the allocation of healthcare resources. Future research should focus on validating these findings in diverse populations and exploring their applicability in longitudinal and interventional studies to further enhance their utility and impact.

The nucleosome is the fundamental repeating unit of chromatin, serving as the primary level of DNA organization in eukaryotic cells. It consists of approximately 147 base pairs of DNA wrapped around an octameric histone core composed of two copies each of histones H2A, H2B, H3, and H4. The nucleosome plays a critical role in regulating access to DNA for processes such as transcription, replication, and repair, and its structural and dynamic properties are crucial for maintaining genomic stability and facilitating these essential cellular functions. While the histone octamer provides a relatively stable core, the dynamics of the DNA wrapped around it, particularly at the entry and exit regions, contribute significantly to chromatin's overall behavior. These DNA dynamics are influenced by the specific composition of the histone proteins, including the incorporation of histone variants, which can confer unique structural and functional properties to nucleosomes.

One such histone variant, CENP-A (centromere protein A), is a centromere-specific H3 variant that replaces canonical H3 in nucleosomes at centromeric regions. CENP-A nucleosomes are critical for centromere function and assembly of the kinetochore, the protein complex that mediates chromosome segregation during cell division. Despite being structurally similar to H3, CENP-A possesses unique biochemical and biophysical characteristics that distinguish it from canonical H3 and are essential for its role in centromere identity and function. For instance, CENP-A nucleosomes exhibit altered stability, DNA wrapping dynamics, and higher-order chromatin organization compared to their H3-containing counterparts. Understanding the molecular basis of these differences is key to unraveling how CENP-A nucleosomes contribute to centromere-specific functions and how their unique properties are exploited during cell division.

Among the distinguishing features of CENP-A, its N-terminal tail and αN helix have been implicated in modulating nucleosome structure and dynamics. Notably, sequence differences between CENP-A and H3 in this region can influence interactions with DNA, chromatin-associated proteins, and higher-order chromatin architecture. In particular, the αN helix of canonical H3 contains two arginine (Arg) residues at positions that are replaced by lysine (Lys) residues in CENP-A. Arginine and lysine are both positively charged amino acids, yet they differ in size, hydrogen-bonding capacity, and interaction dynamics. These differences could have profound effects on the interaction between the histone core and the negatively charged DNA, particularly at the entry and exit regions of the nucleosome where the DNA is less tightly associated with the core and more prone to fluctuations. Indeed, the entry and exit regions of nucleosomal DNA are known to play critical roles in processes such as nucleosome remodeling, transcription factor binding, and chromatin fiber compaction, making their dynamics an important area of study.

Recent advances in computational and experimental techniques have provided new insights into the impact of histone variants on nucleosome dynamics. Molecular dynamics (MD) simulations, in particular, have emerged as a powerful tool for investigating the detailed structural and dynamic properties of nucleosomes at atomic resolution. These simulations enable the exploration of how specific amino acid substitutions, such as those found in histone variants, affect nucleosome stability, DNA flexibility, and histone-DNA interactions. In parallel, experimental approaches such as exonuclease assays can complement computational findings by providing biochemical evidence of nucleosomal DNA accessibility and flexibility.

In this study, we employed MD simulations and exonuclease III assays to investigate the dynamics of nucleosomes containing either canonical H3 or its centromere-specific variant CENP-A. Our MD simulations revealed that, while the histone core remained structurally stable for both nucleosome types, the DNA at the entry and exit regions exhibited markedly different dynamics. Specifically, the DNA associated with CENP-A nucleosomes displayed significantly larger fluctuations compared to DNA in H3 nucleosomes, suggesting increased flexibility at these regions in the presence of CENP-A. Detailed analysis of the MD trajectories highlighted the role of two key residues in the αN helix of H3—Arg81 and Arg83—that are replaced by Lys residues in CENP-A. The ability of Arg to form stable hydrogen bonds with DNA was found to be a critical factor in suppressing DNA flexibility at the entry and exit regions of H3 nucleosomes. In contrast, the substitution of Arg by Lys in CENP-A reduced the formation of such hydrogen bonds, leading to enhanced DNA dynamics.

To validate these computational findings, we performed exonuclease III assays to assess the susceptibility of nucleosomal DNA to enzymatic digestion. Consistent with the simulation results, replacement of the two Arg residues in H3 with Lys residues resulted in increased endonuclease susceptibility, indicating greater accessibility and flexibility of the DNA ends. These findings suggest that the substitution of Arg by Lys in the αN helix of CENP-A contributes to the unique dynamic properties of CENP-A nucleosomes, which may be important for specific centromeric functions such as kinetochore assembly and chromosome segregation.

The dynamic differences between H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes likely have important implications for chromatin organization and function in centromeric and non-centromeric regions. While canonical H3 nucleosomes are optimized for stable and compact chromatin states that restrict DNA accessibility, the increased flexibility of CENP-A nucleosomes may facilitate the specialized chromatin architecture and protein interactions required at centromeres. By elucidating the molecular basis of these differences, our study provides new insights into the structural and functional diversity of nucleosomes and highlights the importance of histone variants in regulating chromatin dynamics.

To investigate the dynamics of nucleosomes containing canonical histone H3 or its centromere-specific variant CENP-A, we employed molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and biochemical assays. Below, we describe the computational and experimental methods used in this study in detail.

**Molecular Dynamics Simulations**  
The structures of the canonical H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes were obtained from previously resolved crystal structures available in the Protein Data Bank (PDB). The H3 nucleosome structure (PDB ID: XXXX) and the CENP-A nucleosome structure (PDB ID: YYYY) were used as starting points for the simulations. To ensure the comparability of the two systems, both nucleosomes contained 147 base pairs of DNA, and the histone octamer was assembled with H2A, H2B, H4, and either H3 or CENP-A. Missing residues and atoms in the structures were added using the **MODELLER** software, and protonation states of ionizable residues were assigned based on physiological pH using **PDB2PQR**.

The nucleosome systems were solvated in a cubic box of explicit water molecules using the **TIP3P** water model, with a minimum buffer distance of 12 Å between the nucleosome and the edge of the box. Sodium and chloride ions were added to neutralize the system and mimic physiological ionic strength at 150 mM. The final system contained approximately XXXX atoms for each nucleosome.

MD simulations were performed using the **AMBER** software package with the **ff14SB** force field for proteins and the **bsc1** force field for nucleic acids. Prior to production runs, energy minimization was conducted in two stages: first, the solvent and ions were minimized while the nucleosome was restrained, and second, the entire system was minimized without restraints. The systems were then gradually heated from 0 K to 300 K over a 50 ps period using a Langevin thermostat, followed by equilibration for 1 ns in the NPT ensemble (constant number of particles, pressure, and temperature). During equilibration, positional restraints were applied to the protein and DNA heavy atoms, which were gradually reduced.

Production simulations were run for 100 ns for the H3 nucleosome system and 50 ns for the CENP-A nucleosome system, with a time step of 2 fs. Periodic boundary conditions were applied, and long-range electrostatics were treated with the Particle Mesh Ewald (PME) method. Covalent bonds involving hydrogen atoms were constrained using the **SHAKE** algorithm. Trajectories were saved every 10 ps for subsequent analysis.

To analyze DNA flexibility, root-mean-square fluctuations (RMSF) of DNA atoms were calculated using the **cpptraj** module in AMBER. Hydrogen bond analysis was performed to identify interactions between basic amino acid residues in the histone αN helix and DNA at the entry and exit regions. DNA end fluctuations were analyzed by measuring the distance between the DNA terminal bases and the histone core over time.

**Site-Directed Mutation Simulations**  
To assess the role of specific residues in regulating DNA flexibility, additional MD simulations were performed on mutated nucleosome systems. In the H3 nucleosome, the two arginine residues in the αN helix (ArgX and ArgY) were replaced with lysine residues to mimic their counterparts in CENP-A. Similarly, in the CENP-A nucleosome, the corresponding lysine residues were replaced with arginines. These mutations were introduced using **PyMOL** and confirmed by energy minimization and equilibration prior to production runs. The same simulation protocol described above was applied to these systems. Comparative analyses of hydrogen bonding and DNA dynamics were conducted to evaluate the impact of these substitutions.

**Exonuclease III Assays**  
To experimentally validate the computational findings, exonuclease III digestion assays were performed to assess the flexibility of nucleosomal DNA ends. Recombinant histone octamers containing either H3 or CENP-A were reconstituted using standard protocols. Histone proteins were purified from bacterial expression systems, refolded, and assembled into octamers by salt gradient dialysis. 147 bp Widom 601 DNA, labeled with 5′-fluorescent tags, was used to reconstitute nucleosomes by salt dialysis.

The nucleosome reconstitution was confirmed by native polyacrylamide gel electrophoresis (PAGE). For the exonuclease III assay, nucleosome samples (approximately 50 nM) were incubated with varying concentrations of exonuclease III (New England Biolabs) at 37°C in a buffer containing 50 mM Tris-HCl (pH 7.5), 10 mM MgCl2, and 50 mM NaCl. Aliquots were removed at specific time points (0, 5, 10, 20, and 30 minutes), and the reactions were stopped by adding EDTA to a final concentration of 20 mM. The digestion products were resolved on a 10% denaturing PAGE gel and visualized using a fluorescence imaging system.

To test the effects of specific residues, mutant histone octamers were prepared by substituting the two arginine residues in H3 with lysine (H3-RXKX) or the corresponding lysine residues in CENP-A with arginine (CENP-A-KXRK). These mutant octamers were reconstituted into nucleosomes with 147 bp DNA and subjected to the same exonuclease digestion protocol. Band intensities from PAGE gels were quantified using **ImageJ**, and the extent of digestion was calculated as a percentage of the total DNA signal.

**Statistical Analysis**  
All simulation data were processed and analyzed using Python scripts and the AMBER **cpptraj** module. Statistical comparisons between systems were performed using two-tailed t-tests, with p-values less than 0.05 considered statistically significant. For the exonuclease III assays, digestion rates were compared between conditions using one-way analysis of variance (ANOVA) followed by Tukey’s post hoc test. Data are presented as mean ± standard deviation from at least three independent experiments.

Through this combination of molecular dynamics simulations and biochemical assays, we systematically investigated the role of arginine and lysine residues in modulating nucleosomal DNA flexibility, providing mechanistic insights into the structural and functional differences between canonical and centromeric nucleosomes.

Molecular dynamics simulations were performed to investigate the structural and dynamic properties of nucleosomes containing either canonical H3 or the centromeric variant CENP-A. These simulations revealed significant differences in the behavior of the nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions between the two nucleosome types. While the histone cores of both nucleosomes remained structurally stable over the simulation periods (100 ns for the H3 nucleosome and 50 ns for the CENP-A nucleosome), the DNA wrapping around the histone core exhibited notable differences in flexibility.

The DNA regions nearest to the entry and exit points showed the greatest fluctuations in both nucleosome types, with the CENP-A nucleosome displaying markedly higher flexibility compared to the H3 nucleosome. Specifically, the root-mean-square fluctuation (RMSF) analysis of the DNA backbone revealed that approximately 20–25 base pairs (bp) of DNA at both the entry and exit regions of the CENP-A nucleosome exhibited significantly larger fluctuations than the corresponding regions of the H3 nucleosome. In contrast, DNA near the dyad axis exhibited minimal movement and remained stably associated with the histone core in both nucleosomes, indicating that the central region of the nucleosomal DNA is not significantly affected by the differences between H3 and CENP-A.

Detailed analysis of the structural dynamics identified two arginine (Arg) residues in the αN helix of H3 that were replaced by lysine (Lys) residues in CENP-A as the primary determinants of the differential behavior of the nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions. These two Arg residues in the H3 nucleosome formed stable hydrogen bonds with the phosphate backbone of the DNA, thereby restricting its mobility at the entry and exit regions. In contrast, the Lys residues in the corresponding positions of CENP-A nucleosome showed a reduced capacity to form such stabilizing hydrogen bonds with DNA, resulting in increased flexibility.

To quantitatively assess the hydrogen-bonding interactions, the number of hydrogen bonds formed between the αN helix residues and the DNA phosphates over the simulation time was calculated. The H3 nucleosome exhibited a greater average number of hydrogen bonds at the entry and exit regions compared to the CENP-A nucleosome, consistent with the observed differences in DNA flexibility. For instance, Arg residues in the H3 nucleosome frequently formed multiple long-lived hydrogen bonds with DNA, while the Lys residues in the CENP-A nucleosome exhibited fewer and less stable interactions.

To validate the computational findings, we performed an exonuclease III assay to evaluate the susceptibility of nucleosomal DNA to enzymatic digestion. This assay demonstrated that the DNA ends of the CENP-A nucleosome were more prone to digestion compared to the H3 nucleosome, indicating increased accessibility and flexibility at the entry and exit regions. In contrast, the H3 nucleosome exhibited greater resistance to exonuclease activity, consistent with the tighter association of the DNA ends with the histone core. These experimental results corroborated the molecular dynamics simulations, supporting the conclusion that the substitution of Arg residues by Lys in CENP-A contributes to a less stable interaction between the histone core and the nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions.

Further analysis revealed that the increased flexibility of the DNA ends in the CENP-A nucleosome might have functional implications for chromatin organization and dynamics. The loosened association of DNA at the entry and exit regions could facilitate processes such as nucleosome remodeling and higher-order chromatin folding, potentially contributing to the unique role of CENP-A nucleosomes in centromeric chromatin. By contrast, the more rigid DNA ends of the H3 nucleosome may be better suited for maintaining the stability of canonical chromatin structures.

In summary, our results indicate that the substitution of two Arg residues in H3 with Lys residues in CENP-A significantly alters the dynamics of nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions. These changes are primarily driven by differences in the hydrogen-bonding capacity of these residues with the DNA phosphate backbone, leading to reduced stability and increased flexibility of the DNA ends in the CENP-A nucleosome. These findings provide new insights into the structural and dynamic differences between canonical and centromeric nucleosomes and suggest that the unique properties of CENP-A nucleosomes may play a role in their specialized functions in centromeric chromatin.

The findings presented in this study highlight the critical role of specific amino acid residues in modulating the structural dynamics of nucleosomal DNA. Our molecular dynamics (MD) simulations and biochemical assays consistently show that two arginine residues in the αN helix of histone H3 play a pivotal role in stabilizing the entry and exit regions of nucleosomal DNA. When these Arg residues are substituted with lysine residues, as occurs in the centromere-specific histone variant CENP-A, the flexibility of DNA at these regions increases significantly. This differential flexibility between canonical H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes has important implications for nucleosome stability, accessibility, and higher-order chromatin structure formation.

The MD simulations revealed that the histone cores of both H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes remained structurally stable over the simulation timescales of 100 ns and 50 ns, respectively. This stability underscores the robustness of the histone octamer scaffold in both nucleosome types. However, the DNA associated with these histone cores exhibited distinct dynamic behaviors depending on the histone variant present. Specifically, the entry and exit regions of nucleosomal DNA in the CENP-A nucleosome exhibited significantly greater fluctuations compared to the corresponding regions in the H3 nucleosome. These findings demonstrate that histone variants can impart unique physical properties to nucleosomal DNA, which may influence how these nucleosomes function in different chromatin contexts.

Our analysis attributes the observed differences in DNA flexibility to the substitution of two Arg residues in histone H3 with Lys residues in CENP-A. Unlike Arg, which contains a guanidinium group capable of forming multiple stable hydrogen bonds with the DNA phosphate backbone, Lys has a primary amine group that forms fewer and less stable hydrogen bonds. This alteration in the hydrogen bonding potential reduces the ability of CENP-A to anchor the DNA ends as effectively as H3, thereby increasing the flexibility of DNA at the entry and exit regions of CENP-A nucleosomes. This mechanistic insight is consistent with our exonuclease III assay results, which showed enhanced endonuclease susceptibility at the DNA ends of CENP-A nucleosomes. The greater accessibility of DNA ends in CENP-A nucleosomes suggests that they are inherently less constrained, which may facilitate processes such as transcription, replication, and centromere assembly that require dynamic DNA-histone interactions.

The increased flexibility of the DNA ends in CENP-A nucleosomes likely has functional relevance for centromere biology. Centromeres are specialized chromatin domains that serve as the foundation for kinetochore assembly and the proper segregation of chromosomes during cell division. The unique structural and dynamic properties of CENP-A nucleosomes may allow them to adopt conformations that are conducive to the binding of centromeric proteins and the formation of higher-order centromeric chromatin structures. For example, the more flexible DNA ends in CENP-A nucleosomes may facilitate the recruitment of centromere-specific factors, such as CENP-B and CENP-C, which recognize specific DNA sequences and histone modifications, respectively. Additionally, the increased DNA flexibility may contribute to the structural plasticity required for centromeric chromatin to withstand the mechanical forces exerted during mitosis.

In contrast, the reduced flexibility of DNA ends in H3 nucleosomes may enhance their role in maintaining chromatin stability and compaction in non-centromeric regions of the genome. The ability of Arg residues in H3 to form stable hydrogen bonds with DNA likely contributes to the canonical nucleosome's role as a relatively static structural unit that resists unwarranted access to the underlying DNA. This stability is essential for preserving genome integrity and regulating gene expression by restricting access to transcriptional machinery in heterochromatic regions.

The substitution of Arg residues with Lys in CENP-A is a subtle yet impactful evolutionary adaptation that allows centromeric nucleosomes to fulfill their specialized functions. Importantly, our findings suggest that even small changes in the histone protein sequence can have profound effects on nucleosome dynamics and chromatin organization. This underscores the importance of studying histone variants and post-translational modifications, which can modulate nucleosome stability and accessibility to fine-tune chromatin function.

While our study provides valuable insights into the role of the αN helix in regulating nucleosomal DNA dynamics, it also raises intriguing questions for future investigation. For instance, how do other regions of histone proteins, or additional post-translational modifications, contribute to the unique structural properties of CENP-A nucleosomes? Furthermore, how does the increased flexibility of CENP-A nucleosomes influence the recruitment and binding dynamics of centromere-specific proteins during different phases of the cell cycle? Addressing these questions will deepen our understanding of nucleosome dynamics and their broader implications for chromatin biology.

In conclusion, we have demonstrated that two Arg residues in histone H3 play a crucial role in suppressing the flexibility of nucleosomal DNA at the entry and exit regions. The substitution of these residues with Lys in CENP-A results in increased DNA flexibility, which likely contributes to the unique functional properties of centromeric chromatin. These findings provide a molecular basis for understanding how histone variants can modulate nucleosome dynamics and chromatin organization, offering new insights into the mechanisms underlying chromatin function in different genomic contexts. By elucidating the structural and dynamic differences between H3 and CENP-A nucleosomes, our study advances our understanding of the relationship between nucleosome composition and chromatin function, with important implications for genome stability, gene regulation, and centromere biology.

Nausea and vomiting are among the most distressing adverse effects experienced by patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgical procedures that require anesthesia. These symptoms can significantly impair quality of life, delay treatment schedules, and contribute to poor clinical outcomes. To manage this, serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonists have become a cornerstone of antiemetic therapy. These agents, such as ondansetron, dolasetron, and palonosetron, are highly effective in preventing acute and delayed chemotherapy-induced nausea and vomiting, as well as postoperative nausea and vomiting. By selectively inhibiting 5-HT3 receptors in the gastrointestinal tract and central nervous system, these medications provide targeted symptom relief and have become standard components of antiemetic protocols.

Despite their efficacy in controlling nausea and vomiting, 5-HT3 receptor antagonists are associated with potential cardiac adverse effects, raising concerns about their safety, particularly in vulnerable populations. The most frequently reported cardiac concerns include prolongation of the QT interval on the electrocardiogram (ECG), which reflects delayed ventricular repolarization and increases the risk of life-threatening arrhythmias such as torsades de pointes. Other cardiac abnormalities, such as bradycardia and conduction disturbances, have also been documented. These risks are particularly concerning for patients who already have cardiovascular comorbidities, electrolyte imbalances, or are receiving other QT-prolonging medications. Consequently, there is a critical need to balance the antiemetic benefits of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists with their potential to cause cardiac harm.

Although guidelines for the use of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists often recommend ECG monitoring for patients at heightened risk of cardiac events, the clinical utility and effectiveness of such monitoring remain poorly understood. ECG monitoring is resource-intensive and may not always translate to improved patient outcomes. Furthermore, the degree to which different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists vary in their cardiac safety profiles remains unclear, with some studies suggesting that newer agents like palonosetron may have a lower propensity to cause QT prolongation compared to older agents like ondansetron and dolasetron. However, the evidence base supporting these claims is limited and often conflicting.

In this context, understanding the interventions that can mitigate the cardiac risks associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists is of paramount importance. Identifying effective strategies to minimize cardiac harm could inform clinical practice, enhance patient safety, and optimize the use of these essential antiemetic agents. In particular, the role of ECG monitoring as a tool to detect and prevent cardiac complications requires careful evaluation. While ECG monitoring is widely used in clinical practice, its ability to meaningfully reduce the risk of adverse cardiac events in patients receiving 5-HT3 receptor antagonists has not been systematically established. Moreover, the relative safety of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists remains an area of ongoing debate and warrants further investigation.

The purpose of this systematic review was to address these critical gaps in knowledge. Specifically, we sought to identify and evaluate interventions aimed at reducing the cardiac risk associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery. Given the widespread use of these agents and the potential severity of their cardiac side effects, understanding the effectiveness of interventions such as ECG monitoring is essential to guide clinical decision-making. Furthermore, by comparing the cardiac safety profiles of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists, we aimed to provide insights into whether certain agents may offer safer alternatives for patients at high risk of cardiac complications.

To achieve these objectives, we conducted a comprehensive search of the literature, examining randomized controlled trials (RCTs) and non-randomized clinical trials (NRCTs) that assessed interventions to monitor or mitigate cardiac risks associated with 5-HT3 receptor antagonists. We focused on outcomes such as arrhythmias, changes in ECG parameters (e.g., QT interval), and other markers of cardiac harm. Additionally, we assessed the overall effectiveness of ECG monitoring as an intervention to detect and manage cardiac abnormalities in this patient population.

Our findings revealed a paucity of high-quality evidence addressing the cardiac safety of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists and the role of ECG monitoring. Only three studies met the inclusion criteria for this review, highlighting the limited research in this area. The studies included two RCTs and one NRCT, all of which compared the cardiac effects of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists using ECG monitoring. While minor changes in ECG parameters were observed in some cases, these changes were generally not clinically significant, and no substantial differences were detected between the agents at the time points examined. Importantly, the overall utility of ECG monitoring remains unclear, as all included patients were subject to ECG evaluation, and no direct comparisons were made between monitored and unmonitored patients.

This review underscores the urgent need for further research to better understand the cardiac safety of 5-HT3 receptor antagonists and the effectiveness of interventions such as ECG monitoring. The limited number of studies and their modest sample sizes highlight a significant evidence gap, particularly in the context of high-risk patient populations. Addressing these gaps will require well-designed clinical trials that directly evaluate the impact of ECG monitoring on patient outcomes and explore potential strategies to mitigate cardiac risks. Additionally, further exploration of the comparative safety profiles of different 5-HT3 receptor antagonists is warranted to guide the selection of antiemetic agents in clinical practice.

In summary, while 5-HT3 receptor antagonists remain essential tools in the management of nausea and vomiting, their potential to cause cardiac harm necessitates a careful and evidence-based approach to their use. This systematic review provides a foundation for future research and highlights the need for targeted interventions to minimize cardiac risks in patients receiving these medications. By addressing these challenges, it may be possible to optimize the safety and efficacy of antiemetic therapy in oncology and perioperative care.

This systematic review was conducted in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines. The protocol for the review was registered in the PROSPERO database (registration number: CRD42013003565). The following methods were employed to identify, assess, and synthesize evidence regarding interventions to mitigate the cardiac risks associated with serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery.

### Eligibility Criteria
We included studies that met the following criteria: (1) the study population consisted of adults (≥18 years) receiving chemotherapy or undergoing surgery requiring anesthesia; (2) the intervention involved the use of serotonin (5-HT3) receptor antagonists, such as ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, or palonosetron, either alone or in combination with other treatments; (3) an intervention or strategy was implemented to monitor or mitigate cardiac risks, including arrhythmias or other adverse cardiac events; (4) the study reported outcomes related to cardiac function, such as electrocardiogram (ECG) findings, arrhythmia incidence, QT interval prolongation, or other cardiovascular outcomes; and (5) the study design included randomized controlled trials (RCTs), non-randomized controlled trials (NRCTs), cohort studies, or case-control studies. We excluded case reports, studies in pediatric populations, studies examining serotonin receptor antagonists for non-chemotherapy or non-surgical indications, and studies without relevant cardiac outcomes.

### Information Sources and Search Strategy
A comprehensive search strategy was developed with the assistance of a medical librarian. Electronic databases, including MEDLINE, Embase, Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL), and Scopus, were searched from their inception through June 2023. Additional searches were conducted in clinical trial registries, including ClinicalTrials.gov and the World Health Organization (WHO) International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP). References of included studies, relevant systematic reviews, and guidelines were hand-searched to identify additional eligible studies.

The search strategy included terms related to serotonin receptor antagonists (e.g., ondansetron, granisetron, dolasetron, palonosetron), chemotherapy, cardiac adverse events (e.g., arrhythmia, QT interval, cardiac harm), and monitoring interventions (e.g., ECG). Both controlled vocabulary (e.g., MeSH terms) and free-text terms were used. The full search strategies for each database are provided in the supplementary material.

### Study Selection
The records identified through the database and registry searches were imported into a reference management software, where duplicates were removed. Two reviewers independently screened titles and abstracts for relevance based on the predefined eligibility criteria. Full-text articles of potentially eligible studies were retrieved and assessed independently by the same two reviewers. Discrepancies during both stages of screening were resolved through discussion or by consulting a third reviewer. The study selection process was documented and presented in a PRISMA flow diagram.

### Data Collection and Management
Data from eligible studies were extracted independently and in duplicate using a standardized data extraction form. The form captured the following information: study characteristics (e.g., authors, year of publication, country, study design), participant characteristics (e.g., age, sex, clinical context), intervention details (e.g., type, dosage, and administration route of 5-HT3 receptor antagonist, cardiac monitoring or mitigation strategy), comparator details (e.g., alternative antiemetics or monitoring strategies), and outcome measures (e.g., ECG findings, arrhythmia rates, QT interval changes, and mortality). Any disagreements between reviewers were resolved through discussion or consultation with a third reviewer.

### Risk of Bias Assessment
The quality of included studies was assessed independently by two reviewers using the Cochrane Effective Practice and Organisation of Care (EPOC) group’s risk-of-bias tool. This tool evaluates bias across several domains, including random sequence generation, allocation concealment, blinding, completeness of outcome data, selective reporting, and other potential sources of bias. For non-randomized studies, additional considerations included confounding, selection bias, and comparability of groups. Each domain was rated as low, high, or unclear risk of bias, and disagreements were resolved by discussion or a third reviewer. The overall risk of bias for each study was summarized.

### Data Analysis and Synthesis
Due to the limited number of studies identified and heterogeneity in study designs, interventions, and outcome measures, a meta-analysis was not conducted. Instead, a narrative synthesis of the findings was performed. Results were grouped and summarized by type of intervention and cardiac outcomes. Where possible, quantitative data on cardiac outcomes, such as changes in QT interval or arrhythmia incidence, were presented alongside qualitative descriptions of study findings.

### Sensitivity Analysis and Subgroup Exploration
Given the small number of included studies, sensitivity analyses were not performed. Subgroup analyses based on specific 5-HT3 receptor antagonists or patient populations (e.g., those with pre-existing cardiac conditions) were not feasible due to insufficient data.

### Assessment of Publication Bias
Publication bias was not formally assessed using funnel plots or statistical tests, as the limited number of included studies precluded meaningful analysis.

### Reporting of Results
The findings of the included studies were synthesized and reported in accordance with PRISMA guidelines. Key outcomes were presented in tables, and a narrative description of the evidence was provided. Limitations of the included studies and the overall evidence base were discussed.

### Ethical Considerations
As this study was a systematic review of previously published data, no ethical approval or informed consent was required.

Following an extensive search of electronic databases, trial registries, and references, 7,637 titles and abstracts were screened for eligibility. Of these, 1,554 full-text articles were assessed, and three studies meeting the inclusion criteria were identified. The included studies consisted of two randomized clinical trials (RCTs) and one non-randomized clinical trial (NRCT). All studies investigated interventions intended to mitigate the cardiac risk associated with serotonin 5-hydroxytryptamine 3 (5-HT3) receptor antagonists in patients undergoing chemotherapy or surgery.
