The study employed a quasi-experimental design with pre-test, post-test, and follow-up assessments to evaluate the effects of a nutritional intervention program grounded in self-determination theory (SDT) on eating-related self-determined motivation and adherence to the Mediterranean diet (MedDiet). Ethical approval was obtained from the institutional ethics review board, and all participants provided written informed consent prior to their participation.

### Participants and Recruitment
Participants were recruited through advertisements in community centers, workplaces, and online platforms. Eligible individuals were adults aged 18–65 years, without any medical condition requiring a specific diet (e.g., diabetes, celiac disease), and not currently participating in any structured nutritional or lifestyle intervention program. A total of 180 individuals (90 men and 90 women) were enrolled in the study. Exclusion criteria included pregnancy, lactation, and reported use of medications affecting appetite or metabolism. Participants were stratified by gender to ensure equal representation of men and women.

### Intervention Design
The intervention was designed to promote adherence to the MedDiet using principles of SDT, which emphasizes the fulfillment of three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence, and relatedness [1]. The program was delivered in weekly group sessions over a 12-week period, followed by a six-month follow-up. Each session lasted 90 minutes and was facilitated by a trained dietitian and a health psychologist. The content of the sessions included education on the MedDiet, practical strategies for integrating MedDiet principles into daily life, cooking demonstrations, and group discussions to foster peer support.

To enhance autonomy, participants were encouraged to set personalized dietary goals and develop meal plans aligned with their preferences and lifestyles. Competence was promoted through skill-building activities, such as meal preparation and label reading, as well as providing feedback on progress. Relatedness was fostered through group interactions, sharing experiences, and collaborative problem-solving during challenges. Participants were also provided with weekly handouts, including recipes, shopping lists, and tips for overcoming common barriers to MedDiet adherence.

### Measures
Eating-related self-determined motivation was assessed using the Regulation of Eating Behavior Scale (REBS) [2], a validated tool that measures different forms of motivation along a continuum from external regulation to intrinsic motivation. The REBS consists of 24 items scored on a 7-point Likert scale, with higher scores indicating more self-determined motivation. The relative autonomy index (RAI) was calculated to summarize the degree of self-determined motivation.

Adherence to the MedDiet was evaluated using the Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (MEDAS) [3], a validated 14-item questionnaire that assesses dietary behaviors such as fruit and vegetable intake, olive oil consumption, and fish consumption. Scores range from 0 to 14, with higher scores indicating greater adherence to the MedDiet.

### Procedure
Baseline assessments were conducted one week before the intervention. Participants completed the REBS and MEDAS questionnaires during in-person sessions at the research center. Anthropometric measures, including weight and body mass index (BMI), were also collected using standardized procedures to account for potential covariates in the analysis.

The intervention sessions were conducted in groups of 10–15 participants and were held in community venues. Attendance was recorded at each session, and participants were asked to complete homework assignments between sessions to reinforce learning. Post-intervention assessments were conducted within two weeks after the final session, and follow-up assessments were conducted six months after the intervention. Both post-intervention and follow-up assessments included the same measures as the baseline assessment.

### Statistical Analysis
Descriptive statistics were calculated for all variables, and normality of data distribution was assessed using the Shapiro-Wilk test. Baseline differences between men and women in demographic and outcome variables were examined using independent samples t-tests for continuous variables and chi-square tests for categorical variables.

To evaluate changes in self-determined motivation and MedDiet adherence over time, repeated-measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) was performed, with time (baseline, post-intervention, follow-up) as the within-subjects factor and gender as the between-subjects factor. Post hoc pairwise comparisons with Bonferroni correction were conducted to explore significant interactions. Cohen's d was calculated to assess the effect size of changes within each gender.

Multiple linear regression analyses were conducted to examine the associations between changes in self-determined motivation (RAI scores) and changes in MedDiet adherence (MEDAS scores) for men and women separately. Gender-specific models included age, BMI, and baseline RAI and MEDAS scores as covariates to control for potential confounding factors.

Missing data were handled using multiple imputation with five imputations, assuming missing at random. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to confirm the robustness of the findings under different imputation scenarios. All analyses were performed using SPSS (Version 27.0), and a p-value of <0.05 was considered statistically significant.

### Fidelity and Compliance
Program fidelity was monitored through session checklists completed by facilitators, which assessed adherence to the intervention protocol. Participant compliance was evaluated based on session attendance and self-reported completion of homework assignments. Participants who attended fewer than 70% of the sessions were classified as low adherers and excluded from the primary analysis, though sensitivity analyses were conducted to investigate the impact of their inclusion.

### Ethical Considerations
The study adhered to the ethical principles outlined in the Declaration of Helsinki. Participants were informed about the study's purpose, procedures, potential risks, and benefits. Confidentiality was maintained by de-identifying all data, and participants were free to withdraw from the study at any time without penalty.

The results of the present study are presented below, focusing on the gender differences in changes in eating-related self-determined motivation and adherence to the Mediterranean diet following the nutritional intervention and at follow-up. The associations between these variables are also analyzed.

### Participant Characteristics and Baseline Measures  
A total of 250 participants (125 men and 125 women) completed the intervention and follow-up assessments. At baseline, no significant differences were observed between men and women in age, body mass index (BMI), or adherence to the Mediterranean diet (p > 0.05). Similarly, baseline levels of eating-related self-determined motivation did not differ significantly between genders (p = 0.82). The initial adherence to the Mediterranean diet, measured using the Mediterranean Diet Adherence Screener (MEDAS), was low to moderate across the sample (mean ± SD: 6.3 ± 1.8 out of 14 points). 

### Changes in Eating-Related Self-Determined Motivation  
Analysis of changes in eating-related self-determined motivation revealed significant improvements in both men and women from baseline to post-intervention (p < 0.001). However, the magnitude of change was significantly greater in men compared to women (mean difference: 0.45 points, 95% CI = 0.28–0.62, p < 0.001). While both genders experienced a decline in motivation scores between post-intervention and follow-up, men exhibited a more sustained improvement than women. At follow-up, men’s motivation scores remained significantly higher than those of women (mean difference: 0.38 points, 95% CI = 0.21–0.55, p < 0.001). 

Repeated measures analysis of variance (ANOVA) confirmed a significant interaction effect between gender and time (F(2, 496) = 8.94, p < 0.001), indicating that the trajectory of changes in self-determined motivation over time differed between men and women. Post-hoc analyses with Bonferroni correction revealed that men showed greater retention of motivation gains at follow-up compared to women (p < 0.01).

### Changes in Adherence to the Mediterranean Diet  
Both men and women demonstrated significant increases in adherence to the Mediterranean diet from baseline to post-intervention (p < 0.001). At post-intervention, men exhibited a slightly greater increase in MEDAS scores compared to women (mean difference: 0.31 points, 95% CI = 0.12–0.50, p = 0.002). However, by the follow-up assessment, the adherence scores of both genders had declined, with no significant difference between men and women (p = 0.11). 

A time × gender interaction effect was observed for adherence to the Mediterranean diet (F(2, 496) = 4.65, p = 0.01). Post-hoc pairwise comparisons revealed that while men retained a higher level of adherence at follow-up relative to their baseline scores (mean difference: 0.83 points, 95% CI = 0.61–1.05, p < 0.001), women’s adherence at follow-up was only marginally higher than baseline (mean difference: 0.47 points, 95% CI = 0.25–0.69, p < 0.01). 

### Association Between Motivation and Adherence  
Changes in eating-related self-determined motivation were positively correlated with changes in adherence to the Mediterranean diet in men at both post-intervention (r = 0.56, p < 0.001) and follow-up (r = 0.42, p < 0.001). In women, these correlations were weaker and not statistically significant at either time point (post-intervention: r = 0.21, p = 0.08; follow-up: r = 0.19, p = 0.11). 

Linear regression analyses further supported these findings. In men, changes in eating-related self-determined motivation significantly predicted changes in adherence to the Mediterranean diet at post-intervention (β = 0.44, p < 0.001) and follow-up (β = 0.37, p < 0.001). In women, motivation changes did not significantly predict adherence changes at either time point (post-intervention: β = 0.12, p = 0.09; follow-up: β = 0.10, p = 0.13). These results suggest that the intervention’s effect on adherence to the Mediterranean diet was mediated by increases in self-determined motivation in men but not in women.

### Gender Differences in Intervention Effectiveness  
Overall, the intervention was more effective in improving eating-related self-determined motivation and adherence to the Mediterranean diet in men compared to women. Men demonstrated greater initial improvements in both variables and sustained these improvements better over time. The results indicate that the nutritional intervention, based on the self-determination theory, aligns more closely with men’s motivational and behavioral responses. 

### Attrition and Sensitivity Analyses  
Attrition rates were low, with only 6% of participants (n = 15; 7 men, 8 women) not completing the follow-up assessment. Sensitivity analyses were conducted to assess the potential impact of missing data, and results remained consistent across multiple imputation methods. Additionally, subgroup analyses stratified by age and baseline adherence levels indicated no significant differences in the patterns of results, confirming the robustness of the findings. 

### Summary of Key Findings  
In summary, the nutritional intervention successfully enhanced eating-related self-determined motivation and adherence to the Mediterranean diet in both men and women. However, the magnitude and sustainability of these effects were significantly greater in men. Furthermore, changes in self-determined motivation were positively associated with changes in diet adherence in men but not in women, suggesting that the intervention’s mechanisms of action may differ by gender.

The findings from this study provide valuable insights into the impact of a nutritional intervention program grounded in self-determination theory (SDT) and promoting adherence to the Mediterranean diet (MD). Notably, the results highlight significant gender differences in the program's effectiveness, with men demonstrating greater improvements in eating-related self-determined motivation and subsequent adherence to the MD compared to women. These findings underscore the importance of considering gender-specific factors when designing and implementing nutritional intervention programs and contribute to the growing body of literature on the interplay between self-determined motivation and dietary behavior change.

The greater changes in eating-related self-determined motivation observed in men relative to women may be attributed to gender-specific psychological and sociocultural factors. Previous research has shown that men and women often differ in their motivational orientations toward health-related behaviors [1]. Men may be more inclined to respond to interventions that appeal to their sense of autonomy and competence, particularly when these interventions emphasize structured and goal-oriented frameworks, as is characteristic of SDT-based approaches [2]. Additionally, cultural norms and societal expectations may influence the way men and women internalize health-related goals. For example, men may perceive adherence to a healthy diet, such as the MD, as a means of achieving tangible outcomes like improved physical performance or weight management, which could enhance their intrinsic motivation to sustain dietary changes [3]. On the other hand, women may experience additional barriers, such as conflicting societal pressures related to body image or caregiving responsibilities, which may hinder their ability to fully engage with the intervention [4].

The findings also suggest that changes in eating-related self-determined motivation are positively associated with changes in MD adherence in men but not in women. This gender disparity may reflect differences in how motivational constructs translate into behavior change. SDT posits that autonomous motivation—characterized by internalized and self-endorsed reasons for engaging in a behavior—is a key predictor of sustained behavioral adherence [5]. While the intervention may have successfully fostered autonomous motivation in men, it is possible that women faced external or contextual factors that limited their ability to translate motivation into dietary adherence. For instance, women may encounter greater time constraints or responsibilities related to meal preparation for others, which could reduce their capacity to prioritize their own dietary goals [6]. Furthermore, women’s dietary behaviors are often influenced by emotional or relational factors, which may not have been adequately addressed by the intervention [7]. These findings underscore the need for gender-sensitive strategies that account for the unique challenges and motivators experienced by women.

The observed decrease in the magnitude of change in eating-related self-determined motivation over time in both genders aligns with previous research indicating that the effects of behavioral interventions often diminish as individuals transition from the intervention phase to independent maintenance [8]. This decline may reflect a reduction in the external support and reinforcement provided during the intervention, which could weaken participants’ sense of autonomy and competence over time. To address this issue, future interventions could incorporate ongoing support mechanisms, such as periodic follow-up sessions or digital tools, to sustain motivation and reinforce adherence to the MD. Additionally, fostering relatedness—another core component of SDT—through social support networks or group-based activities may enhance long-term engagement and dietary compliance [9].

The findings also raise important implications for the design and implementation of nutritional intervention programs. While the SDT-based approach appears to be more effective for men in this study, it may be necessary to tailor the intervention’s content and delivery to better meet the needs of women. For example, integrating components that address emotional eating, stress management, or family-related dietary dynamics could enhance the program’s relevance and effectiveness for women [10]. Moreover, employing a participatory approach that involves women in the co-design of the intervention may help identify and address gender-specific barriers to dietary adherence. This approach could include qualitative research methods, such as focus groups or interviews, to gain a deeper understanding of women’s experiences and preferences related to nutritional interventions [11].

The relationship between self-determined motivation and dietary adherence also highlights the potential of SDT as a theoretical framework for promoting sustainable dietary behaviors. By emphasizing the importance of autonomy, competence, and relatedness, SDT offers a comprehensive approach to fostering intrinsic motivation and long-term behavior change [12]. However, the differential impact of the intervention on men and women suggests that a one-size-fits-all approach may not be sufficient to achieve equitable outcomes. Future research should explore the mechanisms underlying gender differences in response to SDT-based interventions and identify strategies to optimize their effectiveness for diverse populations.

In conclusion, this study demonstrates that a nutritional intervention program based on SDT and promoting the MD can effectively enhance eating-related self-determined motivation and dietary adherence, particularly in men. However, the limited impact observed in women highlights the need for gender-sensitive adaptations to address the unique challenges and motivators experienced by this group. The findings also underscore the importance of sustained support and reinforcement to maintain motivation and dietary adherence over time. By incorporating these considerations into the design of future interventions, researchers and practitioners can enhance the effectiveness and inclusivity of nutritional programs, ultimately contributing to improved dietary patterns and health outcomes across genders. Future studies should aim to further elucidate the complex interplay between gender, motivation, and dietary behavior, as well as explore innovative strategies to promote long-term adherence to healthy dietary patterns like the MD.
